en: Geologists classify faults partly by dip, the angle the fault plane makes with the horizontal, from steep near-vertical cracks to low-angle slides.
If the slip is mostly up or down the sloping plane, the fault is dip-slip; if the slip is mostly sideways, it is strike-slip.
A thrust fault is a reverse fault with a gentle dip, so hanging-wall rocks ride up a low-angle plane instead of a steep one.
On a dipping fault, you name the slip by what the hanging wall did: down for normal, up for reverse, matching the angle of the plane.
Humans are placed in Class Mammalia because, like other mammals, they have mammary glands that can produce milk for young.
Humans are mammals because they grow hair, the same body covering that, as fur, helps classify dogs, cats, and bats in Mammalia.
The three tiny middle-ear bones are a mammal trait; humans have them, which is one anatomical reason we belong in Class Mammalia.
Humans keep a steady warm body temperature using metabolism, an endotherm trait shared with other mammals and used in classification.
Humans give birth to live young that develop inside the mother, matching the typical mammalian pattern used to place us in Class Mammalia.
A muscular diaphragm that powers breathing is another mammal feature humans share, supporting the Class Mammalia placement.
Skin with sweat glands and mammary glands is part of the mammal package; humans have both, so we are not reptiles or birds.
A four-chambered heart that keeps oxygen-rich blood separate is typical of mammals; humans have that heart plan, matching Class Mammalia.
Mammals have a lower jaw made of one bone on each side; humans show that jaw plan, another reason we are classified as mammals.
Talking and using tools do not put humans in Mammalia; the class is about shared body traits such as hair, milk, and ear bones.
Humans are primates because our eyes face forward with overlapping vision, a primate trait that helps judge distance.
Humans have grasping hands with a mobile thumb, a primate trait used to hold branches or tools and to place us in Order Primates.
Flat nails instead of sharp claws on the fingers and toes are a primate feature humans share with monkeys and apes.
Primates have large brains relative to body size; humans fit that pattern, which is one reason we are placed in Order Primates.
Many primates learn by watching others; humans do this intensely, a behavioral trait that fits Order Primates along with the body traits.
A well-developed collarbone and flexible shoulder help primates climb or reach; humans keep that skeleton plan even if we walk on two legs.
Classification stacks: humans are mammals because of milk and hair, and primates because of forward eyes and grasping hands, not one label alone.
Humans are not classed with fish or reptiles because those groups lack hair, mammary glands, and the mammal ear-bone set.
Apes are primates too; humans sit inside that order with them, which is why we share nails, forward eyes, and a large brain.
Monkeys belong to Order Primates as well; humans are classified there for the same primate body plan, not because people are monkeys.
Binocular vision, seeing one scene with both eyes at once, is a primate trait humans have and a reason for the Order Primates placement.
An opposable thumb that can touch the other fingers is a primate grasping trait; humans use it, which supports the primate classification.
Primates emphasize the neocortex, a brain region for complex sensing and social life; humans show that primate pattern in extreme form.
A shorter snout and more emphasis on vision than smell is typical of primates; the human face follows that primate pattern.
Humans typically have two mammary glands, still the mammal milk organs that place us in Mammalia even though litter size is usually one.
Humans are placental mammals: the young are nourished through a placenta before birth, a mammal subgroup that still sits inside Class Mammalia.
Different tooth types in one mouth, incisors through molars, are typical of mammals; humans have that set, matching Class Mammalia.
Mammalia is a wide class that also holds whales and cows; Primates is the narrower order that groups humans with other forward-eyed, grasping relatives.
Language, clothes, and cities do not define the biological class or order; those are culture, while Mammalia and Primates are body-plan groups.
In the ranked system, Class Mammalia sits above Order Primates; humans belong to both, like an address with a city and a street.
Walking upright is a human specialty, not the trait that puts us in Mammalia or Primates; those groups are defined by older shared characters.
Tarsiers are primates but not monkeys; humans share the order with them because of primate eyes and hands, even though the faces look different.
Feeding young on milk after birth is the everyday mammal clue; humans do this, which is why Class Mammalia includes us.
Two of the mammal middle-ear bones came from jaw bones in earlier animals; humans have that mammal ear, a classification character for Mammalia.
Fingerprints help grip, but they are not the main reason for Order Primates; forward eyes, nails, and grasping hands are the standard characters.
A class table can list mammal traits on the left and primate traits on the right, then tick which ones humans show, which is all of the standard ones.
Whales have milk and hair traces so they are mammals, but they lack grasping hands and forward primate eyes, so they are not in Order Primates.
Lemurs are primates of Madagascar; humans share the order with them because of the primate body plan, even though lemur faces look very different.
A complete explanation uses because: humans are mammals because of hair and milk, and primates because of forward eyes, nails, and grasping hands.
Humans belong to Class Mammalia for mammal body traits and to Order Primates for primate eyes, hands, and nails, two nested reasons, not a single nickname.
A simple proportion to remember is about seven tenths water to three tenths land, so water, not land, makes up most of Earth's face.
The Southern Hemisphere has even more of its surface as ocean than the Northern Hemisphere, which holds most of the planet's land.
On an equal-area world map the blue ocean still clearly outweighs the land, a visual check that water covers most of Earth's surface.
If Earth's surface were ten equal tiles, about three would be land and about seven would be water, so land is the smaller share.
Start with the DOST website or its attached agencies, then write the page title and date so your typhoon-support notes can be checked later.
PAGASA is a DOST-attached agency, so its typhoon bulletins are an official source for how authorities warn communities before landfall.
The NDRRMC site lists how national and local offices share tasks after a typhoon, a reliable place to see who supports which community need.
The Office of Civil Defense runs operations centers that collect situation reports, a support system you can identify on official civil-defense pages.
DSWD pages describe family food packs and other relief goods prepositioned for typhoon-hit towns, an example of material support after a storm.
City and municipal websites often post which schools or halls are evacuation centers, local authority support you should copy from that official page.
When you gather typhoon-support facts, prefer pages ending in gov.ph so you are reading the authority itself, not a copied rumor.
Copy the URL of the DOST, PAGASA, or NDRRMC page you used, because a support claim without a link is hard for classmates to verify.
Authority support starts before landfall: official wind signals and rainfall warnings help communities move early, which you can document from PAGASA.
NDRRMC and local DRRM pages identify search-and-rescue groups sent to flooded or isolated barangays, a life-saving form of typhoon support.
DOST and NTC notices sometimes describe emergency communication support when typhoons cut ordinary phone networks, a technical help communities need.
DILG circulars on official sites tell local governments to prepare evacuation and curfew rules, showing how national authorities back towns during typhoons.
DepEd or LGU pages that announce class suspension are a form of support: they keep students off flooded roads, and you can cite the dated notice.
DOH situation reports can list medical teams and clean-water advice for typhoon-hit areas, health support that belongs in a sourced class report.
Always record the date on a typhoon bulletin, because support instructions change as the storm moves, and an old page can mislead a community.
Official agency pages publish hotlines for rescue and relief; copying those numbers from gov.ph is gathering support information the competency asks for.
A Facebook screenshot is not enough; match the claim to a PAGASA or NDRRMC page before you treat it as how authorities are supporting people.
DSWD and OCD reports often say goods were prepositioned in regional warehouses before landfall, support that happens while the weather is still building.
Official disaster reports may list AFP or PNP help with rescue and security in typhoon zones, national-force support you should attribute to that report.
After the strongest winds, authorities keep evacuation shelters open while flooding lasts, a support step described in many LGU and NDRRMC updates.
Older DOST hazard-map projects such as Project NOAH remain a secondary source for flood-prone places that need extra typhoon support planning.
The PAGASA track forecast on its site is support because it tells communities which provinces should prepare first as the cyclone moves.
Authorities support flood-prone towns with rainfall warnings even when the wind signal is still low, a distinction you can see on PAGASA's warning pages.
When foreign aid arrives, NDRRMC pages often record how it is coordinated, so the official channel for outside support is still a government site.
The Mines and Geosciences Bureau, under DENR, posts landslide-prone maps that authorities use to tell hillside communities when to leave in heavy typhoon rain.
A clear report names each agency's job: PAGASA warns, DSWD feeds and shelters, OCD coordinates, LGUs evacuate, all documented on their sites.
NDRRMC numbered situation reports list affected families and assistance already delivered, a dated official source for support after the typhoon.
The Philippine Red Cross website describes volunteer rescue and blood services that work with government during typhoons, a partner you can cite beside NDRRMC.
Authorities often support communities with drinking water and hygiene kits when floods contaminate wells, details that appear in DOH or DSWD updates.
DOE or electric-coop bulletins can list which towns have power back, infrastructure support after a typhoon that you should date and source.
If you cannot find a hotline on an official page, leave it blank; inventing a number is not gathering information and can send people to the wrong help.
Regional OCD or DRRM office pages show how support is organized closer to the affected provinces, not only from a Manila headline.
PAGASA storm-surge maps on its site support coastal barangays by showing who should move to higher ground before the cyclone arrives.
Compare this morning's PAGASA bulletin with yesterday's to see how official support advice changed as the track shifted toward or away from a province.
DA updates may describe seeds or assistance for farmers whose fields were flooded or wind-damaged, livelihood support after the weather eases.
Some DSWD or UNICEF-partner notes describe child-friendly spaces in evacuation centers, a support service you can record from a named humanitarian page.
PAGASA radar images on the official site help authorities time last-minute warnings, a monitoring support communities depend on during the cyclone.

topic: list what you still cannot find
en: End the investigation by listing questions the websites did not answer, because honest gathering includes gaps in how support was described.
Barangay DRRM committees, described in DILG or LGU pages, are the nearest official support for warning neighbors and opening a local shelter.
If an official DSWD or LGU page lists emergency cash aid after a named typhoon, cite that page rather than a forwarded text message.
PCG or PAGASA marine notices that stop sea travel are support for coastal workers, a safety action you can copy from those official marine pages.
DepEd memos on official sites often allow schools to serve as evacuation shelters, a support use of public buildings during and after typhoons.
Look on NDRRMC or DSWD pages for notes on assisting persons with disabilities in evacuation, a support detail easy to miss if you only skim headlines.
Some OCD reports mention backup radios or satellite links for cut-off towns, communications support when typhoons take down ordinary towers.
Keep a folder per storm with dated printouts from DOST-PAGASA and NDRRMC, so your class can see how official support changed through the event.
DPWH notices can describe clearing blocked drainage after a typhoon, infrastructure support that is still part of how authorities help communities recover.
PHIVOLCS pages are for earthquakes and volcanoes; for typhoon support, stay on PAGASA, NDRRMC, and DSWD so the gathered help matches the hazard.
Some official warnings are issued in Filipino and English; gathering both versions can show how authorities try to reach more households.
Post-disaster NDRRMC reports that count houses repaired or families served are still support information, not only the hours while the wind was strongest.
Authorities use rainfall, wind, and surge forecasts together to decide who should move, a science-based support process documented on PAGASA and NDRRMC sites.
Official situation reports sometimes list accredited volunteer groups, so you can name partners without treating an unsourced chat as government policy.
DA or LGU pages may advise moving animals out of flood plains before a typhoon, livelihood support that sits beside human evacuation orders.
Authorities also support communities by announcing when it is safer to return; gather that all-clear from the same official channels, not from a guess.
Other reliable sites include WMO summaries and academic hazard papers, but local support actions should still be confirmed on Philippine government pages.
Match the local PAGASA name of the cyclone on the support page, so you do not mix relief numbers from two different storms.
Official pages frame evacuation as protection, a way authorities support people in mapped danger zones rather than as a punishment for staying.
The competency is about typhoon-affected communities, so a DOST scholarship page is the wrong source even though it is an official DOST website.
A strong class packet cites at least three official pages, such as PAGASA, NDRRMC, and DSWD, then says what support each one documents.
DPWH or local engineering pages that post passable roads after a typhoon help families and relief trucks, a logistics support you can date and quote.
DOH or DSWD pages may mention psychosocial support in evacuation centers; if you include it, quote the named page and do not give medical advice yourself.
A poster can show screenshots of official homepages with the dates, plus one sentence each on warning, rescue, and relief as the three support layers.
Copy casualty or damage numbers only as printed on the NDRRMC sitrep, and say 'according to that report,' because unofficial counts are often wrong.
Authorities support communities through recovery months with housing and livelihood programs, which later official reports still document after the headlines fade.
Better forecasts from DOST-PAGASA are themselves a form of support: earlier, clearer warnings give families more hours to move and to pack.
Some LGU pages list which office stays open as an emergency operations center, a practical support detail students can gather from the city site.
Before the season, NDRRMC and PAGASA sites post preparedness checklists, support that happens even when no named cyclone exists yet.
Quote one official sentence about support, then paraphrase in your own words, so the gathered fact stays tied to the agency and still reads as yours.
A complete answer names more than warnings: it also identifies relief, rescue, shelter, and recovery actions found on official websites.
Gathering here means opening DOST and other reliable sites, naming the authority, and recording how that office actually helps typhoon-hit communities.
Tidal energy needs a useful difference between high tide and low tide, the range secondary sources measure before anyone builds a plant.
A tidal barrage is built across a suitable estuary so the height difference drives turbines as the basin fills and empties.
Where a narrow channel speeds the tide, underwater turbines can harvest the current without a full barrage wall across a bay.
Secondary energy studies look for large tidal range or fast tidal streams, because a pretty beach with small tides cannot power a plant.
Tide times can be predicted years ahead from astronomy, so tidal energy is regular in a way wind energy is not, a point energy agencies often stress.

topic: twice a day in many places
en: Many coasts have two highs and two lows each day, so a well-sited plant can generate on a repeating daily schedule of tidal difference.
A tidal lagoon uses a walled basin beside the coast so the same rise-and-fall difference turns turbines without closing an entire river mouth.
When you name a site as promising, cite a DOE, IRENA, or peer-reviewed resource map rather than a tourism blog about a pretty strait.
Secondary sources also warn that barrages can change mudflats and fish movement, so a good site must have both energy and an accepted environmental plan.
Wave energy rides wind-driven bumps on the surface; tidal difference is the slower rise and fall from the Moon and Sun, a distinction sources insist on.
Even a strong tide is useless for electricity if there is no grid connection; energy studies list both the water resource and the nearby power lines.
South Korea's Sihwa tidal power plant is a documented barrage-style site that secondary sources use as a working example of exploiting tidal difference.

topic: La Rance as a documented plant
en: France's La Rance plant has generated electricity from tidal difference for decades, a classic secondary-source example of a barrage across an estuary.
Tidal-stream turbines need enough depth to stay submerged at low tide, a site filter that resource maps use besides current speed.
Busy shipping channels may have fast tides but are poor plant sites if turbines would block ships, a conflict energy papers routinely discuss.
Spring tides, when Sun and Moon align, make a larger tidal difference and thus more potential energy than neap tides in the same place.
Neap tides have a smaller high-to-low difference, so a plant's output is not the same every day even though the schedule stays predictable.
DOE and academic papers have screened Philippine straits for tidal-stream potential; cite those studies instead of guessing from a ferry ride.
Energy tables often list a capacity factor for tidal sites; that number, from a secondary source, tells how much of the time the difference is useful.
Some barrage designs generate on both the flood and the ebb, using the difference in both directions to make more of the daily tidal cycle.
A few designs pump extra water into the basin at high tide to enlarge the difference later, a method described in engineering reviews of tidal plants.
A storm surge is weather piled water, not the regular astronomical tide; sources for tidal energy must use tide tables, not typhoon water levels.
The Moon's gravity, with the Sun's, makes the tidal difference; secondary physics pages are the right source for why the water keeps rising and falling.
Before claiming a bay can make power, sources measure months of tide-gauge data; one afternoon of watching the shore is not a resource study.
Some papers describe tidal fences, rows of turbines across part of a channel, another situation for exploiting fast tidal difference without a full dam.
Energy agencies also report high construction cost for barrages, so a suitable tide is necessary but not enough if the project cannot be paid for.
Modern source papers discuss fish passages and turbine slowdowns as ways to exploit tides while reducing harm to migrating animals.
Small island grids might use a modest tidal-stream unit if measurements show a reliable current, a situation different from a giant estuary barrage.
Because tides shift later each day, sources discuss whether generation times match evening demand, a siting question besides the size of the difference.
Barrage basins can trap sediment, shrinking the useful water difference over years, a long-term issue secondary environmental reviews flag.

topic: look up a tide table first
en: A class investigation can start with a published tide table for a bay, then ask whether the listed high-low gap is large enough to interest an energy study.
Tidal energy is called renewable in textbooks because the Earth-Moon orbit keeps making the difference, unlike a coal pile that can run out.
A strait can look fast from a boat yet fail a resource map's speed and depth cuts; the secondary source, not the boat trip, decides suitability.
Some coastal energy papers compare tidal sites with offshore wind; your task is still to identify the tidal-difference cases, not to switch topics to wind.
When you copy a site from a paper, write the typical tidal range in meters and the mean current speed, the two numbers that justify exploiting the difference.
The Bay of Fundy is often cited for an unusually large tidal range, a world example of a place where the difference is large enough to study for power.
A few technology reviews describe tethered tidal kites that fly in a current, another proposed way to exploit tidal-stream difference in deep channels.
Because output follows the tide, some studies pair tidal plants with storage so electricity is still available when the difference is small at slack water.
National energy papers also mention permits for using a waterway, so a scientifically good tide still needs legal clearance to be exploited.
Secondary siting guides call for consulting fishing communities, because a turbine field can change the very channel people already use.
A proper study measures both spring and neap cycles so the smallest useful difference is known, not only the most dramatic high tide of the month.
Some tidal-stream designs use vertical-axis turbines that work with reversing current, matching a tide that flows two ways each day.
Other designs look like underwater wind turbines facing the current; sources still classify them as tidal-stream devices, not wind machines.

topic: head is another word for difference
en: Engineering sources call the high-to-low water gap the tidal head; a larger head means more potential energy per cubic meter of water.
If the listed tidal head is only a few tens of centimeters, secondary sources usually drop the site, because turbines need a more useful difference.
One month of tide data can miss seasonal changes; energy papers prefer multi-year gauges before they call a difference exploitable.
A class can use a government energy outlook, a peer-reviewed siting paper, and a tide table, three secondary sources that together identify a possible site type.

topic: do not promise a local plant
en: Identifying a situation where tides could be used is not the same as promising a plant in your hometown; keep the claim as large as the source.
Some older barrages generate mainly on the ebb, releasing stored high water through turbines when the sea outside has already fallen.
Other schemes generate as the tide floods into a basin, another documented way of using the incoming height difference.
Marine energy reviews mention rust and biofouling on turbines, practical limits on exploiting a good tide that physics alone does not show.
Papers on tidal-stream farms discuss spacing turbines so the wake of one does not steal the current difference from the next.
A global tidal-energy atlas is a secondary source for spotting where the difference is large; local studies then check whether that spot can actually be built.
The competency asks for situations where the tidal difference could be exploited, meaning converted to useful electricity, not merely watched from a pier.
Sources group sites into closed-basin barrages or lagoons versus open-stream turbines, two different situations for using the same tidal rise and fall.
Unlike solar power, a tidal difference still arrives at night, a reason secondary energy comparisons list tides as a complementary renewable.
A typhoon swell is not the tidal resource; exploiting tidal difference means using the regular astronomical cycle, which sources separate from storm waves.

topic: quote the range in about meters
en: If a paper says a mean range of about five meters, copy it as 'about five meters' and name the paper; do not invent a more dramatic number.
A complete identification names a site type that is both physically suitable and discussed as acceptable in the sources, not only a huge tide on a map.
In one sentence: secondary sources look for large, regular high-to-low water differences in estuaries or fast channels, then ask if turbines can safely use them.
Mechanical energy is the kinetic plus potential energy that is still available to do work, such as lifting, turning, or speeding something up.
To state an object's mechanical energy you add the energy of its motion to the energy stored by its position or shape, not only one of those parts.

topic: both can be zero or not
en: A still object high on a shelf has mechanical energy from potential alone, while a sliding object on the floor can have mechanical energy from kinetic alone.
Meteor showers return on nearly the same calendar dates each year because Earth crosses the same dusty orbit at the same point in its year.
To discuss a shower's regular timing, check a current astronomy almanac or PAGASA skywatch page rather than a random social-media date.
A shower is named for the constellation that holds its radiant, and that name stays the same year after year as the stream is crossed again.
Many annual showers come from a parent comet whose orbit still sheds dust, so Earth meets that dust on a schedule set by both orbits.
The Geminids are a regular December shower whose parent is an asteroid-like body, showing that not every annual stream is from a classic comet.
The Quadrantid meteor shower is a regular early-January event, another calendar marker listed in yearly meteor-shower tables.
A shower has a peak night and a wider season; reliable tables list both, so 'regular' does not mean only a single hour each year.
The International Meteor Organization publishes yearly calendars of expected showers, a secondary source students can cite for regular dates.
Random sporadic meteors can appear any night, but a shower is the regular, clustered burst when Earth hits a known dust stream.
Earth's year-long trip around the Sun is the clock: the same stretch of orbit is where a given shower's dust is waiting each year.
The shower still occurs on schedule even if a bright Moon hides many meteors, so regularity is about the stream, not about how many you personally see.
The Lyrids are a regular April shower tied to comet Thatcher, listed on annual sky calendars along with the better-known Perseids.
The Orionids return each October from dust of comet Halley, a regular shower whose parent comet is famous from other years as well.
The Eta Aquariids are a regular May shower also linked to comet Halley, showing one comet trail can make more than one annual meeting.
Secondary sources often list a zenithal hourly rate for the peak; that number describes a typical regular year, not a guarantee for your backyard.
Many annual showers are visible from the Philippines, though some northern radiants sit lower; a local astronomy club table is a useful source.
A meteor storm is a rare extra-dense year, not the usual regular shower; textbooks separate those outliers from the ordinary annual return.

topic: cite the year of the table
en: When you copy a peak date, write the year of the table, because leap years and orbital drift can shift the listed night by a day.
Some streams are centuries old, yet Earth still crosses them on a yearly rhythm, which is why the shower is called regular even if the comet is faint now.
The meteors do not come from the stars of Perseus or Gemini; those names only mark the sky direction of a regular, nearby dust crossing.
Many annual showers are better after midnight because that side of Earth then faces into the dust stream, a regular geometric reason in the sources.
The Ursids are a quieter regular shower near late December, often listed beside the Geminids on the same yearly meteor calendar.
A reliable discussion uses observatory dates, not a story that showers are random wishes; regularity is an orbital fact you can look up.
How many nights a shower lasts depends on how wide the dust stream is, which is why some regular showers are short and others last weeks.
Yearly tables also list typical meteor speed for each shower, another regular property of that stream, not a new surprise each August.
Photographers plan the same showers on the same weeks each year, practical evidence that the occurrence is regular enough to schedule.
Listing both Orionids and Eta Aquariids from Halley is a way secondary sources show that one parent orbit can give two regular Earth crossings.
In one sentence: meteor showers occur regularly because Earth's orbit keeps meeting known dust trails at repeatable times you can look up.
Secondary sources group mutations as beneficial, harmful, or neutral depending on whether they help, hurt, or barely change an organism's survival.
Many sources say most DNA changes are neutral, meaning the protein or the organism works about as before, with no clear help or harm.
A well-studied beneficial mutation lets some adults keep digesting milk sugar, an example textbooks cite from human population genetics.
A mutation that lets a bacterium survive an antibiotic is beneficial for that microbe but harmful for a sick person, so effect depends on whose survival you mean.
Harmful mutations can change a protein's shape so a cell process fails, which secondary biology pages use as the usual disease example without naming a scare list.
When you call a mutation beneficial or harmful, write the textbook or journal you used, because the same DNA change can be judged differently in another environment.
A rare mutation in a human immune receptor can reduce HIV infection risk, a beneficial example sources discuss, not a reason to seek infection.
A mutation that blocks chlorophyll is harmful for a green plant because it can no longer harvest sunlight well, a plant example of a damaging change.
A color mutation may hide a moth on dark bark but expose it on pale bark, showing that beneficial versus harmful depends on the environment.
If a DNA letter changes but the same amino acid is still coded, sources often call the mutation silent or neutral for the protein.

topic: not always in the body you feel
en: A mutation in one skin cell is not the same as a mutation in an egg or sperm; sources separate those when they discuss effects on offspring.
Harmful mutations that disable the brakes on cell division can contribute to cancer, a serious effect sources describe without saying every mutation causes it.

topic: neutral in one place harmful in another
en: A change that does nothing in a unused DNA stretch can be harmful if it later sits in a gene that an organism needs, so context matters.
Some human populations have hemoglobin variants that help at high altitude, beneficial mutations studied in secondary genetics sources.
Mutations that switch a needed gene off are often harmful, which is why sources treat many knock-out changes as damaging unless the gene was unused.
A mutation that gives a new activity can be beneficial, harmful, or both, so secondary sources refuse a single label without naming the trait.
RNA viruses mutate quickly; some changes help the virus spread and are harmful to hosts, an example of benefit and harm at two levels.
Some fruit mutations that stop seeds can be useful to farmers and eaters even if they would be harmful for the plant in the wild.
If one website calls every mutation dangerous, check a textbook: the three-way split into help, harm, and no effect is the consensus view.
Inserting or deleting a letter so the reading frame slips is often harmful because many amino acids downstream go wrong.
Population-genetics sources say many neutral mutations spread by chance, not because they help, which is why 'no effect' still matters in evolution.

topic: sickle cell already known skip restating
en: Do not stop at one famous blood example; sources also list plant, microbe, and silent DNA cases when they explain the three effect types.
Ultraviolet light can damage DNA and raise mutation rate; whether each change helps, hurts, or does nothing is a separate later question.
Cells proofread DNA copies, so many mistakes never become mutations; sources mention this when they explain why not every copying error is harmful.
Lab sources show bacteria gaining a mutation that lets them eat a new sugar, a beneficial change for those cells in that dish.
A harmful mutation can hide if one good copy of the gene still works, so sources warn that 'no effect now' is not always 'never harmful'.
Much DNA does not code for protein; many letter changes there are scored neutral unless a control switch was hit, a distinction textbooks make.
Whole-genome duplications in plants can be beneficial by making bigger fruits or new species, a large mutation sources treat as sometimes helpful.
Class facts may name disease as a harmful effect, but they should not tell anyone they are ill; that judgment belongs to a clinician and a sourced test.
terms: not tell anyone they are ill

en: The same mutation can be beneficial in one habitat and harmful in another, so sources always name the environment when they assign an effect.
Neutral does not mean 'nothing happened in the DNA'; it means the change did not clearly help or hurt the organism's function or survival.
Human-gene databases list many harmful variants, so they can bias a report unless you also sample sources that discuss neutral and beneficial cases.
Plant breeders sometimes keep beneficial mutations for yield or disease resistance, then write those examples in agricultural science sources.
Sources note that many harmful mutations in early embryos never become a born organism, so the surviving population is already filtered.
A class chart with beneficial, harmful, and neutral columns, each with a cited example, matches the competency better than a single scary story.
Some inherited color-vision changes are treated as harmful for certain tasks and nearly neutral for others, a reminder to name the job when labeling an effect.
Changes in already-broken genes are often scored neutral because those sequences were not making a needed protein anyway.
Beneficial means better survival or reproduction in a stated setting, not 'good' in a moral sense, a wording secondary biology sources keep careful.
In one sentence: mutations change DNA, and sources classify those changes as helpful, harmful, or neither, always in a named environment.
Oxygen sits in group 16 of the periodic table, so it has six valence electrons, the ones in its outer shell.
To find oxygen's valence electrons, find oxygen on the table and read its main-group number: group 16 means six outer electrons.
On older tables oxygen is in group VIA; the Roman six is the same count: oxygen has six valence electrons.
For groups 13 to 18, subtract ten from the group number: oxygen is group 16, and 16 minus 10 is six valence electrons.
Oxygen is in period 2, so its valence shell is the second shell, which holds those six outer electrons.
Oxygen's atomic number is eight: two electrons fill the inner shell, leaving six as valence electrons in the outer shell.
A simple shell pattern for oxygen is two, then six; the six is the valence count you also get from its column on the table.
A Lewis symbol for oxygen shows the letter O with six dots around it, one for each valence electron from group 16.
Six valence electrons means oxygen is two short of a full set of eight, which is why it often forms two bonds.
Sulfur sits under oxygen in the same group, so sulfur also has six valence electrons; the column, not the row, gives that number.
Do not give oxygen eight valence electrons; eight belongs to neon in group 18, two columns to the right of oxygen.
Fluorine sits one column right of oxygen, so fluorine has seven valence electrons, while oxygen in group 16 has six.
Nitrogen sits one column left of oxygen, so nitrogen has five valence electrons; stepping right to oxygen adds one, making six.
Carbon in group 14 has four valence electrons; oxygen is two groups farther right, so oxygen has six.
Oxygen heads the chalcogen family, group 16, whose members share six valence electrons even though their atoms get heavier down the column.
You do not have to list all eight electrons every time: oxygen's box on the table already tells you the outer count is six.
Oxygen is in the p-block with four p electrons plus two s electrons in the outer shell, totaling six valence electrons.
Valence electrons are the outer-shell electrons that do the bonding; for oxygen those outer electrons number six, from group 16.
Oxygen's two inner electrons are not valence electrons; only the six in the outer shell, shown by its group, count as valence.
When oxygen gains two electrons to fill its valence shell, it becomes O-two-minus, because six plus two makes eight.
In a water molecule oxygen makes two bonds, matching a need for two more electrons to finish a set of eight around six valence electrons.
On the table, find the symbol O, then look at the top of that column: the group label is how you name oxygen's six valence electrons.

topic: do not use period as valence
en: Oxygen's period number is 2, which is not its valence count; the period is the shell, and the group gives the six valence electrons.
Selenium, farther down oxygen's column, still has six valence electrons; changing period does not change that group-16 outer count.
Tellurium is another group-16 element under oxygen, so it too has six valence electrons even though the atom is much heavier.
Oxygen is not a noble gas, so its outer shell is not full; six valence electrons leave two empty places in an octet.
A full outer shell for oxygen would be eight electrons; starting from six valence electrons, oxygen is two away from that octet.
Do not confuse group 16 with the transition metals of group 6; oxygen is a main-group nonmetal with six valence electrons.
Oxygen's box is on the right side of the table, in the p-block, where group 16 elements show six valence electrons.
From boron in group 13, count four boxes right to oxygen in group 16: 13, 14, 15, 16, matching four, five, then six valence electrons.
Helium in group 18 has a full first shell of two, but oxygen's valence shell is the second shell with six electrons, not two.
In an oxygen molecule each atom still has six valence electrons; they share pairs so both can look like they have eight.
A double bond in O-two uses four shared electrons, which fits two oxygen atoms that each started with six valence electrons.
If a classmate says oxygen has eight valence electrons, check the group header: eight would be group 18, not oxygen's group 16.
The number you write for oxygen's valence electrons is six, not eight; eight is the atomic number, which counts all electrons.
When you draw oxygen, count the dots: if you drew eight dots you used neon's group, not oxygen's six valence electrons.
Nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine share period 2 but not the same valence count: five, six, and seven as you move right.
Left-side metals often have one, two, or three valence electrons; oxygen on the right is a nonmetal with six.
Some textbooks title group 16 the oxygen family; that heading is a reminder that oxygen's valence electron number is six.
Use a printed periodic table, find O, read the group, then write 'oxygen has six valence electrons' as the answer the competency asks.
The outer configuration 2s-two 2p-four adds to six electrons, matching oxygen's group-16 place on the periodic table.
Knowing oxygen has six valence electrons from the table helps you predict it often needs two more electrons in compounds.

topic: do not count protons as valence
en: Oxygen has eight protons, but protons are not valence electrons; the table's group, not the proton count, gives the six outer electrons.
Oxygen-16 has mass number 16, which is not the valence count; mass number is protons plus neutrons, while group 16 gives six valence electrons.
Oxygen-16 and oxygen-18 have the same six valence electrons, because isotopes share the group and the electron count, not the neutron count.
In ozone each oxygen atom still has six valence electrons; the molecule's shape changes, not the group-16 outer count of each atom.
A classroom check is 'sixteen means six' for oxygen: group 16, six valence electrons, after you subtract ten from the IUPAC group number.
The nearest noble gas after oxygen is neon, with eight valence electrons; oxygen has not reached that shell, so it has six, not eight.
Hydrogen is not in oxygen's group, so you cannot copy hydrogen's one valence electron onto oxygen; oxygen's own column says six.
Silicon under carbon has four valence electrons; the analog for oxygen's six is sulfur under oxygen, not silicon.
Moving left to right across period 2, each step adds one valence electron, so oxygen, sixth among B through Ne, has six.
The period-2 sequence boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen has three, four, five, then six valence electrons, matching their group numbers minus ten.
Whether oxygen is a single atom in a problem or O-two gas, its place on the table still says six valence electrons per oxygen atom.

topic: do not use group 8 old iron
en: Some old tables numbered iron in group VIII; that is not oxygen's column and must not be used to guess oxygen's six valence electrons.
Place six electron dots around O, usually as two pairs and two singles, matching six valence electrons from group 16.
Oxygen's six valence electrons are often drawn as two lone pairs plus two unpaired electrons, the unpaired ones ready to form bonds.
The bent shape of water comes from oxygen keeping two lone pairs from those six valence electrons while making two bonds to hydrogen.
In carbon dioxide, oxygen atoms still start with six valence electrons each; they share with carbon so each oxygen is surrounded by eight.
The competency asks you to identify a number: based on oxygen's periodic-table position, that number of valence electrons is six.
A complete answer can say: oxygen is group 16, main-group valence is six, so oxygen has six valence electrons.
Even polonium, near the bottom of group 16, is still counted as having six valence electrons from that same column as oxygen.
Superheavy group-16 elements are not classroom samples, but they sit in oxygen's column, the column that means six valence electrons.

topic: color of box does not matter
en: Whether a table colors oxygen as a nonmetal or a gas, the valence count still comes from the group, which is six.
Oxygen gas at room temperature does not change the valence number; a gas, liquid, or solid of the element still has six valence electrons per atom.
A common oxidation number of minus two for oxygen matches gaining two electrons to finish an octet that started with six valence electrons.

topic: plus two is not typical oxygen
en: Oxygen almost never has a plus-six valence story like some sulfur compounds; the table still says six outer electrons, usually used to gain two.
Scan the p-block until you see the column that starts with oxygen at the top: that whole column is six valence electrons.
Oxygen is the lightest element in its group, but being first does not change the valence count; the group still means six.
Magnesium in group 2 has two valence electrons; oxygen in group 16 has six, so MgO can form when two and six make a full transfer picture.
Sodium has one valence electron from group 1; it does not match oxygen, which has six from group 16.
Aluminum has three valence electrons from group 13; two aluminum atoms can pair with three oxygen atoms that each have six valence electrons.

topic: do not read atomic mass as six
en: Oxygen's atomic mass is about 16, which is not the valence number; ignore the mass in the box when the question asks for valence electrons.
An element box shows atomic number, symbol, and mass; none of those is the valence count except as a clue that eight electrons include six outer ones.
Atomic number 8 tells you there are eight electrons in a neutral oxygen atom; the table's group then splits them as two inner and six valence.
Even when you later talk about oxide ions, you still start from the table: oxygen atoms begin with six valence electrons.
A worksheet can use three steps: locate O, read group 16, report six valence electrons, which is exactly the skill this competency names.
Check a neighbor element: if your table reading gives fluorine seven and nitrogen five, then oxygen between them must be six.

topic: no need to memorize a rhyme only
en: A rhyme can help, but the reliable method is the table position: oxygen's group is the reason the valence number is six.

topic: gases on the right still six
en: Many colored tables mark oxygen as a gas on the right; that color codes physical state, while the group still codes six valence electrons.
If you draw two rings around an oxygen nucleus, put two electrons on the inner ring and six on the outer ring to match group 16.
On a shell drawing the outer ring is the valence shell; for oxygen that outer ring should show six electrons, not eight.
The competency says 'based on its position' because the periodic table is the tool: you read six from oxygen's group, not from a random memory.
Classroom wall charts often print 16 above oxygen's column; that printed 16 is your cue to write six valence electrons for oxygen.
Students sometimes copy carbon's four valence electrons onto every period-2 element; oxygen is not carbon, and its group gives six.
Another common error is giving every right-side element eight electrons; neon has eight, oxygen two boxes left has six.
Phosphorus in group 15 has five valence electrons; it is next to sulfur, not a model for oxygen, which sits above sulfur with six.
Chlorine in group 17 has seven valence electrons; oxygen is not a halogen, so do not give it seven, give it six.
In one sentence: oxygen is in group 16, so a neutral oxygen atom has six valence electrons according to the periodic table.
Later bonding lessons use this number: six valence electrons is why oxygen so often makes two bonds or becomes a two-minus ion.
A trustworthy source for this fact is the periodic table itself: oxygen's position in group 16 identifies six valence electrons.
Modern plate motion is measured with GNSS networks that record a station's position over years, then convert the tiny shifts into a velocity.
Scientists compare continuous GNSS stations that run every day with campaign surveys that reoccupy a mark for a few days each year.
InSAR uses repeated radar satellite images to map how the ground has displaced between two passes, a process for measuring plate and quake motion.
Very-long-baseline interferometry times radio signals from distant quasars at far-apart dishes to detect how those dishes, and their plates, have moved.
Satellite laser ranging times a laser pulse to a reflector satellite and back, a space-geodesy process that helps track plate-scale displacements.
Where plates meet under the ocean, scientists use seafloor geodesy such as acoustic ranging to benchmarks on the bottom, not only land GPS.
PHIVOLCS and partner networks run GNSS stations across the Philippines to detect how fast local crust is displacing along faults and trenches.
NAMRIA maintains geodetic control marks whose repeated GNSS occupations help measure national-scale displacement of the islands.
A single GPS reading is not a plate velocity; scientists need a time series long enough that seasonal wiggles do not hide the slow displacement.
Displacement is reported in a global reference frame so a station's motion is compared with a stable model of Earth's rotation and the other plates.
With many stations, scientists compute strain, how a region stretches or shortens, a process that goes beyond one point's displacement.
Older bathymetry compared with new multibeam maps, tied to GPS, can show how a seafloor feature has been displaced over decades.
Engineers install corner reflectors so InSAR can measure a known point's displacement even in a vegetated Philippine landscape.
Modern papers combine GNSS point velocities with InSAR maps so both the exact station motion and the spatial pattern of displacement are measured.
A seismograph records shaking in seconds; it is not the process used to measure the slow centimeter-per-year displacement of a whole plate.
A campaign GPS survey returns to the same benchmark years later; the difference in coordinates is the measured displacement of that mark.
Published plate velocities include uncertainty; a modern process reports both the displacement rate and how large the measurement error is.
The competency asks you to name processes such as GNSS, InSAR, VLBI, or seafloor acoustics, not only to say that plates move slowly.
To predict the archipelago in 50 million years, first measure today's plate velocity from GNSS, then assume it stays roughly similar unless models say otherwise.
A first sketch multiplies current speed by 50 million years, converting centimeters per year into kilometers of future displacement.

topic: draw a vector on a map
en: Draw today's motion as an arrow on a map of the Philippines, then extend that arrow to represent 50 million years at the same rate.
Use a published plate-motion model, not a freehand guess, so the Philippine Sea plate and neighboring plates have consistent velocities.
The archipelago's future shape depends on more than one plate, so the method is to apply each nearby plate's velocity, not only one number.
Where crust dives into a trench it can be removed, so a fair prediction notes that some seafloor may disappear instead of simply sliding sideways.
State the uncertainty: plate speed and direction can change over millions of years, so the 50-million-year sketch is a model, not a promise.
Some methods step the map forward in smaller intervals, redrawing trenches as they move, instead of one giant jump of 50 million years.
Treat island groups as blocks that can rotate as well as slide, because a velocity at Manila may not equal a velocity at Davao.
Unless a cited model states a distance, write 'about the same direction at today's rate' rather than inventing a kilometer figure for 50 million years.
Check published reconstructions of the last 50 million years; if the method worked backward, using it forward is at least consistent with that tool.
Classroom methods can use a plate-velocity calculator: enter today's vector, choose 50 million years, and plot the predicted point.
Predict both position and shape: blocks may spread or squeeze, so the outline of the archipelago can change even if the center only translates.
Include the Philippine Trench as a boundary that can consume seafloor, a method step so the future map is not just the islands sliding as a rigid sticker.
Use different velocities for the Palawan side and the Pacific-trench side if GNSS shows they are not one rigid block.
Write a map key that lists assumptions: constant velocity, rigid blocks or not, and which plate model you used for the 50-million-year sketch.
Convert units carefully: about two centimeters per year times 50 million years is about 1,000 kilometers if that rate truly stayed constant.
Coastlines will erode and grow, so the method predicts tectonic position of crustal blocks, not the exact beach outline of today's map.
Compare your sketch with a published Cenozoic reconstruction; large disagreement means a method step, such as the chosen velocity, needs checking.
Advanced methods rotate a plate about an Euler pole instead of sliding it in a straight line, a better geometric prediction for 50 million years.
If a nearby ridge makes new seafloor, the method should add area on that side rather than only moving today's pieces like furniture.
If blocks collide, the prediction of shape should allow shortening and mountains, not just a translated copy of today's archipelago.
A method demo uses foam blocks on paper arrows: move each block 50 scaled steps and photograph the new arrangement as the predicted map.
Always write 'in 50 million years' on the sketch so no one reads it as next century; the method is geologic, not a weather forecast.
The 'current velocity' in the competency is the GNSS-measured rate, so the method starts with those published millimeters-to-centimeters per year.
Look up the Philippine Sea plate's published motion relative to the Sunda block, then apply that vector when predicting eastern Philippine positions.
The fingernail-speed metaphor is not a prediction method; replace it with a measured rate, a time span, and a drawn displacement.
Draw an uncertainty band around the predicted islands, because errors in today's velocity grow when they are multiplied by 50 million years.
Ask whether the trench itself will roll back or advance; that method step changes the future space available for the archipelago's shape.
Label the product a scenario under stated assumptions, the scientific way to predict 50 million years without claiming a single certain map.
Put a scale bar on the predicted map so a reader can see how many kilometers the method moved the blocks, not only a pretty new outline.
One student gathers GNSS rates, one converts units, one draws arrows, and one writes uncertainties, a division of labor that matches the method.
The competency is about position and shape of the crust, so the method should not wander into guessing 50-million-year rainfall or cities.
State that treating the Philippines as one rigid plate is an approximation; GNSS already shows internal deformation that a careful method includes.
Finish the prediction with because: the islands should sit farther along today's vectors because we multiplied measured velocity by geologic time.
In one sentence: measure present plate velocity, multiply by 50 million years, draw the new block positions, and say which assumptions could be wrong.
Use dynamics carts on a track as a model: one cart hits another, then you measure speeds before and after to classify the collision.
In a nearly elastic model, the carts bounce apart and the total kinetic energy stays almost the same, which you check with a calculator.
Press clay on the bumpers so the carts stick; that inelastic model shows kinetic energy dropping while momentum is still shared.
A slow-motion phone video is a model of the short contact time, letting you describe the push during the hit without guessing the forces.
With two equal masses in a nearly elastic hit, the moving cart can almost stop while the other takes its speed, a model result to measure, not assume.
During the hit, each cart pushes the other with equal-and-opposite forces for the same short time, a Newton's-third description of the model.
In inelastic models the lasting effect is deformation or heat; look for a dent in clay or a warmer bumper after the carts join.
Photogates or motion sensors give cleaner before-and-after speeds than a stopwatch, a measurement method that makes the model quantitative.
A low-cost model is marbles in a ruler groove: vary mass by taping marbles together and describe bounce versus stick after each run.
Call a run elastic in the lab if the carts rebound and kinetic energy is nearly conserved, an operational definition you can apply to the model.
Call a run inelastic if the objects deform or stay together and kinetic energy clearly falls, even if they do not perfectly glue.
Change only the bumper type or only the mass, keeping the release height the same, so the model test of collision type stays fair.
Sketch force arrows only while the bumpers touch; before and after, those contact forces are gone, an effect of the short interaction.
If the model carts latch and move as one mass, you have a perfectly inelastic case whose shared speed you can predict from momentum conservation.
Drop a superball and a clay ball on the same tile as a qualitative model: one returns most kinetic energy, the other does not.

topic: do not use people as models
en: Investigate with carts and marbles, not by crashing bikes or bodies; the competency is about models of collisions, not dangerous tests.
After an inelastic hit, some kinetic energy has become sound and heat; a microphone or a warm bumper is evidence of that effect in the model.
On a flat table, glancing marble hits let you investigate 2-D collisions, then describe how the forces acted along the line of contact.
Run at least three trials per bumper type so one lucky bounce does not decide whether the model looks elastic or inelastic.
A complete lab sentence names the forces during contact and the effects after: bounce, stick, speed change, dent, or heat.
Say that the cart track is a model of a crash, not a highway crash itself, so the forces you describe are the model's contact pushes.
Change mass ratio on purpose: a heavy cart hitting a light one should send the light cart off faster in the elastic model, a prediction to test.
Video-analysis software can plot velocity dots before and after, a digital model record of the collision you can export to a table.
In one sentence: build a bounce model and a stick model, measure speeds, then describe the contact forces and whether kinetic energy was kept.
Changing momentum always needs a force that lasts for some time; a force of zero duration does not change how much motion an object carries.
The same change in momentum can come from a large force in a short time or a smaller force in a longer time, because both are force times time.
If you push a stationary cart forward for two seconds, you have applied force over time, so the cart's momentum increases in that direction.
To take momentum away you still apply a force over a period of time, which is why brakes need a stretch of road, not an instant halt.
The force that changes momentum must have a component in the direction you want the momentum to change, acting across that interval of time.
If the net force on an object stays zero, its momentum does not change, no matter how long you wait, because no impulse is delivered.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Newton's first law and momentum

en: To identify crash-protection devices, gather crash-test reports from agencies such as NHTSA or your local transport office, then name seatbelts, airbags, and crumple zones.
WHO road-safety pages list seatbelts as a proven way to reduce injury in collisions, a secondary source you can cite beside a local law.
Secondary safety sources also name head restraints that limit neck snap in a rear collision, another way to reduce impact effects besides the three famous devices.
Car-safety papers describe side-impact beams in doors that spread a T-bone crash force, a sourced device that protects occupants from the side.
A collapsible steering column is designed to shorten in a frontal crash so the wheel does less harm to the driver's chest, a device named in engineering sources.
Child seats and booster seats, described in LTO and pediatric safety pages, reduce collision impact on small bodies that adult belts do not fit well.
Some vehicle standards require softer, more crumple-friendly fronts so a collision with a pedestrian delivers less peak force, a source-backed design choice.

topic: do not copy one helmet card
en: When gathering sources, list vehicle systems first: belt, bag, crumple zone, then extras, so the report matches the competency's named examples.
Compare a manufacturer's safety brochure with an independent crash-test page; if they disagree, prefer the independent test for how well a device reduces impact.
Laminated windshields that stay in one sheet are cited as reducing ejection and cutting injuries, another sourced way collisions do less harm.
Bumper-height standards in source documents try to make collisions meet at the same level so energy goes into designed crumple structures.

topic: write the year of the test
en: Copy the year of the crash-test protocol, because airbag and crumple-zone rules have changed, and an old source may describe a weaker design.
WHO also documents motorcycle helmets as impact reducers for riders, a sourced example outside cars that still fits reducing collision harm.
Transport agencies publish that a belt only reduces impact if it is worn; reminder chimes in source specs exist because unused belts cannot help.
Crash-test sources warn that airbags are designed to work with a seatbelt, so gathering 'ways' should present them as a pair, not as rivals.
Engineering sources define a crumple zone as a designed crush space in front or rear, not random damage, so the cabin decelerates over a longer time.
Independent rating pages grade how well structures manage a collision; citing a rating is gathering evidence, not just naming the three devices.
Local transport pages may discuss seatbelts on buses or jeepneys; gather whether those rules exist, because reducing impact is not only for private cars.
If a source does not state a percent reduction, do not invent one; name the device and the agency, which is enough for the competency.
Interior padding on dashboards, listed in safety standards, is another sourced way to lengthen contact time and lower peak force in a crash.
Gather at least two official or test-lab sources, then identify seatbelts, airbags, crumple zones, and one extra device, each with a short because.
Scientists often write a word equation first, naming reactants and products in words, then replace those names with formulas in a second line.
In both word and formula equations the arrow means yields or becomes, a method scientists use so the story of the reaction has a direction.
A method check is to write 'hydrogen plus oxygen yields water' then H2 + O2 → H2O, showing the same reaction in words and in formulas.
Scientists add (s), (l), (g), or (aq) after formulas to show solid, liquid, gas, or dissolved, a detail word equations sometimes skip.
After formulas are written, scientists add coefficients so each element count matches on both sides, a step that word equations cannot show clearly.
A plus sign between formulas means 'and,' not addition in arithmetic; it is the method for listing more than one reactant or product.
A classroom pair is the word equation methane plus oxygen yields carbon dioxide plus water, then the matching balanced formula equation.

topic: do not start with numbers only
en: The competency wants both forms: if you only write formulas, add a word line; if you only write words, add the formula line scientists use.
Scientists may write a triangle or the word heat over the arrow to show that heating was needed, a method symbol used on formula equations.
A method for checking a formula equation is to tally each element on the left and right before you claim the reaction is correctly written.
Write iron plus oxygen yields iron oxide in words, then the formula form, so a common rusting reaction is described the way scientists do.
Scientists describe reactions with equations: first in words, then in formulas with an arrow, plus signs, and coefficients that keep atoms counted.
A food chain shows the order in which living things eat each other, starting with the Sun and ending with a top animal.
The Sun gives energy to plants, which make their own food, so every food chain on Earth begins with sunlight.
Green plants are called producers because they make their own food using sunlight, water, and air.
A herbivore is an animal that eats only plants, like a grasshopper chewing on rice leaves in a field.
A carnivore is an animal that eats only other animals, like the Philippine eagle hunting snakes and small birds.
An omnivore is an animal that eats both plants and animals, like a wild boar digging for roots and small insects.
In a food chain, arrows point from the food to the eater, showing the direction that energy moves.
Most food chains have only about three or four steps because a lot of energy is lost at each step.
The first animal in a food chain, called a primary consumer, is always a herbivore because it eats the plant.
The second animal in a food chain is called a secondary consumer, and it eats the herbivore, so it is usually a carnivore.
In a Philippine mangrove, leaves from bakawan trees are eaten by crabs, which are then eaten by herons.
In a rice field, a grasshopper eats the rice leaves, and a spider eats the grasshopper.
In a freshwater pond, tiny algae are eaten by bangus fry, and larger fish eat the bangus fry.
Herbivores have flat teeth for grinding plants, while carnivores have sharp teeth for tearing meat.
A food web is a group of connected food chains, because most animals eat more than one kind of food.
Plants are food for herbivores, but they are also producers because they make their own food first.
A food chain is really a path of energy, not just a list of who eats whom, because the energy from the Sun travels through it.
A Philippine long-tailed macaque is an omnivore because it eats fruits, leaves, and also insects and small birds.
If one animal in a food chain disappears, the animals that eat it and the animals it eats are both affected.
A simple food chain always starts with the Sun, then a plant, then a herbivore, and finally a carnivore.
The Philippine eagle is a carnivore that hunts monkeys, snakes, and birds, making it a top predator in the forest.
The carabao, or water buffalo, is a large herbivore that eats grasses and leaves, and it is a common sight in Philippine farms.
When a herbivore eats a plant, only about ten percent of the plant's energy becomes new animal body.
In a drawn food chain, each animal is labeled with its name and whether it is a herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore.
An omnivore can be a primary or secondary consumer in a food chain, depending on whether it eats the plant or the herbivore.
Scientists measure friction by pulling a wooden block with a spring scale, and the reading when the block just starts to move is the force of friction.
source: standard friction measurement procedure in school labs

en: To compare surfaces, a class tests the same block on sandpaper, carpet, wood, and tile, recording the spring scale reading for each one.
source: fair-test design with multiple surface conditions

en: Repeating the friction test several times on each surface and averaging the readings gives a more reliable result than a single trial.
source: experimental design: multiple trials improve reliability

en: A spring scale measures force in units called newtons, and a higher reading on a rough surface means that surface has more friction.
source: SI unit of force; spring scale calibration

en: Before testing, a scientist writes a prediction about which surface will show the most friction, then checks the results against that prediction.
The same person should push or pull the block each time, because different people may use different amounts of force and spoil the fair test.
A scientist records the distance the block slides on each surface using a meter stick, and a shorter slide means more friction stopped it sooner.
A data table for the friction experiment lists each surface in one column and the measured force or distance in the next column.
A bar graph of the results shows each surface on the bottom and the friction reading on the side, so the tallest bar has the most friction.
source: bar graph for comparing categorical data

en: Keeping the starting point the same for every trial makes the test fair, because a different starting point would change the distance or speed.
Scientists test one surface at a time and clean the block between trials so that dust or bits of the old surface do not change the result.
To measure friction, scientists first find the force that starts the block moving, then the force that keeps it moving at a steady speed.
source: measurement of static and kinetic friction

en: Scientists pull the block very slowly with the spring scale, because a fast pull gives a higher reading that is not the true friction.
source: measurement practice: slow pull for accurate friction

en: To compare rough and smooth surfaces, a class can use sandpaper for rough and a glossy tile for smooth, keeping the block identical for both.
Scientists compare friction on wet and dry surfaces by testing the same block on each, because wet surfaces often have less friction than dry ones.
source: friction on wet vs dry surfaces

en: The ramp height must stay the same for every test, because a higher ramp gives the car more speed and would hide the effect of the surface.
A good record of the experiment includes the date, the surfaces tested, the measurements, and a note about anything unusual that happened.
If the results show that the block moves farthest on sand, then sand has less friction than the other surfaces tested in the experiment.
A class can test friction with a rubber band: stretching the band to pull a block, and the longer the stretch, the bigger the friction force.
source: elastic band as simple force indicator

en: The conclusion of the experiment states which surface had the most friction and which had the least, using the recorded measurements as evidence.
source: scientific conclusion based on recorded data

en: A fair test of shape change keeps the pushing force the same and changes only the object being pressed, so the results really compare the objects.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, the rest held constant

en: To measure how much a soft object squashes, place it on a flat table and use a ruler to record its height before and after pressing.
source: standard measurement practice with a ruler

en: In a guided activity, learners first predict which objects will change shape, then test each one to check whether their prediction was right.
A good record for a shape-change test is a table with columns for the object, its shape before, the force used, and its shape after.
A spring scale lets a class apply the same measured force to different objects, so the shape-change test stays fair for every object.
source: spring scale use in force measurement

en: To tell elastic from permanent change, press an object once, release it, and watch whether it springs back to its first shape.
A hand lens helps learners see small dents or bends that appear on a soft object after a gentle push.
Drawing a straight line on a soft object before bending it shows exactly where the shape changes when force is applied.
Repeating the same press three times on the same object shows whether the change is the same each time, making the result reliable.
To compare soft and rigid objects, use the same push for both and record which one moves farther or changes shape more.

topic: mass stays the same when reshaped
en: Weighing a clay ball before and after reshaping shows that changing its shape does not change its mass.
Before testing, learners sort objects into rigid and soft groups, then predict which group will change shape more easily.
source: classification as a first step in investigation

en: Drawing the object's outline before and after the push gives a clear picture of how its shape changed.
Measuring a spring's length with a ruler when it is relaxed, stretched, and released shows whether it returns to its first length.
source: measurement with a ruler for elastic behavior

en: Using the same hand push for every object keeps the force the same, so only the object's material is being tested.
A bar chart of how much each object changed shape makes it easy to see which materials are soft and which are rigid.

topic: light and strong pushes on clay
en: To find how force affects shape, press the same clay ball with a light push and then a stronger push, measuring the height each time.
source: varying one variable while keeping the object the same

en: In a shape-change test, look at the object before pressing, press it once, then look again and describe any change you see.
Pushing a soft object with a stick instead of a hand lets learners see the shape change without their fingers blocking the view.
Testing a sponge and a stone with the same press shows that the sponge returns to its shape while the stone does not change at all.
source: comparative testing of elastic and rigid materials

en: The Mohorovičić discontinuity, or Moho, is the invisible boundary where the crust ends and the denser mantle rock begins beneath it.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Mohorovičić discontinuity in standard geology texts

en: The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell made of the crust and the stiff top part of the upper mantle.
The asthenosphere is the hot, soft layer below the lithosphere where rock can slowly flow like very thick syrup.
Earth's tectonic plates are pieces of lithosphere that slowly slide over the flowing asthenosphere underneath them.
Oceanic crust is made mostly of basalt, a dark, dense volcanic rock that forms from cooling lava on the seafloor.
Continental crust is thicker but less dense than oceanic crust, so it floats higher on the mantle like a light block on water.
The mantle is about 2,900 kilometers thick, making it by far the thickest layer of the solid Earth.
The crust makes up less than one percent of Earth's total volume, like the thin skin of a huge fruit.
A Croatian scientist named Andrija Mohorovičić discovered the Moho in 1909 by studying how earthquake waves travel.
Peridotite, the main rock of the upper mantle, is dark green and much denser than the granite and basalt of the crust.
In the upper crust, temperature rises about 25 to 30 degrees Celsius for every kilometer you dig deeper.
source: published geothermal gradient range in crustal rocks

en: Earthquakes happen only in the rigid lithosphere, because the soft asthenosphere below cannot crack or break.
source: encyclopedia-stable; brittle vs ductile rock behavior

en: Mountain ranges have deep crustal roots, just like an iceberg has most of its mass hidden underwater.
The lithosphere is broken into large plates that move in different directions, carrying continents and oceans with them.
Heat from deep inside Earth makes the asthenosphere flow in slow circular currents that help drag the plates above.
source: encyclopedia-stable; convection current model in mantle

en: The Moho is shallower under the oceans and much deeper under tall mountain ranges, following the crust's thickness.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Moho depth variation by crust type

en: Continental crust is rich in silicon and aluminum, while the upper mantle holds more iron and magnesium, which is why it is denser.
source: encyclopedia-stable; elemental composition of crust vs mantle

en: Oceanic crust is constantly created at mid-ocean ridges and destroyed at subduction zones, so it is much younger than continental crust.
source: encyclopedia-stable; seafloor spreading and subduction cycle

en: The asthenosphere is not fully liquid; it is solid rock with just a tiny bit of melted material between the crystals, which lets it flow.
source: encyclopedia-stable; partial melting in upper mantle

en: PHIVOLCS monitors earthquakes and volcanic eruptions in the Philippines, which happen where the lithosphere's plates push against each other.
source: PHIVOLCS mandate; Philippine plate boundary activity

en: Carrying capacity is the largest number of living things an area can support with its food, water, and space.
As a population gets bigger, food and water become harder to find, so each new baby has less to live on.
source: ecological principle: resource limitation slows population growth

en: On a graph, this slowing growth makes an S-shaped curve that starts steep and then flattens out at the top.
source: standard logistic growth model in population ecology

en: If a population has unlimited food and no enemies, it can grow in a J-shaped curve, but that never lasts long in nature.
source: exponential vs logistic growth models in ecology

en: If a population accidentally grows past its carrying capacity, it can crash because the food runs out too quickly.
source: population overshoot and die-off concept in ecology

en: Storms, droughts, and fires can suddenly shrink a population even if it is not crowded at all.
source: density-independent limiting factors in population ecology

en: A herd of deer on a small island grows fast at first, then slows down as the island's plants run out.
source: classic island population study example (e.g., deer on island)

en: Bacteria in a closed dish multiply quickly, but soon their growth slows because the food in the dish is used up.
In a Philippine fish pond, the number of bangus that can grow depends on how much natural food the pond water makes.
source: aquaculture carrying capacity principle in Philippine fishponds

en: When a population is below carrying capacity, births outnumber deaths; near it, births and deaths become almost equal.
source: population growth rate = births - deaths, standard ecology

en: Carrying capacity is not a fixed number, because a good rainy season can raise it and a long drought can lower it.
source: carrying capacity varies with environmental conditions

en: Environmental resistance is the name for all the natural forces that stop a population from growing forever.
source: environmental resistance concept in population ecology

en: Carrying capacity is different for each species, so a field can hold thousands of grasshoppers but only a few eagles.
source: carrying capacity is specific to species and resource needs

en: Pollution from factories can lower an ecosystem's carrying capacity by making the water and soil harmful to living things.
source: human pollution degrades habitat and reduces carrying capacity

en: Adding fertilizer to a rice field, or palay, can raise its carrying capacity so more rice plants can grow in the same space.
source: agricultural inputs increase carrying capacity for crops

en: A watering hole in a dry area sets the carrying capacity for the animals that come to drink, because water is the limit.
source: water availability as a key limiting factor in dry ecosystems

en: Animals need space to build nests and find food, so a limited territory naturally slows down how fast their numbers can grow.
source: space and territory as limiting factors in animal populations

en: When prey animals become plentiful, predators increase and eat more of them, which then slows the prey population's growth.
source: predator-prey dynamics regulate population sizes in ecosystems

en: A forest can only support a certain number of birds because there are only so many nesting holes and seeds to go around.
source: habitat resources (nests, food) determine bird carrying capacity

en: The human population on Earth is still growing, but its growth rate has slowed down as we get closer to the planet's limits.
source: demographic transition and global population growth trends
