en: Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5 degrees from straight up, and this tilt is what makes sunlight hit different places at different angles.
When sunlight hits the ground at a steep angle, it spreads over a smaller area and feels hotter than the same light hitting at a shallow angle.
source: encyclopedia-stable; solar intensity and incidence angle

en: The equator receives fairly steady sunlight all year because the Sun's direct rays stay near it, so its temperature changes little.
The poles receive sunlight at a very shallow angle, so the same amount of sunlight spreads over a huge area and warms the ground very little.
In December, the Southern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, so it is summer there while the Northern Hemisphere has winter.
The Sun's direct rays never go beyond the tropics; they move between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn over a year.
The Tropic of Cancer is the northernmost latitude where the Sun can be directly overhead, which happens around the June solstice.
The Tropic of Capricorn is the southernmost latitude where the Sun can be directly overhead, which happens around the December solstice.
The length of daylight also changes with the tilt: summer days are longer and winter days are shorter, adding more hours of sunlight to warm the ground.
A common mistake is blaming seasons on Earth's distance from the Sun, but the real cause is the tilt that changes the angle of sunlight.
During the equinoxes in March and September, the Sun is directly above the equator, and day and night are nearly equal everywhere.
The Sun's noon height in the sky changes through the year: it climbs higher in summer and sinks lower in winter because of the tilt.
The Philippines, being near the equator, gets strong sunlight all year, but the tilt still shifts the Sun's path and helps bring wet and dry seasons.
source: PAGASA; Philippine climate and solar path

en: When the Sun is high in the sky, its rays travel through less atmosphere, so more energy reaches the ground than when it is low.
The tilt makes the Northern and Southern Hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time of year.
The angle of sunlight is measured from the horizon: a high Sun means direct rays, and a low Sun means slanted rays that spread out.
The Arctic Circle marks the latitude where the Sun can stay above or below the horizon for a full day at the solstices because of the tilt.
Think of a flashlight shining straight down versus at a slant: the slanted beam covers more ground but each spot gets less light, just like sunlight on Earth.
The June and December solstices mark the times when one pole leans most toward the Sun and the other most away, giving the strongest seasonal contrast.
The Tropic of Cancer passes north of the Philippines, while the equator lies south, so the Sun's direct rays cross the country twice a year.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Philippines latitude and solar declination

en: Both electric motors and generators have a coil of wire and a magnet, and the coil spins inside the magnetic field.
In a motor, electricity flowing through a coil inside a magnet gives the coil a push, so it turns.
source: encyclopedia-stable; motor effect (force on current-carrying conductor)

en: In a generator, turning a coil inside a magnet pushes electrons along the wire, creating an electric current.
Motors and generators both convert energy from one form to another, but neither creates or destroys energy.
source: encyclopedia-stable; law of conservation of energy

en: The electric motor in a ceiling fan uses electricity to spin the blades and cool the room.
In a hydroelectric plant, falling water spins a turbine, and the turbine spins a generator to make electricity.
Wind turbines are big generators: wind spins the blades, which spin a coil inside a magnet to produce electricity.
A hand-crank flashlight has a tiny generator that makes electricity when you turn the crank, so no battery is needed.
A bicycle dynamo is a small generator that rubs against the tire to power the headlight while you ride.
Geothermal power plants in Leyte use steam from underground to spin generators and make electricity for many homes.
Both motors and generators need a magnetic field, usually from a permanent magnet or an electromagnet, to work.
In a motor, the coil turns because its own magnetic field pushes against the magnet's field, creating a spinning force.
source: encyclopedia-stable; interaction of magnetic fields in motor

en: In a generator, spinning the coil changes the magnetic field around it, which pushes electrons along the wire to make current.
Both machines have a spinning part called a rotor and a fixed part called a stator that stay close together.
Electric jeepneys use motors to move, while the power plants that charge their batteries use generators, so both work together.
source: encyclopedia-stable; electric vehicles and charging infrastructure

en: A washing machine has a motor that spins the drum, and the electricity it uses comes from a generator somewhere else.
source: encyclopedia-stable; household appliance and power grid

en: Without magnetism, neither motors nor generators can work, because both depend on magnetic fields to function.
Power plants use huge generators that spin coils with steam, water, or wind to supply electricity to entire cities.
Electric motors are everywhere: in fans, blenders, drills, and jeepneys, turning electricity into spinning motion.
In remote villages without power lines, small generators powered by diesel can supply electricity for lights and radios.
source: encyclopedia-stable; diesel generator use in off-grid areas

en: Earthquake focuses are grouped by depth: shallow ones start about 70 kilometers down or less, while deep ones can start hundreds of kilometers underground.
Scientists find an earthquake's epicenter by comparing how early the first wave arrives at three or more different seismic stations.
Magnitude is one number that tells how much energy an earthquake releases at its focus, and it stays the same no matter where you feel it.
Intensity describes how strongly people feel the shaking at a certain place, so it changes with distance from the epicenter and local soil.
Each whole number up the magnitude scale means the earthquake releases about 32 times more energy, so a 7 is far stronger than a 6.
A seismograph is an instrument with a weight and a drum that draws wiggly lines to record how the ground moves during an earthquake.
Earthquake waves travel in two main kinds: P-waves arrive first with a push-pull motion, and S-waves arrive later with a side-to-side shake.
In a reverse fault, rocks squeeze together and one block slides up over the other, which can push the seafloor upward during a quake.
In a normal fault, rocks pull apart and one block drops down, which can make the ground sink and sometimes change the shape of the land.
In a strike-slip fault, rocks slide past each other sideways along a nearly vertical crack, like two hands rubbing against each other.
A tsunami can travel across deep ocean as fast as a jet plane, about 800 kilometers per hour, but its wave is small and low there.
When a tsunami reaches shallow water near shore, it slows down and piles up into a tall wall of water that can flood the land.
PHIVOLCS uses its own intensity scale from I to X to rate how strongly people in the Philippines feel an earthquake's shaking.
Scientists today mostly use the moment magnitude scale, which works better than the old Richter scale for very large earthquakes.
The Philippines sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, a belt of active faults and volcanoes where many earthquakes happen every year.
When a big underwater quake shifts the seafloor, the whole column of water above it moves at once, and that push creates a tsunami wave.
A tsunami has a very long wavelength, often hundreds of kilometers, so it acts like a moving wall of water rather than a single tall wave.
A strong earthquake has a high magnitude everywhere, but its intensity can be high near the epicenter and low far away from it.
Shallow-focus earthquakes usually cause more damage than deep-focus ones because their energy has less rock to travel through before reaching the surface.
PHIVOLCS watches earthquakes and sea levels around the Philippines and sends tsunami warnings to coastal communities when a big quake hits the ocean floor.
In a friction experiment, the surface is the independent variable that the scientist changes, and the friction force is the dependent variable that gets measured.
source: experimental design: independent and dependent variables

en: The block, the pull speed, and the table stay the same in every trial so that only the surface changes and the test stays fair.
source: fair-test design: hold all variables constant except one

en: Before measuring, the scientist checks that the spring scale reads zero when nothing pulls on it, so every measurement starts from the same point.
source: measurement practice: calibrate instrument before use

en: The spring scale is held parallel to the table while pulling, because tilting it would add extra force and give a wrong friction reading.
source: measurement technique: keep force direction parallel to motion

en: Testing at least three different surfaces, like sandpaper, carpet, and tile, gives enough data to compare friction fairly.
source: comparative experiment design: multiple conditions for meaningful comparison

en: A good hypothesis predicts which surface will have the most friction and gives a reason, such as roughness creating more rubbing.
source: scientific method: testable hypothesis with rationale

en: Every friction reading is recorded with its unit, newtons, so the results are clear and can be compared correctly later.
source: measurement convention: SI unit for force is the newton

en: The same block is used for every surface because a heavier block would press down harder and increase the friction by itself.
source: fair-test design: normal force affects friction, so mass must stay constant

en: The average friction reading for each surface is compared, and the surface with the highest average has the most friction.
source: data analysis: compare means across conditions

topic: one changing thing in fair test
en: A fair test has only one changing thing, the surface, so any difference in the friction reading must come from that surface.
source: fair-test principle: isolate the single variable being tested

en: Static friction is the force that holds the block still until the pull becomes strong enough, and it is always bigger than the friction while moving.
source: physics of friction: static friction exceeds kinetic friction

en: Scientists check that the table is level with a small bubble level so the block does not slide on its own before pulling.
source: experimental setup: ensure no unintended motion from slope

en: The scientist decides before starting how many trials to do on each surface, such as three, and does exactly that many.
source: experimental design: predetermined number of repetitions

en: Writing down the steps in order before starting helps the scientist follow the same method for every surface tested.
source: scientific method: written procedure ensures consistency

en: The measurement is written down right after each pull, because waiting and writing from memory can make the data wrong.
source: data collection practice: record immediately to avoid error

en: If the results do not match the prediction, the scientist still records them honestly and explains what might have caused the difference.
source: scientific integrity: report actual data even when unexpected

en: The same spring scale is used for all the measurements because different scales may be calibrated differently and give different readings.
source: measurement consistency: same instrument avoids calibration differences

en: A labeled diagram of the setup shows the block, spring scale, and surface, so someone else can repeat the same experiment.
source: scientific communication: labeled diagram aids reproducibility

en: After the block is moving, the scientist reads the spring scale again to get the kinetic friction, which is usually smaller than static friction.
source: physics of friction: kinetic friction is less than static friction

en: The conclusion states which surface had the most friction using the recorded numbers, not just what the scientist expected to happen.
source: scientific method: conclusions must be supported by evidence

en: Taping a small marker on one coil of a slinky shows that the spring itself does not travel; the marker swings in place as the wave passes.
source: standard wave demonstration: medium stays in place

en: A fair comparison of longitudinal and transverse waves uses the same spring, the same stretch length, and the same push strength, changing only the direction of the hand.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, the rest held constant

en: Wave speed in a slinky is measured by marking start and end points, timing the wave with a stopwatch, and dividing distance by time.
A light paper ball at the far end of a stretched slinky moves when the wave arrives, showing the wave carried energy to it.
source: standard demonstration: wave transfers energy to an object

en: A good record of a wave demonstration includes a drawing with arrows showing the wave's direction and the material's direction, plus the measured distances.
source: science notebook practice: labeled diagram with directions

en: The wavelength of a transverse wave on a rope is measured with a meter stick as the distance between two neighboring crests.
For a longitudinal wave, the wavelength is the distance between two neighboring compressions, measured with a ruler on the stretched spring.
A graph of a wave's motion shows time on the horizontal axis and the position of one point on the medium on the vertical axis.
source: standard graphing convention: time on x-axis

en: Placing three paper markers along a slinky shows that wave energy weakens with distance, because the farthest marker moves the least.
source: standard observation: amplitude decreases with distance

en: A clear transverse wave needs a tight rope and a steady rhythm at the free end so the crests stay even and easy to measure.
source: standard demonstration technique: steady driving motion

en: PHIVOLCS scientists read the time gap between the longitudinal and transverse waves on a seismograph to estimate how far an earthquake is.
In a ripple tank, scientists keep the water depth the same and change only the wave maker's speed to see how wave energy spreads.
source: standard ripple tank experiment: one variable changed

en: Comparing wave speeds uses the same long spring for both wave types, timing each over the same distance.
source: fair comparison: same medium, same distance

en: A floating cork on water bobs up and down as a wave passes but stays in place, showing the wave moves energy, not water.
source: standard demonstration: wave transfers energy, not matter

en: Testing how push strength affects wave energy keeps the same spring and stretch, changing only how far the end is pulled back.
source: fair-test design: change only the independent variable

en: A results table for wave experiments lists wave type, push strength, distance traveled, and how far a marker moved, so patterns are easy to see.
source: science notebook practice: organized data table

en: The amplitude of a transverse wave is measured with a ruler as the height from the rest position up to a crest.
source: standard wave measurement: amplitude = crest height from rest

en: A reliable wave speed comes from timing the wave three times with the same spring and push, then taking the average of the times.
source: standard measurement practice: repeated trials and averaging

en: A wave sent along a rope tied to a fixed post bounces back upside down, showing reflection at a fixed end.
source: standard demonstration: reflection of a wave at a fixed boundary

en: A slinky laid on a smooth, flat floor and stretched to the same length each time lets the wave travel in a straight, even path.
source: standard demonstration technique: controlled setup on flat surface

en: A tertiary consumer is a carnivore that eats other carnivores, like a snake that eats a bird which ate a caterpillar.
In a coconut grove, a coconut beetle eats palm leaves, and a monitor lizard eats the beetle, making a three-link food chain.
The number of living things usually gets smaller at each step of a food chain, so there are more plants than herbivores and more herbivores than carnivores.
A food chain with only two living things is possible, such as a plant and the animal that eats it, but most chains have more steps.
A food chain is a straight line of arrows, not a circle, because energy moves in one direction from the Sun to the top animal.
A mango tree is a producer, and a fruit bat that eats its fruit is a herbivore, starting a food chain in a backyard.
In a freshwater river, tiny algae are eaten by small fish, and a Philippine crocodile eats the fish, forming a food chain.
A fruit bat eats fruits and is a herbivore, while a python that eats the bat is a carnivore, showing a forest food chain.
Decomposers like fungi and bacteria are not usually drawn in a simple food chain, but they break down dead plants and animals.

topic: food chain does not show size
en: A food chain shows the feeding order, but it does not show how big the animals are or how strong they are.
A food chain can be found in a garden, a pond, a forest, or a rice field, because every habitat has living things that eat each other.
The Philippine tarsier is a carnivore that eats insects, so it is a secondary consumer when the insects eat plants.

topic: producer can be tree or algae
en: A food chain always has a producer, which is a green plant, but the plant can be a tree, grass, or algae.
A food chain shows interdependence: each living thing depends on the one before it for energy.
A food chain is a model that simplifies real feeding relationships, which are often more complex.
When energy moves from one step of a food chain to the next, some is lost as heat, so each step has less energy.
A food chain can be drawn with labels for each organism's role, like producer, herbivore, carnivore, to show its job.
A food chain is a straight line, but a food web is a tangle of lines, showing that real feeding is more connected.

topic: food chain does not show amount
en: A food chain shows the order of eating, but it does not show how much food each animal eats.
A food chain always ends with a top predator that nothing else eats in that chain, like a crocodile in a river.
The Philippine Sea Plate is a tectonic plate under the Pacific Ocean that carries the eastern Philippines and moves northwestward toward the Asian mainland.
The Philippine archipelago sits where the Philippine Sea Plate meets the Eurasian Plate, so both plates control where the islands go.
A plate's velocity is its speed and its direction together, so predicting the future needs both, not just how fast the plate moves.
The Philippine Trench is a deep underwater canyon where the Philippine Sea Plate dives beneath the archipelago, marking the boundary that shapes the islands' future path.
On the western side, the Manila Trench swallows the other plate, so the whole archipelago is squeezed between two converging plates.
The Philippines is an island arc, a curved chain of volcanic islands built where one plate dives under another.
The same plate motion that builds mountains and feeds volcanoes today is the motion that will carry the archipelago to a new position.
source: encyclopedia-stable; plate motion and landform formation

en: The eastern islands ride the Philippine Sea Plate while the western islands ride the Eurasian Plate, so the two sides of the archipelago move at different speeds.
source: GNSS studies of Philippine Mobile Belt; simplified

en: Satellites send signals to ground stations on the islands, and the tiny yearly shifts in those signals reveal the plate's true velocity.
Fifty million years ago, the crust that now carries the Philippine islands was in a different part of the ocean, and the same drift that moved it then moves it now.
Fifty million years is far longer than all of human history, so even a slow crawl of centimeters per year adds up to an enormous distance.
source: geologic time vs human history; encyclopedia-stable

en: The Pacific Plate pushes from the east while the Eurasian Plate resists from the west, so the archipelago is slowly compressed between them.
New volcanoes may rise and old islands may sink, so the 50-million-year archipelago will likely have a different lineup of islands than today.
If a car keeps driving at a steady speed, you can predict where it will be later; the same math predicts where the Philippine Plate will be in 50 million years.
The 50-million-year map is called a model because it uses today's measurements and stated assumptions, not a guaranteed future.
To measure how far a soft object moves, a class marks its starting spot on the floor and uses a tape measure after a gentle push.
source: method for measuring displacement in fair tests

en: A class uses a spring scale to pull a rubber band and reads the force when it stretches to a certain length, showing how force changes shape.
source: method for measuring force with spring scale

en: Using a stopwatch, a class times how long a squeezed sponge takes to return to its full shape, which shows if it is elastic.
To compare hardness, a class drops a small ball from the same height onto each object and records how much the object dents.
source: method for comparing hardness by impact

en: A class uses a plastic ruler to press on a soft object, then measures the depth of the dent with a ruler after removing the pressure.
A class takes a photo of a soft object before and after pressing it, then compares the two photos side by side to see the change.
source: method for recording observations with camera

en: To test movement, a class gives the same push to a rigid box and a soft box, then measures how far each slides on the floor.
A class uses a spring scale to apply a measured force to a sponge and records its thickness with a ruler at each force level.
A class wraps a piece of string around a ball before and after squeezing it to measure its circumference and see if size changed.
A class uses a ramp to roll a toy car into different objects and measures how far each object moves from the impact.
source: method for testing force from moving object

en: To see how force stretches a spring, a class hangs different weights on it and measures its length with a ruler for each weight.
A class uses a stopwatch to time how long different soft materials take to return to their original shape after being pressed.
Before testing, a class feels each object and ranks them from softest to hardest to predict which will change shape most.
source: method for predicting based on texture

en: A class draws small dots on a soft object, presses it, then watches how the dots move apart or together to see the shape change.
A class squeezes a plastic bottle filled with water and watches the water level rise, showing how the shape change affects the inside.
A class uses a spring scale to press a soft object and reads the force at which a dent appears, then measures the dent with a ruler.
source: method for finding force needed to deform

en: A class uses a marker to draw a grid on a soft object, then bends it and sees how the grid lines curve to show where the shape changed.
A class uses a pencil to poke a soft object and sees if it leaves a mark, which shows how easily the material is changed.
A class uses a fan to blow air on different objects and observes which ones move, showing that force can move objects without touching them.
A class uses a protractor to measure the angle of a bent object before and after pressing, showing how much the shape changed.
To compare soft and rigid objects, a class gives each one the same gentle push and watches which one moves or changes shape more.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, the rest held constant

en: Before testing, learners make a prediction about which objects will change shape, then they test each object to check their guess.
A class presses the same soft object on a hard table and on a soft cloth to see how the surface changes the object's shape.
source: fair-test design: changing surface, holding object constant

en: To see how much force is needed, a class pushes a rigid box harder and harder until it starts to move, then notes that force.
source: observation practice: threshold force for movement

en: A class records the steps of a shape-change test in order: look at the object, press it, then look again and write down the change.
Using a ruler to measure an object's height before and after pressing gives a clear number that shows how much the shape changed.
The crust is the only layer of Earth that humans have directly drilled into, with the deepest hole reaching about 12 kilometers.
Oxygen and silicon make up about three-quarters of the crust's mass, mostly combined as silicate minerals.
The crust is the coldest layer of Earth, with temperatures starting at the surface and rising gradually with depth.
All known life on Earth lives in or on the crust, from the deepest ocean floor to the highest mountain peak.
Weathering and erosion constantly break down crust rocks into soil and carry the pieces to the sea.
The crust is made of three rock families: igneous from cooled magma, sedimentary from pressed layers, and metamorphic from heat and pressure.
Continental crust has a layered structure: a top of sedimentary rock, a middle of granite, and a deeper layer of denser rock.
Oceanic crust also has layers: a thin sediment cover, then basalt, and below that gabbro.
The crust provides most of the minerals we use, like copper, gold, and iron, which are mined from its rocks.
Scientists map the crust's hidden layers by measuring how seismic waves from earthquakes travel through it.
The crust is the thinnest layer of Earth relative to its size, but it is the only one we can see and walk on.
The crust is the boundary where the solid Earth meets the oceans and atmosphere, shaping coastlines and weather.
The crust breaks into faults, and when the rocks slip along a fault, the energy causes an earthquake.
The crust is recycled at plate boundaries: new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and old crust sinks at subduction zones.
The crust is the least dense layer of Earth, so it floats on the denser mantle below.
The crust is the most varied layer, with different rock types, ages, and structures in different regions.
Mines and drill cores give scientists direct samples of the crust, making it the most accessible layer to study.
Most volcanoes on Earth occur where magma from the mantle rises through cracks in the crust.
The crust under the Philippines is a patchwork of continental and oceanic fragments, making it geologically active.
The subsolar point is the one place on Earth where the Sun is directly overhead at noon, and it receives the most intense sunlight because the rays hit at 90 degrees.
The Sun's noon height changes by about 47 degrees between the June and December solstices, because the tilt moves the Sun's direct rays from 23.5 degrees north to 23.5 degrees south.
The tilt makes the Sun rise and set at different points on the horizon, so in the Philippines the Sun rises more toward the north in summer and more toward the south in winter.
source: observational astronomy; seasonal sunrise azimuth shift

en: A place receives the most intense sunlight when the Sun is directly overhead at noon, because the rays hit the ground at 90 degrees and do not spread out.
The intensity of sunlight depends on the Sun's angle above the horizon, so a Sun at 90 degrees gives full intensity and a Sun at 30 degrees gives about half.
source: sine of solar altitude; trigonometry of insolation

en: The tilt causes the Sun's path across the sky to be a higher arc in summer and a lower arc in winter, so the Sun climbs higher at noon.
In the Philippines, the Sun is directly overhead at noon twice a year, and on those days a vertical stick casts almost no shadow.
source: geography of tropics; PAGASA-consistent solar position

en: The Antarctic Circle is the southern counterpart of the Arctic Circle, where the Sun can stay above or below the horizon for a full day at the solstices.
The tilt causes seasons to be more extreme at high latitudes and milder near the equator, because the angle of sunlight changes more at high latitudes.
source: climatology; seasonal insolation variation with latitude

en: The angle of incidence is the angle between the Sun's rays and a line pointing straight up from the ground, and it is zero when the Sun is overhead.
The total solar energy a place receives in a day depends on both the angle of sunlight and the number of daylight hours.
The tilt is about 23.5 degrees, which is the same as the latitude of the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.
source: axial tilt equals tropical latitudes; encyclopedia-stable

en: The Sun's rays are more slanted in the early morning and late afternoon, so the ground warms less then even though the Sun is shining.
The tilt is the reason the shadow of a stick at noon changes length through the year, getting shorter in summer and longer in winter.
The angle of sunlight can be estimated from shadow length, because a longer shadow means a lower Sun and less intense rays.
source: trigonometry of shadows; simple measurement method

en: In the Philippines, the noontime shadow points south when the Sun is north of the zenith, and north when the Sun is south of the zenith.
source: solar position relative to observer latitude; PAGASA-consistent

en: At the North Pole, the Sun stays above the horizon for about six months of daylight and below for six months of night because of the tilt.
source: polar day and polar night; encyclopedia-stable

en: The dates when the Sun is directly overhead depend on latitude, so places closer to the equator have their two overhead days closer together in the year.
Because of the tilt, the summer hemisphere gets sunlight at a steeper angle and the winter hemisphere at a shallower angle, so the two hemispheres receive different amounts of energy.
The tilt causes the Sun's rays to be more concentrated in the summer, which is why the ground warms up more even though the Sun's output stays the same.
source: solar constant vs. incidence angle; encyclopedia-stable

en: When a population gets crowded, finding a mate becomes harder, so fewer babies are born and the population's growth slows down.
source: population dynamics: mate limitation as a density-dependent factor

en: As a population grows, its own waste builds up in the water or soil, which can poison the environment and slow down further growth.
source: encyclopedia-stable; density-dependent limiting factors include waste accumulation

en: Near carrying capacity, animals must travel farther to find food, using up energy that could have gone to raising young.
source: encyclopedia-stable; resource limitation affects reproductive energy

en: When all the good nesting spots or hiding places are taken, many young animals cannot survive, so the population stops growing as fast.
source: encyclopedia-stable; limited shelter as a limiting factor

en: A population far below its limit might grow by ten percent a year, but near the limit it grows by only one or two percent a year.
source: logistic growth model; rate decreases as N approaches K

en: As a population approaches carrying capacity, the number of new individuals added each year gets smaller and smaller.
source: logistic growth; absolute growth rate decreases near K

en: When a population is small, each individual has plenty of resources, but as it grows, the same amount must be split among many, so growth slows.
In a small Philippine pond, tilapia growth slows down as they eat up the algae, leaving less for each new fish to eat.
In a Philippine bakawan, or mangrove forest, the crab population slows down as they use up the fallen leaves that are their main food.
A population's growth slows down when it runs low on the single resource it needs most, like water during a dry spell.
Overcrowding itself can stress animals, making them produce fewer young and slowing the population's growth.
source: encyclopedia-stable; physiological stress in dense populations

en: Near carrying capacity, the population size does not stay perfectly still but wobbles up and down slightly as births and deaths balance out.
The growth of a population slows down because the death rate rises as resources become scarce, not just because the birth rate falls.
source: population ecology; death rate response to scarcity

en: Growth starts to slow down before the population reaches the absolute limit, because resources get harder to find as it gets closer.
Weeds in a field grow quickly at first, but their growth slows down as they crowd each other out for sunlight and water.
In a forest, the number of squirrels slows down as the acorn supply runs out, because each squirrel needs a certain number of acorns to survive the winter.
source: encyclopedia-stable; seed/food limitation in animal populations

en: If a lake has only a certain amount of oxygen, the fish population slows down as that oxygen gets used up by more fish.
source: aquatic ecology; dissolved oxygen as a limiting factor

en: The birth rate falls as food gets scarce, because mothers have less energy to make healthy babies, so growth slows down.
In a rice field, the number of frogs slows down as the insects they eat become harder to find, so fewer tadpoles survive.
A population that is far below its carrying capacity grows quickly, but one that is near it grows very slowly, because every extra mouth makes the shortage worse.
Earth's lithospheric plates are not just crust; each one includes the crust and the rigid top layer of the mantle, moving as a single slab.
The plates glide on a softer, partly melted layer called the asthenosphere, which lets them shift slowly over millions of years.
Tectonic plates drift about 2 to 5 centimeters per year, roughly the length of a paperclip, so their movement is too slow to feel.
Continental crust is made mostly of light granite, while oceanic crust is made of dark, dense basalt from cooled lava.
Some continental crust is over 3 billion years old, yet the oldest oceanic crust is only about 200 million years because it gets recycled.
At a subduction zone, the sinking oceanic plate drags water and sediment into the hot mantle, where they melt and change.
Deep ocean trenches, such as the Philippine Trench, form at the line where a heavy oceanic plate bends and dives downward.
Melting above a sinking oceanic plate feeds arcs of volcanoes, like Mayon in the Philippines, which grow along the plate edge.
The Philippine Sea Plate carries both oceanic crust and small pieces of continental crust, so one plate can hold two crust types.
When an oceanic plate collides with a continental plate, the ocean floor sinks and the land edge crumples into mountains and volcanoes.
When a continent pulls apart at a divergent boundary, the crack can widen into a new ocean, leaving the two halves on different plates.
At transform boundaries, plates slide past each other, like along the Philippine Fault, grinding without making or destroying crust.
Because continental crust is thick and light, it floats high and does not sink into the mantle, so it survives for billions of years.
The Pacific Ring of Fire is a giant loop of subduction zones where oceanic plates sink, creating many of Earth's volcanoes and quakes.
PHIVOLCS tracks the movement of plates around the Philippines to warn communities about earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.
The Philippines sits in a mobile belt squeezed between two large plates, which is why it has many faults, trenches, and volcanoes.
Slow convection currents in Earth's hot mantle, caused by heat rising and cooling rock sinking, help drag the plates along.
At a subduction zone, the sinking edge of a plate pulls the rest of the plate behind it, like a heavy tablecloth tugging downward.
When two continental plates collide, neither is dense enough to sink, so the crust crumples upward into high mountains like the Himalayas.
Old oceanic crust is swallowed back into the mantle at subduction zones, which is why the ocean floor is always much younger than the continents.
Focal depth is the straight-line distance from an earthquake's focus underground to the epicenter on the surface above it.
source: encyclopedia-stable; earthquake focus and epicenter geometry

en: Scientists calculate an earthquake's magnitude from the size of the wiggles on a seismogram, not from the damage it causes.
source: encyclopedia-stable; magnitude from seismic wave amplitude

en: Intensity is measured by collecting reports from many places about how people felt the shaking and what damage they saw.
source: encyclopedia-stable; intensity from felt reports and damage surveys

en: A tsunami is a series of waves that can last for hours, and the first wave is often not the biggest one.
Not all tsunamis come from earthquakes; underwater landslides and volcanic eruptions can also push water and create tsunami waves.
source: encyclopedia-stable; tsunami triggers include landslides and eruptions

en: Wind makes ordinary ocean waves that only move the surface, but a tsunami moves the whole water column from the seafloor up.
The Philippine Fault is a long crack that runs through the islands, and it can produce strong earthquakes when its blocks slip.
The Marikina Valley Fault runs near Metro Manila, and scientists monitor it because it could move and cause strong shaking.
A simple fault model uses two blocks of wood with sandpaper between them that slide to show how rocks move.
source: classroom model of fault motion; DepEd MATATAG activity

en: In a classroom model, the focus is a point deep inside a box of clay, and the epicenter is the mark on the top surface.
source: classroom model of focus and epicenter; DepEd MATATAG activity

en: The focus of an earthquake is also called the hypocenter, the exact underground spot where the rock first breaks.
A seismograph draws its wiggly lines on paper or a screen, and that record is called a seismogram.
When a tsunami reaches land, the height of the water on the shore is called run-up, and it can be much taller than the wave in the open ocean.
A very deep earthquake under the ocean may not create a tsunami because the seafloor barely moves at the surface.
source: encyclopedia-stable; deep quakes produce little seafloor displacement

en: News reports usually name an earthquake by its epicenter, such as a quake near a town, even though the focus is underground.
source: encyclopedia-stable; epicenter used for locating earthquakes in reports

en: A tsunami's height at the shore depends partly on the shape of the seafloor, so some coastal areas get bigger waves than others.
A fault is a crack in the earth's crust where two blocks of rock can move past each other, and earthquakes happen when they suddenly slip.
The largest earthquakes ever recorded are about magnitude 9, and the magnitude scale has no fixed upper limit.
Many countries use the Modified Mercalli scale from I to XII, while PHIVOLCS's Philippine scale goes from I to X.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Modified Mercalli and PHIVOLCS intensity scales

en: A tsunami can cross an entire ocean and still have enough energy to flood a coast far from the earthquake that made it.
A scientific investigation begins with a clear question, like which surface makes the block hardest to pull, before any measuring is done.
source: scientific method: question first, then plan

en: Scientists pick surfaces that look very different, such as rough sandpaper and smooth glass, so the friction readings are easy to compare.
source: fair-test design: choose contrasting levels of the variable

en: A scientist first pulls the block on a plain table to get a baseline reading, then compares every other surface with that starting value.
source: experimental design: baseline measurement for comparison

en: The scientist reads the spring scale only when the needle stops swinging, so the number is steady and not too high or too low.
source: measurement practice: read instruments when stable

en: Along with the numbers, the scientist writes how each surface feels or looks, like rough or shiny, to help explain the results later.
source: science inquiry: qualitative and quantitative observations

en: The written method is clear enough that another person could follow the same steps and check whether the results come out the same.
Scientists test the surfaces in a mixed order, not always the same sequence, so practice with one surface does not change the later readings.
A flat wooden block is used instead of a rolling toy because the spring scale measures sliding friction between the block and the surface.
source: friction measurement: sliding vs rolling friction

en: After making the bar graph, the scientist looks for a pattern, like rougher surfaces having taller bars, before writing the conclusion.
source: data analysis: look for patterns before concluding

en: The scientist clears the table of extra objects so nothing bumps the block or the spring scale while the measurement is taken.
If one trial gives a reading that is very different from the others on the same surface, the scientist repeats that trial to check it.
A generator cannot make electricity by itself; it needs an outside force like falling water, wind, or steam to keep its coil spinning.
Generators are usually placed at power plants, while motors are inside homes and vehicles, so they are connected by long power lines.
In a motor, electricity makes the coil spin, but in a generator, an outside force like water or wind makes the coil spin, so the cause of the spin is opposite.
A motor gets its energy from a battery or a wall outlet, while a generator gets its energy from a crank, a turbine, or an engine, so their energy sources are opposite.
In the energy chain, a generator changes mechanical energy into electrical energy, and a motor changes it back, so they are opposite steps in the same cycle.
A common mistake is thinking a generator creates electricity from nothing, but it only changes motion into electricity, so it must be kept spinning by an outside force.
A generator only makes electricity while its coil is spinning, so if you stop turning the crank, the light goes out.
In a hydroelectric dam, falling water turns a turbine that spins a generator, and the electricity then runs motors in homes, showing how the two work together.
The upper continental crust is made of lighter rocks like granite and gneiss, while the lower crust is denser and more like basalt.
source: standard geology: upper vs lower crust composition

en: In some continental regions, seismic waves reveal a boundary called the Conrad discontinuity that separates the upper and lower crust.
The upper crust holds most of the world's groundwater in porous rocks like sandstone and limestone, which form aquifers that supply wells.
The oldest rocks on Earth, about 4 billion years old, are found in the upper crust of ancient continents called cratons.
The upper crust is cold and brittle, so it breaks during earthquakes, while the lower crust is hot and can bend without breaking.
The upper crust contains most of the world's coal, oil, and natural gas, trapped in layers of sedimentary rock.
source: fossil fuel reservoirs in sedimentary basins

en: The upper crust is the only part of the crust that is directly exposed at the surface, while the lower crust lies hidden beneath.
The upper crust is less dense than the lower crust because it is richer in silica and lighter minerals like quartz and feldspar.
source: compositional difference between upper and lower crust

en: The upper crust is the layer most shaped by weathering and erosion, creating soil, valleys, and plains on the land surface.
The upper crust holds fossils because sedimentary rocks form on top of it and preserve the remains of ancient organisms.
When tectonic plates collide, the upper crust is squeezed and lifted to build mountain ranges like the Himalayas.
The upper crust is the source of most volcanic rocks on land, such as andesite and rhyolite, which cool from magma underground.
A class uses a spring scale to push a toy car with a measured force, then uses a ruler to measure how far the car slides.
source: standard method for measuring force and distance

en: A class uses a stopwatch to time how many seconds a pushed toy car takes to stop, showing which surface slows it down more.
source: standard stopwatch timing for comparing motion

en: A class draws two dots on a clay cylinder and measures the distance between them with a ruler before and after stretching to see how much it lengthened.

topic: line graph of force and distance
en: A class plots a line graph with force on the left and distance moved on the bottom to see how pushing harder makes an object go farther.
A class makes a data table with a column for each object's predicted change and a column for the actual change, then compares the two.
The labels herbivore, carnivore, and omnivore are used only for animals, not for plants, because plants are producers that make their own food.
An animal's label in a food chain is based on its usual diet, so a pig that eats both plants and scraps is an omnivore even if it sometimes eats only plants.
In a simple food chain, you typically draw one producer, one herbivore, and one carnivore, but you can replace the herbivore or carnivore with an omnivore.
The Sun is not a living thing, so it is never labeled as a herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore; it is only the source of energy.
To draw a correct food chain, you must choose a plant that a herbivore really eats and a herbivore that a carnivore really eats, so the chain is realistic.
A food chain diagram can be drawn with the producer on the left and the top consumer on the right, but the order is determined by who eats whom.
A fair test of photosynthesis raw materials keeps light, temperature, and water the same while changing only the one raw material being tested.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, the rest held constant

en: In this investigation, the raw material that is changed is the independent variable, and the starch the leaf makes is the dependent variable that is measured.
Before testing, a plant is kept in a dark cupboard for about 24 hours so all stored starch is used up.
One setup keeps the raw material present as a control, while the other setup removes it, so the two results can be compared.
To remove carbon dioxide from the air, a scientist puts soda lime or a sodium hydroxide solution inside the sealed jar with the plant.
source: standard CO2-absorption method in photosynthesis labs

en: To test water, two similar potted plants are used, one watered and one kept dry, while both get the same light.
source: standard controlled comparison for water as a reactant

en: A leaf partially covered with black paper tests light needs, because the covered and uncovered halves share the same leaf.
source: classic partial-cover experiment for light requirement

en: The leaf is first boiled in water to kill it and make its cells soft enough for the next steps.
The soft leaf is then boiled in alcohol over a water bath to remove the green chlorophyll that would hide the iodine color.
source: standard decolorization step in starch testing

en: After rinsing the pale leaf in water, iodine solution is dropped on it to reveal any starch that was made.
The result is recorded by drawing the leaf and coloring the blue-black patches that show where starch formed.
source: standard data recording for starch distribution

en: The whole setup is repeated with several leaves or plants so the finding is not due to chance.
A bar graph of the results shows the amount of starch for each condition, making the comparison easy to see.
source: standard graphing practice for experimental data

en: A testable hypothesis states that if carbon dioxide is missing, then the leaf will show no blue-black color with iodine.

topic: soil is not a raw material
en: The investigation compares plants with and without each suspected raw material, which can show that soil is not among them.
source: consensus: soil is not a photosynthesis reactant

topic: BTB to show carbon dioxide use
en: To verify carbon dioxide is used, a plant is sealed in a jar with BTB, and the liquid turning blue shows the gas was consumed.
source: BTB color change as CO2 uptake indicator

en: Limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide is present, so it can check that the jar truly has no carbon dioxide.
source: standard limewater test for carbon dioxide

en: The plant is left in the setup for several hours under bright light so photosynthesis has time to make starch.
Keeping both setups at the same temperature matters because heat changes how fast photosynthesis happens.
source: controlled variable: temperature in fair tests

en: If only the setup without carbon dioxide shows no starch, the result supports that carbon dioxide is a raw material.
To identify a compression, look for the crowded coils of a slinky, and to identify a rarefaction, look for the spread-out coils.
source: classroom observation of longitudinal wave parts

en: To find the crest of a transverse wave, look for the highest point above the rest line, and the trough is the lowest point.
source: classroom observation of transverse wave parts

en: To tell the wave types apart, watch the direction of vibration: transverse moves at a right angle, longitudinal moves along the wave path.
source: comparison of wave types by vibration direction

en: Sound travels through air as a longitudinal wave, with air molecules bunching together and spreading apart along the direction of travel.
Light is a transverse wave, so it can travel through empty space without needing air or any material to carry it.
To distinguish earthquake waves, read the seismograph: the first arrival is the longitudinal P-wave, and the later one is the transverse S-wave.
Frequency is the number of complete waves that pass a point in one second, and it is measured in units called hertz.
To calculate wave speed without timing a wave, multiply the measured wavelength by the frequency, and the product is the speed.
To compare the energy of two waves, measure their amplitudes and remember that doubling the amplitude gives about four times the energy.
source: wave energy proportional to amplitude squared

en: Sound waves need a medium such as air, water, or solid material to travel, so there is no sound in empty space.
To demonstrate reflection of a longitudinal wave, clap near a large wall and listen for the echo that returns.
To measure how mangroves reduce wave energy, compare wave height in front of and behind a mangrove stand.
source: coastal ecology; wave attenuation by mangroves

en: PAGASA uses floating buoys in the ocean to measure wave height, which tells how much energy the waves carry.
A struck tuning fork held near a light paper ball makes the ball sway, showing that sound waves carry energy through the air.
To measure frequency, count how many crests pass a marked point in ten seconds, then divide that number by ten to get hertz.
source: standard measurement procedure for wave frequency

en: A fair test of wave speed uses the same spring and tension, timing a gentle push and a hard push to see if the speed changes.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, others constant

en: A marker taped to a slinky coil moves sideways for a transverse wave and back-and-forth for a longitudinal wave, showing the difference in vibration direction.
To record a wave's shape, lay a long paper under the slinky and trace the outline of the coils as the wave passes.
source: classroom method for recording wave shape

en: To observe a longitudinal wave in daily life, listen to a jeepney horn and feel the sound energy reach your ear.
To correct the idea that sound pushes air forward, observe that a light paper strip near a speaker vibrates but does not fly away.
In a fair test, scientists change only one thing, like the gas tested, and keep all other conditions the same.
The independent variable in the limewater test is the gas bubbled in, such as breath or plain air.
The dependent variable is what scientists watch for, which is whether the clear limewater turns cloudy or stays clear.
To keep the test fair, scientists use the same amount of limewater and the same size of test tube for every trial.
First, pour clear limewater into a test tube, then bubble the gas through it using a clean straw or tube.
Use freshly prepared clear limewater because old limewater may already be cloudy from absorbing carbon dioxide in the air.
A good record writes down the starting color and the change, using clear words like 'clear' and 'milky white'.
If the limewater turns milky white, that result means carbon dioxide gas was present in the sample tested.
A precipitate is a solid that forms when two clear liquids are mixed and react to make a new substance.
To test for a precipitate, keep the same amount of silver nitrate solution and change only the liquid added to it.
To compare how much precipitate forms, let the mixture sit for the same time, then look at the solid at the bottom.
Waiting a few minutes lets the solid settle so scientists can see and measure the precipitate clearly.
The limewater test shows a gas by a color change, while the silver nitrate test shows a solid forming from two liquids.
Bubbling plain air into limewater does not make it cloudy because air has very little carbon dioxide, so the test is specific.
Scientists test water from rivers or ponds for chloride using silver nitrate, and a white precipitate shows the chloride is there.
Instead of numbers, scientists record qualitative data like 'turned cloudy' or 'white solid formed' in a table.
To make the investigation reliable, scientists repeat the test three times and check that the same change happens each time.
A fair test includes a control tube with plain water to show that the change only happens with the tested substance.
A new substance forms because the change is chemical, so the original materials cannot be easily separated back.
In a school lab, a class can use a straw to bubble breath into limewater and compare it with a tube of plain limewater.
To draw a circuit diagram, use straight lines for wires and standard symbols for each part, placing them neatly so another person can follow the path.
To assemble a series circuit, connect the battery, switch, resistor, and ammeter one after another so electric current has only one path to follow.
source: series circuit construction: single current path

en: To assemble a parallel circuit, connect each load across the same two points of the battery, so current splits into separate branches.
source: parallel circuit construction: multiple current paths

en: Before closing a switch, check that every screw terminal is tight and that no bare wire touches another, to avoid a short circuit.
To measure current in a series circuit, open the circuit at one point and insert the ammeter there, and the reading stays the same anywhere.
source: ammeter use: series connection, same current throughout

en: If the voltmeter reads zero across one load in a series circuit, that load is likely shorted or the circuit has a break.
source: circuit troubleshooting: zero voltage across load

en: In a series circuit, add the voltmeter readings across each load, and the total equals the battery's voltage.
source: Kirchhoff's voltage law for series circuits

en: In a parallel circuit, the voltmeter reads the same voltage across every branch, and that reading matches the battery's voltage.
source: parallel circuit property: equal voltage across branches

en: In a parallel circuit, add the ammeter readings from each branch, and the sum equals the current leaving the battery.
source: Kirchhoff's current law for parallel circuits

en: A switch appears in a diagram as a break in the wire with a small lever, and an open switch means no current flows through that line.
Label every component in a circuit diagram with its symbol and value, such as ohms for a resistor, so another person can read it.
When assembling a circuit, keep the switch open while connecting parts, and close it only after checking that every connection is correct.
source: safe assembly order: switch open until verified

en: Draw a circuit diagram with the battery on one side and arrange wires so they do not cross, because crossing lines confuse the reader.
To verify a series circuit works, close the switch and check that the ammeter shows a nonzero reading and the bulb lights up.
In a parallel circuit, unscrew one bulb and the others stay lit, which shows that each branch works independently of the others.
A resistor is drawn as a zigzag line or a small rectangle, and its resistance value is written beside it in ohms.
To compare series and parallel circuits fairly, use the same battery and the same bulbs, and change only how the bulbs are connected.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, rest constant

en: A short circuit occurs when a wire directly connects the two battery terminals, making the ammeter read very high and the wire heat up.
Electricians wire household outlets in parallel so each appliance gets the full voltage and turning off one switch does not shut off the others.
A dominant allele is a gene version that shows its trait even when a different version is paired with it, so only one copy is needed to see the trait.
A recessive allele only shows its trait when a person has two copies of it, so one copy stays hidden if the other allele is dominant.
A person is homozygous for a trait when both alleles are the same, such as having two dominant or two recessive versions of the gene.
A person is heterozygous when the two alleles for a trait are different, so the dominant one usually shows while the recessive one stays hidden.
Genotype is the pair of alleles a person carries, while phenotype is the visible result, like having free earlobes or attached earlobes.
A Punnett square is a simple grid that shows all the possible allele combinations a child could inherit from two parents.
When two parents both carry one recessive allele, about three out of four children will show the dominant trait and one will show the recessive trait.
Free earlobes are dominant over attached earlobes, so a child with one free-earlobe allele and one attached-earlobe allele will have free earlobes.
Being able to roll the tongue is a dominant trait, so a child who cannot roll the tongue must have two recessive alleles for that trait.
A widow's peak hairline is dominant over a straight hairline, so a child needs only one widow's-peak allele to show that pointed hairline.
A carrier is a person who has one recessive allele for a trait but does not show it, because the dominant allele covers its effect.
If both parents are carriers of a recessive trait, each of their children has about a one-in-four chance of showing that trait.
If both parents show a recessive trait, all their children will also show it, because each parent can only pass on the recessive allele.
If one parent has two dominant alleles for a trait, none of the children can show the recessive form, no matter what the other parent carries.
Each child's chance of inheriting a recessive trait is independent, so having one affected child does not change the odds for the next child.
A dominant trait is not necessarily more common in a population, because how often an allele appears depends on many other factors.
Brothers and sisters can inherit different allele combinations from the same parents, which is why siblings may not share the same visible traits.
A person showing a dominant trait could have two dominant alleles or one dominant and one recessive allele, so the same look can come from two genotypes.
Crossing two heterozygous parents gives about one child with two dominant alleles, two with one of each, and one with two recessive alleles.
A child who looks like one parent does not mean the other parent's alleles are absent, because every child gets one allele from each parent for every trait.
Displacement is a vector, meaning it includes both how far a point moved and the direction it moved, like '5 centimeters west'.
A GPS receiver measures the travel time of radio signals from at least four satellites to compute its exact position on Earth.
Modern GPS can measure a point's position to within a few millimeters, even though the satellites are about 20,000 kilometers above Earth.
Because GPS signals cannot pass through seawater, scientists use sound waves to measure the displacement of the seafloor.
During a large earthquake, a GPS station can record a sudden jump of tens of centimeters, showing the ground moved instantly.
The Philippine Sea Plate moves toward the islands at about 7 centimeters per year, a rate that GPS stations on Luzon help measure.
GNSS is the umbrella term for satellite navigation systems like GPS, GLONASS, and Galileo, which all help track plate motion.
GPS records a station's position in three directions: north, east, and up, so scientists see both horizontal and vertical displacement.
A population grows fastest when it is about halfway to its carrying capacity, then slows down as it gets closer to the limit.
source: logistic growth model: maximum growth rate at half carrying capacity

en: As a population grows, the most nutritious food is eaten first, leaving poorer food that gives less energy, so growth slows.
source: ecology: food quality as a limiting factor

en: As a population grows, its waste can make the water or soil more acidic, which harms the organisms and slows their growth.
source: ecology: waste accumulation and pH changes

en: As a population of birds grows, the supply of calcium for eggshells runs low, so fewer eggs hatch and growth slows.
As a population grows, animals fight more over food and space, and injuries from fights can kill or weaken them, slowing growth.
As a population grows, the young are born smaller and weaker because their mothers are underfed, so fewer survive to adulthood.
source: ecology: maternal condition and offspring survival

en: As a population grows, it uses resources faster than they can regrow, so the environment can support fewer individuals and growth slows.
source: ecology: resource renewal rate vs consumption

en: As a population of birds grows, the supply of twigs and leaves for nests runs out, so fewer chicks are raised and growth slows.
source: ecology: nesting material as a limiting factor

en: As a population grows, the death rate of adults from starvation rises, not just the young, so the whole population's growth slows.
As a population of grasshoppers grows, they eat the grass so quickly that it cannot regrow, so their food runs out and growth slows.
As a population grows, the density makes it easier for parasites to spread, weakening individuals and reducing reproduction, so growth slows.
Oceanic crust is only about 7 kilometers thick, while continental crust averages about 35 kilometers, so the difference is like a thin board versus a thick log.
Oceanic crust is about 10 percent denser than continental crust, which is why it sinks when the two types meet at a collision.
When two oceanic plates collide, the older and colder plate is denser, so it sinks beneath the younger, warmer plate.
Island arcs, built by volcanoes above subduction zones, can collide with a continent and weld onto it, adding new continental crust.
Continental crust floats on the mantle like an iceberg in water, with deep roots that balance the height of the mountains above.
The Moho is the sharp boundary where the crust ends and the denser mantle begins, lying deeper under continents than under oceans.
The ocean floor has stripes of normal and reversed magnetism that spread out evenly from mid-ocean ridges, recording seafloor spreading.
New oceanic crust is hot and sits high, but as it cools and moves away from the ridge, it becomes denser and sinks lower.
The Manila Trench west of Luzon is a subduction zone where the South China Sea floor sinks beneath the Philippine plate.
At a subduction zone, sediment scraped off the sinking plate piles up into a wedge-shaped mass that becomes part of the continental edge.
The east coast of the United States has oceanic and continental crust sitting side by side on the same plate, with no boundary between them.
Large earthquakes happen where oceanic plates sink, because the sinking plate sticks to the plate above it and then suddenly slips.
Continental crust is a patchwork of many rock types, from granite to marble, because it has been recycled and reworked for billions of years.
Because continental crust is lighter, it stands higher to form dry land, while heavy oceanic crust sits lower, holding the ocean basins.
When a continent riding on a sinking plate reaches the trench, it does not go under; it scrapes off and stays at the surface.
The islands of the Philippines are pieces of oceanic and continental crust that were welded together by plate collisions over millions of years.
The continental shelf, though underwater, is still continental crust, which is why it is shallow and full of life.
Mount Pinatubo in Luzon erupted because the South China Sea floor is sinking beneath the Philippine plate at the Manila Trench.
Oceanic lithosphere is thinner and bends more easily, which is why it can dive into the mantle at subduction zones.
A single lithospheric plate can carry both a continent and an ocean floor, so the shoreline is not a plate boundary.
source: plate tectonics: plate boundaries vs shorelines

en: Use a graduated cylinder to measure the exact volume of limewater or silver nitrate solution so every trial has the same amount.
source: lab technique: measuring liquids with a graduated cylinder

en: Bubble the gas slowly through the limewater so the gas has enough time to react instead of escaping too fast.
source: lab technique: bubbling gas slowly for complete reaction

en: Keep the temperature of all liquids the same because heat can change how fast the reaction happens or how much gas dissolves.
Hold the test tube against a dark background, like black paper, so the white precipitate is easier to see clearly.
source: lab observation technique: dark background for precipitate

en: Draw a bar graph comparing the height of the precipitate or the cloudiness level across different samples to show results.
source: data presentation: bar graph for comparison

en: Use a fresh, clean straw for each gas sample so the gases from previous trials do not mix into the new test.
source: lab hygiene: fresh straw per sample

en: Compare the cloudiness of the limewater to a standard scale or a plain water tube to judge how much carbon dioxide was present.
source: comparison method: standard scale for cloudiness

en: Wear safety goggles when handling silver nitrate solution because it can stain skin and clothes, so protection is important.
source: lab safety: goggles for silver nitrate

en: Scientists test water samples from Taal Lake for chloride by adding silver nitrate and looking for a white precipitate.
source: real-world application: Taal Lake water testing

en: PAGASA scientists bubble air samples through limewater to check for carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere over time.
Add the silver nitrate solution drop by drop with a dropper to watch the precipitate form slowly and clearly.
A common mistake is bubbling the gas too fast, which can make the limewater look cloudy from bubbles alone, so scientists bubble gently.
source: common misconception: fast bubbling causes false cloudiness

en: If the first trial gives a cloudy result, scientists repeat the test with a fresh sample to confirm it is not from a dirty tube.
Check the limewater against a white paper before starting to make sure it is clear and has not already turned cloudy.
To test an unknown gas, scientists bubble it and a known carbon dioxide sample into two separate tubes and compare the cloudiness.
source: comparison method: known vs unknown gas

en: The record for the silver nitrate test includes the volume of liquid added and the mass of the dried precipitate.
To measure the precipitate, scientists filter the mixture, dry the solid, and weigh it on a balance.
The silver nitrate solution is kept in a dark bottle because light can slowly change it, so scientists use it fresh from the bottle.
source: chemical storage: silver nitrate in dark bottle

en: The investigator writes a step-by-step plan that lists the materials and the order of steps, so the test can be repeated by anyone.
Each setup is labeled with its condition, such as 'no carbon dioxide' or 'no water,' to avoid confusing the results.
The same kind and size of leaf is used in every setup so that any starch difference comes only from the changed raw material.
All setups are placed in the same spot with equal light and temperature, so only the tested raw material differs.
A control setup that has all raw materials is included to show that the test can produce starch when nothing is missing.
The investigator uses a timer to give each setup exactly the same number of hours in the light.
The investigator records the room temperature with a thermometer at the start and end of the experiment.
The investigator measures the water given to the watered plant with a graduated cylinder to keep the amount exact.
The investigator seals the jar with plastic wrap to keep outside air from changing the carbon dioxide level.
The investigator checks that the soda lime is fresh by blowing through a straw into limewater to see if it still turns milky.
The investigator places the setups on the same shelf, away from direct sunlight, to avoid uneven heating.
The investigator cuts the leaf into equal-sized pieces after testing to compare the starch patches fairly.
The investigator uses a hand lens to look for tiny blue-black specks that show where starch is stored.
The investigator places the leaf on a white tile before adding iodine so the blue-black color is easier to see.
The investigator records the time when each setup is placed in the light and when it is taken out, to give equal light exposure.
The investigator repeats the whole investigation on different days to see if the same pattern appears each time.
The investigator draws a data table with columns for each setup and rows for the starch result.
The investigator compares the starch result of each setup to the control to decide which raw material is needed.
An alternative method uses an aquatic plant like Elodea to count oxygen bubbles, and the setup without carbon dioxide produces fewer bubbles.
The investigator uses a dropper to add iodine drop by drop to cover the leaf evenly without flooding it.
To draw a circuit diagram, place the battery symbol on one side, then add each component along the loop in the order it appears in the real circuit.
When assembling a circuit, use a battery holder and a switch so you can open the circuit quickly to change parts without disconnecting wires.
To measure the battery's voltage, touch the voltmeter's probes to the battery's positive and negative terminals while the circuit is closed.
A good record of a circuit experiment includes a labeled diagram, a table of meter readings, and a note about which bulbs were brighter.
To check for a broken wire, open the switch and use a continuity tester or a fresh bulb to see if the circuit is complete.
When drawing a circuit diagram, include a legend that explains each symbol, so a reader who does not know the symbols can still follow.
To measure the current in one branch of a parallel circuit, open that branch and insert the ammeter in series with that branch only.
When using a multimeter, set it to the ammeter function before connecting in series, and to the voltmeter function before connecting in parallel.
A circuit diagram should show the switch in the open or closed position used in the experiment, so the reader knows the state.
When assembling a circuit, connect the positive terminal of the battery to the switch first, then to the rest of the circuit.
To record the effect of adding bulbs, measure the current with one bulb, then add a second bulb in series and measure again.
A graph of current versus number of bulbs in series shows a downward curve, because each added bulb lowers the current.
source: standard interpretation of series circuit data

en: To test a switch, connect it in series with a bulb and battery; closing the switch should light the bulb and opening it should turn it off.
When drawing a parallel circuit, draw the battery on one side and each branch as a separate loop connected to the same two points.
A good circuit diagram uses a ruler for straight wires and keeps all symbols the same size, so it looks neat and clear.
To predict which circuit is brighter, compare the total resistance: series adds resistances, while parallel lowers total resistance.
To measure the voltage across one load, place the voltmeter's probes on the two terminals of that load while the circuit is closed.
When assembling a circuit on a board, push each wire into a separate hole and use jumpers to connect the parts in the right order.
In a circuit diagram, draw arrows on the wires to show the direction of current flow, from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.
source: standard circuit diagram current direction convention

en: To measure the total current in a parallel circuit, place the ammeter in the main line before the branches split.
source: standard ammeter placement for total current

en: A fair test of momentum keeps the same cart and the same ramp, and only changes the mass added to the cart.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, rest held constant

en: Measuring stopping distance means rolling the cart off the ramp onto a flat floor and using a meter stick from the ramp's foot to where the cart stops.
source: standard measurement practice in motion labs

en: Changing only the speed means releasing the cart from a higher point on the ramp, which makes it roll faster without changing its mass.
source: energy conversion: higher release gives more speed

en: A fair momentum test keeps the same floor surface and the same wheels on the cart, so friction stays equal for every trial.
Measuring how hard it is to stop a moving cart uses a spring scale attached to it, and the reading shows the force needed to hold it back.
source: spring scale measures force in newtons

en: Repeating each trial three times and averaging the stopping distances gives a more reliable result than a single measurement.
source: standard experimental practice: repeated trials improve reliability

en: A good data table lists the mass, the release height, and the stopping distance for each trial, with all numbers in the same units.

topic: graph of stopping distance vs mass
en: A graph of stopping distance against mass, at the same speed, shows a rising line: more mass means a longer stop.
Comparing momentum at the same speed uses an empty cart and a loaded cart rolled from the same ramp height, and both should reach the floor at the same time.
Adding identical weights, like coins or washers, to a cart changes its mass without changing its shape or how it rolls.
source: practical method for changing mass in a classroom

topic: timing the stop with a stopwatch
en: Measuring how long a cart takes to stop uses a stopwatch started when the cart leaves the ramp and stopped when it comes to rest.
source: standard timing method in motion experiments

en: The floor must be level and clear, because a tilted or cluttered floor changes how far the cart rolls and ruins the comparison.
source: fair-test design: keep path conditions constant

en: A control trial with the empty cart gives a baseline stopping distance to compare against every loaded trial.
Before rolling, each cart is weighed with a balance or scale so its mass is known and can be written in the data table.
If a loaded cart stops farther than an empty one from the same height, the result means the heavier cart had more momentum.
source: momentum relationship: more mass means more momentum at same speed

en: A photo gate at the bottom of the ramp measures the cart's speed by timing how long it blocks a light beam.
source: photo gate timing principle in school labs

en: Releasing the cart from the exact same mark on the ramp each time keeps the starting speed the same across repeated trials.
source: fair-test design: hold initial conditions constant

en: Writing down what happens, like how far the cart rolled and whether it wobbled, helps spot mistakes in the method later.
Placing a light block at the end of the track and measuring how far it slides shows how much momentum the cart carried.
source: indirect measurement of momentum through impact

en: Rolling the same cart from a low and a high ramp point lets you compare momentum at two speeds while mass stays the same.
source: controlled comparison: hold mass constant, vary speed

en: A gene is a section of DNA that holds the instruction for a trait, and alleles are the different forms that gene can take.
In a pedigree chart, a square stands for a male and a circle stands for a female in the family.
In a pedigree chart, a shaded shape means the person shows the trait, while a half-shaded shape means the person is a carrier.
In a pedigree chart, a horizontal line connects parents, and a vertical line connects parents to their children.
In a pedigree chart, generations are labeled with Roman numerals, like I for grandparents and II for parents.
A dominant trait usually appears in every generation of a family, so an affected child almost always has an affected parent.
In a pedigree, a recessive trait often appears in children whose parents are both carriers, even though the parents do not show it.
If a child shows a recessive trait, both parents must carry at least one recessive allele, even if they look normal.
If a child shows a dominant trait, at least one parent must also show the trait, because the dominant allele has to come from somewhere.
Freckles are a dominant trait, so a child with one freckle allele from a parent will have freckles.
Dimples are a dominant trait, so a child with one dimple allele will have dimples even if the other allele is for no dimples.
A cleft chin is dominant over a smooth chin, so a child needs only one cleft-chin allele to have that chin shape.
A hitchhiker's thumb is a recessive trait, so a child must have two copies of the allele to have that bendy thumb.
If one parent is a carrier and the other has two dominant alleles, about half of their children will be carriers.
If both parents are carriers, about half of their children will be carriers, one quarter will show the trait, and one quarter will have no recessive allele.
If one parent has two dominant alleles and the other has two recessive alleles, all their children will be carriers.
If one parent has two recessive alleles and the other is a carrier, about half of their children will show the recessive trait and half will be carriers.
A pedigree chart helps predict the chance that a future child in the family will show a trait.
In a pedigree, if two unaffected parents have an affected child, the trait must be recessive.
