In a pedigree, if an affected parent has an unaffected child, the trait could be dominant or recessive, so you need more generations to tell.
Recording a slinky wave with a phone camera in slow motion lets you see the compressions and rarefactions move slowly enough to count and measure.
source: classroom observation method using video playback

en: A line of people standing and squatting one after another makes a transverse wave, because each person moves up and down while the wave travels along the line.
source: classroom modeling of transverse wave motion

en: A line of people passing a gentle shove from one to the next models a longitudinal wave, because each person leans forward and back while the shove travels along the line.
source: classroom modeling of longitudinal wave motion

en: The period of a wave is measured by timing ten complete waves passing a marked point with a stopwatch, then dividing the time by ten.
source: standard method for measuring wave period

en: A fair test of stretch length keeps the same spring and push strength, and changes only how far the spring is stretched.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, the rest held constant

en: A fair test of whether frequency changes wave speed keeps the same spring and stretch, and compares a slow wiggle with a fast wiggle.
source: fair-test design comparing slow and fast oscillations

en: Wave energy in a water tray is compared by keeping the same tray and water depth and measuring how high the wave splashes at the far end.
source: classroom fair-test method for comparing wave energy

en: A line of touching marbles shows energy transfer: when one marble strikes the end, the last marble rolls away while the middle marbles stay in place.
source: Newton's cradle principle simplified for classroom model

en: Using a dark background and a light-colored slinky makes the compressions and rarefactions easy to see and count during a wave demonstration.
source: classroom observation technique for wave demonstrations

en: A fair test of water depth in a ripple tank keeps the same wave maker and changes only the water depth.
source: fair-test design in ripple tank experiments

en: Comparing how much energy each wave type carries uses the same spring and push strength, and measures how far a paper cup at the far end slides.
source: fair-test method comparing longitudinal and transverse wave energy

en: An investigation is valid when the result truly answers the question asked, with no hidden factor causing the change.
source: validity in experimental design: measuring what is claimed

en: An investigation is reliable when repeating the exact same steps gives the same result every time, so the finding can be trusted.
source: reliability in experimental design: repeatability of results

en: The white solid that makes limewater milky is calcium carbonate, the same mineral found in chalk, coral, and some rocks.
source: encyclopedia-stable; calcium carbonate = CaCO3, chalk and coral composition

en: Limewater is a clear solution of calcium hydroxide in water, and it stays clear until carbon dioxide gas reacts with it.
source: encyclopedia-stable; limewater = dilute calcium hydroxide solution

en: A new substance is forming when the color changes, a solid appears, bubbles rise, or heat is given off without being added.
Melting ice is a physical change because the water can freeze again, but turning limewater cloudy is chemical because the white solid is a new substance.
source: encyclopedia-stable; physical vs chemical change distinction

en: The more carbon dioxide gas bubbled into limewater, the milkier it becomes, so cloudiness can show how much gas is present.
source: quantitative relationship: CO2 concentration vs turbidity of limewater

en: The white precipitate from silver nitrate and chloride is silver chloride, a compound that does not dissolve in water.
source: encyclopedia-stable; AgCl is insoluble in water

en: Coral reefs and seashells are made of calcium carbonate, the same substance that forms when carbon dioxide meets limewater.
source: encyclopedia-stable; marine organisms secrete calcium carbonate

en: Label each test tube with the sample name before testing so the results from different gases or liquids are not mixed up.
source: good laboratory practice: labeling samples before testing

en: Scientists write down what they observe, like 'milky white', and then infer that carbon dioxide was present in the gas.
source: observation vs inference in scientific method

en: Wash the test tubes with clean water between trials so leftover chemicals from one sample do not change the next result.
source: good laboratory practice: cleaning apparatus between trials

en: The time it takes for limewater to turn cloudy can be measured with a stopwatch to compare how fast different gases react.
source: reaction rate observation: time to turbidity as a comparison

en: The investigator uses a ruler to set the lamp at the same distance from every setup, so each plant gets the same amount of light.
source: fair-test design: controlled variables held constant

en: The setup without carbon dioxide is sealed with a rubber stopper, while the setup with carbon dioxide is left open to the room air.
source: method for isolating carbon dioxide variable

en: The investigator uses forceps to move the hot leaf from boiling water to alcohol, so the leaf is not touched by bare hands.
source: lab safety practice for handling hot materials

en: The investigator draws the leaf outline on white paper with a pencil before adding iodine, because pencil marks do not wash away in the liquids.
source: standard record-keeping in leaf starch tests

en: The investigator rates the blue-black color of each leaf from zero to three, where zero means no starch and three means very dark.
source: qualitative scale for starch color intensity

en: The leaf is cut into small squares before boiling in alcohol, which lets the green chlorophyll come out faster and shortens the waiting time.
source: technique to speed up chlorophyll extraction

en: The investigator chooses a healthy, bright green leaf for the test, because a yellow or damaged leaf already has little starch or chlorophyll.
source: plant selection criteria for photosynthesis experiments

en: The investigator places the setups under a steady fluorescent lamp and away from the window, so the light does not change with passing clouds.
source: control of environmental light in experiments

en: The investigator writes a conclusion that states whether the evidence supports the hypothesis, based on which setups turned blue-black.
If both the control setup and the setup missing a raw material still make starch, the investigator concludes that the missing material is not actually needed.
The investigator checks that the control setup makes starch at the end, because a control that fails means the whole test did not work properly.
source: validation of control setup in experiments

en: A ticker tape timer makes dots on a paper tape as the cart moves, and the spacing of dots shows how speed changes during stopping.
source: standard physics lab technique for recording motion

en: A motion sensor sends out sound or light pulses and records the cart's position each moment, giving a graph of speed against time.
source: common classroom motion sensor (e.g., ultrasonic) for kinematics

en: Recording the cart's motion with a video camera and playing it frame by frame lets you measure its speed and stopping distance accurately.
source: video analysis technique used in school physics labs

en: Setting the ramp to the same angle with a protractor keeps the starting speed the same for every trial.
source: fair-test design: controlling ramp angle as a constant

en: Checking the floor with a bubble level makes sure it is flat, so the cart rolls the same way each time.
source: standard practice for leveling surfaces in experiments

en: Measuring the release height with a ruler lets you set the same speed for repeated trials.
source: controlling initial height to keep speed constant

en: A stop block at the end of the track stops the cart, and measuring how far the block slides shows the momentum transferred.
source: method for observing momentum transfer via a movable block

en: A force sensor attached to the cart records the force during stopping, and the peak reading shows the maximum force needed.
source: standard force sensor use in dynamics experiments

en: A graph of force against time during stopping shows a curve, and the area under it equals the change in momentum.
source: impulse-momentum theorem: area under F-t graph equals Δp

en: A hanging ball hit by the cart swings up, and the height it rises shows how much momentum the cart carried.
source: ballistic pendulum-style method for measuring momentum

en: Rolling the cart into a sand-filled box makes a dent, and the depth of the dent shows how much momentum the cart had.
source: impact depth method used in simple collision experiments

en: Measuring the depth of the dent with a ruler gives a number that compares momentum across trials.
source: quantifying impact depth for comparison in experiments

en: Timing how long the cart takes to roll down the ramp with a stopwatch gives its speed at the bottom.
source: timing method to estimate speed from ramp descent

en: A data logger connected to sensors records time, speed, and force automatically, making the measurements more accurate.
source: automated data collection in school physics labs

en: A meter stick measures the vertical height of the ramp, which sets the cart's speed at the bottom.
source: measuring ramp height to control gravitational potential energy

en: A level track with a slight incline slows the cart down gradually, letting you measure stopping distance easily.
source: using controlled incline to study deceleration and stopping

en: A video analysis app tracks the cart's position in each frame and calculates its speed and momentum automatically.
source: modern smartphone video tracking for physics experiments

en: A moving cart collides with a stationary cart of the same mass, and the distance the second cart moves shows the momentum transferred.
source: momentum transfer observation using equal-mass carts

en: Using a spring scale to pull a loaded cart up a ramp shows the force needed to overcome gravity and friction, which relates to momentum.
source: measuring force components to understand momentum effects

en: A spring-loaded launcher gives the cart a known starting speed, so you can compare momentum without changing the ramp.
source: using a launcher to standardize initial velocity in experiments

en: When drawing a circuit diagram, place the ammeter symbol in the main loop and the voltmeter symbol across a load, so the diagram shows their real connections.
To check if a wire is broken, set a multimeter to its ohmmeter function and touch the probes to the wire's ends; a zero reading means the wire is continuous.
To keep the voltage constant while testing different resistors, use a battery eliminator instead of a battery, because batteries weaken as they drain.
To compare the brightness of bulbs in series and parallel, record each bulb as bright, dim, or off in a table, because brightness is a qualitative measure.
To control only one branch of a parallel circuit, place a switch in that branch, so opening that switch stops only that branch's current.
To check if a switch is working, measure the voltage across it: an open switch should read the battery's voltage, while a closed switch should read zero.
To assemble a circuit with both an ammeter and a voltmeter, connect the ammeter in series with the load first, then connect the voltmeter across the load without breaking the loop.
To test if a bulb is blown without a battery, set a multimeter to ohmmeter and touch the bulb's base; a very high reading means the filament is broken.
To count the paths in a circuit diagram, trace from the battery's positive terminal to its negative terminal, and each separate route is one branch.
To read an analog ammeter, look straight at the needle from above to avoid a parallax error, then read the scale line it points to.
To protect a circuit from too much current, connect a fuse in series with the battery, so the fuse blows and breaks the loop if current gets too high.
To record circuit data, make a table with one column for circuit type, one for current, and one for voltage, so you can compare series and parallel.
The law of conservation of mass says the total mass of substances before a reaction equals the total mass after, so nothing is lost or gained.
Balancing an equation applies the conservation of mass, since the total mass of reactants must equal the total mass of products.
In a balanced equation, a coefficient like the 2 in 2H2O multiplies every atom in that formula, so 2H2O means 4 hydrogen and 2 oxygen atoms.
When balancing, you may change coefficients but never subscripts, because changing a subscript like H2O to H2O2 makes a different substance.
The balanced equation for water is 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, showing 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms on each side.
Burning methane balances as CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O, with 1 carbon, 4 hydrogen, and 4 oxygen atoms on both sides.
Lavoisier heated tin in a sealed glass vessel and found the total mass stayed the same, proving matter is conserved in reactions.
Burning sugar seems to make it vanish, but it actually becomes carbon dioxide and water vapor, so the total mass is conserved.
Balancing an equation is like following a recipe: you need the same number of each ingredient on both sides, or the reaction won't match reality.
In a closed container, the total mass before and after a reaction is exactly the same, even if a gas forms or bubbles appear.
source: conservation of mass in closed systems

en: When iron rusts, it gains mass because it combines with oxygen from the air, but the total mass of iron plus oxygen equals the rust.
Burning fuel in a jeepney engine follows conservation of mass: the fuel and oxygen together weigh the same as the exhaust gases and water produced.
The coefficients in a balanced equation give the ratio of molecules that react, like 2 hydrogen molecules for every 1 oxygen molecule in water.
An unbalanced equation cannot be true because it shows atoms appearing or vanishing, which would break the conservation of mass.
The arrow in a chemical equation means 'produces' or 'yields', separating the starting reactants on the left from the products on the right.
To check if an equation is balanced, count each element's atoms by multiplying the coefficient by the subscript in each formula.
Conservation of mass holds for every chemical reaction, from burning wood to digesting food, so no reaction ever loses mass.
A balanced equation lets you predict how much product a certain amount of reactant will produce.
Heating calcium carbonate decomposes it as CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, and the mass of the two products equals the original mass.
Subscripts in a formula show how many atoms are in one molecule, like the 2 in CO2 meaning two oxygen atoms bonded to one carbon.
Scientists use a capital letter for a dominant allele and a lowercase letter for a recessive allele, like D and d.
In pea plants, purple flowers are dominant over white flowers, so a plant with one purple allele and one white allele will have purple flowers.
In simple dominant-recessive inheritance, traits do not blend; a child shows either the dominant form or the recessive form, never a mix of both.
A Punnett square shows the possible chances for one set of parents, while a pedigree chart shows the actual traits that appeared across many generations.
Alleles are located on chromosomes, which come in pairs, and each parent passes one chromosome from each pair to a child.
Farmers and plant breeders use knowledge of dominant and recessive traits to predict which offspring will show a desired feature, like a certain fruit color.
A trait that shows up in every generation and appears equally in boys and girls is most likely a dominant trait.
In a pedigree, siblings are placed in a row and connected by a horizontal line above them.
A pedigree chart is built from the top down, with the oldest generation at the top and children placed below their parents.
In cats, short hair is dominant over long hair, so a kitten with one short-hair allele will have short hair.
A parent who shows a dominant trait can still pass a recessive allele to a child, so the child might not show the trait at all.
The carabao, or kalabaw, is a Philippine animal that lives on land, so it is called a terrestrial animal.
Bangus, also called milkfish, lives in rivers and fishponds, so it is an aquatic animal that stays in water.
The Philippine eagle flies high in the sky and nests on tall trees, so it is an aerial animal.
Rice plants, called palay, grow on land in fields and paddies, so they are terrestrial plants.
Bakawan, or mangroves, grow in salty water along the coast, so they are aquatic plants.
Water lilies float on ponds and lakes, so they are aquatic plants that live in water.
Frogs can live on land and in water, so they are not purely terrestrial or aquatic but amphibious.
Bats fly in the air at night, so they are aerial animals even though they are mammals.
Chickens, or manok, are birds that stay mostly on the ground, so they are terrestrial animals.
source: DepEd MATATAG science; common Philippine animals

en: Corals are animals that live attached to the ocean floor, so they are aquatic animals.
Grasslands are a type of terrestrial habitat where animals like horses and cows graze on grass.
Rivers and lakes are freshwater aquatic habitats, while oceans are saltwater aquatic habitats for many animals.
Orchids that grow on tree branches high above the ground are aerial plants because they live in the air.
Crabs live in water or near the shore, so they are aquatic animals that need moisture.
Snakes live on land and some climb trees, so they are terrestrial animals that do not live in water.
The tarsier is a small Philippine animal that lives in trees on land, so it is a terrestrial animal.
Butterflies fly from flower to flower in the air, so they are aerial animals that move through the sky.
Fish have gills to breathe underwater, which is why they are aquatic animals that live in water.
A desert is a dry terrestrial habitat where only some plants and animals can survive without much water.
A habitat is the natural home of a plant or animal, and it provides food, water, and shelter.
The flat surface along which two rock blocks slide is called the fault plane, and the focus is just one point on that plane.
A subduction zone is where one tectonic plate dives beneath another, and the big quakes there can push the seafloor and create tsunamis.
After a big offshore earthquake, a tsunami can reach the nearest coast within minutes, so coastal people have very little time to move to higher ground.
A tsunami can form when the seafloor moves up or down by about a meter, and that shift pushes the whole water column above it.
The Philippine Trench is a deep underwater crack east of the country where one plate dives under another, and it can cause very large earthquakes.
The elastic rebound theory says rocks bend and store energy for years, then suddenly snap back and release that energy as an earthquake.
Aftershocks are smaller earthquakes that follow the main quake, and they happen because the rocks around the fault are still adjusting.
Foreshocks are small earthquakes that sometimes happen before a big one, but they are not a reliable way to predict the main quake.
Scientists use pressure sensors on the ocean floor to detect a tsunami passing overhead before it reaches the shore.
Surface waves travel along the ground and arrive after P and S waves, and they cause most of the shaking damage.
An intensity map uses colors to show how strongly different places felt an earthquake, with the strongest colors near the epicenter.
A life cycle is the order of stages an animal passes through from its birth until it can produce young of its own.
Metamorphosis is a big body change, like a caterpillar turning into a butterfly, that happens in some animals but not in chickens or humans.
A butterfly's life cycle has four stages: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, and adult butterfly, each looking completely different from the last.
A frog's life cycle starts with eggs in water, then tadpoles that breathe with gills, then froglets with legs, and finally adult frogs that breathe air.
A chicken starts as an egg, then a chick inside, then hatches, and grows into an adult hen or rooster without changing body shape.
Unlike caterpillars and tadpoles, human babies look like small adults from birth, just needing to grow bigger.
Both butterflies and frogs go through metamorphosis, but butterflies have a resting pupa stage while frogs have a swimming tadpole stage.
Chickens and humans have similar life cycles because both grow gradually and do not have a metamorphosis stage.
A flow chart of a life cycle uses arrows to show the correct order of stages, like egg to caterpillar to chrysalis to butterfly.
In a butterfly's life cycle, the caterpillar eats a lot and grows, then forms a chrysalis where it changes into an adult.
Frog eggs are laid in water and look like clear jelly balls, while chicken eggs have a hard shell and can develop on land.
A chicken egg needs about 21 days of incubation before the chick hatches, a number you can picture on a calendar.
A butterfly's adult stage is short, often just a few weeks, but it is the stage that lays eggs to start the cycle again.
A frog's tadpole stage lives only in water, but the adult frog can live on land, showing a change in habitat during its life cycle.
A common mistake is thinking a caterpillar is a baby butterfly, but actually the butterfly hatches from an egg as a caterpillar first.
In a flow chart, comparing life cycles side by side helps you see that butterflies and frogs have more stages than chickens and humans.
The purpose of a life cycle is to keep the species alive by producing new young, and each stage has a role in that process.
A human baby is born after about nine months inside its mother, and then grows slowly for many years before it can have its own baby.
Butterflies change what they eat as they grow: caterpillars chew leaves, but adults sip nectar from flowers.
In the Philippines, you can see frogs in rice paddies and chickens in backyards, and their life cycles happen right around us.
A habitat is the natural home of a plant or animal, and it supplies everything the living thing needs like food, water, and shelter.
Plants and animals live in a habitat that matches their needs, so a fish lives in water while a bird lives where it can fly and nest.
A garden habitat can grow food plants like okra, eggplant, and pechay, which attract small animals like butterflies and earthworms.
source: encyclopedia-stable; common garden plants and animals

en: In a garden, common animal visitors include bees that pollinate flowers and spiders that catch tiny insects for food.
The rice field is a wet habitat where palay, or rice plants, grow in standing water during the planting season.
Besides frogs, rice fields also shelter golden apple snails and small fish that swim in the shallow water between the rice rows.
Egrets and herons are birds that visit rice fields to eat snails, insects, and small fish found in the muddy water.
The seashore habitat has salty water and sandy soil, so only tough plants like sea grasses and some shrubs can grow there.
On the seashore, hermit crabs and sand crabs dig into the wet sand to hide from the sun and from birds.
Empty seashells on the beach are the old homes of sea animals like clams and snails that once lived in the water.
Mangrove trees, called bakawan in Filipino, have special roots that stand above the water and help them breathe in muddy soil.
Mudskippers are fish that can walk and jump on mud, and they are often seen in the roots of mangrove swamps.
A garden and a rice field have fresh water, while a seashore and a mangrove swamp have salty water that mixes with the tide.
Habitats can be on land like a garden, or in water like a seashore, and each one has its own set of living things.
A habitat is more than just a location; it is the whole environment that gives a plant or animal its food, water, and protection.
To list animals and plants in a habitat, scientists first observe the place and then write down every living thing they can find.
Animals choose a habitat where they can find food and build a safe place, so a crab stays near the sea and a worm stays in the soil.
The rice terraces in the Philippines are habitats where farmers grow palay and where fish and snails live in the water.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Philippine rice terraces as habitat

en: In Philippine coastal towns, the seashore habitat provides food and work for people who catch fish and gather shells.
When making a table, you can group animals and plants by their habitat, like putting all seashore animals in one column.
A fair test changes only one thing at a time, while all other conditions stay the same, so the result shows what caused the change.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, the rest held constant

en: To test whether air has mass, compare the balance reading of an empty sealed bag with the same bag filled with air.
source: simple mass comparison for gases; balance use

en: To measure the mass of a liquid, weigh the empty container first, then weigh the filled container, and subtract the first reading.
A thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius, the same unit used for weather reports in the Philippines.
source: thermometer units; Celsius in Philippine weather reporting

en: A comparison setup where nothing is changed is called a control, and it helps show whether the changed setup really differs.
Scientists record each measurement in a table with one column for what they changed and one column for what they measured.
source: data recording practice in school science

en: Taking the same measurement three times and averaging the readings makes the result more trustworthy.
Mass is measured in grams or kilograms, and temperature in degrees Celsius, so every measurement has a clear unit.
source: standard units for mass and temperature

en: Using the same balance for every weighing keeps the comparison fair because different scales can disagree slightly.
source: fair-test design: same instrument for all trials

en: When weighing a gas, the container's mass is part of the reading, so always use the same container for both weighings.
source: mass measurement includes container for gases

en: The thing you change on purpose is the changed variable, and the thing you measure is the result you watch.
If a two-pan balance tips down on one side, that side holds more mass than the other side.
Placing a cup of water on a balance shows the water has mass because the scale gives a number above zero.
A line graph of how mass changes with added water shows a pattern that is easier to read than a list of numbers.
Before measuring, scientists write down what they expect to happen, then compare it with the actual result.
source: prediction and comparison in scientific method

en: Drying and cleaning the container before weighing prevents leftover water or dirt from adding extra mass.
A balance must read zero when empty before you start, and if it does not, you adjust it first.
The unit gram is about the mass of one small paper clip, so a kilogram is one thousand grams.
When the investigation is done, scientists write a short conclusion that says whether the evidence supports the prediction.
source: conclusion from evidence in scientific method

en: A thermometer should hang in the middle of the liquid, away from the sides and bottom, to read the true temperature.
In a garden, caterpillars eat the leaves of plants, and birds eat the caterpillars, showing how food moves through a habitat.
Rice fields are shallow and open, which lets wading birds like egrets and herons spot and catch small animals in the water.
When the tide goes out, water stays in hollows of rocks, and these tide pools shelter small crabs, snails, and tiny fish.
Mangrove swamps act as nurseries for young fish and shrimp, giving them hiding places among the roots until they grow bigger.
A garden is a dry land habitat, while a rice field is a wet one, so they host very different plants and animals.
Sea grasses have strong roots that hold them in sandy soil, even when waves and tides push against them.
Earthworms in a garden eat dead leaves and make tunnels in the soil, which helps air and water reach plant roots.
Dragonflies are common around rice fields because they eat mosquitoes and other small insects that live near the water.
Mud crabs live in mangrove swamps, where they hide in the mud and among roots during low tide to stay safe from predators.
Sandpipers are shorebirds that run along the beach and poke their beaks into the sand to find worms and small crabs.
A garden with flowering plants attracts butterflies, which lay eggs on leaves, and the eggs hatch into caterpillars that eat those leaves.
Besides palay, rice fields have other plants like water lilies and grasses that grow in the shallow water and provide shelter for small animals.
The tangled roots of mangrove trees make a maze where small fish can escape from bigger fish that hunt in open water.
source: encyclopedia-stable; mangrove root structure and fish shelter

en: Clams and oysters that live on the seashore have hard shells that protect their soft bodies from waves and from animals that eat them.
Fruit trees in a garden, like mango and papaya, give food to bats, birds, and insects that help spread their seeds.
Farmers sometimes let fish like tilapia swim in their rice fields, where the fish eat insects and weeds without harming the rice.
Herons and kingfishers build their nests in mangrove trees, where the branches over the water keep their eggs safe from land predators.
Ghost crabs on the seashore dig deep burrows in the sand, and they stay inside during the hottest part of the day.
Plants in each habitat have different needs, so sea grasses need salt water while garden plants like pechay need fresh water and rich soil.
To make a list of living things in a habitat, scientists watch quietly, record what they see, and use pictures to identify unknown plants or animals.
A chemical equation is like a recipe that tells scientists which ingredients react and what new substances they make.
When scientists describe a reaction, they often start by writing the names of the substances in words before switching to chemical symbols.
source: chemistry convention: word equation precedes formula equation

en: The arrow in a chemical equation points from the starting substances to the new substances, showing the direction the reaction goes.
The plus sign in an equation means 'and' for listing multiple reactants or products, not a math addition sign.
Scientists add small letters in parentheses like (g) for gas or (aq) for dissolved in water to show each substance's physical state.
Balancing a chemical equation is a bookkeeping step where scientists add numbers in front of formulas so atoms match on both sides.
source: law of conservation of mass; balancing method

en: Writing a word equation first helps scientists check that they have the right substances before they worry about formulas and numbers.
Scientists group reactions into types like combination, decomposition, and combustion, and the equation pattern helps them identify the type.
If a reaction needs a catalyst to speed it up, scientists write the catalyst's name above the arrow instead of counting it as a reactant.
source: chemistry convention for catalysts in equations

en: To verify a formula equation, scientists count the atoms of each element on the left and right, and the counts must be equal.
source: law of conservation of mass; verification method

en: For methane burning, scientists write methane plus oxygen yields carbon dioxide plus water, then balance it to CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O.
To describe rusting, scientists write iron plus oxygen yields iron oxide, and they can show the same reaction using chemical formulas.
source: common oxidation reaction; word and formula forms

en: For photosynthesis, scientists write carbon dioxide and water plus sunlight yield glucose and oxygen, then translate each name into its formula.
To show neutralization, scientists write acid plus base yields salt plus water, then replace the acid and base names with their formulas.
The total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products, so scientists balance equations to obey this conservation law.
In a formula, a subscript number belongs to one molecule, but a coefficient number in front multiplies the whole molecule.
The arrow in an equation means the reactants change into products, not that they are equal or that a physical mixture is formed.
A classroom example is vinegar and baking soda yields carbon dioxide, water, and a salt, written first in words then in formulas.
source: common classroom reaction; word and formula forms

en: When a reaction needs heating, scientists write a small triangle above the arrow to show that heat was supplied to make it happen.
source: chemistry notation for heat in reactions

en: Before balancing, scientists must write each formula correctly using the right symbols and subscripts, because a wrong formula changes the whole equation.
Multiplying the cart's mass, read from a balance, by its speed at the ramp's bottom gives its momentum in kilogram-meters per second.
source: momentum = mass × velocity; standard measurement procedure

en: A foam pad placed in front of the cart lengthens the stopping time, and a force sensor shows that the longer stop needs a smaller force.
source: impulse-momentum theorem: force × time = change in momentum

en: An air track blows a thin cushion of air under the glider, removing almost all friction so the momentum change comes only from the collision.
source: air track apparatus standard in physics laboratory

en: Rolling a light cart into a stationary heavy cart shows the light one slowing sharply and the heavy one moving forward slowly, meaning momentum was shared.
A rolling cart and a sliding block with the same mass and speed have the same momentum, but the block stops sooner because sliding friction is stronger than rolling friction.
source: rolling friction is less than sliding friction for the same materials

en: Multiplying the average force recorded during stopping by the stopping time gives the impulse, which equals the change in momentum.
A dynamics cart with low-friction wheels rolls almost freely, so its stopping distance mainly shows its momentum rather than wheel friction.
source: dynamics cart design for low-friction motion

en: Two photo gates placed along the track measure the cart's speed at different positions, showing how speed changes as the cart slows down.
source: photo gate timing method for measuring speed

en: The law of conservation of mass is also called the law of conservation of matter, because matter is never created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.
In a chemical reaction, atoms only rearrange their bonds, so the same atoms are present before and after the change.
The number of molecules can change in a reaction, but the total number of atoms of each element stays exactly the same.
source: law of conservation of mass; atomic theory

en: Coefficients in a balanced equation tell the number of molecules or moles, not the mass in grams, of each substance.
A balanced equation uses the smallest whole-number ratio of coefficients, so you divide all numbers by their greatest common factor.
To balance an equation, start with the element that appears in only one reactant and one product, like carbon in methane.
State symbols like (s), (l), (g), (aq) are not part of balancing; they only tell the physical state of each substance.
The balanced equation for photosynthesis is 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, showing 6 carbon atoms on each side.
The balanced equation for cellular respiration is C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O, the reverse of photosynthesis.
Burning propane gas balances as C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O, with 3 carbon atoms on both sides.
The law of conservation of mass works for chemical reactions, but in nuclear reactions, mass can turn into energy.
A balanced equation does not tell you how fast a reaction happens or how much energy it releases or absorbs.

topic: balanced equation doesn't tell if reaction happens
en: A balanced equation does not tell you whether a reaction will actually happen; it only shows the correct atom counts.
The balanced equation for making ammonia is N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, showing 2 nitrogen and 6 hydrogen atoms on each side.
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes as 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2, so 4 hydrogen and 4 oxygen atoms are on both sides.
In a chemical equation, the plus sign means 'and' between reactants or products, while the arrow means 'produces'.
You can use fractional coefficients while balancing, then multiply all coefficients by the same number to get whole numbers.
In a reaction, total mass stays the same, but the volume can change if gases form, expand, or get used up.
source: physical properties vs conservation of mass

en: Sodium reacts with water as 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2, showing 2 sodium atoms on each side.
Ethanol burns as C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O, with 2 carbon atoms on both sides of the equation.
To classify an animal, look at where it usually lives, feeds, and rests, not just a single moment.
The tamaraw, a wild buffalo, lives only on Mindoro's grasslands, so it is a terrestrial animal.
The dugong, a sea cow, grazes on seagrass in shallow coastal waters, so it is an aquatic animal.
The Philippine crocodile lives in freshwater rivers and lakes, so it is an aquatic animal.
The coconut crab climbs trees on land and breathes air, so it is a terrestrial animal, not aquatic.
The Philippine flying lemur glides from tree to tree but does not flap wings, so it is not an aerial animal.
Aerial animals have wings or special body parts that let them stay in the air, like birds, bats, and insects.
The Philippine swiftlet builds its nest on cave walls and catches insects while flying, so it is an aerial animal.
Seaweed grows attached to rocks underwater, so it is an aquatic plant that does not need soil.
The nipa palm grows in swampy water along coasts, so it is an aquatic plant.
Terrestrial plants get water from the soil through their roots, while aquatic plants get water from the water around them.
The water hyacinth floats on rivers and ponds, so it is an aquatic plant that drifts with the current.
The Philippine mouse-deer, or pilandok, lives on the forest floor, so it is a terrestrial animal.
The whale shark is a fish that lives in the open ocean, so it is an aquatic animal.
The Philippine duck lives near lakes and feeds in water, so it is an aquatic bird.
The coconut palm grows on sandy soil near the beach, so it is a terrestrial plant, not aquatic.
The monitor lizard, or bayawak, can swim and climb, but it lives on land, so it is a terrestrial animal.
To classify a plant, ask if its roots are in soil, water, or air, because that tells you its habitat.
source: classification rule: plant habitat based on root location

en: A diagram that shows a carabao on land and a bangus in water makes it easy to see their different habitats.
The Philippine hornbill, or kalaw, is a bird that flies through the forest canopy, so it is an aerial animal.
An active volcano is one that has erupted in recorded history or is showing signs that it might erupt soon.
PHIVOLCS uses seismographs, gas sensors, and satellite images to watch volcanoes and warn communities before an eruption.
You can find the nearest volcano by checking PHIVOLCS maps or asking your local government, which keeps records of nearby hazards.
source: PHIVOLCS maps and local government records

en: Volcano hazard maps show areas that could be hit by ashfall, lava, or lahar, helping families know if their home is at risk.
Lahar is a fast-moving mudflow of volcanic ash, rock, and water that can rush down river valleys long after an eruption ends.
A pyroclastic flow is a cloud of hot gas, ash, and rock that races down a volcano's slope faster than a car can drive.
Ashfall from an eruption can cover roofs, roads, and crops, and heavy ash can even collapse weak roofs.
The Philippines uses alert levels from 0 to 5 to show how dangerous a volcano is, with 5 meaning a major eruption is happening.
Mayon in Albay is the most active volcano in the Philippines, having erupted more than 50 times in the past 400 years.
The Philippines sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, a horseshoe-shaped zone where many of the world's volcanoes and earthquakes happen.
The risk from a volcano depends on how close your town is, which way the wind blows, and what kind of eruption happens.
PHIVOLCS has volcano observatories near active volcanoes where scientists watch for changes day and night.
Barangay officials and local disaster teams use PHIVOLCS warnings to plan evacuation routes before a volcano erupts.
Areas close to a volcano's crater are often permanent danger zones where building homes is not allowed.
Hazard is what a volcano can do, while risk is how much damage it might cause to people and property.
To assess eruption risk, families can check if their home is inside a hazard zone and listen to PHIVOLCS alerts.
Volcanoes release sulfur dioxide gas, which can turn into acid rain and damage plants and buildings.
source: Encyclopedia-stable; volcanic gases and acid rain

en: Before an eruption, volcanoes often swell, shake with small earthquakes, and release more steam, giving scientists warning signs.
When a volcano shows danger signs, authorities order evacuation to keep people safe from ash, gas, and fast-moving flows.
Local stories and old records can help identify volcanoes that erupted long ago but are now covered by forest.
source: Encyclopedia-stable; local knowledge in hazard identification

en: Nipa palms grow in the brackish water of Philippine mangrove swamps, and their leaves are used by people to make roofs.
Ladybugs are helpful insects in a garden because they eat aphids, tiny pests that suck the sap from plant leaves.
The maya, or rice bird, is a common visitor to Philippine rice fields, where it eats grains of palay as they ripen.
Seaweed and algae are plants that grow on seashore rocks, and they provide food for small animals like sea snails.
Fiddler crabs live on the mud of mangrove swamps, and the males wave one large claw to attract females.
A habitat table often groups plants in one column and animals in another, then notes where each one is found, like 'on the mud' or 'in the tree'.
source: DepEd MATATAG Science G4-L-4 table-making skill

en: A single rice field can shelter hundreds of tiny animals, such as snails, insects, and small fish, all living together in the water and mud.
To tell plants apart in a habitat, look at their leaves and roots, because sea grasses have long blades while mangrove trees have tall trunks.
A butterfly and a frog each have four stages in their life cycle, while a chicken has three and a human has five.
source: encyclopedia-stable; stage counts for common animals

en: In a flow chart of a life cycle, the last arrow points back to the first stage because the adult produces eggs to start the cycle again.
source: flow chart representation of cyclical processes

en: A chick that hatches already has eyes, legs, and a beak, so it looks like a tiny version of its parents.
A tadpole has a long tail for swimming, but the adult frog has no tail and uses its legs to jump.
Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body breaks down and rebuilds into a butterfly with wings.
Butterfly eggs are tiny and laid on leaves, frog eggs are jelly-like in water, chicken eggs have hard shells, and human eggs are microscopic inside the mother.
source: encyclopedia-stable; egg types in different animals

en: A chicken spends about three weeks inside its egg, but a butterfly may spend only a few days as an egg.
Humans have a long childhood that lasts many years, giving time to learn and grow before becoming an adult.
A tadpole is not a fish; it is a baby frog that will grow legs and lose its tail.
source: common misconception corrected in life cycle studies

en: The chicken's life cycle has no larva or pupa stage, so it never changes body shape like a butterfly does.
Only the adult butterfly can fly, while the caterpillar crawls and the chrysalis stays still.
A chicken egg needs warmth from the mother hen, while a butterfly egg is left alone on a leaf to develop.
A human baby is born helpless and needs years of care, while a chick can walk soon after hatching.
The froglet is a young frog with small legs and a short tail, before it becomes a full adult frog.
The human life cycle is the longest of the four, because people can live for many decades, while a butterfly lives only weeks as an adult.
The stages in a life cycle always happen in the same order, so the egg comes before the young and the young before the adult.
A chicken egg must stay warm at about 37 degrees Celsius for the chick to develop inside.
source: incubation temperature for chicken eggs (rounded value)

en: Butterflies go through complete metamorphosis, meaning they have four very different-looking stages, while chickens have only three similar-looking stages.
The butterfly's caterpillar sheds its skin several times as it grows bigger before forming a chrysalis.
A human's life cycle repeats when the adult has a baby, and that baby will grow through the same stages.
On a tracking map, a typhoon's position is marked at its center, and the marks are connected in time order to show the path.
source: meteorological plotting convention for storm tracks

en: A typhoon tracking record lists the date, time, latitude, and longitude of the storm center for each observation.
source: standard weather log format for storm positions

en: Latitude lines run east-west and longitude lines run north-south, so a typhoon's location is read where the two lines cross.
Connecting the plotted points with a solid line shows the typhoon's past path, while a dashed line extends it to show the predicted future.
source: track-map convention: solid for observed, dashed for forecast

en: Plotting a typhoon's position every 6 hours gives a smooth track line, so forecasters can see the direction and speed clearly.
source: WMO standard observation interval for tropical cyclones

en: The direction a typhoon moves is read from the track line, such as northwest, and is described by the compass direction.
source: compass-rose convention in weather map reading

en: The distance between two plotted points divided by the time between them gives the typhoon's forward speed in kilometers per hour.
source: speed = distance / time applied to storm track data

en: The PAR boundary is drawn as a rectangle on the tracking map, so a typhoon is inside when its plotted position falls within that box.
source: PAGASA-defined Philippine Area of Responsibility boundary

en: A map scale, like a bar marked in kilometers, is used to measure the real distance between plotted typhoon positions.
A forecast track line is drawn ahead of the actual plotted points, and forecasters compare it with new data to check accuracy.
source: verification practice in operational typhoon forecasting

en: The typhoon's position is the location of its calm center, called the eye, which is what forecasters plot on the map.
source: tropical cyclone structure: the eye defines storm center

en: Arrows on a tracking map show wind direction at each position, helping forecasters see how the typhoon is turning.
source: wind-barb and arrow convention on weather maps

en: Each PAGASA bulletin gives the typhoon's latest coordinates and wind speed, which are used to update the plotted track.
To predict the next position, forecasters extend the straight line of the recent track in the same direction at the same speed.
source: persistence method in short-term track forecasting

en: A tracking map has a grid of latitude and longitude lines, so every typhoon position has a unique coordinate pair.
source: geographic grid standard on navigational maps

en: Comparing a typhoon's actual track with the forecast track shows how accurate the prediction was and how to improve the next one.
A pencil, ruler, and compass are used to plot typhoon positions and draw the track line on a paper map.
Along with position, the tracking record notes the maximum wind speed at each time, so the storm's strength is tracked too.
A straight track means steady direction, while a curved track means the typhoon is turning, often due to steering winds.
source: synoptic meteorology: steering flow and track shape

en: Each new observation is added to the same map, so the track line grows and the forecast is revised with fresh data.
source: operational track-updating workflow in weather agencies

en: The word 'terrestrial' comes from the Latin word 'terra' meaning land, so a terrestrial animal is one that lives on land.
The Philippine brown deer, or usa, lives in forests on land, so it is a terrestrial animal.
Kangkong, also called water spinach, grows in wet fields and ditches, so it is an aquatic plant.
The Philippine flying fox, a large bat, flies at night to find fruit, so it is an aerial animal.
A sea turtle swims in the ocean and only comes ashore to lay eggs, so it is an aquatic animal.
In a habitat diagram, the ground is drawn at the bottom, water as a blue area, and the sky above, so you can place each animal in its proper zone.
The narra tree, the national tree of the Philippines, grows on land, so it is a terrestrial plant.
The sampaguita flower, the national flower, grows on a vine on land, so it is a terrestrial plant.
A scientific investigation follows a plan: first ask a question, then predict, measure, record, and conclude.
source: scientific method sequence in DepEd MATATAG Science

en: A hypothesis is a testable guess, so the plan must include steps that can prove it right or wrong.
A balance measures mass, while a thermometer measures temperature; each tool answers a different question.
Using a balance to measure mass works the same anywhere because mass does not change with gravity.
source: mass as invariant property vs weight

en: Inflating a balloon and weighing it on a balance shows that the air inside adds measurable mass.
source: simple demonstration that gases have mass

en: Two liquids with the same volume can have different masses, so the balance tells which one is heavier.
source: density concept: same volume, different masses

en: Read the balance scale at eye level so the pointer is not seen from an angle.
source: parallax error avoidance in balance reading

en: A graduated cylinder measures liquid volume in milliliters, so you know exactly how much liquid to weigh.
source: graduated cylinder as standard volume tool

en: Taring means setting the balance to zero with the empty container already on it, so only the liquid is weighed.
Every number recorded in the data table must include its unit, like 250 grams or 30 degrees Celsius.
A bar graph compares the masses of different objects side by side, making the heavier one easy to spot.
source: bar graph for comparing discrete measurements

en: If the balance stays level, the two sides have equal mass, so the known weights match the object.
When comparing two liquids, use the same volume of each so the comparison is fair.
Warm liquids expand, so measure temperature and volume at the same time to keep the comparison fair.
source: thermal expansion of liquids affects volume readings

en: Hold the thermometer steady and read it after the liquid stops moving, so the number is accurate.
A clear question like "Does air have mass?" tells you what to plan and measure.
source: inquiry-based investigation starts with a question

en: Scientists share their findings by showing their data table and graph to others, so the work can be checked.
A wrong prediction is useful because it shows the result was a surprise to learn from.
Repeating a measurement and getting the same number each time builds confidence in the result.
source: repeatability as evidence of reliable data

en: Label the x-axis with what you changed and the y-axis with what you measured, so the graph is clear.
source: graph conventions: independent vs dependent variable

en: Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces, giving digestive juices more surface to attack, so digestion works faster.
source: encyclopedia-stable; mechanical digestion increases surface area

en: Salivary glands in the mouth release saliva, which moistens food and begins breaking down starch into sugar.
Waves of muscle called peristalsis squeeze food down the esophagus and through the whole digestive tract, even if you are upside down.
source: encyclopedia-stable; peristalsis in the digestive tract

en: The stomach churns food into a soft liquid called chyme, mixing it with gastric juice to start digesting proteins.
source: encyclopedia-stable; stomach mechanical and chemical digestion

en: Gastric juice in the stomach contains acid and pepsin, an enzyme that chops proteins into smaller pieces.
Most digestion and absorption happen in the small intestine, the longest and busiest part of the digestive tract.
Tiny finger-like villi line the inside of the small intestine and absorb digested nutrients into the blood.
Bile from the liver breaks big fat globules into tiny droplets so fat-digesting enzymes can work on them.
The pancreas releases enzymes into the small intestine that digest carbohydrates, proteins, and fats from your meal.
The large intestine absorbs water and salts from the leftover food, making the waste more solid before it leaves.
Elimination is the last step, when the rectum and anus push the leftover waste out of the body as feces.
Mechanical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces, while chemical digestion uses enzymes to break molecules apart.
Digestion starts in the mouth, not the stomach, because chewing and saliva begin the process before you swallow.
source: encyclopedia-stable; digestion begins in the mouth

en: A meal can take about one to three days to travel through the whole digestive tract, from first bite to leaving the body.
source: encyclopedia-stable; whole-gut transit time rounded value

en: Fiber in vegetables and fruits is not digested, but it helps push food along the intestines and makes waste easier to pass.
The tongue rolls chewed food into a ball and pushes it to the back of the mouth to begin swallowing.
The small intestine is about six meters long, and its folded walls give a huge surface for absorbing nutrients.
source: encyclopedia-stable; small intestine length rounded value

en: Digestive organs release juices at the right moments, like saliva when you smell food, so digestion starts on time.
After nutrients pass through the intestinal walls into the blood, blood carries them to every cell in the body.
A flap called the epiglottis closes over the windpipe when you swallow, so food goes down the esophagus, not the lungs.
To trace a typhoon's path, a forecaster reads the date and time from each tracking record to know the exact interval between plotted points.
A forecaster looks at the landmasses on the tracking map to see if the typhoon's path might hit a country or island.
A forecaster checks the time interval between plotted points, such as six hours, to calculate the typhoon's speed correctly.
A forecaster marks the exact point where the typhoon's track crosses the PAR boundary to record the entry time.
A forecaster draws a smooth curve through the plotted points, rather than connecting them with straight segments, to show the typhoon's continuous path.
Each plotted typhoon position is labeled with its observation time, so the forecaster can tell the order of the points on the map.
A forecaster may draw a cone of uncertainty around the forecast track to show where the typhoon might possibly go.
A forecaster uses the wind arrows on the tracking map to infer the steering winds that are pushing the typhoon along its path.
A forecaster converts all observation times to a single time zone, like Philippine Standard Time, before plotting the track.
A forecaster uses the recorded wind speed to classify the typhoon's strength, such as tropical storm or typhoon.
To measure the distance a typhoon traveled, a forecaster places a ruler between two plotted points and reads the map distance.
When a typhoon's coordinates fall between grid lines, a forecaster estimates its exact position by dividing the space between the lines evenly.
An arrow is drawn along the track line to show the direction the typhoon is moving, pointing from the older to the newer position.
A forecaster checks the coordinates from two different bulletins to make sure the plotted position matches the recorded data.
A forecaster checks the units of the tracking data, such as kilometers or miles, before measuring distances on the map.
A protractor can be used on the tracking map to measure the angle of the track line from north, giving the exact direction.
A forecaster may draw a circle around the plotted eye to show the typhoon's outer rainbands on the tracking map.
A forecaster also marks the point where the typhoon's track leaves the PAR boundary to record the exit time.
To read a typhoon's location, a forecaster looks at the grid lines and reads the latitude and longitude numbers printed on the map edges.
A forecaster reads the map's legend to understand the symbols used for the typhoon's eye and track line.
The liver and pancreas are accessory organs that send digestive juices into the small intestine, even though food never passes through them.
source: standard anatomy: liver and pancreas are accessory digestive organs

en: The gallbladder stores bile made by the liver and releases it into the small intestine when you eat fatty food.
source: standard physiology: bile storage and release

en: Stomach acid is strong enough to kill many germs in swallowed food, and it also helps activate the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin.
source: standard physiology: gastric acid kills pathogens and activates pepsin

en: Fats are absorbed into tiny lymph tubes called lacteals inside the villi, while other nutrients go straight into blood.
source: standard histology: lacteals absorb fats in the small intestine

en: Helpful bacteria in the large intestine make some vitamins, like vitamin K, which the body then absorbs from the waste.
source: microbiome: gut bacteria synthesize vitamin K

en: Digestion follows a fixed order: mechanical breakdown, chemical digestion, absorption, and elimination, with each step preparing for the next.
Conservation of mass also applies to each element, so the mass of carbon in the reactants equals the mass of carbon in the products.
source: law of conservation of mass: each element's atoms are conserved

en: Physical changes like melting ice also conserve mass, but they do not need balancing because no new substances form.
source: chemistry textbook: physical change vs chemical change

en: In a balanced equation, the total atomic mass on the reactant side equals the total atomic mass on the product side, so you can check by adding up the masses.
source: law of conservation of mass applied to atomic masses

en: A balanced equation shows only the atom counts, not the temperature, pressure, or catalyst needed for the reaction.
source: encyclopedia-stable: information not contained in a balanced equation

en: The coefficients in a balanced equation give the ratio of molecules, so you can scale a reaction from a test tube to a factory by multiplying the amounts.
source: stoichiometry: coefficients as mole ratios for scaling

en: The law of conservation of mass holds even when a reaction releases heat or light, because energy changes do not affect the total mass.
source: law of conservation of mass: energy changes separate from mass

en: The law of conservation of mass applies to any amount, from a single molecule to a whole factory, so a balanced equation works at any scale.
source: law of conservation of mass: universal for all amounts

en: Stoichiometry is the branch of chemistry that uses balanced equations to calculate the amounts of reactants and products, based on the law of conservation of mass.
Metamorphosis lets young and adult animals eat different foods, so they do not compete for the same food in the same place.
A frog can lay hundreds of eggs at once, a chicken usually lays one egg at a time, and a human usually has one baby at a time.
A chicken egg from the store is not fertilized, so it will never hatch, but a fertilized egg from a hen can grow a chick.
A butterfly's metamorphosis is complete because its caterpillar looks nothing like the adult, but a grasshopper's is incomplete because its nymph looks like a small adult.
A tadpole eats plants in water, but an adult frog eats insects on land, so its food changes with each stage.

topic: caterpillar sheds skin vs human growth
en: A caterpillar sheds its skin several times to grow, but a human child grows without shedding skin, showing different ways of growing.
A human child spends many years learning to talk and read, while a chick can peck and walk within a day of hatching.
A tadpole swims in water, but a chick walks on land, so the young of frogs and chickens move in very different ways.
A plate boundary is the meeting line where two tectonic plates touch, and the Philippines sits on several of these lines.
Deep ocean trenches are topographical evidence of plate boundaries because they form where one plate slides beneath another.
Volcanoes line up in chains along plate boundaries, so the row of Philippine volcanoes maps where the plates meet.
Earthquakes happen most often along plate boundaries, which is why the Philippines experiences many of them.
The Philippines lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire, a horseshoe-shaped zone of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific Ocean.
The Sierra Madre mountain range rose from the collision of plates, showing geological evidence of a boundary.
The Philippine Fault Zone is a long crack in the ground where two plates slide past each other sideways.
Mayon Volcano's perfect cone grew from lava and ash pushed up where the Eurasian Plate meets the Philippine Sea Plate.
Taal Volcano sits inside a caldera formed by an ancient eruption, marking the plate boundary zone in Luzon.
The Marikina Valley Fault is an active fault line running through Metro Manila that moves because of plate pressure.
Ocean trenches are the deepest places on Earth, and the Philippine Trench reaches about 10,000 meters down.
PHIVOLCS, the Philippine volcano and earthquake agency, watches the ground to track what the moving plates are doing.
Scientists map plate boundaries by plotting where volcanoes and earthquakes cluster, and the Philippines shows a clear pattern.
Convergent boundaries push plates together, divergent boundaries pull them apart, and the Philippines has both convergent and transform boundaries.
The Philippine archipelago itself was built by millions of years of volcanic eruptions and plate collisions.
Seafloor spreading makes new ocean crust at mid-ocean ridges, while subduction destroys old crust at trenches.
The pattern of earthquake epicenters across the Philippines draws the exact lines of the plate boundaries.
Hot springs and geothermal areas in the Philippines mark places where plate movement heats up underground water.
source: encyclopedia-stable; geothermal energy in the Philippines

en: The curved chains of Philippine islands mirror the curved lines where the plates meet beneath the sea.
Scientists use GPS instruments to measure how the Philippine plates move a few centimeters each year.
source: encyclopedia-stable; geodetic GPS studies of plate motion

en: To weigh a gas, use a container that can be tightly sealed, like a zip-lock bag, so the gas stays inside during the weighing.
Place the object in the center of the balance pan so the pointer moves freely and gives a stable reading.
Keep the room temperature steady while weighing liquids, because warm liquids expand and change their volume.
source: effect of temperature on liquid volume

en: After each weighing, check that the balance returns to zero to confirm it is still working correctly.
Pour the liquid slowly into the container to avoid spills that would change the mass reading.
Write the date and time next to each measurement in the data table to track any changes in conditions.
When using a digital balance, wait for the number to stop changing before recording the mass.
To compare the masses of a gas and a liquid, use the same container for both, but seal the gas container tightly.
source: fair comparison of gas and liquid

en: A forecaster uses the compass rose printed on the map to name the direction of the track line, such as northeast or southwest.
source: map reading: compass rose for cardinal directions

en: Before plotting, a forecaster sorts the tracking records by date and time so the path is drawn in the correct order.
source: data organization: chronological sorting before plotting

en: A forecaster plots the points with a pencil so that a mistaken mark can be erased without ruining the map.
source: cartographic practice: pencil for error correction

en: A forecaster reads the map's title to know which typhoon and which dates the tracking map covers.
source: map elements: title identifies subject and time span

en: A forecaster writes the observation time in 24-hour format, like 1400, to avoid confusion between morning and evening.
A forecaster checks that the map is oriented correctly, with north pointing up, before plotting the typhoon's path.
A forecaster compares the current track with tracks of past typhoons to see if the path is similar to a known one.
source: forecasting practice: comparing with historical tracks

en: A forecaster uses a compass to draw a circle around the eye to show the typhoon's area of strong winds on the map.
source: map drawing: compass for circular wind zones

en: A tropical rainforest gets about 200 centimeters of rain each year and stays warm all year, which helps many plants and animals live there.
In a tropical rainforest, dead leaves and wood rot quickly in the warm, wet conditions, so nutrients are recycled fast.
Many monkeys, birds, and insects live in the rainforest canopy, the top layer of leaves, and rarely come down to the ground.
A swamp is a wetland with trees and shrubs growing in soil that is flooded with water for at least part of the year.
Swamps act like natural filters, trapping mud and pollution from water before it flows into rivers or seas.
The water in a swamp has little oxygen because rotting plants use it up, so some fish have special ways to breathe air.
An estuary is a place where a river meets the sea, mixing fresh water with salt water to make brackish water.
Many young fish and crabs grow up in estuaries because the shallow, calm water hides them from bigger predators.
The mixing of river and ocean water in an estuary brings nutrients that feed tiny plants and animals, which then feed larger creatures.
Mangrove trees have roots that stick up out of the mud to get air because the soil is waterlogged and lacks oxygen.
Mangrove forests protect coastlines by slowing down waves and trapping soil, which reduces damage from storms and floods.
Mangrove trees survive in salty water by pushing extra salt out through their leaves or storing it in old bark.
Coral reefs are made by tiny animals called coral polyps that build hard skeletons from calcium carbonate in seawater.
Most reef corals have tiny algae living inside them that give the coral food and their bright colors.
Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor but are home to about one quarter of all marine species.
Tropical rainforests and coral reefs are both hotspots of biodiversity, but one is on land and the other is underwater.
A swamp is different from a marsh because a swamp has trees, while a marsh is mostly grasses and reeds.
The Philippines is part of the Coral Triangle, the area with the highest coral reef biodiversity in the world.
In the Philippines, mangrove trees are called bakawan, and they are planted along coasts to protect against typhoon waves.
Sunlight is an abiotic factor that reaches the shallow water of estuaries and coral reefs, allowing algae and seagrass to grow.
source: encyclopedia-stable; abiotic factors in aquatic ecosystems

en: To test a GMO crop's safety, scientists feed the crop to lab rats and compare their health with rats fed the non-GMO version.
source: standard toxicology feeding study for GMO safety

en: To measure gene flow, scientists plant a GMO field next to a non-GMO field and test the seeds for the inserted gene.
source: field trial design for gene flow assessment

en: A class debate on biotechnology has opening statements, rebuttals, and closing arguments, with each side given equal time to speak.
To judge a biotech claim, check if the study used many samples and was published in a peer-reviewed journal.
To see if a GMO crop harms insects, scientists count the number and types of insects in GMO and non-GMO fields.
In debating ethics, a class can weigh the benefits of a biotech product against its risks to people and the environment.
To check if a GMO food could cause allergies, scientists compare its proteins with known allergens and test them on immune cells.
A fair test of GMO yield keeps soil, water, and sunlight the same, changing only the seed variety planted.
source: fair test design: one variable changed, rest constant

en: During a debate, students record each side's points on a T-chart with pros on one side and cons on the other.
To test Bt corn's effect on beneficial insects, scientists count ladybugs and bees in Bt and non-Bt plots.
source: Bt corn field monitoring in the Philippines

en: To judge a biotech product's true value, researchers look at yields and health data over several seasons, not just one.
In a structured debate, a moderator gives each team three minutes to speak and one minute for rebuttals.
To find unintended changes in a GMO, scientists sequence its entire genome and compare it with the original plant.
To compare nutrient levels, scientists use lab instruments to measure vitamins and minerals in GMO and non-GMO foods.
To assess social impact, researchers survey farmers about their income and health after planting GMO crops.
source: social survey methodology in agricultural studies

en: In a debate, each side must state the ethical principle they use, such as doing no harm or maximizing benefit.
To check for pest resistance, scientists monitor pest populations each year to see if they become harder to kill.
A decision matrix for biotech lists criteria like cost, safety, and environment, then scores each option against them.
A fair debate gives both teams the same evidence packet and the same time to prepare and present their arguments.
To show GMO versus non-GMO yield, scientists make a bar graph with error bars to show the variation in the data.
source: data visualization best practices for field trials

en: When magma erupts on the deep ocean floor, it cools instantly into rounded pillow-shaped rocks that pile up to form the top layer of new oceanic crust.
source: encyclopedia-stable: pillow lavas form at submarine eruptions

en: Water squeezed out of a sinking oceanic plate lowers the melting point of the mantle above it, which is why volcanoes form in a line along the subduction zone.
source: encyclopedia-stable: flux melting at subduction zones

en: Earthquakes along a sinking oceanic plate can happen as deep as 700 kilometers, tracing the cold slab's path as it dives into the mantle.
source: encyclopedia-stable: Wadati-Benioff zone, deep earthquakes to about 700 km

en: Behind some volcanic arcs, the overriding plate stretches and tears open a small ocean basin, creating new oceanic crust far from a mid-ocean ridge.
Continental crust is rich in silica, which makes it light and pale, while oceanic crust has less silica, which makes it dark and dense.
source: encyclopedia-stable: felsic vs mafic crust composition

en: Scientists tell oceanic crust from continental crust by timing earthquake waves, because the dense rocks of the ocean floor carry the waves faster.
source: encyclopedia-stable: seismic wave velocities differ by rock density

en: Fresh oceanic crust near mid-ocean ridges releases more heat than old continental crust, because it is still cooling from molten rock beneath.
source: encyclopedia-stable: heat flow is highest at mid-ocean ridges

en: Magma that rises above a sinking oceanic plate cools into new rock that is lighter than the ocean floor, adding fresh material to continental crust.
source: encyclopedia-stable: arc magmatism contributes to continental growth

en: Plates carrying large areas of heavy oceanic crust move faster, because the dense sinking edge pulls the rest of the plate along behind it.
source: encyclopedia-stable: slab pull drives faster plate motion

en: Oceanic crust has a simple three-layer stack of sediment, basalt, and gabbro, while continental crust is a complex jumble of many rock types.
source: encyclopedia-stable: oceanic crust structure from ocean drilling

en: Over hundreds of millions of years, oceans open where continents split apart and close where oceanic crust sinks, cycling Earth's crust through repeated breakups and collisions.
source: encyclopedia-stable: Wilson cycle of ocean basin opening and closing

en: The Philippines has about 300 volcanoes, and only about 24 are active, so most of the mountains you see are inactive.
An inactive volcano is one that has no recorded eruption and shows no signs of waking up, but it is still a volcano.
source: PHIVOLCS classification of active and inactive volcanoes

en: A dormant volcano is quiet but could erupt again, while an extinct volcano has cooled down and is very unlikely to ever erupt.
The Philippines has many volcanoes because one piece of Earth's crust slides under another near the country, melting rock into magma.
Magma collects in a pocket underground called a magma chamber, and when pressure builds, it pushes up and erupts through the volcano.
source: encyclopedia-stable; magma chamber and eruption process

en: Thick, sticky magma traps gas and causes explosive eruptions, while thin, runny magma lets gas escape and flows out gently.
source: encyclopedia-stable; magma viscosity and eruption style

en: Volcanic ash is made of tiny sharp fragments of rock and glass, so it is not soft like the ash from burned wood.
Volcanic soil is rich in minerals, so many farms in the Philippines grow good crops on the slopes of old, inactive volcanoes.
Scientists read a volcano's history in its layers of ash and lava, like pages in a book, to learn how often it erupts.
A volcano that has erupted many times before is likely to erupt again, so its past eruptions are the best clue to its future.
Hot springs around a quiet volcano show that hot rock still lies underground, which is why scientists do not call it completely extinct.
PHIVOLCS is the Philippine government agency that studies volcanoes and keeps the official list of which ones are active or inactive.
A volcano's danger zone is not a perfect circle; it follows valleys and the shape of the land, so some towns are safer than others at the same distance.
Schools and barangays near active volcanoes hold practice drills so families already know the safe route when a real eruption comes.
source: DRRM practice in Philippine schools and barangays

en: A volcanic eruption can close schools and roads for weeks, so the disruption to a community lasts longer than the eruption itself.
Mount Arayat in Pampanga is an inactive volcano with no recorded eruption, but it still stands as a landmark for nearby towns.
Scientists can warn that a volcano is likely to erupt, but they cannot name the exact day, so communities stay prepared for weeks.
Volcanic eruptions over millions of years helped build the Philippine islands, creating many of the mountains and hills we see today.
A big eruption can change a volcano's shape by blasting away its top or creating a new crater, so the mountain looks different after.
Many Philippine towns are built on the old lava flows of inactive volcanoes, because the land is flat and easy to build on.
The Moon takes about 29.5 days to complete all its phases, from one new moon to the next new moon.
Moon phases happen because we see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half as it travels around Earth.
At full moon, Earth lies roughly between the Sun and the Moon, so the entire sunlit face of the Moon points toward us.
A half moon, called first quarter, occurs when the Moon is at a right angle to the line from Earth to the Sun.
Right after new moon, a thin crescent appears; it is just a small sliver of the Moon's sunlit side facing Earth.
A gibbous moon looks more than half lit but less than full, appearing between the half and full phases.
Waxing means the lit part of the Moon grows each night; waning means it shrinks, from full back to new.
The Moon orbits Earth counterclockwise when seen from above the North Pole, so its phases progress in a steady order.
One complete set of phases, called a lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days, which is close to one calendar month.
Because the Moon moves eastward in its orbit, it rises about 50 minutes later each day, changing where we see it.
At new moon, the Moon rises and sets with the Sun, so it is in the daytime sky and hidden by sunlight.
At full moon, the Moon rises at sunset and sets at sunrise, so it stays in the night sky all night long.
Everyone on Earth sees the same moon phase on a given day, because the Moon is so far away that the angle is almost the same.
The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees from Earth's orbit around the Sun, so most months have no eclipse at full moon.
The bright edge of a crescent moon always points toward the Sun, which helps you find where the Sun is even after sunset.
At first quarter, the Moon is highest in the sky at sunset, then sets around midnight, so it is visible in the early evening.
At last quarter, the Moon rises around midnight and is high in the morning sky, showing its left half lit in the Northern Hemisphere.
The Moon spins slowly on its axis, taking about 27 days, but because it also orbits, the same side always faces Earth.
In the Philippines, PAGASA uses moon phases to predict tides, which help fishermen and coastal communities plan their days.
Earth spins once every 24 hours, while the Moon circles Earth once every 29.5 days, so we see the Sun rise daily but moon phases slowly.
Tropical rainforest soil is thin and poor because most nutrients are stored in the plants themselves, not in the ground.
Swamps provide feeding and nesting grounds for many birds, such as herons and egrets, that wade in the shallow water.
The saltiness of estuary water changes with the tides, so the animals there must tolerate different salt levels throughout the day.
Mangrove roots are home to many animals like crabs, mudskippers, and monitor lizards that climb and dig among the tangled roots.
Coral reefs need water with low nutrients, because too many nutrients cause algae to overgrow and smother the corals.
Estuaries are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth, producing more food per area than most farmlands.
