To start using a dichotomous key, you first look at the rock's visible features like grain size, color, and whether it has layers.
A dichotomous key gives you two choices at each step, and you pick the one that matches your rock to move to the next pair.
To test hardness, you try scratching the rock with a fingernail, a copper coin, and a steel nail, from softest to hardest.
The streak test rubs a rock on a white porcelain tile to see the color of its powder, which is more reliable than surface color.
A fair classification uses the same lighting and a plain background so that color and texture are judged the same way for every rock.
When using a dichotomous key, you must start at the first pair of questions and never skip steps, because each answer narrows the choices.
A good record of rock classification lists the rock's properties, the answers you chose in the key, and the final rock name.
If two people use the same key on the same rock, they should get the same name if they observe the features carefully and honestly.
A common mistake is judging a rock by its stained surface; you should look at a fresh break to see the true color inside.
To test for calcite, a teacher places a drop of dilute acid on the rock; if it fizzes, the rock contains calcite.
The texture of a rock—whether its grains are coarse, fine, or glassy—is a key feature that directs you to the next question.
Many rock keys first ask if the rock has visible layers; this separates sedimentary rocks from igneous and metamorphic ones.
If a rock shows interlocking crystals, the key likely leads to igneous; if it shows rounded grains, it may be sedimentary.
To check for magnetic minerals, you hold a small magnet near the rock; a strong pull suggests magnetite or iron-rich rock.
A fair hardness test uses the same set of scratch tools on every rock, so you can compare which rocks scratch each other.
After the key gives you a name, you confirm by checking that the rock's properties match the description in a rock guide.
A dichotomous key works like a flowchart: each pair of questions leads to another pair until you reach the rock's name.
When classifying, place the rock on a paper towel so you don't lose tiny grains that could change your observation of its texture.
First look at grain size and layers, then do hardness and streak tests, because later tests can scratch or damage the rock.
A reliable result from a dichotomous key includes the path of answers you chose, because that path shows why you named the rock.
Momentum is the amount of motion an object carries, found by multiplying its mass by its velocity, so a fast bike and a slow truck can match.
In any collision, the total momentum of all objects together stays the same before and after, even when they bounce or stick.
A car's crumple zone lengthens the time of a crash, and a longer stopping time means a smaller force on the people inside.
An airbag cushions a person by making the head slow down over a longer time, so the force of the stop is much smaller.
Newton's cradle is a model of elastic collisions: one ball swings in, one swings out, and the middle balls stay still.
A bowling ball hitting a pin is nearly elastic: the pin flies off with most of the ball's speed while the heavy ball keeps rolling slowly.
source: encyclopedia-stable; elastic collision of unequal masses

en: Momentum is the quantity of motion, while kinetic energy is the energy of that motion; a collision can lose kinetic energy but never momentum.
source: encyclopedia-stable; momentum vs kinetic energy distinction

en: The force in a collision acts only during the brief moment the objects touch, often just a tiny fraction of a second.
The same change in momentum needs less force if the push lasts longer, which is why mats and sand pits soften landings.
A jeepney driver slows before a bump because a slower hit means less momentum to absorb, so the force on the passengers is smaller.
A coconut falling and hitting the ground is an inelastic collision: the shell cracks and the ground absorbs some of the motion energy.
A tennis ball hitting a racket squashes and rebounds, showing that even bouncy collisions lose a little energy to heat and sound.
Crash-test dummies with sensors record the forces a human body would feel in a car crash, helping engineers design safer vehicles.
The total momentum before a collision is shared among all objects after, so the more mass that moves, the slower it must go.
A ball bounces higher on a hard floor than on a soft mat because the hard surface returns more of the ball's kinetic energy.
In a head-on crash between a truck and a car, the truck feels the same force as the car, but the lighter car changes speed much more.
A helmet spreads the force of a hit over a larger area and a longer time, reducing the force that reaches the head.
Even the bounciest ball loses a little energy to sound and heat, so perfectly elastic collisions exist only as ideal models.
A clay ball thrown at a wall sticks and stops, turning all its motion energy into heat, sound, and a flattened shape.
A basketball dribble is an inelastic collision: the ball squashes against the floor, loses some energy, and bounces back lower than it fell.
The Philippines is not one single plate but a jigsaw of small crustal blocks called the Philippine Mobile Belt, squeezed between two big plates.
Besides the Philippine Trench, the Manila, Negros, and Cotabato trenches are other subduction zones where plates dive beneath the Philippines.
Deep earthquakes, occurring hundreds of kilometers underground, trace the sinking slab beneath the Philippines, proving that subduction is happening.
The Zambales ophiolite is a slab of ancient ocean floor now on land, evidence that seafloor was pushed up by plate collisions.
Mount Pinatubo's 1991 eruption, which sent ash high into the sky, happened because the Eurasian Plate is subducting beneath the Manila Trench.
The Cordillera Central mountain range in Luzon was formed by the slow collision of the Philippine Sea Plate with the Eurasian Plate.
Marble and schist found in Philippine islands are metamorphic rocks, squeezed and heated by ancient plate collisions, showing geological evidence.
The Negros Trench, west of the Visayas, is a subduction zone where the Sulu Sea Plate slides beneath the Philippine Mobile Belt.
The Cotabato Trench in Mindanao is a subduction zone that has caused strong earthquakes and tsunamis in southern Philippines.
The Philippine Fault Zone is a long transform fault that runs from Luzon to Mindanao, moving sideways as the plates grind past each other.
The Tiwi Geothermal Plant in Albay uses heat from plate boundaries to make electricity, showing that underground heat is close to the surface.
source: encyclopedia-stable; geothermal energy in the Philippines

en: The collision of the Palawan microcontinent with the western Philippines formed the Zambales and Mindoro mountains, adding land to the archipelago.
The gold and copper mines in the Philippines are found near volcanic arcs, which formed from hot fluids at plate boundaries.
The Philippine Sea Plate moves northwest, causing the Philippine islands to slowly shift and rotate over millions of years.
The Philippine islands are made of many terranes, or crustal fragments, that were welded together by plate collisions over millions of years.
The Philippines has two parallel volcanic arcs, one on the west and one on the east, each marking a different subduction zone.
The Philippine Fault Zone is a system of many parallel faults, not just one crack, that run across the islands and cause earthquakes.
The volcanic rocks in the Philippines, like andesite and basalt, come from magma formed when subducted plates melt.
The Philippine Sea Plate's movement is causing the island of Luzon to rotate slowly clockwise over millions of years.
Coral reefs found on top of old volcanic islands in the Philippines show that the land has risen or sunk as plates move.
A water cycle model must be sealed so that the same water keeps cycling, showing that Earth's water is a closed system.
Using a shallow dish with a wide mouth in a water cycle model increases the surface area, so evaporation happens faster and is easier to observe.
source: evaporation rate and surface area principle

en: To make condensation visible in a model, place a clear plastic wrap with ice cubes on top so the vapor turns back to liquid droplets.
source: condensation on cool surface in water cycle model

en: Sloping the plastic wrap in the model makes condensed drops run to one corner and fall, mimicking real precipitation.
To measure evaporation in a model, mark the water level on the container with a marker and measure the drop each hour with a ruler.
source: measurement of evaporation in classroom model

en: A fair test of a water cycle model changes only the heat source, like using a lamp versus shade, while keeping water amount and container the same.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, rest constant

en: To measure condensation, count the drops that fall from the plastic wrap in one minute and record the number in a table.
source: quantitative observation in water cycle model

en: A line graph of water level over time shows a steady downward slope, which means evaporation is happening at a constant rate.
The steps to build a water cycle model are: add water, seal the container, place it in the sun, wait, then observe and record the changes.
source: standard procedure for water cycle model

en: A lamp can replace the Sun in a water cycle model, but it must be placed at a safe distance to warm the water without melting the plastic.
source: safe alternative heat source for classroom model

en: An open container in a model loses water vapor to the air, so it does not show the full cycle, while a closed one recycles all the water.
source: closed-system principle in water cycle models

en: Adding sand and a rock to the model's bottom mimics the ground where water collects, helping show the collection stage.
A good model includes labels for evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection, so viewers can see each process clearly.
Observing the model every 10 minutes for an hour shows the sequence of evaporation, condensation, and precipitation in order.
source: timed observation of water cycle model

en: In a fair test, the amount of water, the size of the container, and the type of wrap are kept the same, while only the heat is changed.
To see how temperature affects the model, place a thermometer inside the container and record the temperature along with the water level.
A small bag model shows the water cycle but leaves out oceans and clouds, so scientists use it only to explain the basic processes.
In the Philippines, PAGASA measures rainfall with rain gauges, just as a model collects condensed drops to measure precipitation.
A sealed model shows that water is never lost, only changed, which is why Earth's water supply stays about the same.
source: conservation of water in Earth's system

en: To test which material works best, make two identical bags and change only one thing, like using a clear bag versus a dark bag.
A collision in physics does not need objects to touch; two magnets repelling each other without contact still exchange momentum and change each other's motion.
source: encyclopedia-stable; physics definition of collision as an interaction that changes motion

en: A volcano's risk to a town depends on how many people and buildings are in the danger zone, so a crowded city far away can be riskier than a small village near the volcano.
Lahar can rush down river valleys for many kilometers, so a town far from the volcano but beside a river can still be in danger.
During an eruption, ash falls mostly on the side where the wind blows, so a town downwind of a volcano gets heavier ash than a town upwind at the same distance.
After a major eruption, PHIVOLCS redraws hazard maps because new craters and valleys change where lava and lahar can flow.
If heavy rain falls on fresh volcanic ash, it can form lahar, so towns near rivers face higher risk during typhoons after an eruption.
Local governments use volcano hazard maps to decide where to build schools and hospitals, keeping important buildings away from the highest risk zones.
PHIVOLCS hazard maps use colors like red, orange, and yellow to show risk levels, so families can check their barangay's color.
Hazard maps are updated as towns grow, because more buildings and people mean higher risk even if the volcano hasn't changed.
source: disaster risk reduction practice: maps updated with development

en: To make a wet mount, place the thin specimen in a drop of water on the glass slide first.
source: standard wet-mount protocol for light microscopy

en: Lower the coverslip onto the slide at an angle to push out air bubbles that blur the view.
source: standard wet-mount protocol for light microscopy

en: Start looking at a slide with the lowest power lens to find the cells before switching to high power.
Use the coarse focus knob only on low power to move the lens close to the slide.
Turn the fine focus knob slowly on high power to make the cell parts look sharp.
Adjust the diaphragm under the stage to let in the right amount of light for a clear image.
Carry a microscope with one hand on its arm and the other under its base to keep it safe.
The specimen must be very thin so light can pass through it and show the cell parts.
source: light microscopy principle: transmission of light

en: The nucleus often looks like the darkest round spot inside the cell under the microscope.
source: standard microscopy observation of cell structures

en: The cell membrane shows as a thin boundary line around the cytoplasm when you focus carefully.
source: standard microscopy observation of cell structures

en: Mitochondria are very small, so you need a high power lens to see their shapes.
A good observation record includes a labeled drawing and the magnification number of the lens.
source: standard scientific drawing and recording practices

en: When looking at plant cells, you see a stiff outer wall, but animal cells only have a thin membrane.
source: encyclopedia-stable; plant vs animal cell structure

en: To stain a slide, put a drop of dye at the edge of the coverslip and let it soak under.
source: standard staining technique for microscope slides

en: Always center the specimen in the low power view before switching to a higher power lens.
Wipe the lens with special paper, not your finger, because dirt makes the image blurry.
source: microscope maintenance and care standard rules

en: To see animal cells, gently scrape the inside of your cheek with a clean toothpick and spread it on a slide.
source: standard safe cheek cell sampling technique

en: In the cytoplasm, you might see tiny moving particles, which shows the fluid is alive and active.
source: standard microscopy observation of cytoplasmic streaming

en: A microscope helps identify cell parts by making them look bigger and separating them clearly.
source: encyclopedia-stable; function of a light microscope

en: A cost-benefit analysis lists each benefit and cost of a biotech product in a table, then compares the totals to see if the benefits outweigh the costs.
To find who is affected by a biotech product, scientists and debaters list all groups like farmers, consumers, and the environment, then consider each one's interest.
When a biotech product has unknown risks, the precautionary principle says to act cautiously by limiting its use until more studies are done.
To judge a biotech study, check who paid for it, because a study funded by the product's maker may have a conflict of interest.
To measure a GMO crop's effect on soil, scientists take soil samples from GMO and non-GMO fields and count the types of microbes in each.
To compare water use, scientists record the amount of water applied to GMO and non-GMO fields over a whole season.
To learn how people feel about GMO food, researchers give a survey to a large group of consumers and count the number who support or oppose it.
To see how GMO crops affect small farmers, researchers interview farmers about their expenses and harvests before and after planting GMO seeds.
In a debate, a speaker makes a claim, supports it with evidence from a study, and then explains the reasoning that connects the two.
To spot a weak argument, debaters check for logical fallacies like attacking the person instead of the evidence.
To weigh effects, debaters separate short-term benefits like higher yield from long-term risks like resistance that may appear after many years.
To decide if GMO food should be labeled, a class can survey what information consumers want and then debate whether that need is strong enough.
To strengthen a debate, one person plays devil's advocate by arguing the opposite side, forcing the team to find weak points in their own case.
After a debate, the class can vote on a resolution or try to reach a consensus by discussing which arguments were most convincing.
A life cycle assessment measures the environmental impact of a biotech product from making the seeds to growing, harvesting, and selling the crop.
To debate fairness, a team can ask if the benefits of a biotech product go to rich farmers while poor farmers bear the risks.
To respect choice, a debate can consider whether people have the right to know if their food is GMO and to choose non-GMO options.
A risk matrix scores a biotech product's harm by multiplying how likely it is to happen by how serious the harm would be.
To track long-term effects of a GMO crop, scientists return to the same field each year to record yield, pests, and soil health.
To compare the carbon footprint, scientists measure the fuel used by tractors and the energy for making fertilizer on GMO and non-GMO farms.
To read a formula equation aloud, scientists say the coefficient as a number of molecules, then the formula name, like 'two water molecules' for 2H2O.
Scientists use a periodic table to find the correct symbols and subscripts for each element before writing any formula equation.
source: standard practice in writing chemical formulas

en: When a reaction gives off a gas, scientists write an upward arrow (↑) after the gas product to show it escapes into the air.
source: standard chemical equation notation for gas evolution

en: When a reaction forms a solid from two liquids, scientists write a downward arrow (↓) after that solid to show it settles.
source: standard chemical equation notation for precipitate formation

en: For a reaction that needs light, scientists write the word 'light' above the arrow to show the energy source.
For a reaction that needs electricity, scientists write the word 'electricity' above the arrow to show the energy source.
To show a reaction can go in both directions, scientists use two arrows pointing opposite ways instead of one.
source: standard notation for reversible chemical reactions

en: To describe a reaction between a metal and an acid, scientists write the metal name, plus acid name, yields salt and hydrogen gas.
source: standard word equation pattern for metal-acid reactions

en: To write a formula equation for a metal and acid reaction, scientists write the metal symbol, plus acid formula, yields salt formula and H2.
source: standard formula equation pattern for metal-acid reactions

en: To describe a reaction between a carbonate and an acid, scientists write the carbonate name, plus acid name, yields salt, water, and carbon dioxide.
source: standard word equation pattern for carbonate-acid reactions

en: To write a formula equation for a carbonate and acid reaction, scientists write the carbonate formula, plus acid formula, yields salt, H2O, and CO2.
source: standard formula equation pattern for carbonate-acid reactions

en: To describe a combustion reaction, scientists write the fuel name plus oxygen yields carbon dioxide and water.
source: standard word equation pattern for combustion reactions

en: To write a formula equation for a combustion reaction, scientists write the fuel formula plus O2 yields CO2 and H2O.
source: standard formula equation pattern for combustion reactions

en: Scientists write a word equation for a reaction that produces a precipitate, like lead nitrate plus potassium iodide yields lead iodide and potassium nitrate.
source: standard word equation example for precipitation reactions

en: To write a formula equation for a precipitate reaction, scientists write Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI → PbI2 + 2KNO3.
source: standard formula equation example for precipitation reactions

en: Scientists write a word equation for a reaction that produces a gas, like hydrogen peroxide yields water and oxygen.
source: standard decomposition reaction example producing a gas

en: Peel a thin, single layer of onion skin and lay it flat on the slide to see its box-like plant cells clearly.
source: standard microscope specimen preparation for plant cells

en: A drop of iodine on onion cells makes the nucleus stand out as a dark brown or blue spot inside the cytoplasm.
source: standard staining technique; iodine binds to starch and reveals cell structures

en: Gently scrape the inside of your cheek with a clean cotton swab and smear it on a slide to see animal cells.
source: standard technique for observing human epithelial cells

en: Methylene blue dye stains the nucleus of cheek cells blue, making it easy to spot among the lighter cytoplasm.
source: standard staining protocol for animal cells

en: Start with the lowest power objective to find your specimen, then switch to higher power to see details like mitochondria.
Use the coarse focus knob only with the low power lens to bring the specimen into rough view without crashing the lens.
source: standard microscope safety and focusing protocol

en: After rough focusing, turn the fine focus knob slowly to make the cell membrane and nucleus look sharp and clear.
Adjust the diaphragm to control the light passing through the slide, so the cell parts are not too dark or too bright.
Cut or tear the specimen very thin so light can pass through it, making the internal parts visible under the lens.
A good observation record includes a labeled drawing of the cell parts and the magnification number of the lens used.
source: standard scientific observation and documentation practice

en: Under a microscope, plant cells show a stiff, rectangular outer wall, while animal cells appear rounder with only a thin membrane.
source: encyclopedia-stable; difference between plant and animal cell structure

en: Look at a thin strand of pond algae to see green chloroplasts moving slowly inside the cells without any staining.
source: standard observation of living plant cells; chloroplasts are naturally pigmented

en: Mitochondria are tiny and almost colorless, so you need high power and good lighting to see their rod-like shapes.
source: encyclopedia-stable; mitochondria are small and require high magnification

en: Wipe the glass slide and coverslip clean before use, because dust or fingerprints can look like cell parts under the microscope.
Lower the coverslip at a 45-degree angle onto the water drop to push air bubbles out and keep the view clear.
source: standard wet mount technique to avoid air bubbles

en: Always center the specimen in the middle of the low power view before switching to high power so it stays in sight.
source: standard microscope procedure to keep specimen in field of view

en: Use special lens paper to wipe the microscope lenses, because other cloths can scratch the glass and blur the image.
Compare an onion cell and a cheek cell side by side to see that both have a nucleus, but only the onion has a cell wall.
source: standard comparative observation of plant and animal cells

en: In a living cell, you may see tiny particles moving in the cytoplasm, which shows that the cell is active and not dead.
source: observable characteristic of living cells under a microscope

en: Write down the magnification number, like 100x or 400x, next to your drawing so others know how big the cells looked.
source: standard scientific documentation of microscope observations

en: To compare soil fertility, scientists take soil samples from GMO and non-GMO fields and test them for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium.
To prepare for a debate, students read at least three scientific articles and write down the main claim and evidence from each.
To test water quality near a biotech farm, scientists collect water samples and measure the amount of dissolved oxygen and nitrates.
To score a debate, judges use a rubric that rates each team on clarity, evidence, and respect for the other side.
To compare profit, farmers record the money spent on seeds and pesticides and the money earned from selling GMO and non-GMO harvests.
Using a dichotomous key is a process of elimination, where each answered question removes whole groups of rocks from the list.
A hand lens magnifies small grains so you can see texture and tiny crystals that the eye alone misses.
Before using the key, sort the rock samples into rough piles by one big feature, such as having layers or not.
The key uses only features of the rock itself, never where it was found or what it is called.
Household vinegar is a safe acid for the fizz test, bubbling on rocks that contain calcite.
source: encyclopedia-stable; calcite reacts with weak acids

en: Lifting a rock to feel if it is heavy for its size hints that it contains dense minerals like iron.
If neither choice in a pair fits your rock, go back one step and look at the rock again with fresh eyes.
Before starting the key, write each rock's features in a table so you do not forget what you saw.
Describe a rock's grain size by comparing it to everyday things like sand, salt, or sugar.
A dichotomous key starts with broad features like layers, then uses finer details to narrow the name.
Many different kinds of rocks share the same color, so color alone can never identify a rock.
A rock is a mixture of minerals, so the key asks about the whole rock's features, not one crystal.
Luster, whether a rock shines like metal or looks dull, is a feature that helps you choose between questions.
Having a partner read the key aloud while you observe the rock helps catch careless mistakes.
Wash and dry a dirty rock first so dust and mud do not hide its true color and texture.
If you classify the same rock on two different days, you should get the same name by following the same steps.
Measuring the largest grain with a ruler helps you decide if the rock is coarse grained or fine grained.
Every question in a dichotomous key asks about something you can see or test on the rock, never its name.
After the key names a rock, write the name on a small label and attach it to the sample.
source: museum and lab specimen labeling practice

en: The same dichotomous key works on rocks from any place, including volcanic rocks found near Taal and Mayon.
source: PHIVOLCS; volcanic rocks of Taal and Mayon

en: Oceanic crust is the thin, heavy rock that forms the sea floor, made mostly of a dark rock called basalt.
Continental crust is the thick, lighter rock that makes up the land we live on, composed mostly of granite.
Earthquakes mostly happen where Earth's plates push, pull, or slide past each other, because the rocks suddenly break and shake.
When two pieces of continental crust collide, neither sinks, so they crumple and fold upward to form tall mountain belts like the Himalayas.
Where oceanic crust sinks under continental crust, earthquakes can happen deep underground, far below the surface, because the slab keeps breaking.
A curved chain of volcanoes, called a volcanic arc, builds up on the continental crust directly above where the oceanic plate slides down.
The Ring of Fire is a huge horse-shoe shaped belt around the Pacific Ocean where many volcanoes and earthquakes are found.
PHIVOLCS is the Philippine agency that maps active volcanoes and faults, helping people know where earthquakes and eruptions may happen.
Taal volcano sits inside a lake on Luzon, and its location is linked to the crack where two tectonic plates meet nearby.
New oceanic crust is made at mid-ocean ridges, while old oceanic crust sinks back into the Earth at deep ocean trenches.
Continental crust floats higher on the mantle because it is less dense, which is why it stays above sea level.
The Andes mountains in South America formed where the dense oceanic Nazca plate dives beneath the lighter continental crust.
The Mariana Trench is the deepest part of the ocean, where heavy oceanic crust bends and sinks down into the mantle.
If you plot all earthquake epicenters on a world map, they form narrow bands that trace the edges of Earth's tectonic plates.
Volcanoes are not scattered randomly; they line up along the cracks between plates, which is why they form long chains.
The Philippines sits where the Philippine Sea Plate and the Eurasian Plate push against each other, causing many earthquakes and volcanoes.
Where oceanic crust sinks, it drags the sea floor down to form a deep trench, like a giant underwater crack.
Major mountain belts on land, like the Alps, are found where continents have crashed into each other over millions of years.
A few earthquakes happen far from plate edges, inside a single plate, when old faults deep in the crust suddenly slip.
The youngest oceanic crust is found near mid-ocean ridges, and the oldest is found far away near the edges of continents.
A water cycle model works best in a clear plastic container, because you can see the vapor, drops, and water level without opening it.
source: model design: transparency needed for observation

en: Place a small cup inside the model under the sloped cover, so the drops that fall are collected and can be measured as precipitation.
source: model construction: collecting output for measurement

en: Wipe the inside of the container dry before sealing it, so any droplets that appear later are new condensation and not leftover water.
Stretch the plastic wrap tight across the top of the model, so condensed drops roll down instead of hanging in place.
source: model construction: directing condensed water flow

en: Put a white paper behind the model so the clear water drops and the changing water level are easier to see and record.
source: observation technique: contrast for clear liquids

en: Set the model on a flat, level surface so the water spreads evenly and the collected drops gather in one predictable corner.
source: model setup: even distribution and predictable collection

en: Use warm water from the tap, not boiling water, so the model heats up safely and evaporation still happens quickly.
Draw arrows on the outside of the container to show the path of water from liquid to vapor to drops and back.
source: communicating the model: visual flow path

en: Use a small dropper or syringe to measure the water collected in the cup, so you can compare precipitation between trials.
source: measurement technique: small volumes of water

en: Leave the model in a sunny spot for a whole day, so you can observe all four stages happen in order from morning to afternoon.
source: observation duration: capturing the full cycle

en: Run the same water cycle model twice and compare the results, because repeating a test shows that the findings are dependable.
To test wind, place one model near a fan and another in still air, keeping the water amount and container exactly the same.
source: fair test design: changing one variable (wind)

en: Place the model where it gets steady sunlight all morning, because moving shade changes the heat and makes the results uneven.
Before starting, write a prediction of which part of the model will show condensation first, then check it against your observations.
Add a drop of food coloring to the water in the model, so you can trace the path of the liquid as it moves through the cycle.
A good observation table has columns for time, water level, number of drops, and temperature, so all changes are recorded together.
Seal the edges of the plastic wrap with tape so no vapor escapes, which keeps the water inside and the cycle complete.
source: model construction: airtight seal for closed system

en: A bar graph of the drops collected each hour shows how precipitation changes over time, with taller bars meaning more rain.
source: data representation: bar graph for precipitation over time

en: Use a pencil and write the date and time on every observation page, so your records stay clear and can be corrected easily.
source: data recording practice: clear and editable records

en: Liquid particles slide past each other, so a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
source: encyclopedia-stable; kinetic molecular theory of liquids

en: Most of a gas is empty space, because its particles are spread so far apart that they barely bump into each other.
When a solid melts, heat makes its particles vibrate faster until they break free from their fixed positions.
Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid when some particles gain enough energy to escape into the air.
In a solid, particles are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern, while in liquids and gases the arrangement is random.
Water boils at about 100 degrees Celsius, when liquid particles throughout the water gain enough energy to form bubbles of gas.
source: boiling point of water at sea level, encyclopedia-stable

en: Condensation is when gas particles lose energy, slow down, and stick together to form a liquid, like drops on a cold glass.
Freezing happens when a liquid cools and its particles slow down enough to lock into fixed positions, forming a solid.
Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide that turns directly into gas without melting, a process called sublimation.
Frost on leaves forms when water vapor in the air turns directly into ice without becoming liquid first.
Gas particles have the most energy, liquid particles have less, and solid particles have the least energy of all.
source: encyclopedia-stable; energy levels of particle states

en: In a gas, particles are about ten times farther apart from each other than in a liquid or solid.
source: rounded value for gas vs liquid particle spacing

en: Even in ice, particles still vibrate in place, so cold does not completely stop their motion.
source: encyclopedia-stable; particles in ice vibrate in place

en: A drop of food coloring spreads through water because moving liquid particles bump into the color and carry it around.
The smell of cooking adobo spreads through the house because gas particles from the food move and mix with the air.
A solid has a fixed shape and volume, a liquid has fixed volume but takes the container's shape, and a gas takes both.
source: encyclopedia-stable; shape and volume of states

en: Gas particles move in straight lines until they collide with each other or with the walls of their container.
Ice floats on water because water particles arrange in a more open pattern when frozen, making ice less dense.
When PAGASA reports rain, water vapor in clouds condenses into droplets that grow heavy enough to fall.
source: PAGASA weather reporting; condensation in clouds

en: Hot lava from Mayon volcano cools and solidifies into rock as its particles slow down and lock into place.
source: PHIVOLCS / encyclopedia-stable; lava cooling to rock

en: To communicate a water cycle model, point to each stage and name it, like saying 'this is evaporation' while showing the vapor.
source: method of verbal labeling during model presentation

en: To show the cycle as a loop, trace one drop of water from the bottom to the top and back down again.
source: method of demonstrating a continuous cycle by following a particle path

en: To measure how fast the cycle works, note the time from placing the model in the sun until the first drop falls.
source: method of measuring cycle rate using time-to-first-event

en: The plastic wrap in the model stands for the cool upper air where real clouds form, so its condensation mimics cloud formation.
source: analogy between model component and atmospheric layer

en: To predict the next stage, watch the water level drop and the vapor appear, then say 'condensation will happen next'.
source: method of predicting the next stage from observed evidence

topic: showing the cycle has no end
en: To show the cycle has no start or end, move your finger around the model in a circle, following the water's path.
source: method of demonstrating the cyclic nature of the water cycle

en: Total magnification is the eyepiece lens power times the objective lens power, so a 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective gives 400x.
Under a compound microscope, the image is upside down and reversed, so moving the slide left makes the image move right.
The stage clips hold the slide firmly on the stage so the specimen stays in place while focusing.
For a long observation, a drop of water is added at the edge of the coverslip to keep the specimen from drying out.
To see chloroplasts, a thin layer from the underside of a leaf is peeled and mounted in a drop of water on a slide.
To see the cell membrane clearly, the diaphragm is closed a little to reduce light and make the outline stand out.
Digestion breaks down food into nutrients, and excretion removes the waste products that the body cannot use.
The small intestine absorbs digested food into the blood, and the blood then carries these nutrients to every cell.
The kidneys filter blood to remove urea and extra water, making urine that leaves the body.
The liver makes bile to help digest fats, and it also turns harmful ammonia into urea for the kidneys to remove.

topic: large intestine and kidney water balance
en: The large intestine absorbs water from leftover food, while the kidneys also balance water to keep your blood just right.
Your lungs are part of excretion because they release carbon dioxide, a waste gas made by your cells.
The skin excretes sweat, which carries out water, salt, and a little urea, helping cool the body.
The digestive system gives glucose to the blood, the respiratory system gives oxygen, and the excretory system takes away the wastes.
The pancreas sends enzymes to the small intestine to finish digestion, and it also sends hormones to control blood sugar.
The kidneys filter about 180 liters of blood each day, but they send only about 1 to 2 liters out as urine.
source: published values for renal filtration and urine output

en: The urinary tract is a tube system—kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra—that works together to store and remove urine.
When you drink a lot of water, the kidneys make more urine so the amount of water in your blood stays balanced.
The small intestine has tiny finger-like villi that give it a huge surface area to absorb digested food into the blood.
Digestion and excretion both depend on the circulatory system to carry nutrients to cells and wastes away from them.
The liver breaks down proteins into urea, and then the kidneys filter that urea out of the blood to make urine.
The digestive system turns food into molecules your cells can use, while the excretory system removes what your cells cannot use.
A flow chart of digestion shows food moving from mouth to stomach to small intestine, where nutrients enter the blood.
The large intestine forms solid waste from undigested food, while the kidneys form liquid waste from extra water and toxins.
The circulatory system connects digestion and excretion by picking up nutrients from the gut and dropping off wastes at the kidneys.
The kidneys work with the lungs to keep your blood's pH stable, removing acids and balancing carbon dioxide levels.
Gas pressure comes from countless tiny particles hitting the inside walls of a container, each collision giving a small push.
source: kinetic molecular theory: gas pressure from particle impacts

en: When a substance is heated, its particles gain energy and move faster; when cooled, they slow down and move closer together.
source: temperature as average kinetic energy of particles

en: Strong forces hold solid particles in fixed positions, weaker forces allow liquid particles to slide, and gas particles have almost no forces pulling them together.
source: intermolecular forces in states of matter

en: Most substances expand when heated because their particles move faster and spread farther apart, taking up more space.
source: thermal expansion due to increased particle motion

en: The Manila Trench and the Philippine Trench are subduction zones on opposite sides of the Philippines, with the Eurasian Plate diving east and the Philippine Sea Plate diving west.
Marine fossils found on Philippine mountain tops prove that these rocks were once under the ocean, pushed upward by plate collisions.
The Philippine Sea Plate is an oceanic plate, so it is denser than the continental crust, which makes it sink beneath the Philippine Mobile Belt at the Philippine Trench.
source: plate tectonics; oceanic vs continental crust density

en: The Philippine archipelago is still growing as new volcanic islands form from eruptions along the subduction zones, adding land over millions of years.
source: plate tectonics; ongoing volcanic activity in Philippines

en: In the Philippines, shallow earthquakes happen along the fault zones, while deep earthquakes happen near the trenches, showing two different boundary types.
The Philippine Trench is about 10,000 meters deep, which is deeper than Mount Everest is tall, showing how much the seafloor bends at a subduction zone.
The Philippines has about two dozen active volcanoes, many of which are located along the plate boundaries, making it one of the most volcanic countries on Earth.
The Philippine archipelago is an island arc, a curved chain of volcanic islands formed above a subduction zone.
When one oceanic plate slides under another, the melted rock builds a curved chain of volcanic islands called an island arc, like the Philippines.
source: plate tectonics: oceanic-oceanic subduction creates island arcs

en: At boundaries where plates slide sideways past each other, earthquakes are common but volcanoes are not, because no crust melts.
source: plate tectonics: transform boundaries lack volcanism

en: Oceanic crust is always being recycled at trenches, so it is never older than about 200 million years, while continental crust can be billions of years old.
source: geology: published values for crustal age and recycling

en: Major mountain belts like the Himalayas mark old continental collisions, while active volcanoes and earthquakes show where plates are moving today.
source: geology: mountain belts are ancient collision zones

en: At the top of its swing, a pendulum has mostly potential energy and almost no kinetic energy; at the bottom, it has mostly kinetic and almost no potential.
A stretched rubber band has elastic potential energy, and when released, that stored energy becomes kinetic energy that can fling a small stone.
A hydroelectric dam stores water high up, giving it gravitational potential energy; when the water falls, that energy becomes kinetic and spins turbines to make electricity.
A jeepney rolling down a hill speeds up because its gravitational potential energy is turning into kinetic energy.
A bouncing basketball loses a little mechanical energy to heat and sound each time, so it never bounces back to its original height.
A 1-kilogram ball held 10 meters high has about 100 joules of potential energy, which is part of its mechanical energy.
A 1-kilogram ball moving at 2 meters per second has about 2 joules of kinetic energy, which is part of its mechanical energy.
A wind-up toy stores mechanical energy in a spring; as the spring unwinds, that potential energy becomes kinetic energy that moves the toy.
A pendulum clock uses the mechanical energy of a swinging weight or spring to keep time, showing how stored energy does work.
A basketball thrown upward slows down as its kinetic energy becomes potential energy, then speeds up as potential becomes kinetic on the way down.
The mechanical energy of an object depends on the reference point you choose for height, so the same ball can have different potential energies.
source: physics: reference point for potential energy

en: Real pendulums slowly lose mechanical energy to air resistance, so they eventually stop swinging on their own.
source: physics: air resistance and energy loss

en: A windmill's blades have mechanical energy from their motion, and that energy can turn a generator to produce electricity.
A jeepney going up a hill slows down because kinetic energy is being converted into potential energy.
source: physics: kinetic to potential on incline

en: The mechanical energy of an object can be zero if it has no motion and no height relative to a chosen reference point.
A battery stores chemical energy, not mechanical energy, but a motor can turn that chemical energy into mechanical energy to move a toy car.
The unit of mechanical energy is the joule, and one joule is about the energy needed to lift a small apple one meter.
A book on a high shelf has more mechanical energy than the same book on a low shelf, because its potential energy is greater.
source: physics: potential energy depends on height

en: A lever uses mechanical energy to lift a heavy load, converting the energy of your push into work on the load.
A compressed spring has potential energy because of its shape; when released, it can push a ball, turning that stored energy into kinetic energy.
source: physics: elastic potential energy in spring

en: During transpiration, plants lose water vapor from their leaves into the air, which adds moisture to the water cycle.
Animals return water to the air when they breathe out and sweat, so they also help keep the water cycle moving.
Trees and other plants store carbon in their trunks, branches, and leaves, so forests act like big carbon banks for the planet.
When animals breathe out, they release carbon dioxide gas into the air, which plants then use for photosynthesis.
Most of the oxygen in the air comes from green plants and tiny ocean algae, which make it during photosynthesis.
Burning wood or fuel uses up oxygen from the air, just like animals do when they breathe, so fire and life compete for the same gas.
The sun's heat is the engine of the water cycle, because it turns liquid water into vapor that rises into the sky.
source: textbook-stable; solar energy drives water cycle

en: High in the sky, cool air turns invisible water vapor into tiny droplets that group together to form clouds.
When cloud droplets get too heavy, they fall back to the ground as rain or snow, which refills rivers and lakes.
When plants and animals die, tiny decomposers break them down and release the stored carbon back into the air.
Coal, oil, and natural gas are ancient plants and animals that stored carbon for millions of years, and burning them releases it.
When a jeepney burns gasoline or diesel, it releases carbon dioxide into the air, adding to the carbon cycle from human activity.
Mangrove forests, called bakawan in the Philippines, store large amounts of carbon in their roots and muddy soil.
Plants give off oxygen that animals need to breathe, while animals give off carbon dioxide that plants need to grow.
Plants pull water up from the soil through their roots, and that water eventually travels up to their leaves to be released.
Animals drink water and later release it through urine and sweat, so they carry water across the land as they move.
Cutting down too many trees means less carbon is absorbed from the air, so more carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere.
Oxygen makes up about 21 percent of the air around us, and that amount stays steady because of the oxygen cycle.
Photosynthesis stores energy from the sun into food, while respiration releases that energy so animals and plants can live.
Rainwater that falls on land soaks into the ground or flows into rivers, lakes, and oceans, where it can evaporate again.
A fair test of soil types keeps the same kind of seed, same pot size, and same water, changing only the soil.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, rest held constant

en: In a soil experiment, plant the same number of seeds at the same depth in each pot of different soil.
source: standard procedure for controlled plant experiments

en: Use a ruler to measure the height of each plant stem every few days and record the numbers.
source: common measurement in plant growth studies

en: Count the number of leaves on each plant as another way to compare growth among soil types.
Water each pot with the same amount of water, using a measuring cup, at the same time each day.
Place all pots in the same sunny spot so each plant gets equal light and temperature.
Label each pot with its soil type, like sand, clay, or loam, to avoid mixing up the data.
After two weeks, compare the average plant height in each soil type to see which grew best.
Repeat the experiment with three seeds per pot and take the average to make results more reliable.
Draw a bar graph with soil types on the bottom and average plant height on the side to show results.
Gently remove a plant from its pot at the end to observe root growth differences between soil types.
Use the same amount of soil in each pot, just different types, so the volume is equal.
Keep the same type of pot with the same drainage holes so water drains equally in all setups.
Use a hand lens to observe tiny differences in plant leaves grown in different soils.
Start all seeds on the same day so every plant has the same number of growing days.
source: controlled start time for fair comparison

en: Write down the color and firmness of leaves as qualitative data to support the measurements.
If the plant in loam grows tallest, the result shows loam is better for that plant's growth.
The crust is the thinnest layer of Earth, like the skin of an apple compared with the whole fruit, and it is only about 5 to 70 kilometers thick.
The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell of Earth, made of the crust and the stiff upper part of the mantle.
The asthenosphere is a soft, slowly flowing layer beneath the lithosphere, and the plates of Earth's surface move on top of it.
source: mechanical layers of Earth; plate tectonics

en: The outer core is a liquid layer of iron and nickel about 2,200 kilometers thick, and it lies below the mantle.
The inner core is a solid ball of iron and nickel about 1,200 kilometers thick, kept solid by enormous pressure.
The crust is only about 5 to 70 kilometers thick, while the mantle below it is about 2,900 kilometers thick.
A scale drawing shows real sizes in a smaller, matching way by using one fixed ratio for every part of the picture.
source: scale drawing concept; math and science

en: To make a scale drawing, divide each layer's real thickness by the scale number, then draw that many centimeters on paper.
source: scale drawing procedure; math and science

en: If the crust is 30 kilometers thick and the scale is 1 centimeter per 100 kilometers, it is only 0.3 centimeter on paper.
The mantle is roughly 2,900 kilometers thick, so in a scale drawing it takes up far more space than the crust.
source: Earth layer thicknesses; scale drawing comparison

en: The lithosphere is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates, and these plates carry the continents and oceans.
The asthenosphere is hot and partly melted, which lets the rigid lithosphere above it slide slowly.
source: mechanical layers of Earth; plate tectonics

en: Earth's core has a radius of about 3,500 kilometers, and it is divided into a liquid outer part and a solid inner part.
The crust under the ocean is thinner, about 5 to 10 kilometers, while the crust under continents is about 30 to 70 kilometers thick.
In a scale drawing of Earth's layers, the crust appears as a very thin line next to the thick mantle and core.
PHIVOLCS studies earthquakes and volcanoes in the Philippines, which come from movements of the lithosphere above the asthenosphere.
The Moho is the boundary between the crust and the mantle, and scientists found it by studying how earthquake waves travel.
Earth is not solid all the way through; the outer core is liquid iron and nickel that flows around the solid inner core.
The inner core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, making it one of the hottest parts of Earth.
When drawing Earth's layers, use the same scale for every layer so their true sizes can be compared on one page.
Loam is a mixture of sand, silt, and clay, so it holds water well but still lets extra water drain away.
Silt particles are smaller than sand but larger than clay, and dry silt feels smooth like flour.
In a water-holding test, clay keeps the most water, sand keeps the least, and loam stays in between.
Loam is often the best soil for garden plants because it holds enough water for roots but still lets air reach them.
source: soil suitability for plant growth; encyclopedia-stable

en: Silt feels smooth and slippery when wet, like wet flour, and it holds more water than sand but less than clay.
The spaces between soil particles are called pores, and water sits in these pores where plant roots can reach it.
Clay can hold water so tightly that some plant roots struggle to pull the water out of the tiny pores.
source: soil water availability to plants; encyclopedia-stable

en: Sandy soil feels gritty between your fingers because its grains are large and rough, unlike smooth silt.
Silt is often carried by rivers and settles on floodplains when the water slows down, making the soil rich.
Loam feels crumbly and soft, not sticky like clay or gritty like sand, and it holds its shape when squeezed.
To compare soils, put the same amount of each soil in a funnel and time how long the water takes to drip out.
source: simple soil water-holding experiment; class activity

en: Soil is made of tiny pieces of weathered rock mixed with dead leaves and other decayed matter.
Farmers choose crops by soil type — rice loves clay-rich paddies, while root crops grow better in loose sandy soil.
In the Philippines, rice paddies are often built on clay-rich soil because it keeps water standing for the rice.
Sandy soil near the coast drains fast, so plants there must survive with little water between rains.
Clay soil is used to make pots and bricks because it is sticky and holds its shape when wet.
source: clay use in pottery and construction; encyclopedia-stable

en: When you squeeze wet soil, sandy soil falls apart, clay soil stays in a tight ball, and loam holds a soft shape.
Loam has both big and small pores, so it drains well yet still stores water for plants.
source: soil pore size and water retention; encyclopedia-stable

en: Soil that holds too much water can drown plant roots, because roots need air as well as water.
source: soil aeration and root health; encyclopedia-stable

en: A soil's texture tells you how much sand, silt, and clay it has, and texture controls how it feels and holds water.
A classification table has rows and columns, so you can line up living things and see which characteristics they share.
Flowering plants like rice and mango make seeds inside fruits that grow from their flowers, which are the plant's reproductive parts.
Mosses are non-flowering plants that reproduce by releasing tiny spores instead of seeds, and these spores can grow into new mosses.
Mammals have hair or fur on their bodies and use lungs to breathe air, even if they live in water like whales.
Reptiles have dry, scaly skin and lay eggs with leathery shells, like snakes and turtles, and they are cold-blooded.
Insects have three body parts and six legs, and they wear a hard outer shell called an exoskeleton.
Birds are the only animals with feathers, and they lay eggs with hard shells, like chickens and eagles.
Fish live in water, breathe with gills, and use fins to swim, like tilapia and bangus, and they have scales.
Amphibians have moist, smooth skin that helps them breathe, and they usually stay near water, like frogs and toads.
Fungi like mushrooms and molds are living things that break down dead plants and animals, and they do not make their own food.
Bacteria are tiny single-celled living things so small that you need a microscope to see them.
A classification table lets you check each living thing's characteristics, like whether it has feathers, fur, or scales.
Whales are mammals, not fish, because they breathe air with lungs and have hair on their bodies.
Mangroves, called bakawan in Filipino, are flowering plants that grow in salty coastal water and have special roots.
Microorganisms include fungi and bacteria, and they are too small to see without a microscope, living in soil and water.
Insects have no backbone, while mammals, reptiles, birds, fish, and amphibians all have backbones, so insects are invertebrates.
Plants are classified as flowering or non-flowering by whether they produce flowers and seeds, like mango versus moss.
To classify an animal, you can ask if it has feathers, fur, scales, or moist skin, and then compare with a table.
Some bacteria are helpful, like the ones that turn milk into yogurt, and these bacteria are safe to eat.
A table can show that a frog and a fish are different because one has moist skin and the other has scales.
Muscles in your esophagus and intestines squeeze food along in waves called peristalsis, so food moves even if you are standing on your head.
source: encyclopedia-stable; smooth muscle contractions of the digestive tract

en: The gallbladder is a small pouch that stores bile from the liver and releases it into the small intestine when you eat fatty food.
Your stomach makes strong acid that kills most germs in food and helps break down proteins into smaller pieces for digestion.
Each kidney contains about one million tiny filters called nephrons that clean your blood and produce the urine you pee out.
source: encyclopedia-stable; kidney nephron count ~1 million per kidney

en: The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle below your lungs, moves for breathing and also gently pushes on your stomach and intestines.
The liver stores extra glucose from meals as glycogen and releases it between meals to keep your blood sugar steady.
source: encyclopedia-stable; liver glucose storage as glycogen

en: Tiny lymph vessels in the small intestine pick up digested fats that are too big to go straight into the blood.
source: encyclopedia-stable; lacteals in intestinal villi absorb fats

en: Your body's cells constantly produce waste as they use energy, and the blood collects it for the kidneys and lungs to remove.
source: encyclopedia-stable; cellular metabolism produces waste products

en: The rectum stores solid waste until it leaves the body through the anus, the last stop of the digestive tract.
The kidneys also make a hormone that tells your bone marrow to make more red blood cells when oxygen is low.
source: encyclopedia-stable; erythropoietin from kidneys stimulates red blood cell production

en: Your brain can tell your stomach to make acid even before you eat, just from seeing or smelling food.
Chewing tears food into smaller pieces while saliva in your mouth starts breaking down starch into sugar.
Your small intestine is about six meters long and coiled in your belly, giving digested food plenty of room to be absorbed.
source: encyclopedia-stable; small intestine ~6 m in adults

en: Helpful bacteria in the large intestine make some vitamins, like vitamin K, which your body absorbs from the leftover food.
source: encyclopedia-stable; gut microbiota produce vitamin K

en: The kidneys help control blood pressure by deciding how much water stays in your blood and how much leaves as urine.
source: encyclopedia-stable; kidneys regulate blood volume and pressure

en: The esophagus is a muscular tube that pushes swallowed food from your throat down to your stomach in a few seconds.
Your digestive tract is one long tube from mouth to anus, with different sections doing different jobs along the way.
The liver does hundreds of jobs, including making bile, storing vitamins, cleaning the blood, and processing nutrients from food.
source: encyclopedia-stable; liver has many metabolic functions

en: Excretion removes waste made by your cells, while defecation removes undigested food that never entered your blood.
source: encyclopedia-stable; distinction between excretion and defecation

en: Mucus lines your stomach and intestines to protect them from acid and help food slide through smoothly.
source: encyclopedia-stable; mucosal lining of digestive tract

en: First, pick one object to study and ignore everything else so only the forces on that object appear.
source: free-body diagram method: isolate one object

en: Before drawing any arrows, list every force acting on the object so you do not leave one out.
source: free-body diagram method: identify all forces before drawing

en: Label each arrow with short letters like F_g for gravity and F_N for normal force so the diagram is clear.
source: free-body diagram convention: label force vectors

en: Gravity's arrow always points straight down toward the center of Earth, no matter how the object is tilted.
The normal force arrow points perpendicular to the surface, meaning it makes a 90-degree angle with the surface.
source: normal force is perpendicular to contact surface

en: Friction's arrow points opposite to the direction the object moves or tries to move across a surface.
Tension arrows point along the rope or string, pulling away from the object at the point where they attach.
Use a ruler to draw arrows so that forces of equal size have exactly the same arrow length.
source: free-body diagram drawing: equal forces, equal arrow lengths

en: To check if forces are balanced, compare arrows pointing in opposite directions and see if their lengths match.
source: free-body diagram analysis: compare opposite arrows

en: If one arrow is longer than the arrow pointing opposite it, that force is unbalanced and the object will accelerate.
source: unbalanced force causes acceleration (Newton's second law)

en: After comparing, draw one separate arrow to show the net force, pointing where the longer arrows point.
source: net force is the vector sum of forces

en: On graph paper, let one square or one centimeter stand for one newton so arrow lengths match force sizes.
source: drawing to scale on graph paper (classroom convention)

en: Check your finished diagram by asking whether the object would stay still, speed up, or slow down from those arrows.
source: free-body diagram check: predict motion from arrows

en: Keep the dot near the center of the paper so every force arrow has enough room to point in its direction.
source: free-body diagram layout: leave room for all arrows

en: After drawing all arrows, count the forces you listed at the start to make sure none is missing from the diagram.
source: free-body diagram verification: match arrows to initial list

en: Include only forces acting ON the object, not forces the object itself exerts on other things.
source: free-body diagram includes only forces on the object

en: When two opposite arrows are exactly equal in length, those two forces are balanced and cancel each other out.
For a lamp hanging still from a ceiling, draw the tension arrow upward and the gravity arrow downward at equal lengths.
source: example: hanging lamp at rest (balanced forces)

en: For a jeepney speeding up on a flat road, draw the forward friction arrow longer than the backward air resistance arrow.
Before planting, sift each soil type to remove stones and large clumps so all pots start with similar texture.
Use seeds from the same packet to ensure all plants have the same genetic background.
Place the pots in a random order on the shelf so no single spot favors one soil type.
Rotate the pots a quarter turn every two days so each plant gets equal light from all sides.
Write all measurements in a table with rows for days and columns for each soil type.
Calculate the average growth per day by dividing the height change by the number of days.
Use a line graph to show how plant height changes over time for each soil type.
Compare the thickness of the main stem by wrapping a string around it and measuring the string.
Count only fully opened leaves, not tiny buds, each time to get a consistent leaf count.
Weigh the same amount of dry soil for each pot before adding water to ensure equal mass.
Use a spray bottle to water gently so the soil surface is not disturbed or seeds uncovered.
Place a tray under each pot to catch excess water and check that drainage is equal.
After the experiment, dry the plants in an oven and weigh them to compare total biomass.
Use a soil moisture meter to check that all pots have similar wetness before watering.
Take a photo of each pot at the same distance and angle each week to document growth.
After washing away the soil, measure the length of the longest root with a ruler.
Compare the number of days to flowering if the plants are allowed to grow longer.
Oceans absorb carbon dioxide from the air, acting as a huge carbon sink that helps keep the carbon cycle balanced.
The water molecules on Earth have been cycling for billions of years, so the water you drink is the same water dinosaurs drank.
Plants respire at night, releasing carbon dioxide, but during the day their photosynthesis makes more oxygen than they use.
Most of the water vapor in the air comes from the oceans, because they cover most of the Earth's surface.
When animals eat plants, the carbon in the plant's body becomes part of the animal, moving carbon through the food chain.
source: ecology; carbon transfer in food webs

en: Oxygen gas dissolves in water, which is how fish and other aquatic animals breathe underwater.
Wind carries clouds across the sky, so water vapor from one place can fall as rain somewhere else.
Rusting is a slow reaction that uses up oxygen from the air, just like burning but much slower.
Groundwater slowly moves through soil and rocks, eventually reaching rivers and oceans to complete the water cycle.
Marine animals like clams use dissolved carbon dioxide to build their shells, storing carbon in the ocean.
Respiration is the process where living things break down food for energy, releasing carbon dioxide as a waste product.
The water cycle is a closed loop: water never leaves Earth, it just changes from liquid to gas and back.
Volcanoes release carbon dioxide from deep inside the Earth, adding natural carbon to the atmosphere.
Planting trees adds more leaves that absorb carbon dioxide, helping to pull extra CO2 out of the air.
The carbon cycle has fast parts like photosynthesis and respiration, and slow parts like fossil fuel formation.
Decomposers use oxygen when they break down dead plants and animals, so they also take part in the oxygen cycle.
Tropical rainforests, like those in the Philippines, are major oxygen producers because of their many trees.
When water evaporates from the ocean, it leaves behind salts, which is why the ocean stays salty.
Animals that eat other animals get carbon from their prey, so carbon moves up the food chain.
Flooded rice paddies in the Philippines release methane, a carbon compound that adds to the greenhouse effect.
Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving, and a faster object has more kinetic energy than a slower one of the same mass.
Potential energy is stored energy that an object has because of its position or shape, like a ball held above the ground.
When you push a toy car, your work adds kinetic energy to the car, so its mechanical energy increases.
A roller coaster car at the top of a hill has mostly potential energy, which becomes kinetic energy as it speeds down the track.
source: encyclopedia-stable; energy conversion on a roller coaster

en: If you double an object's speed, its kinetic energy becomes about four times larger, because speed is squared in the formula.
source: kinetic energy formula KE = 1/2 mv^2; encyclopedia-stable

en: A heavier object at the same height has more gravitational potential energy than a lighter object, because weight is part of the stored energy.
Kinetic energy is energy in action, while potential energy is stored energy waiting to be released.

topic: lifting a box adds potential energy
en: Lifting a box from the floor to a table does work on the box, giving it more potential energy and more mechanical energy.
When a car brakes, its kinetic energy changes into heat in the brakes, so the car's mechanical energy decreases.
A water wheel turns because flowing water transfers its kinetic energy to the wheel, and that mechanical energy can power a rice mill.
When a moving marble hits a resting marble, some mechanical energy is transferred to the resting marble, making it move.
source: momentum and energy transfer in collisions; encyclopedia-stable

topic: mass and speed determine kinetic energy
en: The kinetic energy of an object depends on both its mass and its speed, so a heavy slow object can have the same kinetic energy as a light fast one.
source: kinetic energy formula KE = 1/2 mv^2; encyclopedia-stable

en: On the Moon, where gravity is weaker, the same ball at the same height has less gravitational potential energy than on Earth.
source: gravitational potential energy depends on g; encyclopedia-stable

en: At the middle of its swing, a pendulum has both kinetic and potential energy, because it is moving and still has some height.
Mechanical energy is not the same as force; a force is a push or pull, while mechanical energy is the energy that can do work.
source: distinction between force and energy; encyclopedia-stable

en: A moving hammer has kinetic energy, and when it hits a nail, that mechanical energy does work by driving the nail into wood.
source: work done by moving object; encyclopedia-stable

en: A ceiling fan's spinning blades have mechanical energy from motion, and that energy moves air around the room.
source: mechanical energy of rotating blades; encyclopedia-stable

en: Kinetic energy is always zero or positive, never negative, because an object either moves or it does not.
source: kinetic energy is a scalar, always >= 0; encyclopedia-stable

topic: negative potential energy in a hole
en: If you choose the ground as zero, a ball in a hole has negative potential energy because it is below the reference point.
source: reference point choice in gravitational potential energy; encyclopedia-stable

topic: mechanical energy of a train system
en: The mechanical energy of a whole system, like a moving train, is the sum of the kinetic and potential energy of all its parts.
source: mechanical energy as sum over system parts; encyclopedia-stable

en: Earth's layers are thousands of kilometers thick, so drawing them at true size would need a page as wide as the planet, which is why we use a scale.
source: encyclopedia-stable; concept of scale in mapping

en: A scale like 1:10,000,000 means 1 centimeter on paper represents 10 million centimeters, or 100 kilometers, of real Earth.
With a scale of 1 cm = 1,000 km, the 2,900 km mantle becomes 2.9 cm, while the 30 km crust becomes only 0.03 cm, too thin to see.
The crust is less than 1% of Earth's radius, so on a scale drawing it is usually just a thin line or even invisible.
source: Earth radius ~6,371 km; crust ~5-70 km; encyclopedia-stable

en: The lithosphere is about 100 kilometers thick, which is thicker than the crust but still only a small fraction of the mantle.
source: geology textbooks; rounded average lithosphere thickness

en: In a scale drawing, the asthenosphere appears as a thin band just below the lithosphere, much thinner than the mantle.
source: mechanical layer model; relative thickness comparison

en: The mantle makes up about 84% of Earth's volume, so it takes up most of the space in a scale drawing.
In a scale drawing, the core takes up about half of the circle's diameter, leaving the mantle and crust as a thin shell around it.
source: core radius ~3,500 km vs Earth radius ~6,371 km; rounded

en: Many textbook pictures exaggerate the crust's thickness, but a scale drawing shows it as a hairline compared to the thick mantle.
source: common visual misconception; scale drawing corrects it

en: Choose a scale so that the mantle fits on your paper, then use that same scale for all other layers to keep the comparison fair.
A scale drawing of Earth's layers works like a city map, where one centimeter on paper stands for many kilometers in real life.
Because the crust varies from 5 to 70 km thick, a scale drawing might use an average value like 35 km for simplicity.
source: published range of crust thickness; rounded average

en: The inner core is about 1,200 km thick, which is roughly two-thirds the length of the Philippine archipelago.
source: inner core radius ~1,200 km; Philippine archipelago length ~1,800 km

en: The outer core is about 2,200 km thick, which is longer than the whole Philippine archipelago from north to south.
source: outer core thickness ~2,200 km; Philippine archipelago length ~1,800 km

en: The mantle is about 2,900 km thick, which is more than one and a half times the length of the Philippines.
source: mantle thickness ~2,900 km; Philippine archipelago length ~1,800 km

en: A scale drawing of Earth's layers can be drawn on a long strip of paper, with the crust as a thin line at the edge and the core in the middle.
A scale drawing keeps the same ratio for every layer, so the drawn thicknesses match the real proportions exactly.
source: definition of scale drawing; consistency requirement

en: PHIVOLCS uses scale maps to show how deep earthquake sources are, which helps people picture the thin crust and thick mantle.
source: PHIVOLCS public information; scale map usage

en: After drawing, you can multiply the paper length by the scale to find the real thickness, which checks that your drawing is correct.
A scale of 1:100,000,000 means the drawing is 100 million times smaller than the real Earth, so all layers shrink by the same factor.
Conifers like pine trees are non-flowering plants that make seeds inside cones instead of flowers, so they never have petals.
Mammals are warm-blooded, meaning their bodies keep a steady temperature, while reptiles are cold-blooded and change with the surroundings.
Birds have beaks and wings, and most can fly, but flightless birds like ostriches still have feathers and lay eggs.
Fish are cold-blooded and have scales, but some fish like sharks have cartilage instead of bones, so their skeletons are lighter.
Amphibians lay eggs in water, and their eggs are soft and jelly-like, unlike reptile eggs with leathery shells.
Insects have antennae that help them smell and feel, and they also have compound eyes made of many tiny lenses.
Fungi like mushrooms are not plants because they lack chlorophyll and cannot make food from sunlight; instead, they get food from other things.
Bacteria are single-celled and have no nucleus, so their genetic material floats freely inside the cell, unlike plant and animal cells.
To classify an unknown animal, scientists look at its body coverings, how it breathes, and whether it feeds its young milk.
The Philippine eagle is a bird because it has feathers and lays eggs, even though it is a hunter.
A bat is a mammal, not a bird, because it has fur and nurses its babies with milk, even though it flies.
Yeast is a fungus that makes bread rise by releasing gas, and it is a microorganism you can see only with a microscope.
A classification key uses yes-or-no questions, like "Does it have feathers?" to sort an animal into its group.
Insects molt or shed their hard exoskeleton to grow, because the shell cannot stretch, so they make a new one.
Reptiles like snakes bask in the sun to warm up because they are cold-blooded and need outside heat.
The tarsier is a Philippine mammal with fur and long fingers, and it feeds its young milk like all mammals do.
Bacteria can live in extreme places like hot springs and even inside your body, and they are the most numerous living things.
Flowering plants like gumamela have petals that attract insects, which help carry pollen from flower to flower.
Non-flowering plants like ferns have leaves that uncurl as they grow, and they reproduce using spores.
Fish have gills to breathe underwater, and they have fins for steering, but they do not have eyelids.
Clay particles are flat and plate-like, so they pack tightly together and leave only tiny spaces for water.
source: soil science: particle shape and packing

en: Water climbs up tiny spaces in soil by capillary action, which is why clay stays moist longer than sandy soil.
source: soil physics: capillary rise in porous media

en: Humus, made from decayed leaves and roots, acts like a sponge and helps soil hold more water.
source: soil science: organic matter and water retention

en: Adding compost to sandy soil gives it more organic matter, so it can hold water longer instead of draining away.
Gravity pulls water down through large soil pores, but tiny pores hold water in place, so clay keeps water longer.
source: soil physics: gravitational water vs capillary water

en: Water holding capacity is how much water a soil keeps after extra water has drained away.
Sandy soil has large pores that let water drain fast, but those same pores also let air reach roots easily.
source: soil science: pore size and aeration

en: Water moves very slowly through clay because its tiny pores are like narrow winding paths.
source: soil physics: hydraulic conductivity in clay

en: In a drainage test, sandy soil may release water in seconds, while clay takes much longer to drip.
Volcanic soil from places like Mayon is often loamy and holds water well, which helps crops grow.
source: PHIVOLCS and soil science: volcanic ash soils

en: Scientists use a soil texture triangle to name a soil by its mix of sand, silt, and clay.
Because clay particles are tiny, they have a huge surface area that can hold water films around each particle.
source: soil science: specific surface area of clay

en: Wet clay is sticky because its flat particles slide and cling together, while wet sand falls apart.
Silt settles on riverbanks during floods, making the soil rich and able to hold water for plants.
source: geology: floodplain deposition and soil fertility

en: Plant roots have a hard time growing in tight clay because the tiny pores leave little room for air.
source: plant science: soil aeration and root growth

en: Dark soil often has more humus, so it tends to hold more water than light-colored sandy soil.
source: soil observation: color as indicator of organic matter

en: Plants like cactus and some beach grasses grow well in sandy soil because it drains fast and doesn't stay wet.
source: ecology: adaptations to dry, well-drained soils

en: The size of soil particles determines how much space is between them, and that space controls water flow.
source: soil physics: relationship between particle size and porosity

en: The amount of water a soil can hold depends on how much organic matter it has, not just particle size.
source: soil science: organic matter influence on water retention

en: When clay soil dries, it becomes hard and cracked, so water runs off instead of soaking in.
source: soil behavior: shrinkage and cracking of clay

en: Spiders are not insects because they have eight legs and two body parts, while insects always have six legs and three body parts.
Fungi and bacteria are both microorganisms, but fungi have a nucleus (the cell's control center) while bacteria do not.
source: encyclopedia-stable; cell structure of fungi and bacteria
