en: A flying airplane has mechanical energy from both its forward motion and its height above the ground, so its total mechanical energy is the sum of its kinetic and potential energies.
source: encyclopedia-stable; physics of mechanical energy as a sum

en: Mechanical energy is a single number, so you simply add the kinetic and potential energy values, ignoring direction, to get the total.
source: encyclopedia-stable; mechanical energy is a scalar quantity

en: Photosynthesis and respiration are opposite reactions: plants use carbon dioxide and water to make food and oxygen, while living things use food and oxygen to release carbon dioxide and water.
source: textbook: photosynthesis and respiration are reverse chemical processes

en: When sea animals with shells die, their shells can slowly turn into limestone rock, storing carbon in the earth for millions of years.
source: geological carbon cycle, limestone formation from marine organisms

en: In cold places, water can freeze into glaciers that hold water for a long time, and when they melt, the water keeps moving through the water cycle.
source: water cycle includes storage in glaciers and ice caps

en: When leaves and roots die, some of their carbon stays in the soil as humus, so soil stores carbon for many years.
source: soil organic matter and carbon storage in terrestrial ecosystems

en: Plants need water from the water cycle to combine with carbon dioxide and make food, so the water and carbon cycles work together in every leaf.
source: photosynthesis requires water and carbon dioxide, linking the two cycles

en: Earth's shadow does not cause moon phases; it only creates lunar eclipses when Earth blocks the Sun's light from the Moon.
The Moon's orbit around Earth takes about 27.3 days relative to the stars, but its phases repeat every 29.5 days because Earth moves around the Sun.
source: astronomy stable; sidereal and synodic periods

en: The Moon's phase changes gradually, so each night it looks slightly different from the night before.
The Moon can be seen in the daytime sky during many of its phases, not only at night.
The Moon's distance from Earth changes slightly, but this does not change the phase; only the angle between Sun, Earth, and Moon matters.
The Moon's phases are not caused by Earth's rotation; they come from the Moon's own movement around Earth.
The Moon's phase cycle is used in many calendars, such as the Islamic lunar calendar, to mark months.
In a model of the solar system, the Sun is the light source, Earth moves around the Sun, and the Moon circles Earth, showing how phases depend on the Moon's position.
The Moon's phase at any time is determined by the angle between the Sun and the Moon as seen from Earth.
The Moon's phases repeat in a cycle, so if you know today's phase, you can predict the phase for any future date.
The Moon moves about 13 degrees eastward each day relative to the Sun, which is why it rises later each night.
The word 'month' comes from 'moon' because the Moon's phase cycle takes about a month.
To draw moon phases, place the Sun on one side, Earth in the middle, and show the Moon in different positions around Earth.
The order of moon phases is always new, crescent, first quarter, gibbous, full, then back to new.
The Moon's crescent looks thin because we see only a small edge of its sunlit half.
The Moon's phase can be used to estimate the time of night, but it is not a precise clock.
The Moon's phase cycle is used in many cultures for religious festivals, such as Eid al-Fitr.
The Moon's path through space is a wavy line because it circles Earth while Earth circles the Sun.
Everyone on Earth sees the same moon phase on a given day, but the time it rises and sets changes with your location.
Before planting, write a hypothesis that predicts which soil type will grow the tallest plant.
Use a pH strip to test the acidity of each soil type before planting, and record the color change.
Use a measuring cup to collect and measure the water that drains from each pot after watering.
Use a thermometer to check that the soil temperature is the same in all pots before watering.
Use a ruler to measure the width of the largest leaf on each plant to compare leaf size.
Use a stopwatch to time how long it takes for water to soak into each soil type.
Use a magnifying glass to look for tiny root hairs that help the plant take up water.
Blood from the intestines goes straight to the liver first, so the liver can process nutrients and catch harmful substances before they reach the rest of the body.
source: hepatic portal circulation; liver first-pass metabolism

topic: Flow chart of digestion and excretion
en: A flow chart of digestion and excretion shows food becoming nutrients in the small intestine, then wastes traveling through the blood to the kidneys and lungs.
source: flow chart of digestive and excretory pathways

en: Your kidneys keep the right amount of water in your blood, which your digestive system needs to make saliva and stomach juices.
source: kidney water balance; digestive secretions require water

en: A meal can take about one to three days to travel through your digestive tract, while your kidneys filter your blood continuously.
source: gastrointestinal transit time ~1-3 days; continuous renal filtration

en: The liver checks the blood right after it leaves the intestines, and the kidneys check it again later, so wastes and toxins are caught twice.
source: liver portal processing and kidney filtration

en: To make the results fair and unbiased, ask someone else to measure the plants without knowing which soil each pot holds.
source: scientific method: blinding to reduce observer bias

en: A cell is the smallest unit of a living thing that can carry out life processes like getting energy and making copies of itself.
A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to do one job, like muscle tissue that helps you move.
An organ is made of two or more different tissues that work together, such as the heart pumping blood using muscle and nerve tissue.
An organ system is a team of organs that work together, like the digestive system breaking down food from mouth to stomach to intestines.
An organism is any living thing that can carry out all life processes on its own, from a single bacterium to a human being.
A population is all the individuals of the same species living in one area, like all the mango trees in a school yard.
A community is all the different populations that live and interact in the same place, such as fish, water lilies, and insects in a pond.
An ecosystem includes a community of living things plus the non-living parts of their environment, like water, soil, and sunlight.
Each level of biological organization contains the level below it, so a tissue is made of cells and an organ is made of tissues.
When cells are grouped into tissues, they can do jobs that a single cell cannot, like pumping blood or thinking.
In the human body, muscle cells form muscle tissue, which makes up the heart organ, which is part of the circulatory system.
A leaf is an organ made of different tissues, such as the outer skin tissue and the inner food-making tissue.
A human body contains about 37 trillion cells, and they are organized into tissues, organs, and systems to keep you alive.
A population is just one species, but a community includes many species; for example, all the tilapia in a lake are a population, while the tilapia, snails, and algae together are a community.
An ecosystem is not only living things; it also includes the non-living parts like rocks, water, and air that living things depend on.
The tropical rainforest biome in the Philippines contains many different ecosystems, from mountain forests to lowland swamps.
In a labelled diagram, arrows from cell to biosphere show that each higher level is made up of the levels below it.
Cells become specialized for different jobs, and this specialization allows tissues, organs, and systems to perform complex tasks.
An organ is not just a bigger cell; it is a structure made of many different tissues, each with its own role.
In a rice field, a single palay plant is an organism, all the palay plants are a population, and the field with frogs and insects is a community.
When shaken with water, soil particles settle in layers with the largest sand at the bottom, silt in the middle, and the smallest clay at the top.
source: standard classroom demonstration: particle size affects settling rate in water

en: Farmers water sandy soil more often because it drains quickly, while clay soil stays wet longer and needs less watering.
source: agricultural practice: irrigation scheduling based on soil texture and water retention

en: The lithosphere and asthenosphere are not extra layers but zones within the upper mantle, so a scale drawing shows them as parts of the mantle's thickness.
source: mechanical layering of Earth's interior; encyclopedia-stable

topic: outer core vs inner core thickness
en: The outer core is about 2,200 km thick, which is nearly twice the inner core's radius of about 1,200 km, so it appears as a thicker ring in a scale drawing.
source: rounded values from Earth structure models

en: The mantle is about 2,900 km thick, which is nearly half of Earth's radius of about 6,400 km, so it takes up the largest portion of a scale drawing.
source: rounded values of mantle thickness and Earth's radius

en: The asthenosphere lies roughly between 100 and 350 kilometers deep, so it is a soft zone within the upper mantle that appears as a thin band in a scale drawing.
source: commonly cited depth range for asthenosphere

en: Using a scale of 1 cm = 100 km, the 2,900 km mantle becomes 29 cm on paper, which is about the length of a long ruler.
source: scale conversion example with 1 cm = 100 km

en: The geologic time scale is built from the order of rock layers and the fossils inside them, so it tells the sequence of Earth's past events.
In undisturbed rock layers, the oldest layer lies at the bottom and the youngest at the top, giving a natural order to Earth's history.
Certain fossils called index fossils appear in only a short span of time, so they help match rock layers of the same age across different places.
Radiometric dating measures the decay of radioactive elements in rocks, giving scientists a number of years for when the rock formed.
The geologic time scale combines the relative order of rock layers with absolute ages from radiometric dating to give a complete timeline.
source: combination of relative and absolute dating

en: The boundaries between divisions of the geologic time scale often mark major changes in life, such as a sudden appearance or extinction of many species.
source: geologic time scale boundaries and biotic events

en: The Cambrian explosion, about 541 million years ago, marks a time when many major animal groups first appear in the fossil record.
The Phanerozoic eon, meaning "visible life," covers the last 541 million years, when abundant fossils make Earth's history easier to read.
The geologic time scale shows Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, far older than any written human record, which only goes back a few thousand years.
By reading the geologic time scale, scientists can see that life evolved from simple single-celled organisms to complex multicellular animals over billions of years.
The geologic time scale lets scientists match rock layers of the same age on different continents, showing that they formed at the same time.
Many geologic period names come from places where their rocks were first studied, like the Jurassic period from the Jura Mountains in Europe.
The geologic time scale helps geologists find coal and oil because these resources are trapped in rocks of specific ages.
The geologic time scale acts like a giant calendar, allowing scientists to place events such as volcanic eruptions and asteroid impacts in order.
source: geologic time scale as chronological framework

en: The geologic time scale reveals that mass extinctions, like the one that killed off the dinosaurs, have punctuated Earth's history.
source: mass extinction events in geologic record

en: Matching rock ages and fossils across continents using the geologic time scale supports the idea that continents have moved over time.
source: evidence for plate tectonics from rock correlation

en: The geologic time scale records past climate changes, including ice ages and warm periods, helping scientists understand today's climate.
In the Philippines, scientists use the geologic time scale to date rocks and fossils found in areas like Palawan and Cebu.
The geologic time scale is not fixed; scientists keep refining it as new fossils and dating techniques provide better evidence.
source: dynamic nature of geologic time scale

en: The geologic time scale works like the chapters of a book, each division telling a part of Earth's story from its birth to now.
For a box sliding at constant speed on a flat floor, the push arrow and the friction arrow are drawn equal in length because the forces are balanced.
source: balanced forces: constant velocity means net force is zero

en: To find the net force from a free-body diagram, subtract the shorter arrow's length from the longer arrow's length when they point in opposite directions.
source: net force = vector sum; opposite forces subtract

en: When drawing a free-body diagram for an object on a ramp, tilt the coordinate axes so one axis runs along the ramp surface and the other is perpendicular to it.
source: inclined plane analysis: axes along and normal to surface

en: When a rope pulls an object at an angle, draw the tension arrow from the object's point at that exact angle, not along the horizontal or vertical.
source: force direction follows the rope's actual orientation

en: For an object that is not moving, every force arrow in the diagram must have a matching arrow of equal length pointing the opposite way.
source: equilibrium: net force zero for objects at rest

en: When two forces act on an object in the same direction, draw both arrows from the same point pointing the same way, with the longer one showing the larger force.
source: multiple forces: each drawn separately from the point

en: A free-body diagram for a ball rolling across the floor and slowing down shows a longer friction arrow pointing backward and a shorter push arrow pointing forward.
source: unbalanced force opposite motion causes deceleration

en: Draw the arrow for gravity first in a free-body diagram because it always points straight down and gives a reference for the other forces.
source: gravity direction is fixed downward; serves as reference

en: When drawing a free-body diagram for an object hanging from two ropes, draw each tension arrow along its own rope, pointing away from the object toward the ceiling.
source: tension acts along each rope away from the object

en: A free-body diagram of an object moving at constant velocity shows balanced forces, so opposite arrows are equal even though the object is moving.
source: Newton's first law: constant velocity means zero net force

en: When a force acts at an angle, use a protractor to measure the angle from the horizontal or vertical axis before drawing the arrow.
For an object being pushed but not moving, the push arrow and the friction arrow are equal in length, showing the forces are balanced.
source: static friction balances applied force until motion starts

en: Draw the arrow for the applied force in the direction the hand or machine pushes, and the friction arrow in the opposite direction along the surface.
source: applied force direction matches push; friction opposes motion

en: For an object with three forces, draw all three arrows from the same point, then check if any two opposite arrows are equal to spot balanced pairs.
source: systematic check of force pairs in a diagram

en: To draw a free-body diagram for an object on a table being pulled to the right, draw the pull arrow to the right, friction to the left, gravity down, and normal force up.
source: complete set of forces for a pulled object on a surface

en: For a person walking forward, draw the friction arrow pointing forward, because friction from the ground pushes the person in the direction of motion.
source: friction as the driving force for walking

en: When drawing a free-body diagram for an object in an elevator accelerating upward, draw the normal force arrow longer than the gravity arrow.
source: apparent weight: normal force exceeds gravity during upward acceleration

en: A free-body diagram for a ball kicked into the air shows the gravity arrow pointing down and a shorter air resistance arrow pointing opposite to the ball's motion.
source: projectile with air resistance: two forces acting

en: For an object floating in water, draw the buoyancy arrow upward and the gravity arrow downward at equal lengths because the object is not sinking or rising.
source: buoyancy balances gravity for a floating object

en: Draw a free-body diagram before solving a force problem so the balanced and unbalanced forces are visible and the net force direction is clear.
source: free-body diagram as first step in force analysis

en: A clear aim names the one thing you want to find out, such as whether more water makes seeds sprout faster.
source: scientific investigation steps: aim defines the question

en: The materials list tells what you need and how much, like 100 grams of soil, so another person can prepare the same setup.
source: scientific investigation: materials and equipment step

en: Choose the measuring tool that matches what you measure, such as a ruler for length, a graduated cylinder for liquid, and a balance for mass.
source: measurement instruments match the property measured

en: Number each step in the method so the experimenter knows the exact order, from preparing the setup to recording the final reading.
source: scientific investigation: method or procedures step

en: A fair test changes only one thing on purpose and keeps all other conditions the same, so the results truly show that one thing's effect.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, rest constant

en: The variable you change on purpose is the independent variable, and the variable you measure as the outcome is the dependent variable.
source: experimental design: independent vs dependent variable

en: The conditions you keep the same, like temperature and amount of light, are called controlled variables and they make the test fair.
source: experimental design: controlled variables held constant

en: Doing the experiment three or more times and averaging the results helps you spot mistakes and makes the data more dependable.
source: repeated trials improve reliability of data

en: Use a bar graph to compare different groups and a line graph to show how one measurement changes as another value increases.
source: graph choice: bar for categories, line for trends

en: Read measuring instruments at eye level and read liquid volume at the bottom of the curved surface to get an accurate value.
source: accurate instrument reading: eye level and meniscus

en: Results can be quantitative, like 40 degrees Celsius, or qualitative, like describing the liquid as clear and slippery.
source: types of data: quantitative numbers vs qualitative descriptions

en: In the conclusion, you compare your actual results with your aim and say plainly what the data show, even if it is not what you wanted.
source: scientific investigation: conclusion answers the aim

en: Even if the results do not match what you expected, the investigation is a success because you learned the true answer.
Write down observations during the experiment, not later from memory, because details like color changes fade quickly.
Safety items such as goggles, gloves, or an apron are listed as materials when the procedure uses heat, chemicals, or sharp tools.
source: safety equipment part of materials list

en: Every graph has labeled axes with units and a title, so a reader knows what each bar or line represents.
source: graph conventions: labeled axes, units, title

en: A weather scientist at PAGASA records rainfall amounts in a table each day, then looks for patterns across the wet season.
The aim guides your choice of materials and steps, because what you want to find out decides what you measure and how.
The method is written clearly enough that another scientist can follow it and get similar results, which makes the investigation reliable.
Atoms share electrons to fill their outer shells, and a filled outer shell makes each atom more stable than it was alone.
source: encyclopedia-stable; octet rule and chemical stability

en: Many nonmetal atoms become stable when their outermost shell holds eight electrons, so they share electrons to reach that number.
An oxygen atom needs two more electrons to fill its outer shell, and each hydrogen atom needs one, so they share to form water.
source: encyclopedia-stable; valence electron counts for H and O

en: A carbon atom needs four more electrons, and each oxygen atom needs two, so carbon shares two pairs with each oxygen in CO2.
source: encyclopedia-stable; valence electron counts for C and O

en: When two atoms share two pairs of electrons, the bond is called a double bond, and it holds the atoms more tightly than a single bond.
When two atoms share only one pair of electrons, the bond is called a single bond, like each hydrogen-oxygen link in water.
Covalent bonds happen between nonmetal atoms, which all tend to gain electrons instead of giving them away like metals do.
In a covalent bond, the shared pair of electrons belongs to both atoms at the same time, so each atom can count them as its own.
Forming a covalent bond releases energy, which is why atoms bond willingly and why molecules stay together instead of falling apart.
Because oxygen has two lone pairs of electrons, a water molecule is bent like a V, not a straight line.
Carbon dioxide is a straight molecule because carbon has no lone pairs, so the two oxygen atoms line up on opposite sides.
In water, oxygen pulls the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen, so one end of the molecule is slightly negative and the other slightly positive.
In carbon dioxide, the two oxygen atoms pull electrons equally from both sides, so the molecule has no slightly positive or negative ends.
Water is a liquid at room temperature but carbon dioxide is a gas, because of the weak forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds inside them.
source: encyclopedia-stable; physical states of molecular compounds

en: A Lewis dot structure shows a covalent bond as a pair of dots or a line placed between the symbols of the two atoms.

topic: bonding pairs and lone pairs in water
en: In water, oxygen has two bonding pairs shared with hydrogen and two lone pairs that are not shared with any other atom.
A carbon atom can form four covalent bonds, which is why it can join with two oxygen atoms using two double bonds in CO2.
Every living thing on Earth, including plants and people in the Philippines, is mostly made of water molecules held together by covalent bonds.
The carbon dioxide that people breathe out and that jeepneys release is a covalent molecule made of one carbon and two oxygen atoms.
Covalent compounds like sugar do not conduct electricity because their neutral molecules have no free charged particles to carry a current.
source: encyclopedia-stable; electrical conductivity of molecular compounds

en: Table salt melts at about 800°C because its ions are locked in a strong crystal lattice, while sugar melts at a much lower temperature.
When salt dissolves in water, its ions break free and move, so the solution conducts electricity; sugar water does not because sugar molecules stay whole.
source: electrolyte behavior of ionic vs covalent compounds

en: Tapping an ionic crystal like salt shatters it into smaller cubes because pushing layers brings same-charged ions together, which repel.
source: ionic crystal brittleness due to ion repulsion

en: Ionic compounds usually form between a metal and a nonmetal, while covalent compounds form between nonmetals only, like oxygen and hydrogen in water.
source: periodic table trends in bonding types

en: In ionic bonding, atoms transfer electrons to become ions; in covalent bonding, atoms share electrons to make molecules.
The formula NaCl means one sodium ion for every chloride ion in the entire crystal, not a single molecule like H2O.
source: ionic formula unit vs molecular formula

en: Water is a covalent compound: each H2O molecule is a separate unit, and many molecules stay near each other but do not form a lattice.
Carbon dioxide is a covalent compound where each CO2 molecule is separate, so it is a gas at room temperature.
In salt farms like those in Pangasinan, seawater evaporates and leaves cubic salt crystals because ions arrange in a repeating cube pattern.
source: Philippine salt industry; ionic crystal habit

en: Most ionic compounds are solid at room temperature because their ions are held tightly in a rigid lattice, unlike many covalent compounds that are gases or liquids.
source: states of matter for ionic vs covalent compounds

en: Covalent compounds like methane have individual molecules that move freely as a gas, with no repeating crystal structure at all.
Ionic crystals are hard because strong ionic bonds hold the lattice, but covalent solids like wax are soft because their molecules are only weakly attracted.
source: physical properties of ionic and molecular solids

en: Sugar is a covalent compound that forms separate molecules, while salt is ionic and forms a giant repeating lattice of ions.
source: comparison of sucrose and NaCl structures

en: When melted, ionic compounds also conduct electricity because the ions can move; covalent liquids like oil do not.
Some think salt is made of molecules, but it is actually a huge repeating pattern of ions, so each grain is one big crystal.
Even solid covalent compounds like ice are made of separate water molecules held by weak forces, not a lattice of charged ions.
Ionic bonds holding a crystal lattice are much stronger than the weak forces between covalent molecules, so ionic solids have higher melting points.
source: comparison of bond strengths in ionic and molecular compounds

en: In a ball-and-stick model, an ionic compound looks like a 3D grid of alternating balls, while a covalent compound looks like separate small clusters.
source: common modeling of ionic and covalent structures

en: Ionic compounds have very high boiling points because breaking the whole crystal lattice takes a lot of energy, unlike boiling a covalent liquid.
source: boiling points of ionic vs molecular compounds

en: Oxygen gas is a covalent compound made of separate O2 molecules that move freely, not a repeating lattice like salt.
Energy from the sun flows through plants to animals, linking the organism level to the ecosystem level in a food chain.
source: ecology: energy transfer through food chains

en: Every level from a cell to the biosphere is made of cells, because all living things are made of cells and the biosphere contains all living things.
source: cell theory: all living things are composed of cells

en: A change at one level can affect the levels above and below it, like when pollution kills the plants in a pond, the animals that eat them also disappear.
In DNA, the base adenine always pairs with thymine, and cytosine always pairs with guanine, like two puzzle pieces that only fit each other.
The two DNA strands are held together by weak hydrogen bonds between paired bases, so the ladder can unzip when the cell needs to copy it.
source: molecular biology; hydrogen bonding between base pairs

en: In the DNA double helix, the sugar-phosphate backbones run along the outside, while the paired bases form the rungs on the inside.
The two strands of DNA run in opposite directions, so one goes upward while the other goes downward along the twisted ladder.
A DNA double helix is only about 2 nanometers wide, so about 25,000 of them side by side would fit across a human hair.
Each full turn of the DNA helix is about 3.4 nanometers long and holds about 10 base pairs, like ten steps on a spiral staircase.
source: Watson-Crick model; ~3.4 nm pitch, ~10 bp per turn

en: The DNA in one human cell is about 2 meters long when stretched out, yet it is packed into a nucleus too small to see.
source: encyclopedia-stable; ~2 m per diploid human cell

en: To fit inside the nucleus, DNA wraps around proteins called histones, like thread winding around tiny spools to stay tidy.
The order of the bases A, T, C, and G along the DNA strand is the code that carries the instructions for building your body.
Because each base has only one perfect partner, each DNA strand can act as a template to build the other strand exactly.
Rosalind Franklin's X-ray image called Photo 51 showed an X-shaped pattern that helped reveal DNA's helical shape.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Franklin's X-ray diffraction of DNA

en: The letters A, T, C, and G stand for adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine, the four chemical bases that make DNA.
In human cells, DNA lives mostly inside the nucleus, packed into rod-shaped structures called chromosomes that carry it.
The DNA double helix works like a zipper: the bases are the teeth that match up, and the backbones are the two tapes.
A human cell's DNA contains about 3 billion base pairs, enough to fill about 3,000 books with 1,000 pages each.
A mutation is a change in the order of bases in DNA, like a typo in a long instruction book that may change the meaning.
The twisted shape of the double helix makes DNA strong and stable, protecting the genetic instructions packed inside the cell.
The phosphate groups in DNA's backbone carry a negative charge, which helps DNA dissolve and stay spread out in the watery cell.
DNA is a double helix with the sugar deoxyribose, while its cousin RNA is usually a single strand with ribose sugar instead.
source: molecular biology; DNA vs RNA structure

en: When a cell divides, the DNA double helix unzips down the middle, and each half builds a new partner to make two copies.
The line that separates the lit and dark parts of the Moon is called the terminator, and its curved shape changes as the Moon's phase changes.
The first quarter moon is called 'first quarter' because the Moon has completed one quarter of its orbit around Earth, not because it is half lit.
The last quarter moon is called 'last quarter' because the Moon has completed three quarters of its orbit, leaving only one quarter to go.
The crescent moon's lit side points toward the Sun, but which side is lit (right or left) depends on whether you are in the Northern or Southern Hemisphere.
The phase of the Moon is the fraction of its sunlit side that faces Earth, from 0% at new moon to 100% at full moon.

topic: weather does not change moon phase
en: Clouds or weather do not change the Moon's phase; on any given day, the phase is the same no matter what the sky looks like.
To measure air temperature fairly, place the thermometer in the shade and read it at the same time every day.
source: standard method for measuring air temperature

en: A rain gauge collects falling rain, and you read the water level on its marked scale each morning.
A wind vane points to the direction the wind is coming from, like north or east, so you can record that.
source: standard method for observing wind direction

en: A daily weather log uses a table with columns for date, temperature, rain, wind, and sky condition.
A bar graph of daily rainfall makes it easy to see which days were wetter and which were drier.
To compare weather over several days, record the same measurements at the same time each day.
source: fair test principle in weather observation

en: To see how weather changes in one day, record the temperature and sky condition in the morning, noon, and afternoon.
source: standard observation schedule for daily change

en: Place a rain gauge in an open area away from trees and buildings so it catches only the falling rain.
Scientists describe cloud cover by looking at the sky and saying if it is clear, partly cloudy, or overcast.
Read a thermometer at eye level and wait until the liquid stops moving to get the true temperature.
When recording wind direction, write the direction the wind comes from, such as 'north wind' or 'east wind'.
A barometer measures air pressure, and a falling air pressure often means rainy weather is coming.
To predict rain, look for thick, dark clouds that grow taller, because they often bring a storm.
source: standard cloud observation for rain prediction

en: A weather chart uses simple symbols like a sun for sunny, a cloud for cloudy, and raindrops for rainy.

topic: setting up a home weather station
en: A simple home weather station has a thermometer, a rain gauge, and a wind vane placed in an open spot.
source: standard setup for a simple weather station

en: After a week of records, you can count how many days were sunny, rainy, or cloudy to find the pattern.
source: standard data analysis for weekly patterns

en: PAGASA weather stations measure temperature, rain, and wind, and their reports help us know the daily weather.
To describe the sky condition, look up and note if the sun is shining, if clouds cover the sky, or if it is raining.
A fair weather observation keeps the same place and the same time every day, changing only what the weather does.
source: fair test principle in weather observation

en: To record a sunny day, scientists note that the sun is shining and there are no rain clouds in the sky.
On a cloudy day, scientists describe the sky as mostly covered with clouds, making the sunlight dimmer.
A rainy day is recorded when raindrops fall from clouds, and scientists note if the rain is light or heavy.
To describe a windy day, scientists observe how strong the wind is and whether it moves leaves or branches.
A weather log table has rows for each day and columns for temperature, rain, wind, and sky, making patterns easy to see.
Scientists record weather at the same time each day, like 8 in the morning, so the data can be compared fairly.
To measure air temperature, scientists use a thermometer and read the number where the liquid stops moving.
source: instrument use in weather observation; encyclopedia-stable

en: A rain gauge is a container that catches rain, and scientists read the water level on its marked scale to know how much fell.
source: instrument use in weather observation; encyclopedia-stable

en: A wind vane spins to point where the wind comes from, so scientists can record the wind direction like north or east.
source: instrument use in weather observation; encyclopedia-stable

en: Scientists describe cloud cover by looking at the sky and saying if it is clear, partly cloudy, or fully overcast.
A weather chart uses a sun picture for sunny, a cloud for cloudy, and raindrop pictures for rainy days.
After a week of weather records, scientists count how many days were sunny, rainy, or cloudy to find the pattern.
To see how weather changes in one day, scientists compare the temperature and sky in the morning with the afternoon.
Scientists describe wind strength by watching if leaves barely move, branches sway, or trees bend in the wind.
A barometer measures air pressure, and scientists note if it is rising or falling to help predict weather changes.
source: instrument use in weather observation; encyclopedia-stable

en: Scientists predict rain by watching for thick, dark clouds that grow taller, because these often bring storms.
A pictograph uses small pictures to show how many sunny, rainy, or cloudy days happened in a week.
To get a true air temperature, scientists place the thermometer in the shade, not in direct sunlight.
source: instrument use in weather observation; encyclopedia-stable

en: At noon, scientists check the sky to see if the sun is high and bright or hidden by clouds, describing the midday weather.
Scientists use PAGASA reports to compare their local weather records with official data from weather stations across the Philippines.
The geologic time scale gives scientists a shared timeline, so a geologist in Japan and one in Brazil can agree on when a rock formed.
The oldest rocks found on Earth are about 4 billion years old, but the time scale starts at 4.5 billion, leaving a mysterious early gap.
The Quaternary period, where humans live, is very short on the time scale, lasting only about 2.6 million years so far.
When a volcano erupts, it leaves a thin ash layer that can be dated, giving a precise age to the rocks and fossils above and below it.
The time scale records times when Earth's magnetic poles flipped, and these flips are frozen in rocks, helping match layers of the same age.
Most Philippine rocks are young in the time scale, forming in the Cenozoic era, which is why the islands have no dinosaur fossils.
source: PHIVOLCS / geology of Philippines; island arc formation

topic: life moved from sea to land
en: The time scale shows that life first filled the oceans, and only later, in the Paleozoic era, did plants and animals move onto land.
The extinction of the dinosaurs about 66 million years ago marks the boundary between the Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras on the time scale.
The geologic time scale helps scientists see that Earth has changed gradually, with each division showing a different stage in its long development.
source: encyclopedia-stable; gradual change in Earth history

en: The time scale reveals that some species, like certain shellfish, stayed almost the same for hundreds of millions of years, while others changed quickly.
The time scale helps scientists tell both relative age, which rock is older, and absolute age, how many years old a rock is.
By looking at the order of marine and land fossils in the time scale, scientists can see when seas rose and fell over millions of years.
The time scale shows that places now covered by desert were once under the sea, and today's mountains were once flat plains.
The time scale places the formation of the Moon very early, about 4.5 billion years ago, right after Earth itself took shape.
The time scale shows that the first mammals appeared long before the dinosaurs died out, living alongside them for over a hundred million years.
The time scale shows that the Himalayas, Earth's highest mountains, are young, having formed in the last 50 million years during the Cenozoic.
The geologic time scale is built from careful evidence in rocks and fossils, so it is a scientific story, not a guess or a myth.
Scientists use the time scale to compare Philippine fossils, like those in Cebu, with fossils from other countries to see which are older.
The time scale helps scientists understand the history of the solar system, because Earth's oldest rocks hold clues to its early formation.
The time scale lets scientists assign a rock layer to a specific period, such as the Jurassic, based on the unique fossils it contains.
Before drawing a free-body diagram, choose a scale so that the largest force arrow fits on the paper, then use that same scale for every arrow.
source: standard practice in drawing scaled vector diagrams

en: When two forces on an object point in the same direction, add their arrow lengths to get the net force and draw that total as one arrow.
source: vector addition of forces in the same direction

en: For an object at rest, draw any unknown force (like friction) with the same length as the known applied force but pointing the opposite way.
source: equilibrium condition for objects at rest

en: A hypothesis is a testable guess you write before the experiment, and it states what result you expect to see.
source: standard scientific method: hypothesis before experiment

en: A control setup is the group you do not change, so you can compare it with the setup where you changed the variable.
When you record data, write the unit with every number, like 25 mL or 30 seconds, so the data has clear meaning.
A data table has a title and columns for the independent variable and the dependent variable, with units in the headings.
source: data table organization: variables and units

en: To measure time accurately, start the stopwatch at the exact moment you begin the action and stop it at the exact end.
To measure temperature, keep the thermometer bulb in the liquid and wait until the reading stops changing before writing it down.
A prediction is a specific statement about what you think will happen, while a conclusion is a statement about what actually happened based on the data.
If one result is very different from the others, check your method and repeat that trial to see if it was a mistake.
Write the aim as a question that names the thing you will change and the thing you will measure.
List materials in a table with columns for name, quantity, and unit, so the list is easy to read.
source: materials list format: table with quantities

en: Write each step in the method with a specific amount and time, like 'add 10 drops' or 'wait 2 minutes'.
To get accurate results, use the same measuring instrument for all trials, like the same ruler or the same thermometer.
A good data table lets another person read your results without asking you, so it needs clear headings and units.
When you do an experiment, you should record the date and time of each trial to keep your data organized.
A control group is the setup that does not receive the treatment, so you can see the natural result without your change.
When you write a procedure, use action words like 'measure', 'pour', and 'mix' so the steps are clear.
The results section includes both the data table and the graph, so the reader can see the numbers and the pattern.
The method should include a step for cleaning up and disposing of materials safely after the experiment.
To measure the mass of a solid, place it on a balance and wait until the reading is stable before writing the number.
To measure the length of an object, place the ruler's zero mark exactly at one end and read the number at the other end.
Hydrogen is an exception to the octet rule: it needs only two electrons to be stable, so in water each hydrogen shares one pair with oxygen.
source: octet rule exception for hydrogen, encyclopedia-stable

en: In a covalent bond, the shared pair of electrons is attracted to both nuclei at once, and that pull is what holds the atoms together in water and carbon dioxide.
source: covalent bond model, electrostatic attraction between electrons and nuclei

en: Because covalent bonds share electrons rather than transfer them, water and carbon dioxide molecules have no electric charge and are electrically neutral.
source: covalent bonding results in neutral molecules, encyclopedia-stable

en: Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5 degrees from the vertical, and this steady tilt is what makes daylight length change across the year.
Earth's axis always points toward Polaris, the North Star, so the direction of the tilt stays the same while Earth circles the Sun.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Earth's axis points to Polaris

en: At the equator, every day of the year has about 12 hours of daylight and 12 hours of night, because the Sun's path is steady there.
Around March 21 and September 23, the equinox, nearly every place on Earth gets about 12 hours of daylight and 12 hours of night.
The Tropic of Cancer at 23.5 degrees north is the northernmost latitude where the Sun can be directly overhead at noon.
The Arctic Circle at 66.5 degrees north is the southernmost place in the north where the Sun can stay up for 24 hours on the summer solstice.
The Antarctic Circle at 66.5 degrees south is where the Sun stays up for 24 hours on the December solstice, while the north has short days.
The length of daylight changes little by little each day, not suddenly, as Earth moves along its orbit around the Sun.
When the Northern Hemisphere has long summer days, the Southern Hemisphere has short winter days, and the reverse happens half a year later.
In summer, the Sun takes a higher and longer arc across the sky, which gives more daylight hours than the lower, shorter arc of winter.
The farther a place is from the equator, the bigger the difference between its longest and shortest day of the year.
source: encyclopedia-stable; latitude effect on day length

en: The Philippines sits near the equator, so its day length changes by only about an hour or two across the entire year.
A model with a tilted globe and a flashlight shows that the lit half of Earth shifts, so some latitudes get more sun time than others.
The Sun rises and sets at different points on the horizon each day, moving north in summer and south in winter.
At the North Pole, the Sun is above the horizon for half the year and below it for the other half, but the change happens slowly.
Earth's distance from the Sun does not cause the changes in daylight length; the tilt of its axis is the real reason.
source: encyclopedia-stable; tilt causes seasons, not distance

en: When the Sun is higher in the sky at noon, the day is longer, and when it is lower, the day is shorter.
source: encyclopedia-stable; solar altitude vs day length

en: At about 60 degrees north, a summer day can have over 18 hours of daylight, while a winter day has fewer than 6 hours.
source: encyclopedia-stable; day length at high latitude

en: On the summer solstice, the Sun rises earliest and sets latest, giving the maximum daylight hours for that latitude.
The tilt makes the Sun's direct rays move between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn over the year, changing day length.
When you reach a pair in a dichotomous key, read both choices before picking, because the better match may be the second one.
source: standard practice in dichotomous key use

en: A rock's streak and hardness do not change with the size of the sample, so a small chip and a large boulder of the same rock type give the same key result.
source: physical properties are intrinsic to rock type

en: When classifying a set of rock samples, you use the same dichotomous key for each one, so you can fairly compare their names.
A dichotomous key for rocks uses only simple tests with everyday tools like a coin, a nail, and a tile, so you can identify rocks outside a laboratory.
source: rock identification uses simple field tests

en: A dichotomous key never uses a rock's weight because weight changes with size, while features like hardness and streak stay the same.
source: weight is not a diagnostic feature in rock keys

en: A geological fault is a crack in the Earth's crust where the rocks on either side have moved.
The block of rock above a fault plane is the hanging wall, while the block below it is the footwall.
When rocks are pulled apart by tension, the hanging wall slides down the fault plane, forming a normal fault.
When rocks are squeezed by compression, the hanging wall is pushed up the fault plane, forming a reverse fault.
Shear stress, where forces push rocks in opposite sideways directions, is what creates strike-slip faults.
An oblique-slip fault combines sideways and up-or-down movement, so the blocks slide diagonally along the fault plane.
Normal faults usually dip steeply at about 60 degrees, while thrust faults dip gently at about 30 degrees or less.
source: standard geology textbook; rounded typical values

en: A strike-slip fault's plane is usually steep and near-vertical, letting the two sides grind past each other horizontally.
In a rift valley, two normal faults drop the middle block down, forming a long trough like the East African Rift.
Reverse and thrust faults push rock upward during compression, helping build mountain ranges like the Himalayas.
California's San Andreas Fault is a famous strike-slip fault where the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other.
Subduction zones create very low-angle thrust faults called megathrusts, which can produce powerful earthquakes and tsunamis.
The Manila Trench west of Luzon is a subduction zone where the seafloor dives under the island, creating low-angle thrust faults.
A fault scarp is a steep cliff left when a fault moves, showing where the ground broke and slipped.
Slickensides are polished scratches on a fault plane that show the direction the blocks slid.

topic: classifying faults by dip and slip
en: Geologists name a fault by putting together its dip angle and its slip direction, such as a steep normal fault or a gentle thrust fault.
PHIVOLCS maps active faults in the Philippines, recording each fault's type and slip direction to assess earthquake hazards.
To read a graduated cylinder, place it on a flat surface at eye level and read the bottom of the curved liquid surface, called the meniscus.
source: standard lab technique: meniscus reading at eye level

en: Before measuring mass on a triple beam balance, check that the pointer swings freely and the balance reads zero with nothing on the pan.
Carry a microscope with one hand on the arm and one hand under the base to keep it steady and prevent dropping it.
When focusing a microscope, start with the lowest power objective lens and use the coarse focus knob only while looking from the side.
To light a Bunsen burner, close the air hole first, hold the striker to the side of the barrel, and open the gas valve slowly.
When heating a test tube, point the open end away from yourself and others, and move it gently through the flame to heat evenly.
Use a rubber bulb to draw liquid into a pipette, never your mouth, and release the liquid slowly against the wall of the receiving container.
Before using any glass container, inspect it for cracks or chips because damaged glass can break suddenly when heated or squeezed.
Label every container with the name of its contents and the date before storing it so nobody mistakes one substance for another.
Use a graduated cylinder instead of a beaker when you need a precise volume because the cylinder has finer markings for accurate measurement.
Read a thermometer at eye level and wait until the liquid inside stops moving to get a steady, correct temperature reading.
When filtering, place the filter paper as a cone inside the funnel, wet it slightly, and pour the liquid down a glass rod to avoid splashing.
Hold a spring scale vertically and read the number at eye level while the object hangs still, so the stretch shows the true force.
Turn off a hot plate and unplug it after use, and remember that the surface stays hot for several minutes even when it looks cool.
Squeeze a dropper's bulb before putting the tip into liquid, then release slowly to draw up the exact small amount you need.
Hold a reagent bottle with the label facing your palm and pour slowly so drips do not smear or wash off the label.
Place a ruler flat against the object, start at the zero mark, and read the length at the line that lines up with the object's end.
Rinse glassware with water right after use, then wash with soap and a brush, and rinse again so no residue affects the next experiment.
Start a stopwatch at the same moment the action begins and stop it at the same moment it ends to measure time accurately.
Use forceps or tweezers to pick up small or sharp solid objects so your fingers stay clean and the object stays where you put it.
The FaultFinder tool lets you type your barangay or school name, then it draws the nearest active fault lines on a map around that spot.
A fault is called active if it has moved within the last 10,000 years, so PHIVOLCS marks it on hazard maps as a red line.
Scientists measure an earthquake's magnitude with seismographs, while intensity describes how strongly people feel the shaking at a place.
When a strong earthquake hits, the ground can split along the fault line, so buildings directly on the fault are the most dangerous.
To measure your distance from a fault, you use the FaultFinder's ruler tool to draw a straight line from your house to the nearest red line.
Liquefaction happens when loose, wet soil shakes like a liquid during an earthquake, so sandy coastal areas near faults have extra risk.
PHIVOLCS and local governments set a buffer zone of at least five meters on each side of an active fault where no building is allowed.
A hazard map has layers you can turn on and off, like fault lines, liquefaction zones, and landslide areas, to see all risks at once.
After finding a nearby fault, you compare your house's distance to it with the building's age and materials to judge how much danger it faces.
Geologists find and map faults by digging trenches across suspected lines and dating the soil layers to see when they last moved.
The shaking you feel during an earthquake depends on how far you are from the fault and what kind of rock or soil is under your feet.
Steep mountain slopes near a fault can slide during an earthquake, so the FaultFinder map also shows landslide-prone areas.
A class can use FaultFinder to check if their school building sits within the danger zone of a fault and then practice safe drop-cover-hold drills.
Seismic hazard is the natural danger like shaking or rupture, while risk is how much harm that hazard can do to people and buildings.
The fault trace is the actual line where the fault meets the ground surface, and FaultFinder shows this trace as a thin red line.
PHIVOLCS uses old church records and newspaper reports of past earthquakes to estimate how often a fault moves.
Scientists place GPS stations on both sides of a fault to measure how slowly the ground is creeping or building up stress.
The National Structural Code sets rules for how strong buildings must be, and areas near active faults need stricter earthquake-resistant designs.
source: National Structural Code of the Philippines

en: A barangay uses its hazard map to mark safe evacuation routes that stay far from fault lines and liquefaction zones.
To confirm a fault's location, you compare the FaultFinder result with the printed PHIVOLCS hazard map for your municipality.
The aim states what you want to find out, while the hypothesis states what you expect to find, so you write both before starting the experiment.
source: standard scientific method: aim and hypothesis are distinct planning steps

en: For repeated trials, give each trial its own row in the data table, and label each column with the measurement and its unit.
source: standard practice for recording repeated experimental trials

en: In the conclusion, you state whether your hypothesis was supported by the data, using the numbers from your results as evidence.
source: conclusion writing in scientific method: compare hypothesis with results

en: The geologic time scale shows gaps where rock layers are missing, so scientists know that some parts of Earth's history are not recorded.
The geologic time scale places the first fish before the first amphibians, and reptiles later, so scientists can tell the order of life's history.
In DNA, a large base always pairs with a small base, so the ladder's width stays the same all the way along.
The DNA double helix twists to the right, like the threads of a standard screw, which scientists call a right-handed helix.
The flat bases inside the DNA ladder stack on top of each other like coins, and this stacking helps hold the double helix together.
The sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA loves water and stays on the outside, while the bases avoid water and hide inside the helix.
Each DNA building block, called a nucleotide, has one base, one sugar, and one phosphate group, and many nucleotides link to form a strand.
In DNA, adenine and thymine pair with two hydrogen bonds, while cytosine and guanine pair with three, making C-G pairs a bit stronger.
The DNA double helix has a wide groove and a narrow groove spiraling along it, where proteins can grip and read the bases inside.
Every DNA double helix has the same twisted-ladder shape, but the order of bases along the ladder changes, giving each gene a different message.
DNA is a long chain made of repeating units called nucleotides, so it is a polymer, just like many other large molecules in your body.
The base pairs in DNA are not perfectly flat; they are slightly tilted, which helps the helix twist smoothly without breaking.
All living things, from tiny bacteria to humans, store their genetic instructions in the same double-helix DNA structure.
The bases are tucked inside the double helix, which protects the genetic code from being damaged by chemicals in the cell.
When DNA is heated, the weak bonds between the two strands break, and the double helix unwinds into two separate strands.
The wide groove of the DNA double helix is a common spot where proteins attach to read the genetic code without unwinding the DNA.
The sugar-phosphate backbone carries a negative charge, which helps DNA stick to positively charged proteins inside the cell.
The sugar in DNA, deoxyribose, has one less oxygen than ribose, which makes DNA more stable than RNA.
The two strands of DNA wind around each other in a spiral, so the molecule looks like a twisted rope rather than a straight ladder.
The two strands of DNA are complementary, meaning each base on one strand has a matching base on the other, so they fit together like a lock and key.
Extreme pH can separate the two strands of DNA by breaking the hydrogen bonds, just like heat does.
The DNA double helix is held together by both hydrogen bonds between bases and stacking of the flat bases, making it strong yet able to unzip.
Opposite charges pull ions together while same charges push them apart, so ions settle into a neat repeating grid that balances both forces.
The smallest repeating part of an ionic crystal is called a unit cell, and a whole grain of salt is billions of these cells stacked together.
In table salt, every sodium ion touches six chloride ions and every chloride touches six sodium ions, making a balanced cube pattern.
A space-filling model of salt shows spheres packed tightly in a grid, while a model of water shows separate clusters with empty space around them.
Some ionic crystals, like ammonium nitrate, contain groups of atoms called polyatomic ions that still line up in a repeating lattice.
Ionic bonds pull equally in every direction, so ions pack into a crystal, while covalent bonds point between two atoms, making a molecule.
Ionic crystals have flat faces and sharp edges because their ions lie on straight planes inside the lattice.
Because covalent bonds point in fixed directions, each molecule has a definite shape, like the bent shape of a water molecule.
A model of an ionic compound shows a small part of the lattice with a note that the pattern repeats, while a model of a covalent compound shows one complete molecule.
When salt melts, its ions stay close and move around, but when ice melts, the water molecules slide past each other freely.
source: behavior of ions vs molecules in liquid state

en: A covalent molecule has a fixed number of atoms, like three in water, but an ionic crystal has no fixed number of ions, so it can grow large.
The shape of an ionic crystal comes from how its ions pack together, so different ionic salts can form different geometric shapes.
An ionic crystal is made of a huge number of ions, so it is much larger than a single covalent molecule.
Covalent molecules are so small that a single molecule is invisible, but ionic crystals can grow into visible grains.
The force that holds ions in a crystal is the same electrostatic attraction that makes a balloon stick to a wall after rubbing.
To show an ionic crystal in a model, you draw a small fragment of the lattice and use lines to show it continues in all directions.
The regular arrangement of ions in an ionic crystal makes it symmetric, so salt crystals look the same from many angles.
In an ionic crystal, each ion is bonded to several neighbors around it, not just one, so the bonds form a network.
The pattern of ions in an ionic crystal is so orderly that scientists can predict its shape from the sizes of the ions.
source: ionic radius and crystal structure prediction

en: The lattice of an ionic crystal is a network of ions, while a covalent molecule is a single isolated group of atoms.
A dominant allele masks a recessive allele, so an organism with one dominant and one recessive copy shows the dominant trait.
A recessive allele only shows its trait when an organism has two copies of it, one from each parent.
Genotype is the pair of alleles an organism carries, while phenotype is the visible trait that those alleles produce.
Homozygous means two identical alleles for a gene, and heterozygous means two different alleles for that gene.
To make a Punnett square, put one parent's alleles on top and the other's on the side, then fill each box with the combined letters.
source: Standard method for predicting offspring genotypes

en: A test cross pairs an organism with a dominant trait to a homozygous recessive one to find out if it is homozygous or heterozygous.
Because each parent gives only one allele per gene to its offspring, a Punnett square shows all possible pairs from those two alleles.
In a dominant/recessive pair, a heterozygote shows the dominant trait, not a blend of both traits.
When a homozygous dominant parent (AA) crosses with a heterozygous one (Aa), all offspring show the dominant trait, but half are AA and half are Aa.
source: Punnett square prediction for AA x Aa

en: When a heterozygous (Aa) crosses with a homozygous recessive (aa), the offspring have a 1-to-1 ratio of dominant to recessive traits.
source: Punnett square prediction for Aa x aa

en: A dominant allele is not necessarily more common in a population; it just means it masks the recessive allele in a heterozygote.
Recessive traits are not always harmful; they are simply hidden when a dominant allele is present.
Each box in a Punnett square is equally likely, so a 3-to-1 ratio means three chances for the dominant trait out of four.
With complete dominance, a heterozygote looks like the dominant homozygote, but with incomplete dominance it looks different, giving different ratios.
In rice, the allele for glutinous (sticky) grain is recessive, so a plant shows sticky grain only if it has two copies of that allele.
source: Rice genetics: glutinous trait is recessive

en: In dogs, the allele for floppy ears is recessive to pointy ears, so a floppy-eared dog must have two floppy alleles.
To write genotypes, use a capital letter for the dominant allele and a lowercase letter for the recessive allele, like B for brown and b for blue.
A heterozygous parent makes two kinds of gametes for that gene, one with each allele, while a homozygous parent makes only one kind.
A 1-to-1 ratio from a cross means two equally likely outcomes, like half dominant and half recessive.
In pea plants, yellow seed is dominant over green, so crossing a yellow heterozygote (Yy) with a green (yy) gives half yellow and half green offspring.
In every collision, elastic or inelastic, the combined momentum of the objects before the crash is exactly the same as after the crash.
source: conservation of momentum: closed system total momentum constant

en: Two billiard balls colliding on a pool table are a near-perfect elastic collision because they barely deform and bounce apart with almost no energy lost.
source: encyclopedia-stable; billiard ball collisions as near-elastic

en: When two lumps of clay are thrown together, they stick into one lump and move together, making a perfectly inelastic collision.
source: perfectly inelastic collision: objects stick and move together

en: Most real collisions are neither perfectly elastic nor perfectly inelastic, but somewhere in between, with some energy lost but objects still separating.
source: real collisions are partially elastic; textbook physics

en: When a car crumples in a crash, the energy that folds the metal comes from the car's motion, so the car slows down as the metal bends.
source: energy transfer in deformation; car crash physics

en: Elastic collisions happen with hard, springy materials like steel or glass that return to their original shape right after the hit.
source: elastic collision requires energy storage and return; material property

en: Inelastic collisions happen with soft or sticky materials that stay deformed after the hit, like a crumpled soda can.
source: inelastic collision: permanent deformation; material property

en: A basketball bounces back up but never reaches its original height because each bounce loses a little energy to heat and sound.
Scientists measure how elastic a collision is with a number from zero to one, where one means perfectly elastic and zero means perfectly inelastic.
source: coefficient of restitution definition; 0 to 1 scale

en: When two identical billiard balls meet head-on in an elastic collision, they simply swap their speeds and directions.
source: elastic collision of equal masses; velocity exchange

en: A tennis ball hitting a racket is a mostly elastic collision because the ball compresses, springs back, and flies off with most of its energy.
source: tennis ball compression and rebound; sports physics

en: A bullet that buries itself inside a wooden block is a perfectly inelastic collision because the bullet and block end up moving together.
source: bullet embedding in wood; perfectly inelastic example

en: A hammer hitting a nail is inelastic because the hammer keeps moving with the nail and much of the energy goes into pushing the wood apart.
source: hammer-nail collision; energy transfer to wood

en: A superball is made of a rubber that stores energy when squashed and returns almost all of it, so it bounces very high in a nearly elastic collision.
Car crumple zones are designed to be inelastic on purpose, crushing slowly to absorb crash energy and protect the people inside.
source: car crumple zone design; safety engineering

en: Two magnets that repel each other can have an elastic collision without even touching, because the magnetic field pushes them apart.
source: magnetic repulsion as contactless elastic collision

en: Bicycle helmets are designed to be inelastic, crushing and cracking on impact to absorb crash energy instead of bouncing the rider's head.
source: helmet energy absorption design; safety engineering

en: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the two objects stick together and move at one single speed, like two train cars coupling.
source: perfectly inelastic collision; train coupling example

en: A basketball player catching a pass is an inelastic collision because the ball and hands end up moving together and the ball's energy is absorbed.
source: catching a ball as inelastic collision; sports physics

en: Momentum has direction, so two objects crashing head-on can cancel each other's motion, and the total momentum after depends on both speeds and directions.
source: momentum as vector quantity; direction matters

en: To add a switch to a simple circuit, cut the wire between the battery and bulb and attach the two loose ends to the switch's terminals.
source: standard circuit assembly: switch placed in series to control flow

en: When a toy motor replaces the bulb, close the switch and watch for the motor's shaft to spin, which shows current is flowing.
source: observable outcome of closed circuit with motor

en: A circuit diagram uses straight lines for wires and standard symbols for each part, arranged in a closed rectangle shape.
A clear record of a circuit test includes a labeled drawing of the setup and a note saying whether the bulb lit or not.
To check if a circuit is complete, trace the path from one battery terminal through every component and back to the other terminal.
To swap a bulb for a motor, disconnect the two bulb wires and attach them to the motor's two terminals instead.
A buzzer works like a bulb: when the switch closes, it makes a sound, so you listen instead of looking for light.
source: buzzer as output device in circuit

en: To test which materials conduct electricity, keep the same battery, bulb, and wires, and only change the material placed in the gap.
If the bulb does not light, check that every wire end is tightly touching its terminal and that the switch is fully closed.
In a circuit diagram, draw the switch on one side of the loop, between the battery and the bulb, not inside the battery symbol.
The order of connecting the battery, switch, and bulb does not matter as long as the loop is unbroken and complete.
To make a bulb brighter, add more batteries by connecting the positive terminal of one to the negative terminal of the next.
Reversing the battery connections in a motor circuit makes the motor spin in the opposite direction.
source: motor direction depends on current polarity

en: To turn off a simple circuit, open the switch to create a gap in the wire, which stops the flow of current.
source: switch function: break in circuit stops current

en: To test if a switch works, close it and see if the bulb lights; if it does, the switch is functioning properly.
In a circuit diagram, a toy motor is drawn as a circle with the letter M inside, connected by wires to the other parts.
To verify a circuit diagram, trace a line from the battery's positive symbol to the negative symbol, passing through each component.
A battery holder keeps the battery steady and makes it easier to attach wires to its two metal clips.
When comparing circuits, note whether the bulb is dim or bright, which tells you how much current is flowing.
When you type a school name into FaultFinder, it places a marker on the map, which you then use as the starting point for measuring distances.
The measure tool in FaultFinder measures straight-line distance, so you should draw the line perpendicular to the fault line to get the shortest distance.
A good record of a FaultFinder check includes a screenshot that shows the scale bar, the north arrow, and the red fault line clearly.
When comparing two possible house sites, you keep the same map zoom level and the same measure tool settings so the distances are fair to compare.
Scientists verify the FaultFinder map by walking the fault trace on the ground with a GPS device and marking the exact line.
The FaultFinder map lets you click on a fault line to see its name and the date of its last known movement.
To see if your school is in a liquefaction zone, you turn on the liquefaction layer in the FaultFinder menu and look for the shaded area.
The FaultFinder's legend explains that red lines mean active faults, while yellow or orange areas mean liquefaction or landslide risk.
A class can use the FaultFinder's print button to save a map that shows the school and the nearest fault, which they can attach to a report.
If the FaultFinder shows the fault line passing directly under a building, that building is in the highest risk zone.
The FaultFinder map is updated by PHIVOLCS, so it shows the most recent fault lines that scientists have confirmed.
If the FaultFinder shows no red line near your barangay, you still check the liquefaction and landslide layers for other risks.
If the measure tool is not available, you can use the map's scale bar to estimate the distance from your house to the fault line.
The FaultFinder map has a basemap option that lets you switch to satellite view to see actual buildings and roads near the fault line.
A good way to record the result is to write down the fault name, the measured distance, and the date you checked it on the map.
The search function in FaultFinder lets you type a barangay name, and the map will zoom to that barangay automatically.
To see liquefaction zones clearly, you can turn off the fault line layer in the FaultFinder menu.
To compare the risk of two different barangays, you use the same FaultFinder tool and the same layers turned on for both places.
Wear safety goggles during experiments so splashes or flying bits of glass do not hurt your eyes.
Place test tubes in a test tube rack so they stand upright and do not roll off the table.
Use a clean spatula to scoop solid chemicals from their containers so your fingers stay clean.
Put a solid on a watch glass before weighing it on a balance so the pan stays clean.
Set a beaker on a tripod over a flame, with a wire mesh between them, so the heat spreads evenly.
Grind a solid into a fine powder with a mortar and pestle so it dissolves faster in liquid.
Use a wash bottle to squirt a fine stream of water into glassware to rinse it thoroughly.
Clean microscope lenses with special lens paper because cloth or tissue can scratch the glass.
Hold a thermometer steady with a clamp so it does not touch the bottom of the container.
To find the volume of an odd-shaped solid, drop it into a graduated cylinder and read the water rise.
Use a funnel to pour a liquid into a narrow bottle so it does not spill outside.
Wipe up a spilled liquid right away and tell the teacher so nobody slips or touches it.
Place a heat-proof mat under a hot plate or Bunsen burner to protect the table from burns.
When using a balance, put the object on the left pan and add weights to the right pan to find its mass.
Use a hand lens to look closely at small details of a leaf, rock, or insect.
Heat a substance gently by placing its container in a water bath of hot water instead of direct flame.
Place a specimen on a glass slide and cover it with a cover slip before putting it under a microscope.
After washing and drying equipment, return each piece to its proper storage place so the lab stays organized.
To measure weight with a spring scale, hook the object onto the bottom hook and let it hang freely.
Rocks are hard, solid pieces of the Earth made of minerals, and they come in many sizes from tiny pebbles to huge mountains.
Some rocks form from cooled lava, like the black basalt near Mayon Volcano in the Philippines.
Water can be a solid, liquid, or gas: ice is solid, rainwater is liquid, and water vapor in the air is a gas.
Air is all around us even though we cannot see it, and it is a mixture of gases like oxygen and nitrogen.
Wind is moving air, and it can be gentle like a breeze or strong like a typhoon.
Metals such as iron and aluminum are shiny, hard, and can be shaped into things like cans, wires, and jeepney bodies.
Sunlight gives us both light and heat, and it is the main source of energy for life on Earth.
Rainwater collects in rivers, lakes, and underground, and this fresh water is used by people, plants, and animals.
Rocks break into smaller pieces over time because of wind, water, and temperature changes, and these pieces become part of soil.
A rock's color and texture can tell us what it is made of; for example, granite has visible specks of different minerals.
Water takes the shape of its container, so it can flow as a stream or fill a glass.
Air has weight, so a balloon filled with air is heavier than an empty balloon.
Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity, which is why cooking pots are made of metal and wires are made of copper.
Sunlight can be blocked by clouds, which is why it is darker and cooler on a cloudy day.
A rain gauge is a tool that collects rainwater so we can measure how much rain fell in a day.
Water evaporates from oceans, lakes, and soil when heated by the sun, turning into water vapor that rises into the air.
Some rocks are soft and crumble easily, like chalk, while others are very hard, like diamond.
Soil holds water and air between its tiny particles, giving roots the moisture and oxygen they need.
Metals can rust when they stay wet, like the brown rust on an old iron nail.
Sunlight is a form of energy called solar energy, and it can be used to make electricity with solar panels.
For main-group elements, the group number on the periodic table matches the number of electrons in the outermost shell, called valence electrons.
source: periodic table group number = valence electrons for main-group elements

en: Moving from left to right across a period, each element adds one more outer electron, which is why properties change gradually across the row.
source: periodic table period trend: outer electron count increases by one per step

en: Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways, like lithium and sodium both being soft metals.
source: periodic table groups share valence electron count and similar chemistry

en: Sodium's 11 electrons sit in three shells as 2-8-1, so it belongs in period 3, group 1, just below lithium.
source: sodium electron configuration 2-8-1; position period 3 group 1

en: Atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to reach eight in their outer shell, and this drive shapes how elements in each group behave.
Halogens in group 17 have seven outer electrons, so they need just one more to fill their shell, making them very reactive nonmetals.
Alkali metals in group 1 have a single outer electron that they easily give away, which is why they are the most reactive metals.
source: alkali metals: group 1, one valence electron

en: In transition metals, new electrons go into an inner shell rather than the outer one, which is why they sit in the middle block of the table.
source: transition metals fill d orbitals in inner shell

en: The lanthanides and actinides sit below the main table because their extra electrons fill deep inner f-orbitals, not the outer shell.
Helium has only two electrons, but because its first shell is full, it sits with the noble gases in group 18.
Elements in the same period have the same number of shells but different outer electron counts, while elements in the same group share the same outer count.
source: period = shell count; group = outer electron count

en: An element's group is decided by its outer electrons only, not by the total number of electrons in the atom.
source: group number determined by valence electrons, not total

en: Electrons fill the innermost shell first, then the next, and this filling order is what gives each element its row and column.
source: aufbau principle: electrons fill lowest energy levels first

en: No two elements have the same electron arrangement in their shells, which is why each element gets its own unique box on the table.
source: each element has a unique electron configuration

en: The outer electrons are the ones that interact during chemical reactions, so atoms with the same outer count land in the same group.
source: valence electrons participate in chemical bonding

en: Chlorine's 17 electrons are arranged 2-8-7, placing it in period 3, group 17, where it pairs with sodium to make table salt.
source: chlorine electron configuration 2-8-7; forms NaCl with sodium

en: Metals tend to lose their outer electrons, while nonmetals tend to gain them, and this difference in electron structure shows up in their table positions.
source: metals lose electrons; nonmetals gain electrons

en: The second electron shell can hold eight electrons, and the third shell fills to eight before the next shell begins, so periods 2 and 3 each have eight elements.
source: shell capacities: second shell 8; third shell fills to 8 before 4th starts

topic: nearly full vs nearly empty shells
en: An atom with a nearly full outer shell, like oxygen with six, tends to gain two electrons, while one with a nearly empty shell tends to lose them.
source: octet rule: atoms gain or lose electrons to reach eight

en: The periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number, and electron shells fill in that same order, so position matches electron structure.
source: periodic table ordered by atomic number; electron filling follows same order

en: A fair test of conductors keeps the same battery, bulb, and wires, and only changes the material placed in the gap.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, the rest held constant
