en: To test a motor, watch which way its shaft spins when you close the switch, then reverse the battery to see it spin the other way.
source: observable behavior of DC motors with reversed polarity

en: When a buzzer is in a circuit, closing the switch makes a sound, so you listen for the buzz to know current is flowing.
source: observable behavior of buzzers in a closed circuit

en: Alligator clips grip wire ends and terminals firmly, so they make a secure connection that is easy to change between tests.
source: common classroom tool for temporary circuit connections

en: In a circuit diagram, the switch must be drawn as an open gap or closed line on the wire, never as a separate floating part.
source: standard circuit diagram conventions for switches

en: In the DNA backbone, each phosphate group connects two sugar molecules with a strong covalent bond called a phosphodiester bond.
In the DNA double helix, each base pair lies flat and perpendicular to the long axis, like the steps of a spiral staircase.
When building a circuit, connect the battery, wires, switch, and bulb first, then close the switch last to test it.
source: standard practice for assembling simple circuits

en: To draw a circuit diagram, place the battery symbol on one side, the bulb on the other, and connect them with straight lines.
An open switch is a gap in the wire, so drawing it as a break in the line shows exactly where the circuit stops.
A good way to check a circuit is to follow the wire from one battery end to the other, looking for any loose or broken spots.
To compare batteries fairly, use the same bulb and wires, and only change the battery to see which one makes the bulb brighter.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, rest held constant

en: The bulb, motor, or buzzer in a circuit is called the load, and it is the part that uses the electricity to do something.
A short circuit happens when a wire connects the two battery ends directly, so the electricity takes a shortcut and skips the bulb.
To test a motor, close the switch and watch which way its shaft spins, then reverse the battery to see it spin the other way.
source: standard method for observing motor direction

en: A complete circuit means every part is connected in one unbroken loop, so electricity can flow from the battery and back again.
To build a circuit from a diagram, match each symbol to its real part, then connect them in the same order as the drawing.
source: standard engineering practice for reading schematics

en: To compare your distance with the 5-meter buffer zone, you multiply the FaultFinder's kilometer reading by 1000 to get meters.
source: PHIVOLCS buffer zone guideline; unit conversion

en: Rocks are sorted into three groups by how they form: from cooled melted rock, from pressed layers, and from heat and pressure.
source: rock classification by origin (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic)

en: Sandy soil feels gritty, clay soil feels smooth and sticky when wet, and loam is a helpful mix of sand, clay, and humus.
source: soil texture types: sand, clay, loam

en: Pure water freezes into ice at 0°C and boils into steam at 100°C at sea level.
source: water phase change temperatures at standard pressure

en: Air takes up space, so a glass that looks empty is actually full of air inside it.
source: air is matter and occupies volume

en: Magnets pull on some metals like iron, but they do not pull on aluminum or copper.
Clouds are made of millions of tiny water droplets or ice crystals so small that they float in the sky.
source: cloud microphysics: droplets and ice crystals

en: When warm air cools, water vapor turns back into tiny droplets, and this process is called condensation.
Your shadow is longest in the early morning and late afternoon, and shortest at noon when the sun is highest.
Limestone is a common rock that people crush and heat to make cement for buildings and roads.
Water can dissolve many things, like salt and sugar, which is why we use it to wash and clean.
Living things need the oxygen in air to breathe, and fire also needs oxygen to keep burning.
source: oxygen's role in respiration and combustion

en: Metals like iron and copper are dug from the ground inside rocks called ores, then melted into useful objects.
Plants use sunlight, water, and air to make their own food, so they grow toward the light.
The Philippines has a rainy season from June to November and a dry season from December to May.
source: PAGASA climate seasons in the Philippines

en: Fog is a cloud that forms close to the ground, like the thick mist you see on cool mountain mornings.
Air is mostly nitrogen, about 78 out of every 100 parts, with about 21 parts oxygen and a little other gas.
source: air composition by volume (about 78% N2, 21% O2)

en: A fair test of a lever keeps the same lever, the same fulcrum, and the same load, while only changing the distance from the fulcrum to your hand.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, the rest held constant

en: To measure how a lever changes force, attach a spring scale to the load and read the number of newtons it takes to lift it.
source: standard force measurement with spring scale

en: In a lever fair test, you change the effort distance by moving your hand along the lever, but you keep the load weight exactly the same.
To test the load side, keep your hand at the same spot and move the load closer to or farther from the fulcrum.
A good record for a lever test is a table listing the effort distance, the load distance, and the measured force for each trial.
Scientists repeat each lever measurement three times and use the average force, so a single mistake does not change the answer.
Plotting the effort force against the effort distance on a graph shows a curve that goes down as the distance gets longer.
To test direction change, watch the load move up when you push the lever down, and record that opposite motion in your notes.
Use the same ruler or board for every trial, because a heavier lever would need a different force to lift the same load.
Mark the exact spot where the lever rests on the fulcrum with a pencil, so you measure all distances from that same point.
Use a meter stick to measure the distance from the fulcrum to the load and from the fulcrum to your hand.
In a lever fair test, the distance you choose to change is called the independent variable, and the force you measure is the dependent variable.
Keeping the load the same is important because if you change the weight, you cannot tell if the force changed because of the lever or the weight.
If the effort arm is shorter than the load arm, the measured force is bigger, meaning the lever does not multiply your force but changes direction.
If the effort arm is longer than the load arm, the measured force is smaller, showing the lever multiplies your input force.

topic: direction change with fulcrum in middle
en: When the fulcrum sits between the load and your hand, pushing down makes the load go up, changing the direction of the force.

topic: no direction change with load in middle
en: When the load sits between the fulcrum and your hand, pushing up makes the load go up too, so the direction stays the same.
A class can use a seesaw as a lever, keeping the same two people on it while moving the fulcrum to test how force changes.
Read the spring scale only when the load is just about to lift off the table, because that is the exact force needed to overcome gravity.
To compare two different levers fairly, use the same load and the same effort distance, and only change the length of the lever itself.
When drawing a circuit diagram, use a ruler to make straight wire lines and write the name of each part beside its symbol for a clear record.
To test a bulb before building the circuit, connect it directly to a battery with two wires; if it lights, the bulb is ready to use.
A family disaster plan is a simple list of safe meeting places and phone numbers so everyone knows what to do when an earthquake hits.
An emergency go-bag holds water, canned food, a flashlight, and a whistle, so your family can survive for about three days after a quake.
Your school's evacuation route is planned and marked by teachers so it leads away from glass windows and heavy shelves.
If you are outdoors when the shaking starts, move to an open space away from buildings, trees, and power lines, then drop, cover, and hold.
If you are riding a jeepney or car during an earthquake, the driver should pull over to a safe spot and stay inside until the shaking stops.
Stay away from windows and glass doors during an earthquake because they can shatter and send sharp pieces flying.
After the shaking stops, use the stairs instead of the elevator because the elevator might be damaged or the power might go out.
Listen to a battery-powered radio or your phone for official announcements from PHIVOLCS and NDRRMC about aftershocks and safe areas.
It is a common mistake to run outside during strong shaking, but staying under a sturdy table is safer because falling debris is the biggest danger.
A barangay disaster plan lists the nearest evacuation center and the quickest safe route to get there, so you know where to go.
Your family plan should have a designated meeting place outside your home, so you can find each other after an earthquake.
Aftershocks can happen minutes, hours, or even days after the main earthquake, so your plan includes staying alert and not going back inside damaged buildings.
Practicing your school's earthquake drill makes the steps automatic, so your body knows what to do instead of freezing during a real quake.
Know the safe spots in each room, like under strong tables or against inside walls, because you might be anywhere when the quake starts.
If you smell gas after an earthquake, turn off the gas valve if you know how, then leave the building and tell an adult.
Local disaster plans are made by schools, families, and barangays together, so everyone knows their role and how to help each other.
The plan tells you to check on elderly neighbors or people with disabilities after the shaking stops, because they may need extra help to evacuate.
If your building looks unsafe after the earthquake, the plan says to evacuate to the assembly area and wait for instructions from authorities.
The West Valley Fault is a major fault near Metro Manila, so local plans there include specific routes and drills for that risk.
A disaster plan is not just a paper; it is a habit you build by walking the evacuation route and checking your go-bag every few months.
The 3-to-1 phenotypic ratio appears because the two heterozygous offspring and the one homozygous dominant offspring all show the same dominant trait.
source: Mendelian genetics: monohybrid cross phenotypic ratio

en: For a monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes, the genotypic ratio is 1:2:1, but the phenotypic ratio is 3:1 because the heterozygote shows the dominant trait.
source: Mendelian genetics: comparing genotype and phenotype ratios

en: In a Bb x Bb cross, each offspring has a 25% chance of showing the recessive trait and a 75% chance of showing the dominant trait.
source: Mendelian genetics: offspring probabilities from heterozygote cross

en: A cross that tracks just one gene, like seed color, is called a monohybrid cross, and its ratios are the simplest to predict.
source: Mendelian genetics: definition of monohybrid cross

en: In pea plants, round seeds are dominant over wrinkled seeds, so a cross of two round heterozygotes gives three round for every one wrinkled.
source: Mendelian genetics: pea plant seed shape trait

en: In corn, purple kernels are dominant over yellow kernels, so a cross of two purple heterozygotes gives a 3-to-1 ratio of purple to yellow.
source: Mendelian genetics: corn kernel color trait

en: In humans, a widow's peak hairline is dominant over a straight hairline, so a child with two straight-hairline parents will have a straight hairline.
source: Mendelian genetics: human dominant trait example

en: The ability to roll the tongue is dominant over not rolling it, so two non-rollers cannot have a roller child.
source: Mendelian genetics: human dominant trait example

en: An organism that is heterozygous is called a carrier of the recessive allele, because it can pass that allele on without showing the trait.
With a large number of offspring, like hundreds of seeds, the observed ratio gets closer to the predicted 3-to-1 ratio.
source: Mendelian genetics: law of large numbers in inheritance

en: Dominant does not mean better or stronger; it simply means the trait shows in a heterozygote, which is why the 3-to-1 ratio appears.
source: Mendelian genetics: common misconception about dominance

en: Predicting ratios means using the parents' genotypes to list the possible genotypes and phenotypes of their offspring before they are born.
The four boxes in a monohybrid Punnett square each represent one possible offspring, so you can count them to get the ratio.
In dogs, the allele for short hair is dominant over long hair, so two short-haired parents can have a long-haired puppy if both carry the recessive allele.
source: Mendelian genetics: dog coat length trait

en: A single-gene cross between two heterozygotes fills a four-box Punnett square with three different genotypes.
The dominant trait appears in the 3 part of a 3-to-1 ratio, while the recessive trait appears in the 1 part.
In pea plants, purple flowers are dominant over white flowers, so crossing two purple-flowered heterozygotes gives a 3-to-1 ratio of purple to white.
source: Mendelian genetics: pea plant flower color trait

en: A genotypic ratio of 1:2:1 and a phenotypic ratio of 3:1 describe the same cross, just looking at genes versus visible traits.
source: Mendelian genetics: comparing genotype and phenotype ratios

en: If a trait skips a generation, it is often recessive, because carriers can pass it on without showing it themselves.
The tsunami warning chain has three steps: detect the earthquake, decide the danger, and alert the coast so people can evacuate.
PHIVOLCS issues tsunami bulletins that tell people whether to evacuate, stay alert, or return to normal.
When a local tsunami is possible, the first waves can arrive within minutes, so people must evacuate immediately without waiting for an official warning.
A natural warning sign of a tsunami is the sea suddenly pulling back from the shore, leaving fish flopping on dry sand.
If you are on the coast and feel a strong earthquake, do not wait for a warning — run to higher ground right away.
Tsunami evacuation maps show the safe zones and the fastest routes to reach them, and every coastal family should know their path.
During a tsunami warning, authorities broadcast alerts over radio, television, sirens, and text messages to reach as many people as possible.
After a tsunami warning is lifted, people must still stay away from the coast because the danger can last for many hours.
The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center watches the whole ocean and sends alerts to countries, including the Philippines, when a huge wave may travel across the sea.
A tsunami warning from a faraway earthquake gives hours to prepare, but a local earthquake gives only minutes, so local knowledge saves lives.
Tsunami sirens are loud, high-pitched alarms placed along Philippine coasts to signal people to evacuate immediately.
Local governments hold tsunami drills so residents practice moving to higher ground quickly and calmly before a real wave arrives.
The first tsunami wave is often not the biggest, so people must not go back to the shore just because the water looks calm.
An emergency 'go bag' with water, food, flashlight, and important documents helps a family evacuate quickly during a tsunami warning.
PHIVOLCS works with local governments to put up tsunami hazard maps that show which coastal areas are safe and which are dangerous.
When a tsunami warning is announced, people should move to high ground or at least one kilometer inland, away from rivers and the sea.
The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council coordinates the response, helping evacuations and rescue during a tsunami.
Never go to the beach to watch a tsunami, because the waves can arrive suddenly and sweep people into the sea.
After a tsunami, people may return home only when authorities say it is safe, because roads, buildings, and water may be dangerous.
A tsunami advisory means the waves may be small but still dangerous, so people should stay off the beach and away from the water.
Pangaea was a supercontinent that included almost all of Earth's landmasses, existing about 300 to 200 million years ago before breaking apart.
Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, suggesting that continents slowly moved across Earth's surface instead of staying fixed.
Glacial scratches and deposits found in Africa and India show these warm places were once covered by ice near the South Pole.
source: paleoclimate evidence from glacial striations; encyclopedia-stable

en: Coal deposits in Antarctica prove it was once warm and forested, because coal forms from ancient swamp plants that cannot grow in ice.
Lystrosaurus was a land reptile whose fossils appear in Africa, India, and Antarctica, lands now separated by oceans.
Glossopteris, an ancient seed fern, left fossils on five continents, showing these lands were once connected.
Continents drift about 2 to 5 centimeters each year, roughly the speed your fingernails grow, so movement is too slow to feel.
Heat from Earth's interior creates convection currents in the mantle, which slowly drag the continents along with the plates.
New ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and pushes older crust sideways, carrying continents apart over millions of years.
Symmetrical magnetic stripes on the ocean floor record reversals of Earth's magnetic field, confirming that the seafloor spreads.
The Appalachian Mountains in North America line up with the Caledonian Mountains in Scotland when the continents are rejoined.
source: geological correlation of mountain belts; encyclopedia-stable

en: South America, Africa, India, Australia, and Antarctica fit together like pieces of a giant puzzle around the South Pole.
The name Pangaea comes from Greek words meaning 'all lands,' fitting a time when all continents were one.
Wegener's idea was rejected at first because he could not explain what force could move entire continents across the ocean.
source: history of continental drift acceptance; encyclopedia-stable

en: Modern GPS satellites track continents moving a few centimeters each year, giving direct proof that they are still drifting.
source: geodesy and GPS plate motion studies; encyclopedia-stable

en: The oldest ocean floor is only about 200 million years old, much younger than continents, because the seafloor is constantly recycled.
Plate tectonics is the modern theory that explains continental drift by dividing Earth's surface into moving plates.
Fossil coral reefs found in cold regions today show that those places once sat in warm tropical waters near the equator.
The Philippine archipelago sits where several plates meet, and its islands formed from ocean floor and volcanic activity rather than from Pangaea itself.
source: PHIVOLCS plate tectonics of the Philippines

en: Earth's continents have joined and split several times, with Pangaea being the most recent supercontinent about 300 million years ago.
The six-kingdom system sorts all living things into Archaebacteria, Eubacteria, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia.
Classification matters because it gives every organism a shared scientific name, so scientists in different countries know they are talking about the same species.
The three-domain system shows that archaea are more closely related to eukaryotes than to bacteria, even though archaea look like bacteria.
In the three-domain system, the six kingdoms fit inside it: Bacteria and Archaea each become a domain, while four kingdoms sit in Eukarya.
A human belongs to domain Eukarya and kingdom Animalia, because our cells have a nucleus and we are animals.
A mushroom is in kingdom Fungi, not Plantae, because fungi absorb food instead of making it with sunlight.
Many archaea live in extreme places like hot springs and deep-sea vents, where other kinds of life cannot survive.
Ribosomal RNA acts like a molecular clock, letting scientists measure how long ago two species split apart.
Archaea have cell walls without peptidoglycan, a material found in bacterial cell walls, so they are placed in different kingdoms.
Knowing an organism's kingdom lets scientists predict its basic traits, such as whether it makes its own food or eats others.
Scientists have described about 1.5 million species, and the six-kingdom and three-domain systems help organize this huge list.
Not all single-celled organisms are bacteria; protists like amoebas are single-celled but have a true nucleus.
The Philippine eagle is in domain Eukarya and kingdom Animalia, the same groups that hold all birds and mammals.
Bakawan, or mangroves, are flowering plants in kingdom Plantae, so they belong to domain Eukarya like all plants.
The six-kingdom system gives single-celled life its own kingdoms, because a microscope shows protists are very different from plants and animals.
Classifying microbes correctly helps scientists tell which ones cause disease and which ones help make food like yogurt.
The three-domain system is newer than the six-kingdom system, and it places kingdoms inside larger domains based on DNA evidence.
Scientists use both systems today: the three-domain system shows the biggest branches of life, while the six-kingdom system shows smaller groups.
Classification helps scientists trace how different species evolved from common ancestors over millions of years.
Earthquakes strike without warning, so a local disaster readiness plan helps you act quickly and calmly instead of panicking.
If you are in bed when an earthquake starts, the plan says to stay there and cover your head with a pillow.
If you are cooking when the shaking begins, turn off the stove if you can reach it safely, then drop, cover, and hold.
After the shaking stops, the plan says to open doors and windows because the quake may have jammed them shut.
After an earthquake, do not use matches or lighters because a gas leak could cause a fire.
After an earthquake, look for fallen power lines and tell an adult so they can report the danger.
If you live near the coast and the shaking is strong, your plan says to move to higher ground right away because a tsunami may follow.

topic: stay away from beach after quake
en: After a strong earthquake near the sea, stay away from the beach for several hours because a tsunami can arrive later.
At the assembly area, teachers do a headcount to make sure every student is safe and no one is missing.
When you evacuate, bring your emergency go-bag so you have water, food, and a flashlight while you wait.
Wear closed shoes and long sleeves when you evacuate, because broken glass and debris can hurt your feet and skin.
During evacuation, the plan says to help younger children or classmates who are scared, so everyone moves together safely.
Use your phone only for emergencies after an earthquake, because too many calls can block the network for people who need help.
Follow the marked evacuation route even if it looks longer, because it is the path that avoids the most dangers.

topic: check walls for cracks before reentry
en: Before going back inside your home after a quake, check the walls and ceiling for cracks that could mean the building is unsafe.
Keep a small copy of your family disaster plan inside your school bag, so you can remember what to do even if you are away from home.
To see a rock's true color, break it open or look at a fresh chip, because the outside surface is often stained by weather or soil.
source: observation method: fresh surface vs weathered surface

en: To see grain crystal size, hold a hand lens close to your eye and bring the rock toward it until the grains look sharp.
To describe texture, run a finger across the rock's fresh surface and note if it feels smooth, rough, gritty, or glassy.
A scratch test for hardness uses a fingernail, a copper coin, and a steel nail, each scratching softer minerals in order.
To find a mineral's streak, rub it firmly across an unglazed porcelain tile and observe the color of the powder left behind.
A good rock record lists each sample's color, texture, grain size, and hardness in a table so comparisons are easy to see.
When collecting rocks, wrap each sample in paper, label it with the date and place, and keep the label with the rock.
To compare colors fairly, look at all rock samples under the same bright light, because shadows can make colors look darker.
To measure grain crystal size, place a ruler against the rock and record the width of the largest visible grain in millimeters.
Scientists sort rocks into groups by first separating them by grain size, then by color, and finally by texture.
To describe luster, hold the rock so light bounces off it and decide if the shine looks metallic, glassy, pearly, or dull.
To describe grain shape, look at the edges of the crystals and note whether they are sharp and angular or smooth and rounded.
To check for layering, turn the rock sideways and look for flat bands or stripes that run in one direction across the sample.
To test for magnetic minerals, hold a small magnet near the rock and see if it pulls or sticks to the surface.
When comparing two rocks, choose chips of similar size, because a big piece can look rougher or darker than a small one.
To compare density, hold one rock in each hand and feel which is heavier for its size, or use a balance scale.
To record where a rock was found, draw a simple map of the school grounds and mark each collection spot with a number.
A weathered rock surface is often brown or gray from rain and air, so scientists always check the fresh break for true color.
A magnifying glass helps count tiny grains, and scientists record whether they can see grains without it or only with it.
To see if crystals have a pattern, look at the rock under a hand lens and note if the grains are packed tightly or have gaps.
A simple circuit is a closed loop of a battery, wires, and a bulb, so electricity can travel around the loop and light the bulb.
A battery has two ends, positive and negative, and it pushes electrical energy through the wires when the circuit path is complete.
Metals like copper, iron, and aluminum conduct electricity because their outer electrons are loose and free to move from atom to atom.
source: encyclopedia-stable; free electron model of metals

en: The bulb lights only when the circuit is complete, meaning there is one unbroken path from one battery end, through the wires and bulb, back to the other end.
A switch is a gap in the circuit that you can open or close; closing the switch joins the path, and opening it breaks the flow of electricity.
Even a tiny gap anywhere in the loop stops the electricity, because electrons need a continuous path from the battery through the bulb and back.
Copper is the most common metal for electrical wires because it conducts electricity very well and is cheaper than gold or silver.
Coins, paper clips, aluminum foil, metal spoons, and keys are everyday conductors that can complete a simple circuit and light a bulb.
Insulators act like a broken bridge in a circuit: electrons cannot cross them, so the current stops at that point.
A short circuit happens when wires touch each other directly without a bulb in between, so too much current flows and the wires can get hot.
A brighter bulb means the material conducts electricity well, while a dim bulb or no light means the material blocks the current.
In a simple circuit, the bulb is the load that changes electrical energy into light and heat, showing that current is flowing.
The wires in a circuit are like pipes for electricity; they guide the electrons from the battery to the bulb and back again.
Dry wood is an insulator, but wet wood can conduct a little electricity because the water in it carries dissolved minerals.
In the Philippines, you can test a metal key, a one-peso coin, and a tin can lid in a simple circuit to see which ones light the bulb.
source: DepEd MATATAG; local materials for circuit testing

en: Electric current is the flow of electrons through a wire, and it only happens when the circuit is closed and unbroken.
A conductor is like an open door that lets electricity pass through, while an insulator is like a wall that blocks it.
A complete circuit needs four parts: a source like a battery, wires to carry current, a load like a bulb, and a closed path.
Electric current is measured in amperes, but in a school circuit you can just watch the bulb to know that current is flowing.
source: encyclopedia-stable; ampere as unit of current

en: A battery stores chemical energy, and when the circuit is complete, that energy pushes electrons around the loop to light the bulb.
Before testing, name the lever class by finding the fulcrum, load, and effort positions, because each class changes the force differently.
source: lever classes: first, second, third class arrangements

en: Hold the spring scale at a right angle to the lever when pulling, so the reading shows only the lifting force and not a sideways pull.
source: force measurement: perpendicular pull for accurate spring scale reading

en: Use a balance to check that the load weighs the same before every trial, so the weight is not a hidden variable.
source: fair-test design: verify constants before trials

en: Start each trial with the lever horizontal and the load resting on the table, so every trial begins from the same position.
To test a second-class lever, place the load between the fulcrum and your hand, and move the load to see how the force changes.
source: lever classes: second-class lever (load between fulcrum and effort)

en: To test a third-class lever, place your hand between the fulcrum and the load, and record that the measured force becomes larger than the load.
source: lever classes: third-class lever (effort between fulcrum and load)

en: Calculate the mechanical advantage by dividing the load weight by the effort force you measured with the spring scale.
source: mechanical advantage formula: MA = load ÷ effort

en: Compare the mechanical advantage to one: a number above one means the lever multiplied your force, and below one means it only changed direction.
source: mechanical advantage interpretation: MA > 1 or MA < 1

en: Use a protractor to keep the pull angle the same in every trial, so only the lever arm distance changes.
source: fair-test design: hold angle constant as a control

en: Mark the hand position on the lever with chalk or tape, so you push at the exact same spot in every trial.
source: fair-test design: mark positions for reproducibility

en: Read the spring scale at eye level so the pointer lines up with the numbers, because looking from above or below changes the reading.
source: measurement practice: read at eye level to avoid parallax

en: Check that the spring scale reads zero before each trial, so every measurement starts from the same baseline.
source: measurement practice: zero the instrument before each use

en: Have the same person pull the spring scale in all trials, so the speed and smoothness of the pull stay consistent.
source: fair-test design: keep operator consistent across trials

en: Pull the spring scale slowly and steadily, because a fast jerk makes the reading jump higher than the true force.
source: measurement practice: slow steady pull avoids dynamic overshoot

en: In a lever fair test, multiplying the effort force by the effort distance gives the same number as multiplying the load force by the load distance.
source: principle of moments / work conservation for an ideal lever

en: When the fulcrum is between the load and your hand on a lever, the effort moves down while the load moves up, reversing the force's direction.
source: lever classification by fulcrum-load-effort order; encyclopedia-stable

en: A tsunami is a series of powerful ocean waves caused by a sudden movement of the seafloor, usually from an underwater earthquake.
When an earthquake lifts or drops the seafloor, it pushes the entire column of water above it, creating waves that spread outward in all directions.
Tsunami warning centers judge the danger by checking the earthquake's size, depth, and whether it happened under the ocean floor.
After a strong earthquake, scientists check tide gauges and ocean buoys to confirm whether a tsunami was actually generated.
Some coastal villages train volunteer lookouts who watch the sea and alert neighbors when they see unusual water behavior.
In flat coastal areas with no hills, people can evacuate upward into tall, strong buildings designed as tsunami shelters.
Mangrove forests along Philippine coasts act as natural barriers that slow tsunami waves and reduce their strength.
Schools near the coast practice tsunami evacuation drills so students know the fastest route to high ground.
A tsunami watch means a distant earthquake may create a tsunami, while a warning means a tsunami is confirmed and people must evacuate.
Barangay officials use megaphones and go door-to-door to warn residents who may have missed the sirens and broadcasts.

topic: tsunami crosses Pacific in a day
en: A tsunami can cross the entire Pacific Ocean in about one day, traveling about as fast as a jet airplane.
The word 'tsunami' comes from Japanese words meaning 'harbor wave,' because the waves become most destructive in harbors and bays.
During a tsunami evacuation, authorities direct traffic and close some roads so emergency vehicles and evacuees can move quickly.
Authorities set up temporary evacuation centers on high ground with food, water, and first aid for displaced families.
Authorities lift a tsunami warning only after monitoring the waves for several hours and confirming the danger has passed.
Families living near the coast should have a plan that includes a meeting place on high ground and a way to contact each other.
A vector is a quantity that has both a size and a direction, so velocity is a vector because it includes which way something moves.
A scalar is a quantity that has only a size, so speed is a scalar because it just tells how fast without any direction.
To draw velocity, you use an arrow whose length shows the speed and whose direction points where the object is going.
A car going around a circular track has a constant speed but its velocity changes every moment because its direction keeps turning.
When a jeepney turns a corner at the same speed, its velocity changes because the direction of its motion changes.
An airplane flying with a tailwind has a faster ground speed, but its velocity is the sum of its own speed and the wind's speed.
PAGASA reports a typhoon's velocity by telling both how fast the storm moves and the direction it is heading.
PHIVOLCS watches the velocity of Mayon's lava flow to know how fast and in which direction the hot rock is moving.
A common mistake is thinking velocity is just a larger speed, but velocity is a different idea because it always has a direction.
If a runner keeps a steady speed on a straight path, their velocity stays the same because both speed and direction are unchanged.
To measure velocity, you need a speedometer for the size and a compass or map to know the direction.
Two velocities can cancel out, like a boat moving forward while the river current pushes it backward at the same speed.
Velocity uses displacement, which is the straight-line change in position, while speed uses the total distance traveled.
A ball thrown straight up has a velocity that points up first, then down, even though its speed just gets smaller and bigger.
A bus moving north on EDSA has a velocity of 40 km/h north, but the same bus moving south has a different velocity.
The unit for velocity is the same as speed, like meters per second or kilometers per hour, but it must include a direction.
source: SI units for velocity and speed

en: A boat crossing a river has a velocity that combines its own engine speed and the river's current speed and direction.
A runner sprinting 100 meters has a velocity pointing toward the finish line, while a runner sprinting back has a velocity pointing the opposite way.
Velocity can be split into parts, like a car moving northeast having a northward part and an eastward part.
A car moving straight at a constant speed has a velocity that is constant, but if it brakes, its velocity changes because speed changes.
To estimate grain crystal size, scientists compare the grains to everyday objects like sugar, rice, or peas on a printed chart.
A field sketch records the rock's outline, visible grains, and any bands, so the shape and details are kept even after leaving the site.
source: standard field geology practice: sketching specimens

en: Before picking up a rock, scientists note whether it lies loose on the ground or is part of a larger layer or outcrop.
source: field observation protocol: note context before collecting

en: Dropping a little vinegar on a rock reveals limestone or marble if it fizzes, because the acid reacts with the mineral calcite.
source: calcite reacts with weak acid; standard field test

en: To see a rock's true colors, scientists wet the surface with water and compare it to the dry surface, because water deepens the colors.
source: field observation: wetting surfaces reveals true mineral colors

en: A rock identification key works like a branching set of questions, each answer sending you to the next question until the rock is named.
source: dichotomous keys in rock identification guides

en: To test porosity, scientists drop water on a fresh surface and watch whether it soaks in quickly, slowly, or beads up on top.
source: porosity test: water absorption on fresh surface

en: Comparing granite from two different provinces shows that the same rock type can vary in color and grain size from place to place.
Scientists record whether a rock looks like a solid mass or is made of visible grains, because that tells if it cooled fast or slow.
source: igneous rock texture: cooling rate determines grain visibility

en: To describe holes in a rock, scientists count the pits and note their size, because gas bubbles once made those cavities in lava.
source: vesicular texture from volcanic gas bubbles

en: Scientists describe a rock's overall shape as rounded, angular, or flat, which hints at how far water or wind carried it.
Scientists use a small brush to dust off loose dirt before examining a rock, so tiny grains and cracks are not hidden by soil.
source: field preparation: clean specimen before examination

en: Scientists note the weather when collecting rocks, because rain can darken surfaces and make colors look different from dry days.
source: field collection protocol: note environmental conditions

en: Projectile motion is the curved path an object follows after it is thrown, kicked, or launched, when gravity is the only force still acting on it.
The path of every projectile is a parabola, a symmetric curved shape that rises to one peak and then falls back down.
source: encyclopedia-stable; trajectory of projectiles is parabolic

en: In ideal projectile motion, after the launch, gravity pulls the object downward at about 9.8 meters per second squared, and no other force acts on it.
When a player shoots a basketball, the ball's arc from hands to hoop is a projectile path, and the release angle decides whether the shot reaches the rim.
source: encyclopedia-stable; basketball as everyday projectile example

en: A football kicked high into the air stays above the ground longer than one kicked low and flat, even if both travel the same forward distance.
source: encyclopedia-stable; time of flight depends on vertical motion

en: Water sprayed from a garden hose follows a projectile arc, so tilting the hose steeper makes the water rise higher but land closer.
source: encyclopedia-stable; water stream as projectile example

en: The upward part of a projectile's launch velocity decides how high it rises, so more upward speed means a higher peak.
source: encyclopedia-stable; vertical velocity determines maximum height

en: Scientists split a projectile's launch velocity into horizontal and vertical parts, then study each part separately because they behave differently.
source: encyclopedia-stable; vector components of projectile velocity

en: Gravity constantly changes a projectile's vertical speed, slowing it down on the way up and speeding it up on the way down.
source: encyclopedia-stable; gravity's effect on vertical velocity

en: On level ground, a projectile's path is symmetric, so the time it spends rising equals the time it spends falling.
In real life, air resistance slows projectiles down, so an actual thrown ball lands a little shorter than the ideal calculation predicts.
In the Filipino game sipa, each kick sends the washer or ball on a projectile path, and a higher kick gives the player more time to prepare the next hit.
Long jumpers take off at about 20 degrees above the ground, because a steeper angle would waste energy going upward instead of forward.
source: biomechanics literature; long jump takeoff angle around 20 degrees

en: Rocks and ash thrown out of a volcano like Mayon follow projectile paths, and their range depends on the speed and angle of the eruption.
Range is the horizontal distance a projectile travels from its launch point to where it lands on the ground.
A projectile launched at a very steep angle, like 80 degrees, goes almost straight up and lands very close to the launch point.
source: encyclopedia-stable; effect of very steep launch angles

en: Doubling the launch speed of a projectile makes it travel about four times farther, because range grows with the square of the speed.
source: range formula v²sin(2θ)/g; doubling speed quadruples range

en: A common mistake is thinking a heavier ball thrown the same way travels farther, but in ideal projectile motion, weight does not change the path at all.
source: Galileo; mass independence in ideal projectile motion

en: A ball launched straight up at 20 meters per second takes about 2 seconds to reach its peak and about 4 seconds to return to the ground.
source: kinematics; v = u + at for vertical launch

en: Water fountains shoot streams that curve like projectiles, and the nozzle angle controls how high and how far each stream sprays.
source: encyclopedia-stable; water fountain as projectile example

en: A circuit tester is built with a gap in the wire, and you place the material you want to test across that gap to see if it completes the loop.
When you test a material, it becomes part of the circuit loop, so a conductor completes the path and lights the bulb, while an insulator breaks it.
A dry cloth is an insulator, but a wet cloth can conduct a little electricity because the water in it carries dissolved minerals.
Sea water conducts electricity better than fresh water because it has more dissolved salt, which helps carry the electric current.
source: electrolyte concentration: sea vs fresh water

en: Charcoal, like the kind used for cooking, is a form of carbon that can conduct electricity and light a bulb in a circuit tester.
A dry bamboo stick is an insulator, so placing it in a circuit tester will not light the bulb, unlike a metal nail.
You can use a circuit tester to sort everyday materials into conductors that light the bulb and insulators that keep it dark.
Testing materials with a circuit helps us choose which ones are safe to use for wires and which ones should cover them.
A dry string is an insulator, but a wet string can conduct a little electricity, so it can light the bulb dimly.
The battery in a circuit tester pushes the electric current through the test material, so the bulb can show if the material lets it pass.
To design a simple circuit tester, you connect a battery, a bulb, and wires in a loop, leaving two free wire ends to touch the material.
A piece of chalk is an insulator, so it will not light the bulb in a circuit tester, unlike a metal key.
When testing materials outside, remember that a dry leaf is an insulator, but a wet leaf can conduct a little electricity.
Antoine Lavoisier made one of the first lists of pure elements, separating true elements from mixtures and compounds.
John Dalton gave each element a relative atomic weight, which let early scientists compare elements by a shared number.
Johann Dobereiner grouped elements into triads, where the middle element's atomic weight was about the average of the other two.
John Newlands arranged elements by atomic mass and noticed a repeating pattern every eighth element, which he called the law of octaves.
Lothar Meyer independently plotted atomic volume against atomic mass and saw a periodic pattern that matched Mendeleev's table.
Mendeleev used his table to correct the atomic masses of some known elements, because their positions showed the old values were wrong.
Henry Moseley discovered that arranging elements by atomic number, the number of protons, fixed the order that atomic mass made confusing.
Glenn Seaborg moved the actinide elements to a separate row below the main periodic table, reshaping how heavy elements are shown.
Early scientists like Lavoisier defined an element as a pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means.
Today's periodic table is ordered by increasing atomic number, which is the exact count of protons in an atom's nucleus.
source: Modern periodic table ordering by atomic number

en: The periodic law states that element properties repeat in a regular pattern when elements are arranged by increasing atomic number.
Jöns Jacob Berzelius introduced the one- or two-letter chemical symbols we still use, like O for oxygen and Fe for iron.
Before Berzelius, scientists used different names and pictures for elements, so a shared symbol system made communication much easier.
Mendeleev's table was powerful because it placed elements with similar chemical reactions in the same vertical column.
Before the periodic table, scientists had no single chart to compare all known elements at a glance, so discoveries were hard to link.
Early lists had fewer than 40 known elements, while the modern periodic table contains about 118 confirmed elements.
Moseley used X-rays to show that atomic number, not atomic mass, is the true basis for ordering the elements.
The periodic table lets scientists predict how an unknown element will react based on its position among known neighbors.
The periodic table grew through the work of many scientists over more than a century, each building on the last person's findings.
In the periodic table, columns group elements with similar properties, while rows show a repeating pattern of electron shells.
source: Structure of the periodic table (groups and periods)

en: The six-kingdom system groups organisms by their cell type and how they get food, making it simpler for students than the DNA-based three-domain system.
source: encyclopedia-stable; six-kingdom system based on cell structure and nutrition

en: Classifying the Philippine crocodile as a separate species helps conservationists protect it, because it is found only in the Philippines and is endangered.
source: IUCN Red List; Philippine crocodile (Crocodylus mindorensis) endemic and endangered

en: A common mistake is thinking all microbes are germs, but classification shows many bacteria and protists help break down waste and make food.
source: encyclopedia-stable; beneficial roles of microbes in decomposition and food production

en: Farmers use classification to choose crop varieties that share resistance to pests, because related plants often have similar defenses.
source: agriculture science; related crop varieties share genetic traits

en: When doctors find a new microbe, they compare its DNA to known groups to predict how it spreads and what medicine might work.
source: medical microbiology; DNA comparison for pathogen identification

en: The word 'bayawak' can mean different lizards in different provinces, so scientific names from classification prevent confusion.
source: encyclopedia-stable; common names vary by region, scientific names are universal

en: Classification helps scientists compare organisms from different regions, so a Filipino frog and an African frog can be checked if they are the same species.
source: biogeography; classification enables cross-regional species identification

en: Classification helps scientists estimate how many species are still unknown by comparing new finds with already grouped organisms.
source: taxonomy; extrapolation from known groups to estimate biodiversity

en: All living things share the same genetic code for building proteins, so the three-domain system shows they all came from one common ancestor.
source: molecular biology; universal genetic code indicates common ancestry

en: The three-domain system shows that bacteria and archaea are as different from each other as animals are from plants.
source: molecular phylogenetics; rRNA comparisons show deep divergence

en: Before building a road, scientists classify the plants and animals in the area to know which rare species need protection.
source: conservation biology; environmental impact assessments require species inventories

en: Many archaea live in extreme conditions like hot springs, so scientists study them to understand how the first life on Earth survived.
source: astrobiology and evolutionary biology; extremophiles as models for early life

en: Field guides use classification to organize species into groups, so a hiker can identify a bird by matching it to its family.
source: natural history; field guides arranged by taxonomic groups

en: If a scientist finds a new fungus, classification tells them it likely lives in damp places because fungi need moisture to grow.
source: ecology; kingdom-level traits predict habitat requirements

en: DNA-based classification can show that two look-alike organisms, like some desert plants, are actually from different families.
source: molecular phylogenetics; convergent evolution can mislead morphology

en: Knowing that archaebacteria and eubacteria have different cell walls helps scientists develop antibiotics that target only harmful bacteria.
source: microbiology; cell wall differences inform antibiotic design

en: Learning the six kingdoms helps Filipino students see the variety of life, from bakawan in the sea to eagles in the sky.
source: educational science; six-kingdom framework introduces biodiversity

en: Meiosis is a two-step division that reduces the chromosome number by half, turning one diploid cell with paired chromosomes into four haploid cells with single chromosomes.
Having genes from two parents creates more variety in a population, which helps the species survive changes in the environment.
source: biology: genetic variation and natural selection

en: A corn kernel gets one set of genes from the pollen parent and one from the seed parent, so kernels on one cob can have different colors.
Unlike mitosis, which makes identical body cells for growth and repair, meiosis makes unique sex cells with half the chromosomes.
Some people think a child gets more traits from the parent they resemble, but meiosis gives an equal number of chromosomes from each parent.
Plant breeders in the Philippines pollinate one rice plant with another so the resulting seeds get DNA from both, a direct use of meiosis and fertilization.
source: agriculture: rice breeding in the Philippines (IRRI)

en: The first division of meiosis separates matched chromosome pairs, so each sex cell ends up with just one chromosome from each pair.
source: biology: meiosis stages (Prophase I to Telophase II)

en: The new cell formed by fertilization is called diploid because it has two complete sets of chromosomes, one set from each parent.
Besides swapping sections, chromosomes also line up randomly during meiosis, so each sex cell gets a different mix of mother's and father's chromosomes.
Asexual reproduction makes clones from one parent, but sexual reproduction uses meiosis and fertilization to create offspring with genes from two parents.
In flowering plants, meiosis makes pollen and egg cells inside the flower, and fertilization joins them to form a seed.
source: botany: plant life cycle and alternation of generations

en: A child's traits come from the specific genes they inherit, not from a blending of parents' blood, because meiosis sorts genes into separate sex cells.
The reason meiosis produces four cells instead of two is that it divides twice, which is why each sex cell ends up with half the original chromosomes.
source: biology: meiosis produces four haploid cells

en: Speed is always a positive number, but velocity can be negative when an object moves backward or opposite a chosen direction.
source: vector sign convention in one-dimensional motion

en: When two velocities combine, you add them like arrows, so 3 m/s east plus 4 m/s east is 7 m/s east, but 3 m/s east plus 4 m/s west is 1 m/s east.
source: vector addition rules for collinear vectors

en: A person walking forward on a moving bus has a velocity that is the sum of the bus's velocity and their own walking velocity.
source: relative velocity concept in moving frames

en: The speed of a car is just the size of its velocity vector, so a car moving 60 km/h north has a speed of 60 km/h.
A car reversing out of a driveway has a velocity pointing backward, while its speedometer still shows a positive speed.
source: direction of velocity vs speedometer reading

en: A car driving up a steep hill has a velocity pointing up the slope, and if it turns around to go down, its velocity points down.
A pendulum swinging has a velocity that changes direction every swing, but its speed is highest at the bottom and zero at the ends.
source: pendulum motion: changing direction, varying speed

en: Two cars moving at the same speed in opposite directions have velocities that are exact opposites, so one is positive and the other is negative.
When a car slows down on a straight road, its velocity gets smaller but still points the same way, so only the size changes.
source: velocity magnitude changes with speed while direction constant

en: When a car speeds up on a straight road, its velocity gets bigger but still points the same way, so the arrow gets longer.
source: velocity magnitude increases with speed while direction constant

en: A projectile launched at a steep angle, like 70 degrees, follows a tall narrow arc, while a flat 20-degree launch makes a low, wide arc.
source: projectile motion geometry; shape depends on launch angle

en: A ball thrown straight up at 20 meters per second reaches about 20 meters high, because gravity slows it down at about 10 meters per second each second.
source: kinematic equation h = v²/(2g) for vertical launch

en: Air resistance also lowers the peak of a projectile, so a real baseball does not fly as high as the ideal calculation predicts.
source: real-world projectile motion; air drag reduces maximum height

en: When a basketball player shoots from above the rim, the ball can be released at a flatter angle and still reach the hoop, because it starts higher.
source: projectile motion with different initial heights; higher start allows flatter trajectory

en: Throwing a ball faster at the same angle makes it stay in the air longer, because it rises higher before gravity pulls it back down.
source: vertical motion independence; greater initial vertical speed increases time of flight

en: At the highest point of its flight, a projectile has already traveled half of its total horizontal range.
source: symmetry of projectile path on level ground

en: A football kicked straight up at 30 meters per second slows to about 20 meters per second after one second, because gravity reduces its speed by about 10 meters per second each second.
source: constant acceleration due to gravity, 9.8 m/s² rounded to 10

en: For a basketball free throw, players often aim for a release angle of about 50 degrees, which gives the ball a high arc and a better chance of dropping in.
source: common coaching advice and biomechanics studies; rounded value

en: At a 30-degree launch, about 87% of the launch speed goes forward, but at a 60-degree launch, only half goes forward and the rest goes upward.
source: trigonometry of velocity components: cos30≈0.87, cos60=0.5

en: Gravity changes a projectile's vertical speed by about 10 meters per second every second, no matter how heavy the object is.
source: Galileo's principle; gravitational acceleration independent of mass

en: Biodiversity is the variety of all living things on Earth—from tiny bacteria to giant whales—and the ecosystems they form together.
Extinction happens when the very last member of a species dies, so that kind of animal or plant is gone from Earth forever.
When roads and farms split a forest into small patches, animals are trapped in tiny areas with too little food, space, and mates to survive.
Fishing boats that scoop up fish faster than they can reproduce empty the ocean of certain species, leaving too few adults to make the next generation.
Chemical pollution from factories and farms can poison rivers and lakes, killing fish and the insects that other animals depend on for food.
When a foreign species like the janitor fish enters a Philippine river, it competes with native fish for food and space, pushing them toward extinction.
source: invasive species biology; Philippine freshwater ecosystems

en: As the planet warms, some animals cannot find the cooler places they need to live, so their populations shrink and may die out.
When seawater gets too warm, corals lose the colorful algae that feed them, turn white, and can die—destroying homes for thousands of fish species.
A species with only a few dozen members left is in danger because a single storm, disease, or hunting event can wipe out the whole group at once.
When a species has very few members left, they must breed with close relatives, and the loss of genetic variety makes them weaker against new diseases.
When a keystone species like the sea otter disappears, its prey multiply out of control and the whole ecosystem collapses like a falling tower.
The Philippines sits in the Coral Triangle, the world's richest marine area, yet overfishing and pollution are destroying reefs that feed millions of people.
source: Coral Triangle Initiative; Philippine marine biodiversity

en: Water hyacinth, a fast-spreading foreign plant, chokes Philippine lakes by blocking sunlight and oxygen, killing the fish that live underneath.
Sea turtles and seabirds mistake floating plastic for food, and eating it fills their stomachs so they starve even when real food is nearby.
Once a species goes extinct, no scientist can bring it back, which is why protecting endangered animals today matters for all time.
Scientists estimate species are disappearing about 1,000 times faster than the natural rate before humans appeared on Earth.
When one species in a food web disappears, the animals that ate it starve and the ones it ate multiply, sending waves of change through the whole ecosystem.
Some birds and butterflies migrate to cooler places each year, but climate change shifts the seasons so they arrive when their food is already gone.
Protected areas like national parks give endangered species a safe place to live, but they work only if the animals' needs for food and space are met.
When a species goes extinct, the ecosystem services it provided—like pollination or pest control—are lost, and people lose food and medicine sources.
Distance and displacement are both measured from a reference point, the fixed place you choose as the starting line for describing motion.
source: encyclopedia-stable; definition of reference point in kinematics

en: Displacement always includes a direction, like north or east, while distance is just a number with no direction attached to it.
Distance can never be negative because it only counts how much ground you covered, and you cannot cover less than zero ground.
source: encyclopedia-stable; scalar quantities are always non-negative

en: Displacement can be negative if you choose one direction as positive, so moving the opposite way gives a negative displacement value.
Displacement is always the straight-line distance from start to finish, so it is never longer than the distance you actually traveled.
source: encyclopedia-stable; definition of displacement as shortest path

en: A jeepney that winds through narrow streets to reach the plaza covers a long distance, but its displacement is just the short line from terminal to plaza.
A farmer walking along the edges of a square rice field travels a distance equal to the perimeter, but his displacement is the diagonal across the field.
source: encyclopedia-stable; geometric example of distance vs displacement

en: A basketball player dribbling from one hoop to the other and back has a large distance, but zero displacement because he returns to the same hoop.
To find displacement on a map, draw a straight arrow from start to finish and measure it, while distance requires tracing the whole path.
Whenever a trip ends exactly where it began, the displacement is zero, no matter how long or winding the journey was.
A car climbing a long winding mountain road to Baguio covers many kilometers of distance, but its displacement is just the straight height gained.
Walking from school to home through a market adds extra distance, but displacement is just the straight-line gap between the school gate and your front door.
Distance and displacement are equal only when you travel in a perfectly straight line without turning or changing direction.
An airplane flying from Manila to Cebu follows a curved route in the sky, so its distance is longer than the straight displacement between the two cities.
Because distance has no direction, speed is just how fast you go, while velocity uses displacement and direction to tell where you are heading.
Ecosystem stability means the place keeps providing food, clean water, and shelter even when conditions like drought or flood change.
source: ecology principle: stability as persistence of functions

en: When a drought kills the main food crop, a farm with many crops still has other plants to eat, so people and animals do not starve.
If a disease wipes out one species in a diverse forest, the other species stay healthy, so the forest keeps standing and feeding its animals.
In a diverse ecosystem, some species can handle heat, others handle cold, so when the climate shifts, at least some survive.
The Philippines grows many rice varieties, so if a new disease attacks one type, the other types still produce grain for harvest.
Many kinds of decomposers, like different fungi and bacteria, break down dead leaves, so if one dies out, the others keep the soil rich.
When many species share a forest, they use different parts of it, so a storm does not destroy all the shelter at once.
A rice field with only one variety can lose everything to a single pest, while a field with many varieties loses only a part.
One hectare of tropical rainforest can hold about 300 tree species, while a plantation has just one, so a single disease can wipe out the plantation.
source: published estimate: ~300 tree species per hectare in tropical rainforest

en: Mangroves along Philippine coasts shelter many species, and if one mangrove type dies, the others still hold the soil during storms.
Ecosystems with few species are easier for invaders to take over, because there are fewer native competitors to stop them.
In a diverse animal community, a disease spreads less because the germ has fewer suitable hosts, so more animals stay healthy.
A coral reef with many coral species recovers faster after bleaching, because some corals can survive warmer water and regrow the reef.
Sea otters are a keystone species because they eat sea urchins, protecting kelp forests that shelter many fish.
When many bird species spread seeds, a forest can regrow after a typhoon, because some birds survive and carry seeds from other trees.
As the climate changes, a diverse ecosystem can rearrange itself, with new species taking over roles that others can no longer fill.
High biodiversity is not just for saving rare animals; it also keeps our farms, water, and air working for people every day.
During a typhoon, a diverse forest loses some trees but keeps its soil, while a single-species plantation may fall down completely.
In a diverse farm, natural enemies like spiders and birds control pests, so a pest outbreak does not destroy the whole crop.
A diverse ocean with many fish species keeps the food chain stable, so a drop in one fish population does not empty the sea for fishers.
Subduction happens when one tectonic plate dives beneath another, forming a deep ocean trench and a line of volcanoes on the overlying plate.
The Philippines lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire, a horseshoe-shaped zone around the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes occur.
The Sierra Madre mountain range on eastern Luzon was pushed up by the slow collision of the Philippine Sea Plate with the Eurasian Plate.
The Cordillera Central in northern Luzon is a high mountain range with many active faults, showing that the region is still being squeezed by moving plates.
Taal Volcano sits inside a large caldera, a bowl-shaped depression left by a huge ancient eruption, and it is one of the most active volcanoes in the Philippines.
Mount Pinatubo's 1991 eruption, one of the largest of the 20th century, happened because magma rose where the South China Sea plate subducts beneath Luzon.
The Cotabato Trench lies south of Mindanao, where the Celebes Sea plate dives under the Philippines, making that area prone to earthquakes and tsunamis.
The Negros Trench, west of Negros and Panay, marks another subduction zone where the Sulu Sea floor slides beneath the Philippine islands.
The Philippine Mobile Belt is a complex region of faults and folds between two large plates, making the archipelago a mosaic of moving blocks.
Earthquakes in the Philippines come from two main sources: fault movements like the Philippine Fault, and subduction at trenches like the Manila Trench.
The country's volcanoes form a chain called a volcanic arc, which runs parallel to the deep trenches where plates are subducting.
The Philippine Trench reaches about 10,540 meters deep, making it one of the deepest places on Earth's surface, even deeper than Mount Everest is tall.
The Philippine Sea Plate moves northwest at about 7 centimeters per year, slowly pushing against the Eurasian Plate to build the islands.
The Philippine Fault is a major strike-slip fault, meaning two blocks of crust slide horizontally past each other, causing many of the country's inland quakes.
The Zambales Mountains in western Luzon are made of volcanic rocks that came from an older subduction zone, showing how plate motion builds mountains.
Volcanoes are not scattered randomly; they line up along plate boundaries, which is why the Philippines has a clear chain of active volcanoes.
Deep earthquakes near trenches occur at increasing depths farther from the trench, tracing the path of the subducting plate into the mantle.
The Pacific Ring of Fire also includes Japan and Indonesia, so those islands share the same pattern of trenches, volcanoes, and earthquakes as the Philippines.
Hot springs and geothermal areas in the Philippines are signs of hot rock beneath the surface, often linked to volcanic activity from plate subduction.
On a map, large mountain ranges on land often sit next to deep ocean trenches, because both are formed by the same plate collision.
A deadly skin fungus called chytrid has wiped out many frog species around the world, because it blocks their skin from absorbing water.
Fishing nets meant for tuna often trap sea turtles and dolphins, which drown because they cannot reach the surface to breathe.
The ocean absorbs extra carbon dioxide from the air, turning more acidic and making it hard for clams and corals to grow their shells.
People dig up rare orchids from Philippine forests to sell, and when too many are taken, the wild plants can no longer make seeds.
source: encyclopedia-stable; orchid trade in the Philippines

en: When crocodiles or eagles attack livestock, farmers sometimes kill them to protect their animals, reducing the wild predator population.
Dams built across rivers stop salmon and other migratory fish from swimming upstream to lay eggs, so their numbers drop sharply.
Warmer sand from climate change makes sea turtle eggs hatch mostly females, so too few males remain to fertilize future eggs.
Bright lights on beaches make baby sea turtles crawl toward the road instead of the ocean, where they often die from cars or heat.
Too many livestock on dry grassland eat every plant, leaving native animals like prairie dogs with no food or cover to survive.
Diseases from farm animals, like distemper, can jump to wild lions and dogs, killing many in a short time and pushing them toward extinction.
When a metal gives electrons to a nonmetal, the resulting ions attract each other and lock into a repeating crystal lattice, not separate molecules.
Dry ice is a covalent solid made of separate CO2 molecules, so it has no crystal lattice, unlike ionic salt.
Plant cells have tiny connecting pores called plasmodesmata, but animal cells do not have these bridges between cells.

topic: cell membrane position in plant and animal cells
en: In a plant cell, the cell membrane sits just inside the stiff cell wall, but in an animal cell, the membrane is the outer boundary.
When a plant cell divides, it builds a new cell plate wall between the two new cells.
When an animal cell divides, its membrane pinches inward to split the cell into two.
Animal cells have lysosomes that break down waste, while plant cells usually use their vacuoles for storage and breakdown instead.
Plant cells have plastids like chloroplasts to make and store food, but animal cells have no plastids at all.
Both cells use mitochondria to release energy, but only plant cells also use chloroplasts to capture energy from sunlight.
A plant cell's large vacuole often pushes the nucleus to the side, while an animal cell's nucleus stays near the center.
Animal cells can change shape to move through tiny spaces, but plant cells stay fixed because of their rigid cell wall.

topic: plant cell size due to vacuole
en: Plant cells are often larger than animal cells because the big central vacuole takes up so much room.
Plant cells store extra sugar as starch, while animal cells store it as glycogen, a different type of stored food.
The cell wall gives plant cells a strong frame, so plants can stand tall, while animal cells rely on other tissues for support.
When a plant vacuole fills with water, it pushes against the cell wall to keep the plant firm, but animal vacuoles do not press against a wall.
Because plant cells have chloroplasts, they can make their own food, but animal cells must eat other organisms to get energy.
Plant cells divide without centrioles, but animal cells use these tiny structures to help pull chromosomes apart.
When two objects touch, heat flows from the hotter one to the cooler one until they reach the same temperature, then heat transfer stops.
source: thermodynamics: heat transfer stops at equilibrium

en: A thermometer works by letting its liquid expand or contract until it matches the object's temperature, so it shows temperature, not heat.
Heat is measured in joules, while temperature is measured in degrees Celsius, so they are different quantities with different units.
source: SI units: joule for heat, Celsius for temperature

en: Ice absorbs heat while melting at 0°C, but its temperature stays the same until all the ice turns to water.
source: phase change: latent heat of fusion

en: Water boils at 100°C and stays at that temperature even as you add heat, because the heat goes into turning liquid into steam.
source: phase change: latent heat of vaporization

en: Cold is not a separate thing; it is simply the lack of heat, so heat always moves from warmer to cooler places.
source: concept: heat is energy, cold is lack of heat

en: The same amount of heat raises a small object's temperature more than a large one, because temperature change depends on mass.
The sun's heat travels through empty space by radiation and warms Earth's surface, raising the temperature of ground and air.
PAGASA's heat index combines air temperature and humidity to tell how hot it feels, because humidity affects how fast sweat cools you.
Mixing hot and cold water gives a final temperature between the two, because heat flows from hot to cold until they match.
A metal spoon in hot soup becomes hot along its whole length because heat conducts through the metal, raising every part's temperature.
A drop of boiling water and a full pot of boiling water have the same temperature, but the pot holds much more heat because it has more particles.
Heat is not a substance that can be stored; it is energy in motion, so it only exists while it is being transferred.
source: definition of heat as energy transfer

en: Water needs more heat to raise its temperature than sand does, so a beach's sand heats up faster than the sea during the day.
source: specific heat of water vs sand

en: Dark-colored objects absorb more heat from sunlight than light-colored ones, so a black shirt feels hotter than a white shirt in the sun.
In a diverse ecosystem, a predator that loses its usual prey can switch to another available species, so it survives food shortages without starving.
source: ecology: predator diet flexibility in diverse food webs

en: A forest with many tree species has roots at different depths, so a drought that dries the topsoil still lets deep-rooted trees find water.
source: plant ecology: root stratification in mixed forests

en: In a diverse meadow, different flowers bloom at different times, so pollinators always find nectar even if one plant fails to flower.
source: plant-pollinator phenology in diverse plant communities

en: A species with many genetic variations has a better chance that some individuals resist a new disease, so the whole population does not die out.
source: population genetics: genetic diversity buffers disease

en: Tree holes, logs, and leaf litter create small shelters, so many species survive storms or droughts even if the main habitat is damaged.
When a favorite fruit is scarce in a diverse forest, animals can eat seeds, leaves, or insects instead, so they do not starve.
source: animal foraging flexibility in diverse habitats

en: A wetland with many plant species filters different pollutants, so the water stays clean even if one plant dies.
source: ecosystem services: phytoremediation in diverse wetlands

en: In a diverse forest, trees with different leaf shapes catch sunlight at different heights, so even if some trees fall, others still get light.
In a diverse grassland, different grasses grow in different seasons, so the soil is covered all year and erosion is prevented.
A diverse forest has many tree species that drop leaves at different times, so the soil gets a steady supply of nutrients.
Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell of an atom, and they decide how that atom bonds with others.
For the main groups, the group number tells you how many valence electrons an atom has, like group 2 means two.
source: periodic table group number = valence electrons for main-group elements

en: Magnesium and calcium are in group 2, so both have two valence electrons and react in similar ways.
Carbon and silicon are in group 14, each having four valence electrons, which lets them form four bonds.
Nitrogen and phosphorus are in group 15, each with five valence electrons, so they often make three bonds.
Elements in group 1 have one valence electron, while group 2 elements have two, so group 1 metals react more easily.
source: comparison of group 1 and group 2 reactivity

en: Moving across a period changes the number of valence electrons, but moving down a group keeps that number the same.
source: periodic table trends across periods and down groups

en: Elements in the same group do not have the same number of electron shells; they have the same number of valence electrons.
source: common misconception about electron shells vs valence electrons

en: Sodium and potassium are both group 1 elements, and both form salts, like table salt and a salt substitute.
source: sodium and potassium compounds in daily life

en: Calcium and magnesium are group 2 elements, and both are important for strong bones and healthy plants.
source: calcium and magnesium in biology and agriculture

en: The outermost electrons are the ones that touch other atoms, so having the same number of them makes elements act alike.
source: chemical reactivity determined by outer electrons

en: To know an element's valence electrons, just look at its group number in the main part of the periodic table.
source: reading group numbers from periodic table

en: Transition metals in the middle columns do not follow the simple group-number rule for valence electrons, so we focus on main groups.
source: transition metals exception to group number rule

en: Helium has two valence electrons, while other noble gases have eight, and this complete set makes them very stable.
Because group 1 elements have just one valence electron, they easily lose it to become a positive ion with a +1 charge.
Because group 17 elements have seven valence electrons, they easily gain one to become a negative ion with a -1 charge.
The number of valence electrons an element has tells you how many bonds it can form, like oxygen with six making two bonds.
Across a period, the number of valence electrons increases from one to eight, which is why properties change gradually.
source: periodic trend of valence electrons across a period

en: Fluorine and chlorine are both group 17 elements, and compounds of them are used to keep drinking water safe.
source: fluorine and chlorine in water treatment

en: Knowing an element's group lets you predict its valence electrons and therefore how it will react with other elements.
source: predicting chemical properties from group number

en: Elements in the same group have the same valence electrons, but those lower down have more shells, so they react faster even though they react in the same way.
source: periodic trends: atomic radius and reactivity within a group

en: Oxygen and sulfur are both in group 16, so each has six valence electrons and typically needs two more to fill its outer shell.
source: periodic table group 16 valence electron configuration

en: Lithium, sodium, and potassium are group 1 metals with one valence electron, so they are stored under oil to keep them from reacting with air.
source: standard laboratory safety for alkali metals

en: A common mistake is thinking elements in a group have the same total number of electrons, but they actually share the same number of outer electrons only.
Bromine and iodine are in group 17, so they each have seven valence electrons and easily gain one to form salts like potassium bromide.
source: group 17 halogens reactivity and ion formation

en: The periodic table is deliberately arranged so that elements with the same valence electron count stack in the same column, which is why the group number matches that count.
