source: periodic table structure and group number significance

en: Strontium and calcium are in group 2, so both have two valence electrons, and they give fireworks their red and orange colors when burned.
source: flame test colors of alkaline earth metals

en: Seismic waves are vibrations that spread out from an earthquake, and the way they travel tells scientists what the ground is made of.
When a seismic wave crosses from one layer to another, it bends, just like a straw looks bent in a glass of water.
source: encyclopedia-stable; wave refraction at layer boundaries

en: The Earth's core is about half the size of the whole planet's radius, making it a huge central sphere.
source: rounded value; core radius ~3500 km vs Earth radius ~6371 km

en: The mantle is the thickest layer of the Earth, stretching about 2,900 kilometers down from the crust.
The crust is the thinnest layer, like the skin of an apple compared to the whole fruit.
The outer core is the only liquid layer of the Earth, made of melted iron and nickel.
The inner core is a solid ball of iron and nickel, kept solid by the crushing pressure around it.
source: encyclopedia-stable; inner core composition and state

en: The temperature at the Earth's core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, around 5,000 degrees Celsius.
The pressure at the center of the Earth is millions of times stronger than the air pressure at the surface.
The Earth's average density is about 5.5 times that of water, but surface rocks are lighter, so the deep interior must be very dense.
source: rounded value; Earth's average density vs surface rocks

en: Scientists use instruments called seismographs to record the exact arrival times of seismic waves from many earthquakes.
By comparing wave arrival times at different stations, scientists build a 3D picture of the inside of the Earth.
source: encyclopedia-stable; seismic tomography and model building

topic: P-wave speed drop in outer core
en: The speed of P-waves suddenly drops when they enter the outer core, which tells scientists that this layer is liquid.
source: encyclopedia-stable; P-wave velocity drop in liquid

topic: P-wave speed increase in inner core
en: The speed of P-waves speeds up again when they reach the inner core, showing that this deepest layer is solid.
source: encyclopedia-stable; P-wave velocity increase in solid inner core

en: The Gutenberg discontinuity is the sharp boundary between the mantle and the liquid outer core, found by studying wave speed changes.
The Lehmann discontinuity is the boundary between the liquid outer core and the solid inner core, discovered by studying P-wave behavior.
The Earth is layered like an onion, with a thin crust, a thick mantle, a liquid outer core, and a solid inner core.
PHIVOLCS uses seismic wave data from local earthquakes to help map the structure beneath the Philippines.

topic: why outer core liquid inner solid
en: The outer core is liquid because the heat is high enough to melt iron, but the inner core is solid because the pressure there is even higher.
source: encyclopedia-stable; state of core layers due to pressure and temperature

en: The model of Earth's layers was built from thousands of earthquakes recorded all over the world, not just one event.
source: encyclopedia-stable; global seismic network and model development

en: On a map of the Philippines, a fault is a crack on land, while a trench is a deep groove under the sea, so they appear in different places.
source: geological definitions of fault and trench

en: The Philippines has about 300 volcanoes, but only about 24 are active, so maps often mark active ones with special symbols.
The Philippine archipelago is made of several island arcs, each with its own trenches and volcanoes, so different regions have different features.
source: plate tectonics theory on island arcs

en: Not all mountains in the Philippines are volcanoes; some ranges were pushed up by plate collisions without volcanic activity.
Mount Apo, the highest peak in the Philippines, is a volcano formed by subduction near the Cotabato Trench.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Mount Apo is a stratovolcano

en: Because the Philippine Fault is a strike-slip fault, it does not create volcanoes, unlike the subduction trenches.
source: plate tectonics: strike-slip faults do not produce volcanoes

en: PHIVOLCS, the agency that studies volcanoes and earthquakes, makes detailed maps of faults and trenches to help people know where hazards are.
To sort the elements, Dmitri Mendeleev wrote each element's properties on a separate card and arranged them by similarity.
source: Historical accounts of Mendeleev's working method

en: William Ramsay's discovery of argon in 1894 forced scientists to add a whole new column for the noble gases.
source: Discovery of argon (1894) and its placement in the periodic table

en: Mendeleev placed tellurium before iodine even though tellurium is heavier, because their chemical properties matched better that way.
John Dalton's atomic theory said each element is made of its own kind of atom, which gave scientists a reason why elements differ.
The lanthanide elements were so similar to each other that scientists placed them in a separate row below the main periodic table.
source: Placement of lanthanides in the periodic table

en: By Mendeleev's time, about 60 elements were known, and his table organized them all into a single chart.
source: Historical count of known elements by 1869

en: Mendeleev's table was not the first attempt, but it was the first to be widely accepted because it predicted new elements.
source: Historical context of Mendeleev's table acceptance

en: Mendeleev's original table had 8 columns, while the modern one has 18 because noble gases were added later.
source: Comparison of Mendeleev's table to modern table structure

en: Humphry Davy used electricity to break down compounds and discover new elements like sodium and potassium.
source: Davy's use of electrolysis to discover elements

en: Mendeleev corrected the atomic mass of beryllium because its position in his table showed the old value was wrong.
source: Mendeleev's correction of beryllium's atomic mass

en: When typhoon winds push against a mountain, the air rises and cools, which drains some of the storm's heat energy and weakens it.
Narrow valleys between mountains can squeeze typhoon winds, making them blow faster in those gaps, just like air speeding through a narrow pipe.
A typhoon gets more fuel when the warm ocean layer is deep, because even after stirring the sea, there is still warm water to keep it going.
As a typhoon churns the sea, it pulls up cooler water from below, which can weaken the storm by taking away its warmth.
The Philippines' many islands act like a series of brakes, so a typhoon that crosses several islands becomes much weaker than one that stays over the ocean.
Tall mountains like the Cordillera weaken typhoons more than low hills because they force air to rise higher, causing more rain and wind disruption.
A bay that narrows inland can make storm surge worse, because the water gets squeezed into a smaller space and rises higher.
A gently sloping seafloor lets storm surge push farther inland, while a steep underwater drop-off keeps the surge closer to the shore.
A typhoon weakens more over a large island like Luzon than over a small island, because there is more land to create friction and cut off the ocean fuel.
Typhoons need a large area of warm ocean water to form and grow, not just a small warm patch, so they typically start in the open Pacific.
A mountain range that runs across a typhoon's path blocks and weakens the wind, but a range that runs parallel lets the wind slide along it.
When a typhoon passes over land, its calm eye often becomes cloudy and ragged because the storm loses its organized structure.
A typhoon weakens faster when it hits a mountainous coast than a flat one, because the mountains cause more friction and disrupt the wind flow.
The western Pacific Ocean has the warmest water on Earth, which is why most strong typhoons form and grow there.
If a typhoon crosses a small island and then returns to warm ocean, it can regain strength, because the sea provides the energy it lost on land.
The periodic table's rows and columns are a direct map of an atom's electron shells and outer electrons.
source: periodic table structure: rows = shells, columns = outer electrons

en: The electron structure of an atom acts like a code, so reading its position on the table reveals its electron arrangement.
source: periodic table as a code for electron configuration

en: The outermost shell of an atom is called the valence shell, and its electrons are the ones that join in chemical bonds.
The electron structure decides if an element is a metal or nonmetal, because metals have few outer electrons while nonmetals have many.
source: metal/nonmetal classification based on outer electrons

en: The electron structure explains the staircase line on the table that separates metals from nonmetals, based on their outer electron counts.
source: periodic table staircase line, metal/nonmetal boundary

en: The electron structure explains why the first period has only two elements, because the first shell can hold only two electrons.
The electron structure explains why the table has a short first row and longer rows below, because each shell can hold more electrons.
source: periodic table row lengths based on shell capacity

en: Magnesium's 12 electrons are arranged 2-8-2, so it sits in period 3, group 2, just below beryllium.
Carbon's 6 electrons are arranged 2-4, placing it in period 2, group 14, where it can form four bonds.
Phosphorus's 15 electrons are arranged 2-8-5, placing it in period 3, group 15, just below nitrogen.
Aluminum's 13 electrons are arranged 2-8-3, placing it in period 3, group 13, just below boron.
The electron structure of an atom determines its position on the table, which is why carbon's position tells us it can form many different molecules.
source: carbon's position and its ability to form diverse molecules

en: The electron structure determines the charge an atom will form when it becomes an ion, like calcium losing two electrons to become +2.
source: ion formation, calcium loses 2 electrons to form +2 ion

en: The electron structure explains why the table is divided into blocks, like the s-block on the left and the p-block on the right.
source: periodic table blocks (s, p, d, f) based on subshell filling

en: The electron structure explains why the periodic table is a tool for predicting an element's behavior without memorizing its properties.
The electron structure explains why some elements are very reactive and others are not, based on how close they are to a full outer shell.
source: reactivity based on distance to full outer shell

en: The electron structure explains why the table is called 'periodic,' because the pattern of outer electrons repeats every row, causing properties to repeat too.
source: periodic law: repeating properties based on electron configuration

en: The electron structure explains why the periodic table is a map of the atom, showing how electrons are arranged in shells and blocks.
source: periodic table as a map of electron arrangement

en: The electron structure of an atom determines its position on the table, which is why the table is a universal tool for chemists everywhere.
source: periodic table universal use in chemistry

en: Seismic waves travel faster through denser and stiffer rock, so measuring their speed tells scientists what each deep layer is made of.
source: seismic wave velocity depends on material properties

en: The mantle is solid because S-waves pass through it, but it can flow very slowly over millions of years, like thick honey.
source: S-wave transmission indicates solid mantle; mantle convection

en: The crust is thicker under mountains and thinner under oceans, a difference that seismic wave travel times reveal clearly.
source: seismic refraction studies of crustal thickness

en: The inner core was discovered when a faint P-wave appeared in the shadow zone, showing that a solid inner core reflects waves.
source: Lehmann's observation of P-wave arrivals in shadow zone

en: By measuring how long seismic waves take to reach stations around the world, scientists calculate the depth of each boundary inside Earth.
The core is about twice as dense as the mantle, so seismic wave speeds tell scientists it is made of heavy metals like iron and nickel.
source: seismic wave speeds and density estimates

en: Seismic waves curve as they travel deeper because their speed gradually increases, so they follow curved paths, not straight lines.
source: seismic refraction in a layered Earth

en: Earth's land is split into separate continents, while the ocean is one connected body of water covering most of the surface.
The Pacific Ocean alone spreads over a larger area than all of Earth's land put together.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Pacific Ocean area vs total land area

en: Even the hemisphere that holds most of Earth's land still has more ocean than land on its surface.
source: geography data; hemispheric distribution of land and water

en: Earth's water fills the low ocean basins, so the higher land sticks out as continents and islands.
source: encyclopedia-stable; formation of ocean basins and continents

en: Because people live on land, it is easy to think land is bigger, but water actually covers most of Earth's surface.
source: common misconception corrected by Earth surface data

en: Looking down from a high airplane, you would see far more blue ocean than brown or green land.
source: observational fact; aerial view of Earth's surface

en: On any world map, the blue of oceans takes up more space than all the other colors of land put together.
Most of the water covering Earth is salty ocean water, not the fresh water we drink.

topic: total area of oceans and land
en: Earth's oceans cover about 361 million square kilometers, while all land covers about 149 million square kilometers.
source: rounded values from Earth fact sheets

en: The amount of silica in magma controls its stickiness: more silica means thicker, stickier lava that forms steep cones.
source: encyclopedia-stable; silica content determines magma viscosity

en: Viscosity is how easily a liquid flows; water has low viscosity and honey has high viscosity, and lava behaves the same way.
Runny lava spreads far from the vent before hardening, widening the base, while sticky lava hardens close by, building height.
source: encyclopedia-stable; lava flow distance vs viscosity

en: Thick lava traps gas bubbles that build pressure until they explode, hurling out ash and rock that build a steep, layered cone.
Runny lava lets gas bubbles escape easily, so eruptions are quiet and the lava flows out to form a wide, gently sloping shield.
Cinder cones are built from loose rock fragments that settle at a steep angle of about 30 degrees, giving them straight, steep sides.
source: encyclopedia-stable; angle of repose for granular materials

en: Basaltic lava is very hot, about 1100 degrees Celsius, so it stays thin and runny, while cooler lava is thicker and builds steeper shapes.
Stratovolcanoes are made of andesite, a rock with medium silica, which makes their lava sticky enough to build tall, steep layers.
Shield volcanoes are made entirely of basalt, a dark rock with low silica, which is why their lava flows so far and wide.
The steepness of a volcano's cone is a clue to its magma's stickiness, so scientists can guess the rock type just by looking at the slope.
A tall, steep volcano does not mean it is more powerful; it simply means its lava is stickier and piles up closer to the vent.
Imagine pouring syrup on a plate: thin syrup spreads flat like a shield volcano, while thick syrup piles up like a steep stratovolcano.
The lava that builds Mayon and other Philippine stratovolcanoes is andesitic, meaning it has enough silica to be sticky and explosive.
A plate boundary is the meeting line where two of Earth's moving crust pieces touch, and most earthquakes and volcanoes happen along these lines.
Plates move because heat inside Earth makes the soft mantle flow in slow loops called convection currents, dragging the crust above them.
source: encyclopedia-stable; mantle convection drives plate motion

en: When an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, the denser oceanic plate sinks beneath, melting to form volcanoes like the Andes.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Andes formed by oceanic-continental subduction

en: When two oceanic plates collide, one sinks and melts, creating chains of volcanic islands like Japan and the Philippines.
When two continental plates crash, neither sinks, so the crust crumples upward into tall mountain ranges like the Himalayas.
At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, new crust is born as magma fills the gap, pushing the plates apart at about 2 to 5 centimeters a year.
The San Andreas Fault in California is a transform boundary where the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other.
The Philippines sits where the Philippine Sea Plate and Eurasian Plate meet, so PHIVOLCS watches for earthquakes and volcanic activity there.
Earth's outer shell is broken into about seven large plates and several smaller ones that all move at different speeds.
Divergent boundaries create new crust while convergent boundaries destroy it, so Earth's surface stays about the same size.
source: encyclopedia-stable; conservation of Earth's surface area

en: Earthquakes happen at all three types of plate boundaries, not just transform faults, because all moving plates build up stress.
source: encyclopedia-stable; earthquakes occur at all boundary types

en: Most of Earth's volcanoes and earthquakes ring the Pacific Ocean, where many plates meet, so the area is called the Ring of Fire.
At subduction zones, the sinking plate carries water down, which helps the mantle melt and rise to feed volcanoes above.
source: encyclopedia-stable; flux melting at subduction zones

en: Combination reactions often release energy as heat and light, which is why burning wood in a campfire is a combination reaction between wood and oxygen.
Decomposition reactions need an energy input like heat, light, or electricity to break a compound apart into simpler substances.
A metal can only replace another metal in a single replacement reaction if it is more reactive, a ranking shown in the activity series.
Iron rusting is a slow single replacement reaction where iron replaces hydrogen in water and oxygen, forming iron oxide.
Double replacement reactions often happen because they form a solid precipitate, a gas, or water, which removes ions from the solution.
source: encyclopedia-stable; driving forces of double replacement

en: Combination and decomposition are opposite processes: combination builds a bigger compound from smaller parts, while decomposition breaks a compound into smaller parts.
Photosynthesis is a natural combination reaction where plants use sunlight to join carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
Baking soda decomposes when heated, releasing carbon dioxide gas that makes cakes and bread rise in the oven.
source: encyclopedia-stable; thermal decomposition of sodium bicarbonate

en: When a metal reacts with an acid, it is a single replacement reaction where the metal replaces hydrogen, producing hydrogen gas and a salt.
Mixing vinegar and baking soda causes a double replacement reaction that forms carbonic acid, which quickly decomposes into water and carbon dioxide gas.
Rust forms through a combination reaction where iron, oxygen, and water join together to create a new reddish-brown compound.
Electrolysis is a decomposition reaction where electricity forces a compound like water to break apart into its elements.
A more reactive metal like zinc can replace copper in a blue copper sulfate solution, turning it colorless as zinc sulfate forms.
Mixing two clear solutions can produce a solid precipitate in a double replacement reaction, like silver chloride forming from silver nitrate and sodium chloride.
When a new substance forms from two simpler ones, like sodium and chlorine making table salt, it is a combination reaction.
Dead plants and animals decompose through chemical reactions that break down complex molecules into simpler nutrients for the soil.
A jeepney's metal body slowly undergoes single replacement reactions with oxygen and water, causing rust to form over time.
An acid-base neutralization is a special double replacement reaction where an acid and a base swap partners to form water and a salt.
Combination reactions are common in daily life, such as when iron combines with sulfur to make iron sulfide, or when hydrogen burns with oxygen to make water.
The four reaction types differ by what happens to the reactants: combination joins them, decomposition splits one, and replacement swaps atoms or ions.
When limestone (calcium carbonate) is heated strongly, it decomposes into calcium oxide (quicklime) and carbon dioxide gas, a reaction used in making cement.

topic: food gives energy to living things
en: A dog gets energy from the food it eats, but a toy dog never needs food because it is not alive.
A stone stays the same size for many years, but a small seedling grows into a tall tree.
A plant slowly bends toward the sunny window, showing it responds to light, while a plastic plant never moves.
A hen lays eggs that can hatch into chicks, so chickens can make new chickens, but a glass of water cannot make more water.
Fire moves and grows bigger, but it is not alive because it does not eat, breathe, or make baby fires.
The sun gives light and heat, but it is not alive because it does not grow, eat, or reproduce.
Water is not alive, yet every living thing from a carabao to a rice plant needs it to survive.
A carabao eating grass in the field is living, but the wooden cart it pulls is non-living because it cannot eat or grow.
A mango tree is living: it grows from a small seed into a tall tree that bears fruit year after year.
A wooden chair was once part of a living tree, but after cutting and drying, it no longer grows or breathes.
A spider's web is not alive, but a living spider made it to catch its food.
Fish take in oxygen from water through their gills, so even underwater animals breathe to stay alive.
A dry seed looks still and lifeless, but it is alive and will sprout when it gets water and warm soil.
Living things need food, water, air, and a place to live, while non-living things need nothing to keep existing.
A rock breaks into smaller pieces only when wind, water, or people act on it, not by itself.
A plant with a broken stem can heal and grow new parts, but a broken plastic toy stays broken forever.
Bakawan, or mangrove trees, are living things that grow in salty water along Philippine coasts and give shelter to fish.
A cat walks, runs, and jumps by itself, while a toy cat moves only when someone pushes or winds it.
Living things live for a time and then die, while stones just wear away and do not die.
Fish need water to live, and worms need soil, but a rock can stay anywhere because it is not alive.
Momentum is a measure of how hard it is to stop a moving object, calculated by multiplying its mass by its velocity.
Momentum is conserved because during a collision, the forces two objects exert on each other are equal and opposite, so their momentum changes cancel out.
When two ice skaters push away from each other on ice, their total momentum stays zero, so they glide apart with equal and opposite momenta.
source: conservation of momentum in a closed system

en: A slow, heavy truck and a fast, light bicycle can have the same momentum, because momentum equals mass times velocity.
A 1,000-kilogram car moving at 10 meters per second has 10,000 units of momentum, and if it sticks to a stationary car, both move at 5 meters per second together.
When a ball stops rolling on the ground, its momentum is not destroyed; it passes to the Earth, which moves a tiny, unmeasurable amount.
source: conservation of momentum with the Earth as part of the system

en: In both elastic and inelastic collisions, total momentum is conserved, but only elastic collisions also keep the total motion energy the same.
In a crash test, a car hits a heavy wall; the wall barely moves, but the car's momentum change is balanced by the wall's tiny momentum change.
source: conservation of momentum with a massive object

en: During a jeepney-tricycle collision, the lighter tricycle changes speed more than the heavier jeepney, but their total momentum stays conserved.
source: conservation of momentum applied to unequal masses

en: When a basketball bounces off the floor, the Earth itself moves upward a tiny bit, so the total momentum of ball and Earth stays conserved.
source: conservation of momentum including the Earth

en: Two identical carts, one moving at 2 meters per second and one at rest, move together at 1 meter per second after a sticky collision.
Conservation of momentum applies to the whole system of colliding objects, not to each object on its own.
source: conservation law for a closed system

en: Momentum has direction, so two objects moving toward each other can have momenta that cancel out to zero.
A light object moving very fast can have more momentum than a heavy object moving slowly, because speed matters as much as mass.
source: momentum depends on both mass and velocity

en: When a firecracker explodes, its pieces fly in all directions, but the total momentum of all the pieces together stays zero.
source: conservation of momentum in an explosion

en: A bowling ball slows down when it hits a pin, but the total momentum of the ball and pin together is the same before and after.
source: conservation of momentum in an elastic collision

en: In any collision, the momentum one object gains is exactly equal to the momentum the other object loses, keeping the total unchanged.
source: Newton's third law and momentum transfer

en: Investigators use conservation of momentum to estimate how fast vehicles were moving before a crash by studying their damage and final positions.
An explosion is like a collision played backward: pieces fly apart, yet the total momentum before and after stays the same.
source: conservation of momentum in reverse collisions

en: Conservation of momentum holds true for every collision, from tiny atoms bumping into each other to entire galaxies interacting.
Fossils give the relative age of a rock—whether it is older or younger than another—but not the exact number of years.
source: relative vs absolute dating in geology

en: Fossil types appear in a fixed order through time, so scientists can tell a rock's age by which fossils are inside it.
Fossils are found only in sedimentary rocks, so scientists use them to date those layers, not rocks that melted or were squeezed.
Tiny fossils called foraminifera, with shells like grains of sand, are used to date the age of deep-sea mud.
source: foraminifera as biostratigraphic markers in marine geology

en: Each fossil species appears in the rock record at one time and disappears later, so its presence marks a specific span of time.
source: biostratigraphy: first and last occurrence datums

en: A group of different fossils found together in a rock layer gives a more accurate age than just one fossil type.
Fossil teeth of Stegodon, a prehistoric elephant, help scientists date the age of river sediments in the Philippines.
source: Stegodon fossils in Cagayan Valley, Philippines

en: Geologists study tiny fossil shells in rock layers to find the age of layers that may hold oil and gas.
The type of marine fossil in a rock layer tells both that it was once underwater and how old the layer is.
source: fossil evidence of marine transgression and age

en: Trilobites, extinct sea animals with three-part shells, are index fossils that date rocks from the Paleozoic era.
Pollen grains from ancient plants, found in lake mud, are fossils that help date the age of the sediment.
Simple single-celled fossils are the oldest known, so a rock layer with only simple fossils is likely from early Earth.
source: oldest prokaryotic fossils in Archean rocks

en: Fossils of ferns and other plants help date the age of coal layers, which formed from ancient forests.
The hottest days of summer usually come about a month after the June solstice, because the ground and oceans take time to absorb and release heat.
If Earth's axis had no tilt, every place would receive about the same sunlight all year, and there would be no seasons.
Insolation is the solar energy received per square meter of ground, and the tilt changes it by changing the angle at which rays arrive.
Solar panels are tilted to face the Sun because a surface facing the rays directly captures more energy than one lying flat.
The equator gets about 12 hours of daylight every day all year, while higher latitudes swing between long summer days and short winter days.
The tilt makes the Sun's angle change gradually through the year, so seasons flow smoothly instead of switching suddenly from hot to cold.
Because the tilt stays at about 23.5 degrees, the seasons repeat at the same time every year.
Filipino farmers use the seasonal rhythm set by the tilt to time their rice planting with the start of the rainy season.
Earth is closest to the Sun in January, yet the Northern Hemisphere has winter then, so the tilt matters more than distance.
The tropics are the warmest region on Earth because the tilt keeps the Sun's rays arriving steeply there all year.
In summer, the ground absorbs more heat from the direct Sun, and the air above it becomes warmer.
A tadpole grows into a frog, changing its body shape, but a pebble stays the same shape forever because it is not alive.
When two objects collide at an angle and then move off in different directions, the total momentum is still conserved, but you must add their momenta as vectors.
source: conservation of momentum is a vector law; holds component-wise in every direction

en: A trophic level is one feeding step in a food chain, like grass making its own food, a goat eating the grass, and a person eating the goat.
source: encyclopedia-stable; trophic level definition in ecology

en: Green plants and algae make their own food from sunlight through photosynthesis, so they are called producers and form the first trophic level.
Herbivores like carabao and grasshoppers eat plants directly, so they occupy the second trophic level just above the producers.
Carnivores that eat herbivores, like a frog eating a grasshopper, sit on the third trophic level, and those that eat other carnivores sit even higher.
Fungi and bacteria break down dead bodies and animal waste, returning nutrients to the soil, but they are not drawn as a level in an energy pyramid.
Most food chains stop at four or five trophic levels because so little energy remains at the top that no organism could survive another step.
source: encyclopedia-stable; food chain length limits from energy loss

en: A pyramid of numbers counts individual organisms at each level, while an energy pyramid measures stored energy, so the two can have different shapes.
The sun is the original energy source for nearly every food pyramid, and plants capture it through photosynthesis to start the whole chain.
source: encyclopedia-stable; solar energy in food webs

en: In a Philippine rice field, palay plants feed rice bugs, frogs eat the bugs, and snakes eat the frogs, passing energy up the pyramid.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Philippine rice field food chain

en: In a bakawan mangrove, young fish and crabs eat fallen leaves and algae, then bigger fish eat them, moving energy upward through the pyramid.
People usually sit near the top of a food pyramid because we eat both plants and animals that have already eaten plants.
Ecologists measure the energy stored at each trophic level in calories or joules, and the amounts get smaller with every step upward.
Animal cells have mitochondria too, even though they lack chloroplasts, so they still release energy from the food they eat.
The inner membrane of a mitochondrion folds into shelves called cristae, giving more space for the reactions that release energy from food.
Before food reaches the mitochondria, a first step called glycolysis happens in the jelly-like cytoplasm outside the mitochondria.
Cellular respiration uses oxygen and glucose to make carbon dioxide, water, and ATP, the molecule that powers cell activities.
Photosynthesis makes glucose and oxygen in chloroplasts, while respiration breaks them down in mitochondria to release energy.
Besides chlorophyll, chloroplasts contain orange and yellow pigments called carotenoids that help capture extra light energy.
A muscle cell that works hard has many more mitochondria than a fat cell, because it needs more energy to contract.
Root cells of a plant have mitochondria but no chloroplasts, so they can only do respiration, not photosynthesis.
The fluid inside a chloroplast, called the stroma, is where the plant builds sugar from carbon dioxide using energy from the thylakoid membranes.
In a chloroplast, the thylakoid membranes are stacked like coins into piles called grana, which trap sunlight for photosynthesis.
Both plant and animal cells use mitochondria to break down food, but only plant cells have chloroplasts to make that food in the first place.
The energy released in mitochondria is stored in ATP, which acts like a rechargeable battery for moving, building, and repairing cells.
Uniform velocity is motion with a constant speed and a constant direction, so the object never speeds up, slows down, or turns.
An object with uniform velocity covers the same distance in each equal time interval, like 5 meters every second.
A car cruising at a steady 60 km/h on a straight highway is an example of uniform velocity, so its distance-time graph is a straight line.
A jeepney moving at a constant speed on a straight road shows uniform velocity, and its distance-time graph is a straight line.
A train traveling at a steady 80 km/h on a straight track has uniform velocity, so its graph is a straight line.
A ball rolling on a smooth, flat floor at a steady speed has uniform velocity, and its distance-time graph is a straight line.
On a uniform velocity graph, the slope calculated from any two points gives the same speed, proving the speed never changes.
source: encyclopedia-stable; slope constancy in uniform motion

en: Uniform velocity differs from uniform speed because uniform velocity also requires a constant direction, though both look like straight lines on distance-time graphs.
source: encyclopedia-stable; distinction between velocity and speed

en: The speed from a distance-time graph is in meters per second, so a uniform velocity line rising 10 meters in 2 seconds has a speed of 5 meters per second.
source: encyclopedia-stable; units of speed from graph slope

en: A distance-time graph of uniform velocity that does not pass through the origin means the object started at a distance away from the reference point.
You can predict where a uniformly moving object will be later by extending the straight line on its distance-time graph.
In uniform velocity, the speedometer reading stays the same, so the line on a distance-time graph has the same steepness all along.
To draw a distance-time graph of uniform velocity, plot equal distance increases for equal time steps and connect the points with a straight line.
In uniform velocity, distance increases linearly with time, meaning the graph is a straight line and the ratio of distance to time is constant.
source: encyclopedia-stable; linear relationship in uniform motion

en: A distance-time graph of uniform velocity has no curves, because a curve would mean the speed is changing.
source: encyclopedia-stable; graph shape for uniform motion

en: The y-intercept of a uniform velocity graph shows the object's starting distance from the reference point.
Uniform velocity is also called constant velocity, and it means the object's velocity vector does not change.
A boat moving at a steady speed on a calm river shows uniform velocity, and its distance-time graph is a straight line.
If a uniform velocity graph passes through the origin, the object started at the reference point at time zero.
Uniform velocity is the simplest motion to graph because its distance-time graph is always a straight line.
source: encyclopedia-stable; ease of graphing uniform motion

en: On a distance-time graph, the horizontal axis measures time in seconds and the vertical axis measures distance in meters, so the slope's unit is meters per second.
source: standard graph conventions for distance-time plots

en: Shield volcanoes like Hawaii's Mauna Loa have broad, gentle slopes because their runny lava flows far before cooling.
Hotspot volcanoes such as Hawaii form far from plate boundaries, where a plume of hot rock rises from deep inside Earth.
Most Philippine volcanoes sit above a subduction zone, where one tectonic plate dives beneath another and melts into magma.
About three-quarters of Earth's volcanoes lie along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a horseshoe-shaped belt around the Pacific Ocean.
source: encyclopedia-stable: Pacific Ring of Fire, about 75% of volcanoes

en: A phreatic eruption happens when groundwater touches hot magma and flashes into steam, blasting rock fragments without new lava.
A Plinian eruption is the most violent type, sending a tall column of ash and gas tens of kilometers high, like Pinatubo in 1991.
A caldera is a large bowl-shaped depression that forms when a big eruption empties the magma chamber and the ground collapses.
Lava with lots of silica is thick and sticky, trapping gas and making explosive eruptions, while low-silica lava flows easily.
source: encyclopedia-stable: silica content and magma viscosity

en: Volcanoes also form where plates pull apart, like along mid-ocean ridges where melted rock rises and makes new seafloor.
PHIVOLCS, the government volcano agency, lists about 24 active volcanoes in the Philippines, including Mayon, Taal, and Kanlaon.
Scientists measure eruption strength with the Volcanic Explosivity Index, and Pinatubo's 1991 blast rated 6 on a scale of 0 to 8.
source: USGS Volcanic Explosivity Index; Pinatubo 1991 VEI 6

en: A lava dome is a rounded mound of thick, sticky lava that piles up inside a crater, like the dome that grew at Pinatubo after 1991.
A timeline of the atomic model shows how each scientist's discovery built on the work of earlier scientists over many centuries.
The current atomic model, called the quantum mechanical model, describes electrons as a fuzzy cloud of probability around the nucleus.
James Chadwick discovered the neutron, a particle with no electric charge, in 1932, completing the picture of the atom's nucleus.
Rutherford's gold foil experiment revealed that an atom is mostly empty space, with a tiny, dense nucleus at its center.
The nucleus of an atom holds protons, which have a positive charge, and neutrons, which have no charge at all.
Electrons, which have a negative charge, zoom around the nucleus in a cloud, making the atom electrically neutral overall.
The number of protons in an atom's nucleus is called the atomic number, and it decides which element the atom is.
Atoms are incredibly tiny; about one million atoms lined up side by side would stretch across the width of a single human hair.
Bohr's model placed electrons in specific circular paths, or energy levels, around the nucleus, like planets orbiting the sun.
Scientists change the atomic model when new experiments provide evidence that the old model cannot explain.
Protons and neutrons are about 1,800 times heavier than an electron, which is why the nucleus holds almost all of an atom's mass.
The atomic model has evolved over about 2,500 years, starting with ancient Greek ideas and reaching today's quantum model.
In the quantum mechanical model, scientists cannot pinpoint an electron's exact location, only the probability of finding it in a region.
The discovery of the nucleus changed the atomic model from a solid sphere to a structure with a tiny center and mostly empty space.
Unlike Bohr's fixed orbits, the modern electron cloud model shows electrons moving in a blurry region of probable locations.
source: electron cloud model vs Bohr model

en: Chadwick's discovery of the neutron explained why atoms of the same element could have different masses, leading to the idea of isotopes.
Scientists use atomic models as simplified pictures to help explain and predict how tiny particles behave, even though they are too small to see.
Thomson's model spread positive charge like pudding, but Rutherford's gold foil test showed that positive charge is packed into a tiny central nucleus.
source: comparison of Thomson and Rutherford models

en: A timeline helps students see the atomic model as a chain of discoveries, where each new model corrects or improves the one before it.
In a neutral atom, the number of positively charged protons equals the number of negatively charged electrons, so the charges cancel out.
Hydroelectric plants use falling water to spin a turbine, and the spinning generator turns that motion into electricity.
Wind turbines catch the breeze with their blades, and the rotating shaft drives a generator to produce electricity.
High-voltage transmission lines are hung from tall steel towers so the bare wires stay far above the ground and out of reach.
Substations also have circuit breakers that automatically cut off power to a section if a fault happens, protecting the grid.

topic: why AC is used in the grid
en: Power plants generate alternating current, or AC, because transformers can easily change its voltage, which is why the grid uses AC.
source: encyclopedia-stable; AC vs DC for power transmission

en: Power plants across the country are linked in one grid, so if a plant stops, other plants can send electricity to keep the supply steady.
Electric meters come as spinning dials or digital screens, but both count the same kilowatt-hours of energy your home uses.
Transmission lines carry bare wires with very high voltage, so they rely on air and tall towers for safety instead of insulation.
source: encyclopedia-stable; overhead line insulation by air

en: Large factories often receive electricity at a higher voltage, like 13,800 volts, and use their own transformers to step it down for machines.
source: typical industrial distribution voltage; rounded value

topic: voltage levels from plant to home
en: Electricity leaves a power plant at about 20,000 volts, is raised to about 230,000 volts for long travel, then lowered in steps to 220 volts for homes.
source: typical grid voltage levels; rounded values

en: A scientific model is a simplified picture that helps explain something too big, too small, or too slow to see directly.
source: science education standard: models as explanatory tools

en: Scientists use models to test ideas about things they cannot observe directly, such as the inside of a cell or the path of a typhoon.
A model is not an exact copy; it leaves out extra details so scientists can focus on the important parts.
Models are not permanent; scientists revise them when new observations do not fit the old picture.
Scientists use a model of Earth's layers—crust, mantle, and core—to explain earthquakes, since we cannot dig that deep.
PAGASA uses computer models of the atmosphere to predict typhoons, which are huge storms that form over the ocean and are hard to see all at once.
A magnetic field model draws curved lines around a magnet to show the invisible force that pulls or pushes other magnets.
Sound waves are invisible, so scientists draw them as wavy lines to show how they travel through air as vibrations.
DNA is too small to see, so scientists use a double helix model that looks like a twisted ladder to show its shape.
The plate tectonics model explains that Earth's outer shell is broken into moving plates, which drift very slowly over time.
A food web model uses arrows to show which animals eat which plants or animals, making hidden energy flow visible.
The greenhouse effect model shows how invisible gases like carbon dioxide trap heat in the atmosphere, like a blanket.
A model of the human heart shows the chambers and valves that pump blood, even though the real heart is inside the body.
Viruses are microscopic, so scientists build models with spikes and shapes to show how they look and attach to cells.
A water molecule model shows two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom at an angle, a shape too small to see.
A solar system model shows the planets orbiting the Sun, which is useful because the real orbits are millions of kilometers wide.
A cell model shows organelles like the nucleus and mitochondria, which are too small to see without a microscope.
The water cycle model uses arrows to show evaporation, condensation, and rain, processes that happen over large areas.
A cutaway volcano model shows the magma chamber and vent underground, which are hidden from view in a real volcano.
Scientists use a model of the respiratory system to show how air moves through the lungs, which are inside the chest.
In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields vibrate at right angles to each other and to the direction the wave travels, making it a transverse wave.
source: encyclopedia-stable; EM waves are transverse (fields perpendicular to travel)

en: All electromagnetic waves travel at about 300,000 kilometers per second in empty space, the fastest speed in the universe.
source: encyclopedia-stable; speed of light in vacuum ≈ 300,000 km/s

en: From lowest to highest energy, the electromagnetic spectrum runs radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays.
source: encyclopedia-stable; EM spectrum ordered by energy/frequency

en: Visible light, the only colors our eyes can see, is just a tiny slice of the whole electromagnetic spectrum.
source: encyclopedia-stable; visible band is a small part of EM spectrum

en: Microwave ovens heat food by making water molecules inside the food vibrate, and that vibration turns into heat.
source: encyclopedia-stable; microwave dielectric heating of water

en: X-rays pass through soft body tissue but are blocked by bones, so bones cast shadows on an X-ray image.
Radio and TV stations broadcast by sending radio waves that carry sound and picture information to receivers.
Cell phones use microwaves, a kind of electromagnetic wave, to carry your voice and messages through the air.
source: encyclopedia-stable; mobile communications use microwave band

en: TV remote controls send invisible infrared waves that the TV detects to change channels or volume.
Ultraviolet waves from the Sun can cause sunburn, which is why sunscreen protects your skin.
Gamma rays are the most energetic electromagnetic waves, coming from radioactive atoms and from explosions in space.
source: encyclopedia-stable; gamma rays from nuclear/astrophysical sources

en: PAGASA weather radar sends out microwave pulses that bounce off raindrops to track typhoons and storms.
Electromagnetic waves that vibrate more times per second (higher frequency) carry more energy than slower ones.
source: encyclopedia-stable; photon energy proportional to frequency

en: Radio waves can be as long as a building, while gamma rays are smaller than an atom's nucleus.
source: encyclopedia-stable; EM wavelength range (radio to gamma)

en: In an electromagnetic wave, a changing electric field creates a magnetic field, and the changing magnetic field creates the electric field again, so they keep each other going.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Maxwell's equations, self-propagating EM wave

en: Microwave ovens use waves that vibrate about 2.45 billion times per second, a frequency water molecules absorb well.
source: encyclopedia-stable; 2.45 GHz ISM band for microwave ovens

en: Every warm object, including your body, gives off infrared waves, which is how thermal cameras see heat.
source: encyclopedia-stable; thermal imaging detects IR emission

en: Lightning bolts send out radio waves, which is why you hear crackling static on a radio during a thunderstorm.
source: encyclopedia-stable; lightning emits radio frequency energy

en: The Sun gives off radio, infrared, visible, and ultraviolet waves all at once, but our eyes only see the visible part.
Fiber-optic cables carry internet data as pulses of light, an electromagnetic wave, traveling through thin glass strands.
source: encyclopedia-stable; fiber-optic communication uses light pulses

en: Democritus imagined atoms through reasoning alone, but later scientists like Rutherford used experiments to test and refine the atomic model.
source: history of atomic theory; shift from philosophical to experimental science

en: Scientists use ball-and-stick models to show how atoms rearrange during a chemical reaction, because the actual movement is too fast and tiny to see.
source: encyclopedia-stable; ball-and-stick models represent atomic rearrangement in reactions

en: When an electromagnetic wave hits a material, it can bounce off, pass through, or be absorbed—like light bouncing off a mirror or passing through a window.
source: encyclopedia-stable; behavior of EM waves at material boundaries

en: Mammals are born alive from their mother's body and drink her milk, which gives them food and strength to grow.
A young mammal, like a puppy or calf, stays close to its mother for food, warmth, and protection until it can fend for itself.
A bird begins life inside an egg, and the parent bird sits on the egg to keep it warm until a chick hatches out.
After hatching, a chick grows feathers, learns to find food, and practices flying until it becomes a mature bird.
A mature bird can lay eggs and care for its own chicks, so the life cycle starts again with a new generation.
A mature plant makes flowers, and each flower can turn into a fruit that holds seeds for new plants to grow.
Mammals give birth to live young, birds lay eggs outside their bodies, and plants produce seeds inside fruits.
A carabao calf grows into a strong adult that helps plow rice fields and later has its own calf to continue the cycle.
source: encyclopedia-stable; Philippine agriculture, carabao life cycle

en: A chicken starts as an egg, hatches into a chick, then grows into a hen or rooster that can produce new eggs.
A mango tree grows from a seed into a seedling, then a tall tree that bears fruit with seeds inside for new trees.
Unlike mammals, birds do not nurse their babies with milk; they bring insects, seeds, or worms to feed their chicks.
A mature plant has roots, a stem, leaves, and flowers, and it can make its own food using sunlight and water.
Every life cycle repeats when a grown animal or plant makes offspring, and those offspring grow up to make their own.
Some mammals, like dogs, become adults in about a year, while elephants take many years to reach adulthood.
A bird's egg has a hard shell that protects the growing chick inside from harm until it is ready to hatch.
For a plant to become mature, it needs plenty of sunlight, water, and nutrients from the soil to grow tall and strong.
A seed sprouts into a seedling, which grows leaves and roots, then becomes a mature plant that can flower and make seeds.
Acceleration is any change in how fast or which way something moves, so speeding up, slowing down, or turning are all acceleration.
A jeepney pulling away from a stop sign speeds up, so it is accelerating because its speed is increasing.
A tricycle braking to stop at a red light is slowing down, which is also acceleration because its speed is decreasing.
A bicycle turning a corner changes direction, so it is accelerating even if its speed stays the same.
A spinning top on the floor shows uniform circular motion because its top point traces a circle at a steady rate.
A ceiling fan's blades move in a circle, so each blade is constantly changing direction and therefore accelerating.
Acceleration has a size and a direction, so a car turning left and a car turning right have different accelerations.
A washing machine's spin cycle spins clothes in a circle at a high speed, so they are in uniform circular motion.
A car going around a rotonda at a steady speed is in uniform circular motion because its direction keeps changing.
Many people think acceleration only means speeding up, but slowing down and turning are also acceleration.
To find acceleration, you divide the change in speed or direction by the time it took for that change to happen.
A jeepney that goes from rest to 30 kilometers per hour in 5 seconds has a bigger acceleration than one taking 10 seconds.
source: hypothetical example based on standard kinematics

en: A dropped ball speeds up as it falls because gravity pulls it, so it is accelerating downward.
A ball thrown straight up slows down going up and speeds up coming down, so it accelerates the whole time.
Speeding up and slowing down are both acceleration, but slowing down is sometimes called deceleration.
A student running around a school oval at a steady pace is accelerating because they keep turning.
PAGASA tracks how fast a typhoon's winds speed up or slow down, which is the acceleration of the air.
A basketball spinning on a finger is in uniform circular motion because its surface moves in a circle.
The nucleus is the atom's central core, and it is packed tightly with protons and neutrons.
Electron shells are the circular paths drawn around the nucleus, showing where electrons are found.
When drawing an atom, put the nucleus in the middle and draw the shells as circles around it.
The first electron shell, which is closest to the nucleus, can hold up to two electrons.
The second electron shell can hold up to eight electrons, but only after the first shell is full.
Electrons fill the shell nearest the nucleus first before they move to the outer shells.
source: Bohr model; lowest energy levels fill first

en: The nucleus has a positive charge because the protons packed inside it are positively charged.
Neutrons in the nucleus have no electric charge at all, so they are neutral particles.
When drawing shells, each one is a complete circle around the nucleus, and the circles never cross each other.
An oxygen atom has eight electrons: two fill the first shell and six sit in the second shell.
A sodium atom has eleven electrons: two in the first shell, eight in the second, and one in the third.
In a neutral atom, the number of protons in the nucleus equals the number of electrons in the shells.
The nucleus is like the yolk of an egg, while the electron shells are like the layers of white around it.
source: common teaching analogy for atom structure

en: Electrons are negatively charged, so they are pulled toward the positive nucleus at the center.
The outermost shell of an atom is called the valence shell, and it decides how the atom reacts with others.
source: encyclopedia-stable; valence shell determines chemical behavior

en: To draw an atom, count its electrons, then place them shell by shell starting from the inside.
Helium has just two electrons, both fitting in the first shell, so its drawing shows only one shell.
The shells in an atom drawing are not solid rings but show where electrons are most likely to be found.
source: modern quantum view vs Bohr model simplification

en: Protons and neutrons are about 1,800 times heavier than electrons, so the nucleus holds almost all the atom's mass.
In the Bohr model, each shell sits at a fixed distance from the nucleus, like floors in a building.
Relative dating arranges events from oldest to youngest, while absolute dating measures actual years, and together they build the geologic time scale.
source: encyclopedia-stable; definitions of relative and absolute dating

en: Sediments usually settle in flat, horizontal layers, so if scientists see tilted rock layers, they know something moved them after they formed.
Fossils appear in a consistent order in rock layers, so a fossil found in one place can help match the age of layers in another place.
An index fossil comes from a species that lived for a short time but spread widely, so its presence marks a specific slice of geologic time.
A gap in the rock record, called an unconformity, means some layers were eroded away or never deposited, so time is missing from that spot.
Scientists choose the dating isotope by the rock's age: carbon-14 suits young remains, while potassium-argon and uranium-lead measure much older rocks.
Potassium-argon dating measures the decay of potassium into argon in volcanic rocks, giving ages from about 100,000 years to billions of years.
Uranium-lead dating uses the decay of uranium into lead inside zircon crystals, and it can date rocks that are billions of years old.
After one half-life, half the parent atoms remain; after two, one-quarter remain, so counting parent and daughter atoms reveals the rock's age.
The geologic time scale is divided into eons, eras, periods, and epochs, and each boundary marks a major change seen in the fossil record.
source: geologic time scale divisions, ICS framework

en: Absolute dating adds real numbers to the relative order of rock layers, turning a simple sequence into a time scale measured in millions of years.
source: integration of relative and absolute dating, encyclopedia-stable

en: Scientists use potassium-argon dating on rocks from Philippine volcanoes like Mayon to estimate when each volcano first began erupting.
source: PHIVOLCS / volcanology dating of Philippine volcanic rocks

en: Relative dating never gives an exact year; it only tells older or younger, so absolute dating is needed to place events on a calendar of deep time.
source: relative vs absolute dating distinction, encyclopedia-stable

en: By matching the same fossil or ash layer in different places, scientists connect rock layers and build one timeline for a whole region.
Geologists built most of the geologic time scale using relative dating first, then radiometric dating added the actual ages we see today.
source: history of geologic time scale development

en: Carbon-14 dating works only for things up to about 50,000 years old, so older rocks and fossils need isotopes with much longer half-lives.
Rock layers usually extend sideways in all directions until they thin out or hit a barrier, so matching layers across hills links their ages.
When the same index fossil appears in two distant rock layers, scientists conclude those layers formed at about the same time.
The Andes Mountains formed when the dense oceanic Nazca Plate slid beneath the lighter South American Plate, a process called subduction.
The Himalayas came from two continents colliding, while the Andes came from an ocean plate sinking under a continent, so they look and grow differently.
As an oceanic plate sinks into the hot mantle, it melts and sends magma upward, building volcanic mountains like those in the Andes.
The Andes are the longest mountain range on land, stretching about 7,000 kilometers along western South America.
The Appalachians are an old, eroded mountain range, while the Himalayas are young and still sharp, showing how mountains change over time.
Many large mountain ranges, including the Himalayas, are folded and faulted from squeezing, not built by volcanic eruptions.
In subduction, the dense oceanic plate sinks, creating deep ocean trenches off the coast, while the lighter continental plate crumples upward.
The Andes' highest peak, Mount Aconcagua, rises about 6,961 meters, making it the tallest mountain outside Asia.
Net force is the combined result of all pushes and pulls on an object; when they cancel out, the net force is zero and the object does not accelerate.
source: Newton's first law; net force concept

en: A heavier object needs a larger net force to get the same acceleration as a lighter one, so a loaded truck accelerates slower than an empty jeepney.
When a jeepney speeds up, the engine's forward force is larger than the backward friction, so the net force is forward and the jeepney accelerates forward.
When a car brakes, the road's friction acts backward, so the net force is backward and the car accelerates backward, which we feel as slowing down.
At the highest point of a ball thrown upward, its speed is zero for an instant, but its acceleration is still downward because gravity never stops pulling.
A satellite in orbit moves at constant speed but keeps changing direction, so it accelerates toward Earth all the time.
Speed only tells how fast something moves, but velocity also includes direction; acceleration changes velocity, so it can change speed, direction, or both.
If two people push a box from opposite sides with equal force, the forces cancel, giving zero net force and zero acceleration, so the box stays still.
A rocket accelerates upward because the thrust from its engines is a net force greater than gravity's downward pull.
A bike rider who pedals harder increases the forward net force, so the bike's acceleration increases and it speeds up faster.
A ball rolling on a flat floor slows down because friction is a net force opposite to its motion, so its acceleration points backward.
When a bus turns left, the road's friction pulls the bus left, so the bus accelerates left even though passengers feel pushed right.
A pendulum at the end of its swing has zero speed for an instant, but it still accelerates because the string's pull changes its direction.
A car that goes from rest to 60 km/h in 10 seconds has an acceleration of about 6 km/h per second, meaning its speed increases by that much each second.
A kite accelerates upward when the wind's upward force is stronger than gravity's downward pull, so the net force points up.
If you double the net force on an object, its acceleration doubles, as long as its mass stays the same.
An object moving in a straight line at constant speed has zero acceleration because its velocity does not change at all.
A basketball thrown at an angle follows a curved path because gravity constantly changes both its speed and direction, so it accelerates throughout its flight.
An element's period, or row, in the periodic table tells you how many electron shells its atoms have, so sodium in row 3 has three shells.
source: periodic table period number corresponds to outermost electron shell

en: A carbon atom has six electrons, so its drawing shows two in the first shell and four in the second shell.
source: carbon electron configuration: 2 in first shell, 4 in second

topic: shell labels K L M N
en: Scientists label the electron shells K, L, M, and N, starting with K as the shell closest to the nucleus.
source: spectroscopic notation for atomic shells (K, L, M, N)

en: The third electron shell can hold up to 18 electrons, but for the first 18 elements it fills with 8 before the fourth shell starts.
source: aufbau principle; first 18 elements fill third shell with 8 before fourth

en: An ionic compound is made when a metal gives electrons to a nonmetal, creating positive and negative ions that attract each other.
A chemical formula uses element symbols and small numbers to show the ratio of ions in a compound.
Magnesium oxide (MgO) forms when magnesium with a +2 charge pairs with oxygen with a -2 charge, balancing one-to-one.
Potassium chloride (KCl) is made of potassium (+1) and chloride (-1) ions in a one-to-one ratio.
The formula MgCl2 tells you there is one magnesium ion and two chloride ions in the compound.
Every ionic compound is neutral overall because the total positive charge of all ions equals the total negative charge.
In a chemical formula, the small subscript number tells how many of each ion are needed, and no subscript means one.
When writing an ionic formula, the metal or positive ion always comes first, followed by the nonmetal or negative ion.
Sodium and potassium always form +1 ions, magnesium forms +2, and chlorine forms -1, so their formulas follow these charges.
Seawater contains dissolved sodium and chloride ions, which is why salt can be harvested from the ocean in many places.
Magnesium oxide is a white powder used in antacids and fireproof materials because it resists high heat.
Potassium chloride is a common fertilizer ingredient that supplies potassium, a nutrient plants need to grow strong.
Potassium chloride tastes salty like table salt but contains potassium instead of sodium, so it is sold as a low-sodium salt substitute.
NaCl does not mean one molecule of salt; it means the crystal has equal numbers of sodium and chloride ions.
Magnesium oxide gets its name from its ions: magnesium (Mg2+) and oxide (O2-), with the metal name first.
Potassium chloride is named by putting the metal name potassium first and changing chlorine to chloride with an -ide ending.
Solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity, but when melted or dissolved in water, their ions move and carry current.
The salt you sprinkle on food is the same NaCl compound found in ocean water and underground salt deposits.
When a meteoroid enters Earth's atmosphere, it burns up as a bright meteor, and if a piece survives to land, that piece is called a meteorite.
A comet's tail always points away from the Sun because the solar wind pushes the gas and dust, so the tail trails behind the comet.
Most comets come from two far-off regions: the Kuiper Belt near Neptune and the Oort Cloud, a huge sphere of icy bodies beyond Pluto.
Meteor showers occur when Earth passes through the dusty trail left by a comet, causing many meteors to light up the sky at once.
Pluto is a dwarf planet because it orbits the Sun, is round, but has not cleared its orbit of other objects like the eight full planets have.
Both Ceres and Pluto are dwarf planets—they are round and orbit the Sun, but they share their orbits with many other small bodies.
Meteorites that fall to Earth are direct samples of asteroids or comets, letting scientists study the solar system's earliest materials in a lab.
Comets are often called 'dirty snowballs' because they are made of ice, dust, and rock that heat up and release gas near the Sun.
Comets are ancient leftovers from the solar system's birth, so the ice inside them preserves clues about the original cloud that formed the Sun.
The asteroid belt sits between Mars and Jupiter, where millions of rocky bodies orbit the Sun, but they never joined to make a planet.
Large asteroid impacts have struck Earth many times, leaving craters that help scientists understand past collisions and the solar system's history.
Dwarf planets like Pluto and Ceres are small worlds that never grew into full planets, showing what the building blocks of planets looked like.
Meteoroids are smaller than asteroids, usually less than a few meters across, while asteroids can be hundreds of kilometers wide.
Jupiter's strong gravity stirs up the asteroid belt, preventing the rocky pieces from clumping together to form a planet.
In the Philippines, the Geminid meteor shower appears every December, when Earth meets the dusty trail of an asteroid called 3200 Phaethon.
A contact force is a push or a pull that happens only when two objects touch, like your hand pushing a book across a table.
When you push a toy car forward, the car rolls forward in the exact direction your hand is pushing.
When you pull a drawer toward you, the drawer slides toward you, following the direction of your pull.
When you kick a football, your foot pushes the ball forward, so the ball flies in the direction of your kick.
Pushing a shopping cart at the market makes it roll forward in the direction you push, not sideways or backward.
Pushing a door away from you makes it swing open in the direction of your push, while pulling it brings it toward you.

topic: pulling a rope with a box
en: When you pull a rope tied to a box, the box moves toward you in the same direction as your pull.
Unlike gravity, which pulls objects without touching them, a contact force like your hand pushing a pencil needs direct contact.
If you push a ball from the side, it rolls sideways, not forward, because objects move in the direction of the applied push.
Even a gentle push can move a light object like a paper boat on water in the direction of the push.
When you push a heavy box, the force from your arms is a contact force that moves the box forward in the direction you push.
A fisherman pushes his bangka off the shore, and the boat moves forward in the direction of the push.
In a simple investigation, place a ball on a flat table and push it gently with your finger — it rolls exactly in the direction your finger pushes.
When you pull a wagon, it follows you in the direction you pull, not in the opposite direction.

topic: pushing a pencil on a desk
en: When you push a pencil across your desk, it moves in the direction of your push, showing that contact force determines motion direction.
A force makes an object accelerate, and that acceleration must last for some time to change the object's speed and therefore its momentum.
A rocket engine pushes with a steady force for minutes, so the rocket's momentum builds up gradually until it reaches a very high speed.
Gravity pulls a falling mango for every second it drops, so its momentum increases steadily until it reaches the ground.
source: Gravity as a constant force (Newton's law of gravitation)

en: When a car accelerates, the engine applies force to the wheels for several seconds, increasing the car's momentum along the road.
Wind pushes a sailboat for a long time, so even a gentle breeze can slowly increase the boat's momentum across the water.
source: Wind force on sails (Newton's second law)

en: If you push with the same force for twice as long, the object's momentum changes twice as much.

topic: quick tap gives small momentum change
en: A quick tap on a ball changes its momentum only a little because the force acts for a very short time.
While a constant force pushes an object, its momentum keeps increasing with each second the force continues to act.
source: Newton's second law: constant force gives constant acceleration

en: A sideways force on a moving ball acts for a short time, changing the ball's direction of momentum without changing its speed.
A trophic level is one feeding step in a food chain, such as producer, herbivore, or carnivore, and each step holds a different amount of energy.
In a food pyramid, the first trophic level is producers like plants, the second is herbivores, and the third is carnivores that eat them.
The sun is the original energy source for every food pyramid, because green plants capture its light to make their own food.
In a Philippine rice field, palay is the producer, rats eat the palay, and snakes eat the rats, forming a three-level food pyramid.
Most food pyramids have only four or five trophic levels, because the energy left after each step is too small to support another level.
Energy flows in one direction through a food pyramid, from the sun to plants to animals, and never flows backward to a lower level.
When energy is lost as heat in a food pyramid, it is not destroyed, but it becomes unusable for the next trophic level.
Planets move across the sky like stars, but they drift slowly against the star patterns, which is why ancient people called them wanderers.
source: astronomy: planets get name from Greek for wanderer

en: A stick's shadow is shortest at noon, so tracing its shadow through the day shows the Sun's curved path across the sky.
The Sun's rising point on the horizon shifts a little each day, moving north for half the year and south for the other half.
The Moon can sometimes be seen in the daytime sky, especially in the afternoon, because it is bright enough to shine through the daylight.
The Moon rises later each day, so its position in the sky at the same clock time changes from one night to the next.
Venus and Jupiter are so bright that you can see them moving across the sky with just your eyes, just like the stars.
The stars you see at 8 PM in December are different from the stars you see at 8 PM in June because Earth travels around the Sun.
The Sun climbs to its highest point at noon, then sinks lower, making an arc across the sky from east to west.
The Moon moves across the sky from east to west because of Earth's spin, but it also moves eastward a little each day because of its own orbit.
source: combined Earth rotation and Moon orbit

en: Using a compass to record where the Sun rises and sets shows that it always rises in the east and sets in the west.
The Sun is a star, and it moves across the sky just like the other stars, but its bright light hides the other stars during the day.
source: Sun is a star, outshines others

en: The Sun, Moon, and planets all travel along a similar path across the sky, called the ecliptic, which is tilted compared to the horizon.
To record the Moon's movement, you can draw its position next to a bright star, and you will see it shift eastward each night.
The Sun's highest point at noon is not the same all year; it is higher in some months and lower in others.
source: seasonal variation of solar noon altitude

en: The Moon's steady movement across the sky is why we can predict when it will rise and set each day.
The symbol for a proton is p+, for a neutron it is n0, and for an electron it is e−.
source: Standard symbols for subatomic particles (IUPAC notation)

en: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus is its atomic number, and that number decides which element the atom is.
source: Definition of atomic number in chemistry

en: Electrons are arranged in energy levels called shells around the nucleus, and each shell can hold only a certain number of electrons.
Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they share the same atomic number but differ in mass.
source: Definition of isotopes in nuclear chemistry

topic: elementary charge of electron and proton
en: The charge on one electron is the smallest unit of electric charge, called the elementary charge, and a proton has exactly the same amount but positive.
source: Elementary charge from Millikan's oil-drop experiment

topic: neutral atom has equal protons and electrons
en: A neutral atom has exactly the same number of protons and electrons, so the positive and negative charges cancel out.

topic: mass number counts protons plus neutrons
en: The mass number of an atom is the total count of protons plus neutrons, since electrons are so light they barely add any mass.
Water squeezed out of the sinking oceanic plate rises into the mantle above, lowering its melting point so it melts and feeds volcanoes on the plate above.
As the oceanic plate sinks, it scrapes off soft sediments that pile up against the front of the plate above, building a ridge called an accretionary wedge.
The sinking plate drags the edge of the plate above downward, bending it like a spring until it snaps, releasing earthquakes that shake the land above.
Behind the volcanic arc, the sinking plate can stretch the plate above apart, cracking it so the sea floor sinks to form a back-arc basin.
The subducting plate squeezes the plate above, compressing it over millions of years so the crust folds and thickens into mountain ranges.
The period number of an element tells how many electron shells its atoms have, so period 3 elements have three shells.
source: periodic table structure: period number = number of electron shells

en: For main-group elements, the group number equals the number of outer electrons, so group 2 elements have two outer electrons.
source: periodic table: group number = valence electrons for main groups

en: Across a period from left to right, elements change from reactive metals to reactive nonmetals because their outer electrons increase.
source: periodic trends: metallic to nonmetallic across a period

en: Periods have different lengths because each new electron shell can hold more electrons, so period 2 has 8 elements and period 4 has 18.
source: periodic table: shell capacity determines period length

en: The 18 groups exist because electron shells can hold many electrons, and transition metals fill inner shells in the middle block.
source: periodic table layout: transition metals and shell filling

en: An element's position in the periodic table predicts its reactivity: Group 1 metals react violently, while Group 18 gases do not react.
source: periodic table: group position correlates with reactivity

en: Although early scientists sorted elements by atomic mass, the modern periodic table sorts them by atomic number, which is the number of protons.
source: history of periodic table: Moseley and atomic number

en: Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, so they form similar compounds and react in similar ways.
source: periodic table: group = same valence electrons → similar chemistry

en: Sodium sits in period 3 and group 1, so its atoms have three electron shells and one outer electron, making it very reactive.
The periodic table's shape comes from electron shells filling in order, so each new row starts when a new shell begins to fill.
source: periodic table construction from electron configuration

en: Metals on the left lose outer electrons easily to react, while nonmetals on the right gain electrons, and noble gases do neither.
source: periodic trends: electron loss/gain and reactivity

en: Scientists use the periodic table to predict unknown element properties, like how reactive a new element might be based on its group.
source: periodic table as predictive tool in chemistry

en: A fair test of an electromagnet keeps the same battery and nail, and only changes the number of wire coils to compare strength.
source: fair-test design: one variable changed, rest constant

en: Plot the number of coils on the x-axis and paper clips picked up on the y-axis to see the trend.
Use the same size and type of paper clips for every trial so the test is fair and results are comparable.
Swapping the battery connections flips the electromagnet's poles, but it still attracts the same number of paper clips.
Replace the iron nail with a wooden pencil and the coil picks up almost no paper clips, proving iron is needed.
Add a switch in the circuit to turn the electromagnet on and off without removing the wire from the battery.
When you disconnect one wire from the battery, the nail drops all paper clips right away because the current stops.
Certain viruses can cause mutations by inserting their own genetic material into a cell's DNA, which can disrupt how genes work.
source: encyclopedia-stable; viral integration into host genome

en: A mutagen is any chemical or radiation that raises the mutation rate by damaging DNA or interfering with how DNA copies.
A chromosomal mutation can delete, duplicate, or flip a large segment of a chromosome, affecting many genes at once.
source: types of chromosomal mutations in biology

en: Cells have repair enzymes that fix most DNA mistakes, so only a small number of mutations remain and cause changes.
Mutations happen by chance, not because an organism needs a new trait, so they are random changes in DNA.
source: mutations as random events in genetics

en: A limitation of parallel circuits is that too many appliances on one line can draw too much current, tripping a circuit breaker.
source: electrical safety: overcurrent protection in parallel wiring

en: An advantage of series circuits is that they use less wire because all parts connect in one simple loop.

topic: series circuit hard to find broken part
en: A limitation of series circuits is that when a bulb burns out, you must test each bulb one by one to find the broken one.
