An advantage of parallel circuits is that a TV and a refrigerator can run at the same time because each branch works on its own.
A limitation of parallel circuits is that a short circuit in one branch can draw a huge current, which may trip the main breaker.
source: electrical safety: short circuit behavior in parallel

en: An advantage of series circuits is that connecting batteries in series adds their voltages, like two 1.5-volt batteries making 3 volts.
source: series connection of cells increases total voltage

en: A limitation of series circuits is that the battery voltage is shared among all bulbs, so each bulb gets less power as you add more.
Jeepney headlights are wired in parallel, so if one headlight burns out, the other still lights the road for the driver.
The main advantage of series circuits is low cost, while the main advantage of parallel circuits is independent operation.
To measure an electromagnet's strength, add paper clips one by one until one falls, then record the number that stayed attached.
source: standard classroom method for quantifying magnetic pull

en: Keep the wire coil tight and evenly spaced around the nail so every trial has the same shape, making the comparison fair.
source: fair-test design: consistent construction controls variables

en: Hydroelectric dams let falling river water spin turbines to make electricity, releasing no carbon dioxide, and the Philippines has many rivers for this clean power.
source: encyclopedia-stable; hydroelectricity is renewable and emits no direct CO2

en: Turning farm waste like rice husks and coconut shells into electricity is renewable because plants regrow, and it can replace some coal in the Philippines.
source: encyclopedia-stable; biomass from agricultural residues is renewable if sustainably managed

en: Solar and wind power now cost less than new coal plants, so switching to them saves money while also cutting the greenhouse gases that warm the Earth.
source: IRENA and market data show declining renewable costs below new coal

en: Solar and wind power depend on weather, but storing their electricity in batteries lets them provide steady power even when the sun sets or wind stops.
source: encyclopedia-stable; energy storage enables grid integration of variable renewables

en: In a normal fault, rocks are pulled apart and the block above the crack slides down, like a sinking sidewalk.
source: fault types by stress direction (normal = extension) — encyclopedia-stable

en: In a reverse fault, rocks are squeezed together and the block above the crack slides up, shortening the ground.
source: fault types by stress direction (reverse = compression) — encyclopedia-stable

en: In a strike-slip fault, two blocks slide horizontally past each other, so the ground moves sideways instead of up or down.
source: fault types by stress direction (strike-slip = shear) — encyclopedia-stable

en: Reverse faults are common in the Philippines because the country sits where two big plates collide and squeeze the crust.
source: PHIVOLCS: Philippine plate convergence creates reverse faults

en: The Philippines also has many strike-slip faults because the plates grind sideways as they push together, not straight on.
source: PHIVOLCS: Philippine Fault accommodates oblique convergence as strike-slip

en: The focus is the underground spot where an earthquake starts; the epicenter is the point on the surface directly above it.
Earthquakes send out waves: P-waves arrive first and push-pull, while S-waves arrive second and shake side to side.
source: encyclopedia-stable: P-waves arrive first, S-waves second

en: Normal faults, where rocks pull apart, are rare in the Philippines because the plates here mostly push together.
source: plate tectonics: Philippines is convergent, not extensional — PHIVOLCS

en: Along the Philippine Trench, an ocean plate dives under the country, bending the crust and creating thrust faults.
source: PHIVOLCS: subduction at Philippine Trench generates thrust faults

en: The force that holds positive and negative ions together in an ionic bond is called electrostatic attraction, and it is very strong.
In table salt, sodium and chloride ions pack into a repeating cube pattern called a crystal lattice, giving salt its cubic crystals.
The charge of an ion equals the number of electrons it lost or gained, so magnesium losing two electrons becomes a +2 ion.
In an ionic compound, the total positive charge from cations always balances the total negative charge from anions, so the compound is neutral.
Calcium loses two electrons, and each chlorine atom gains one, so one calcium ion pairs with two chloride ions to form CaCl₂.
Only the outer-shell electrons take part in ion formation; the inner electrons stay unchanged, so the ion keeps its identity as the same element.

topic: ionic compounds solid at room temperature
en: Because the electrostatic attraction between ions is so strong, ionic compounds like table salt are solid at room temperature.
Valence electrons sit farthest from the nucleus, so they are the first to feel the pull of another atom's nucleus during a reaction.
Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same number of valence electrons, which is why they behave similarly in reactions.
source: periodic table group number = valence electrons for main-group elements

en: Sodium has one valence electron that it easily gives to chlorine, which has seven, so both end up with full outer shells in table salt.
Oxygen has six valence electrons, so it shares two of them with two hydrogen atoms to fill its shell and make water.
When atoms bond, only the valence electrons are rearranged; the inner electrons and the nucleus stay unchanged.
source: atomic structure; bonding involves only outer electrons

en: Most atoms follow the octet rule, aiming for eight valence electrons, but hydrogen and helium are happy with just two.
source: octet rule with exceptions for hydrogen and helium

en: Forming a chemical bond releases energy, which is why bonded atoms like those in water are more stable than separate atoms.
An atom's tendency to lose, gain, or share electrons comes from its valence electrons, not from its inner ones.
source: chemical reactivity depends on valence electrons

en: Nitrogen has five valence electrons, so it needs three more to fill its shell, which is why it forms three bonds in ammonia.
source: covalent bonding in ammonia; nitrogen has 5 valence electrons

en: When scientists observe, they look, listen, and touch carefully, then write down exactly what they notice without adding guesses.
source: science process skills: observing (sensory observation, recording)

en: To predict, scientists use what they already know to guess what will happen next in a test, then they measure to check.
When measuring with a ruler, place the zero mark exactly at one end of the object and read the number at the other end.
source: measuring technique: aligning zero mark on ruler

en: To measure a tiny object, scientists use millimeters, but for a long distance like a room, they use meters instead.
source: unit selection based on object size (mm, cm, m)

en: In a fair test, scientists change only one thing and keep everything else the same, so they know exactly what caused the result.
A good record of a measurement writes the number and the unit together, like 5 centimeters, so everyone understands the exact size.
Daytime length is the number of hours from sunrise to sunset, and Earth's tilt makes that number change through the year.
As Earth orbits, the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun in June, giving longer days, and away in December, giving shorter days.
A model with a tilted globe and a lamp shows that the circle of illumination is tilted, so the day-night boundary is not a straight line.
Daylight length changes fastest near the equinoxes and slowest near the solstices, so the difference per day is not constant.
At about 45 degrees north, the longest day has about 15 hours of daylight and the shortest has about 9 hours.
The summer solstice happens when the Northern Hemisphere tilts most toward the Sun, and the winter solstice when it tilts most away.
In the Northern Hemisphere, summer days have more than 12 hours of daylight, while winter days have less than 12 hours.
Earth's tilt stays the same, but as it orbits the Sun, the orientation of that tilt relative to the Sun changes, so daylight length changes.
The tilt makes the Sun rise earlier and set later in summer, so the total daylight hours increase.
The length of daytime increases at the same rate before and after the winter solstice, and decreases at the same rate before and after the summer solstice.
You can see the tilt's effect by recording sunrise and sunset times each week and watching the daylight hours change.
Earth rotates at a steady speed, so the longer path of the Sun in summer means more hours of daylight.
The closer a place is to the poles, the more hours of daylight it gets on the summer solstice and the fewer on the winter solstice.

topic: model lit half vs facing half
en: A model with a tilted globe and a flashlight shows that the lit half is not the same as the half facing the Sun because of the tilt.
On the equinox, the Sun rises exactly in the east and sets exactly in the west, and day and night are nearly equal everywhere.
The number of daylight hours on a given day depends on both your latitude and the time of year, because of the tilt.
Daylight hours on the summer solstice range from about 12 at the equator to 24 at the Arctic Circle.
In the Southern Hemisphere, the longest day happens in December, and the shortest in June, which is the opposite of the north.
On the equinox, the Sun is directly overhead at the equator, and day and night are equal everywhere.
Shelter is a limiting factor: a forest can hold only as many nesting birds as there are safe tree holes and branches for their nests.
source: encyclopedia-stable; shelter as a resource in carrying capacity

en: The resource that is scarcest, whether food, water, shelter, or mates, sets the ceiling for how many animals an ecosystem can support.
source: Liebig's law of the minimum; encyclopedia-stable

en: A flood can kill or harm animals no matter how crowded they are, so it is a limiting factor that does not depend on population size.
source: ecology standard concept of density-independent factors

en: When food is scarce, animals may survive but produce fewer young, so the population grows more slowly even without extra deaths.
source: ecological principle that food shortage lowers birth rates

en: Work is the total energy transferred, while power is how quickly that energy is transferred.
source: definitional distinction between work and power

en: Just as speed tells how fast distance is covered, power tells how fast work is done.
source: analogy between speed and power as rates

en: One horsepower equals about 746 watts, so a 10-horsepower motor delivers about 7,460 watts of power.
Your electric bill charges for energy in kilowatt-hours, not power, because power is the rate of using energy while kilowatt-hours measure total energy.
source: electric utility billing measures energy, not power

en: A thermoelectric generator uses the heat difference between two sides of special materials to make electricity directly, with no moving parts.
Space probes like Voyager use radioisotope thermoelectric generators, which turn heat from decaying radioactive material into electricity far from the Sun.
source: NASA / encyclopedia-stable; RTG on Voyager missions

en: Concentrated solar power plants use curved mirrors to focus sunlight, heating a fluid until it makes steam that spins a turbine.
Thermoelectric generators can be attached to car exhaust pipes to capture wasted engine heat and turn it into electricity.
source: encyclopedia-stable; automotive thermoelectric waste heat recovery

en: A solar pond is a salty lake that traps the Sun's heat at the bottom, and that stored heat can be used to make electricity.
A Stirling engine uses the difference between hot and cold air to move a piston, and that motion can spin a generator to make electricity.

topic: electrons equal protons in neutral atom
en: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so an aluminum atom with 13 protons also has 13 electrons.
source: electrical neutrality: equal positive and negative charges

en: The mass number of an atom is the total count of protons and neutrons in its nucleus, so it is always a whole number.
source: nuclear physics definition of mass number (A = Z + N)

en: Aluminum has a mass number of about 27, so subtracting its 13 protons leaves 14 neutrons in each aluminum atom.
source: aluminum-27 stable isotope; mass number 27, atomic number 13

en: The atomic number is the element's identity, so any atom with exactly 13 protons must be aluminum, no matter how many neutrons it has.
source: periodic table definition: atomic number = number of protons

en: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they share the same name but have different mass numbers.
The atomic mass of an element is roughly the sum of its protons and neutrons, so aluminum's atomic mass of about 27 matches its mass number.
source: atomic mass rounded to nearest whole number equals mass number

en: Earth spins from west to east, so the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west every day.
source: Earth's rotation direction is a standard astronomy fact.

en: Earth makes one full turn in about 24 hours, which is why the Sun's position and shadows change throughout the day.
source: Earth's rotation period is about 24 hours.

en: Because Earth turns about 15 degrees per hour, a shadow stick's shadow also swings about 15 degrees each hour.
source: Earth rotates 360 degrees in 24 hours, so 15 degrees per hour.

topic: Sun's apparent motion is an illusion
en: The Sun does not travel around Earth; its daily path is an illusion caused by Earth spinning on its axis.
Solar noon, when the Sun is highest and shadows are shortest, can be a few minutes before or after 12:00 on your clock.
source: Equation of time and time zones cause solar noon to differ from clock noon.

en: In the Philippines, a shadow stick's shadow turns clockwise from west to north to east as the Sun moves across the sky.
source: Shadow direction in the Northern Hemisphere.

en: A volcano's life lasts thousands of years, so the last 100 years of records show only a small slice of how it behaves.
source: encyclopedia-stable; volcanoes are long-lived geological features

en: Pinatubo slept for centuries before its huge 1991 eruption, showing that a long quiet period can end with a giant blast.
Volcanoes with thick, sticky magma tend to explode violently, while those with runny magma flow gently, so each volcano's pattern looks different.
source: encyclopedia-stable; magma viscosity controls eruption style
